Having thus rejected that deity's view, now wishing to show the word of the Arahants, she spoke 'Aniccā vata saṅkhārā,' etc. In that verse, 'Aniccā vata saṅkhārā' means all conditioned things belonging to the three planes are impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. 'Uppādawayadhammino' means having the nature of arising and passing away. 'Uppajjitvā nirujjhanti' is a synonym for the previous term. Or, because they arise and then cease, they are called 'uppādawayadhammino.' By taking arising (uppāda) and passing away (vaya) here, the moment of presence (ṭhiti) standing in between is also included. 'Tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho' means Nibbāna, which is the stilling of those conditioned things, is alone happiness. This is the word of the Arahants.

## The Commentary on the Nandana Sutta is finished.
30:
Therefore, it should be understood that they have the nature of arising and ceasing. Furthermore, in this verse, by taking 'arising' and 'passing away' (uppāda and vaya), the 'static moment' (ṭhitikkhaṇa) that exists in the immediate middle of that arising is also included. 'Tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho' means that only Nibbāna, which is the stilling of those formations (saṅkhāra), is true happiness. This is the word of the Arahants. Thus ends the commentary on the Nandana Sutta.

## 2. Nandati Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'nandati' means to rejoice or to have a delighted mind. 'Puttimā' refers to one who has many sons. Some of his sons engage in agriculture and fill the granaries with grain; some engage in trade and bring back gold and silver; some serve the king and obtain vehicles, horses, villages, towns, and so forth. At that time, the mother or the father, enjoying the glory known as the power of those sons, rejoices. Or, seeing the sons adorned on festival days and such, enjoying prosperity, they rejoice. Therefore, it was said, "One with sons rejoices through his sons."

'Gohi tatheva' (likewise with cattle) means that just as one with sons rejoices through his sons, a cattle owner also rejoices through his cattle, seeing a prosperous herd and enjoying the abundance of dairy products derived from them. 'Upadhī hi narassa nandanā' (acquisitions are the joy of man)—here, 'upadhi' (acquisition/attachment) is of four kinds: kāmūpadhi (acquisition of sensual pleasures), khandhūpadhi (acquisition of the aggregates), kilesūpadhi (acquisition of defilements), and abhisaṅkhārūpadhi (acquisition of volitional formations). Sensual pleasures are called 'upadhi' in the sense that "happiness is acquired here," because they are the basis of the happiness described as: "The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure is the gratification (assāda) of sensual pleasures." The aggregates are called upadhi because they are the basis of suffering rooted in the aggregates; defilements because they are the basis of suffering in the lower realms; and volitional formations because they are the basis of suffering in the rounds of existence.

In this context, however, kāmūpadhi is intended. For the five cords of sensual pleasure, presented in the form of three-storied palaces, noble beds, clothes, ornaments, and retinues of dancers, bring about rapture and joy and make a man rejoice. Therefore, it should be understood that just like sons and cattle, these acquisitions are also the joy of man. 'Na hi so nandati yo nirūpadhī' (he who is without acquisitions does not rejoice) means that a poor person who is devoid of the prosperity of sensual pleasures and who finds it difficult to obtain food and clothing cannot rejoice. The deity addressed the Blessed One, saying, "How can such a human-peta or human-denizen of hell rejoice?"

Hearing this, the Teacher thought: "This deity is making the very cause of sorrow (sokavatthu) into a cause of joy (nandavatthu); I shall show him its nature as a cause of sorrow." Then, as if knocking down a fruit with another fruit, he broke the deity's argument using the deity's own analogy, and reversing that very verse, he said 'socati' (sorrows). In that verse, 'socati puttehi' means one sorrows when sons are lost or perishing, such as when they go to foreign lands, or through the fear of loss, thinking, "Now they will perish."
31:
One also sorrows merely by the suspicion of loss. Likewise, when they have died, or are dying, or when they are captured by thieves or king's men, or when they have fallen into the hands of enemies, one sorrows out of fear of their death. When they fall from trees, mountains, etc., and their hands or feet are broken, or while they are being broken, one sorrows out of fear of such breakage. Just as one with sons sorrows because of his sons, a cattle owner likewise sorrows because of his cattle in nine ways. In the phrase "Upadhī hi narassa socanā" (acquisitions are the sorrow of man), just as with sons and cattle, the acquisitions of the five cords of sensual pleasure also cause a man to sorrow, as it is said:

"If those sensual pleasures of a person who desires them
and is filled with longing fade away,
he suffers as if pierced by an arrow." (Sn 773)

By the method already mentioned, they cause a man to sorrow. Therefore, it should be understood that a man's sorrow is indeed based on the objects of sorrow. In the phrase "One without acquisitions does not sorrow," it means: for whom these four kinds of acquisitions do not exist, how could that acquisition-free great Khīṇāsava (Arahant) sorrow? O deity, he does not sorrow.

## Thus ends the commentary on the Nandati Sutta.

## 3. Natthiputtasama Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, the Natthiputtasama Sutta, regarding the statement "There is no love equal to that for a son," even if their own little children are unattractive, parents regard them as if they were golden statues. Carrying them on their heads like garlands of flowers, even when they are soiled by the children's excrement or urine, the parents feel joy as if they had been sprinkled with scented water or perfumes. Therefore, He said, "There is no love equal to that for a son." This means there is no love known that is equal to the love for a son. In the statement "Cattle are the supreme wealth," the deity said, "O Blessed One, there is no other wealth equal to cattle, equal to the wealth of cattle." In "There is no light equal to the sun," it is shown that there is no other light equal to the light of the sun. In "The ocean is the greatest (receptacle of water)," the deity said, "O Blessed One, whatever other lakes or rivers there may be, they all have the ocean as their destination; the ocean is the most excellent among them, and there is no other reservoir of water equal to the ocean."

However, because there is no love equal to the love for oneself—for even though parents may abandon or fail to support their sons and daughters, beings...
32:
Beings support only themselves. There is no wealth equal to grain. When beings face famine, at such a time of scarcity, they take gold, silver, and so forth, as well as cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, to the owners of grain for the sake of obtaining grain. There is no light equal to wisdom. The light of the sun and so forth illuminates only a certain region and dispels only the darkness of the present. But the light of wisdom can illuminate the entire ten-thousandfold world-system at once and destroys the darkness of ignorance that veils the past and so on. There is no river equal to the flow of rain. Whether it be a river or a lake, it is true that there is no river equal to rain. When the flow of rain is cut off, the great ocean does not have even a finger-joint's depth of water; but when it rains, there is a single expanse of water reaching up to the Ābhassara Brahma realm. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to speak a responsive verse to the deity, spoke the words beginning with "Natthi attasamaṃ pemaṃ" (There is no love equal to self-love).

## The Commentary on the Natthiputtasama Sutta is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Khattiya Sutta

In the fourth sutta, "Khattiyo dvipadaṃ" means that among two-footed beings, the king is the best. "Komārī" means a wife taken while she was still a maiden; it means she is the best among other wives. "Pubbajo" means the first-born son; whether he be blind or one of those with crooked limbs, that first-born son alone is the best in the view of this deity. Since the Buddhas and others are the best among bipeds and so forth, the Blessed One spoke the responsive verse. In that verse, although the Blessed One is the best of all beings, including those without feet, when he arises, he arises only among two-footed beings; therefore, he said, "Sambuddho dvipadaṃ seṭṭho" (The Fully Enlightened One is the best of bipeds). The fact that the Blessed One, having arisen among bipeds, is the best of all beings is an unhindered truth. "Ājānīya" means whether it be an elephant or one among horses and so on, the being who knows the cause (reason) is the best among four-footed beings. This is like the horse named Guḷavaṇṇa belonging to King Kūṭakaṇṇa. It is heard that the king, having departed through the eastern gate, reached the bank of the Kalamba River intending to go to the Cetiya Mountain. The horse stood on the bank and did not wish to enter the water. The king called the horse-trainer...
33:
"How wonderful! Even though you have trained the horse well, it does not wish to enter the water," said the King. The horse trainer replied, "Great King, the horse is well-trained. It thinks, 'If I enter the water, my tail will get wet; if the tail is wet, water droplets might fall on the King's body.' Thus, out of fear of water falling on your body, it does not enter. Please have someone hold the tail." The King did as suggested, and the horse quickly entered the water and reached the other bank.

"Sussūsati" means the desire to listen. Whether she was taken as a wife since maidenhood or later, whether she is beautiful or not, the wife who respectfully listens to, serves, and pleases her husband is the best among wives. 

"Assavo" refers to a son who is respectfully obedient to his parents. Whether he is the eldest or the youngest, the son who listens to his parents' words, accepts them, and follows their advice is the best among sons. "O Deity, what is the use of other sons who, like thieves breaking through walls, are disrespectful to their parents?"

## The Commentary on the Khattiya Sutta is finished.

## 5. Saṇamāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "ṭhite majjhaṇhike" refers to the time when the sun is at its zenith in the middle of the sky. "Sannisīvesu" refers to the time when [beings] approach a comfortable place to rest and relax. This noontime is a period when the physical postures of all beings are weak, but here it is shown only through the power of birds. 

"Saṇateva" means making a sound like letting out a great cry. In the summer at noontime, while groups of animals and birds are resting, loud sounds arise in the middle of the forest from hollow tree trunks filled with wind, hollow bamboo joints, and the striking of tree trunks and branches against each other. It is in reference to this that "saṇateva" is said. 

That sound appears to the deity as a danger. That deity of dull wisdom, at that moment, not finding a companion to stay with or talk to, spoke thus. However, at such a time, for a monk who has returned from alms-round and sits in a secluded forest dwelling having taken up a meditation subject, great joy of seclusion (viveka-sukha) arises. In reference to this, it was said: "For the monk who has entered a secluded place, with a peaceful mind, and is clearly perceiving the Dhamma, there is a delight that is not of humans," and "For that monk who lives alone in the forest without anyone else before or behind, there is happiness." Therefore, the Blessed One spoke the second verse beginning with "ṭhite majjhaṇhika."

In that verse, "saṃ arati paṭibhāti manti" means "the delight of living alone at such a time appears clearly to me." The remaining terms are the same as in the previous verse. 

The explanation of the fifth sutta is finished. 

In the sixth sutta, the meaning should be understood thus: "Aggivessana, the Buddha knows that he has reached sleep in the last month of the summer season."
34:
"For the monk who has entered an empty place, whose mind is peaceful, and who clearly sees the Dhamma, there is a delight transcending that of humans." (Dhp. 373) And: "Whether in front or behind, if no other is found, it is exceedingly pleasant for one living alone in the forest." (Thag. 537) (Thus it is preached).

Therefore, the Blessed One spoke the second verse. In that verse, "Sā rati paṭibhāti maṃ" means that such delight, which is the act of sitting alone at such a time, appears clearly to me. The remaining terms are just the same as in the previous verse.

## The Commentary on the Saṇamāna Sutta is finished.

## 6. Niddātandī Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, the Niddātandī Sutta, "sleeping" (niddā) refers to the sloth and torpor (thina-middha) that arises in the prompted unwholesome consciousness (sasaṅkhārika akusala citta) of trainees (sekhas) and worldlings (puthujjanas) in the periods before and after the neutral sleep (abyakata niddā) described as: "Aggivessana, I recall falling asleep in the last month of the summer" (M. Ni. 1.387). "Tandī" refers to the adventitious laziness that arises during times of extreme hunger, extreme heat, extreme cold, and so on. It has also been said: "Therein, what is tandī? That which is laziness, the act of being lazy, the state of having a lazy mind, indolence, the performance of indolence, the state of having reached indolence; this is called tandī" (Vibh. 857). "Vijambhitā" is the stretching of the body. "Arati" is discontent on the side of the unwholesome. "Bhattasammado" is the intoxication or fatigue caused by food. The detailed explanation of these terms like vijambhitā is exactly as it appears in the Abhidhamma in the manner beginning with: "Therein, what is vijambhitā? That which is the bending or stretching of the body is called vijambhitā."

"Etena" means because of being defiled by these aforementioned defilements such as sleep, and thus being prevented from appearing. "Nappakāsati" means it does not shine, it does not manifest. "Ariya maggo" refers to the supramundane path. "Idha" means in this world. "Pāṇinaṃ" means for living beings. "Vīriyena" means by the effort conjoined with the path. "Naṃ paṇāmetvā" means having removed that mass of defilements. "Ariya maggo" refers to the mundane and supramundane path. Thus, it is preached that the purity of the path is achieved by removing the defilements through the path itself.

## The Commentary on the Niddātandī Sutta is finished.
35:
## 7. Dukkara Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, the Dukkara Sutta, "duttitikkhan" means that which is difficult to endure or hard to tolerate. "Abyattena" means by the foolish or unskilled person. "Sāmaññaṃ" refers to the practice of a recluse (samaṇadhamma). By these words, the deity shows this point: Wise sons of good family practice the recluse-dharma, undertaking the holy life for as long as life lasts, even for ten, twenty, or sixty years, by clenching their teeth, pressing the tongue against the palate, and restraining the mind with the mind, while taking only one meal at one sitting. It is shown that the unskilled fool is not able to perform that recluse-dharma. "Bahū hi tattha sambādhā" means that in that Noble Path known as monkhood, there are many obstacles and dangers such as sensual thoughts in the preliminary stage of one practicing to attain the path.

"Cittañce na nivāraye" means if one does not restrain the mind that has arisen through improper attention (ayoniso), for how many days could one practice the recluse-dharma? One could not practice it for even a single day. This is because one who follows the whims of the mind cannot perform the recluse-dharma. "Pade pade" means in every object (ārammaṇa). Here, "pada" is intended to mean the object. In whatever object a defilement arises, the fool is said to sink in that very object. The term for postures (iriyāpatha) is also appropriate here. In whatever posture such as walking a defilement arises, he is said to sink in that very place. "Saṅkappānaṃ" refers to sensual thoughts and so on.

"Kummo vā" means like a tortoise. "Aṅgāni" refers to the five limbs including the neck. "Samodahaṃ" means properly withdrawing and tucking them in. "Manovitakke" refers to the thoughts that have arisen in the mind. By this much, this point is shown: Just as a tortoise, by withdrawing its five limbs including the snout into its own shell, does not give an opportunity to the jackal, and by withdrawing them becomes unassailable to it; even so, a monk, by withdrawing the thoughts arisen in the mind into the shell of his own meditation object, should not give an opportunity to Māra, and by so withdrawing, he becomes unassailable to Māra. "Anissito" means being unattached, without the supports of craving and views. "Aheṭhayāno" means not harming. "Parinibbuto" means cooled by the extinction of defilements. "Nūpavadeyya kañci" means one should not revile or speak to any person with a mind desiring to shame them regarding failures in conduct and so on. Rather, one should speak out of compassion, establishing the five factors within oneself such as "I will speak at the proper time, not at the improper time," with a mind aimed at lifting them up from their moral failure.

## The Commentary on the Dukkara Sutta is finished.
36:
## 8. Commentary on the Hirī Sutta

In the eighth sutta, "hirīnisadho" means one who restrains unwholesome states through shame (hirī). Wishing to ask if such a person exists in the world, it is said, "koci lokasmiṃ vijjatīti." "Yo nindaṃ apabodhatī" means one who knows by removing blame. "Asso bhadro kasāmivā" means just as a noble thoroughbred horse knows the strike of the whip; just by seeing the shadow of the whip, it is startled and does not allow the whip to fall on its body. Similarly, a monk who does not allow the ten grounds for true verbal abuse to fall upon himself, and knows by removing blame. It is asked whether such a type of Khīṇāsava (Arahant) exists in the world. There is no one who is free from false verbal abuse. "Tanuyā" means they are few; it means that the Khīṇāsava (Arahant) individuals who practice by restraining unwholesome states through shame are few. "Sadā satā" means being endowed with abundant mindfulness at all times. "Antaṃ dukkhassa pappuyya" means having reached Nibbāna, which is the end of the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha). The remaining words are as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Hirī Sutta is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Kuṭikā Sutta

In the ninth sutta, "kacci te kuṭikā" means this deity metaphorically called the ten months of staying inside the mother's womb a "little hut" (kuṭikā). Just as birds that go out for food during the day return to their nests (kulāvaka) at night, so too beings, though they go to various places, return to their wives, who are like nests, out of the bond of craving (ālayavasa). Because of the nature of continuing the lineage, children are called "tendrils" (santānaka), and craving is called a "bond" (bandhana). Combining these questions in a verse, the deity asked the Blessed One. The Blessed One, wishing to answer the deity, spoke the words beginning with "tagghā." In that context, "taggha" is an indeclinable (nipāta) expressing the sense of "certainly" (ekaṃsa). "Natthi" means "there is none" because, having renounced everything to become a monk, there is no longer any dwelling in a mother's womb in the round of rebirth, nor supporting a wife, nor the production of children.

The deity thought, "I asked a hidden question, binding it firmly, yet this ascetic answered it as soon as it was asked. Did he speak knowing my intention, or did he speak from memory without knowing?" and spoke again the words beginning with "kintāhanti." In that verse, "kintāhanti" should be broken down into "kiṃ te ahaṃ." Then the Blessed One, wishing to clarify for the deity, spoke the words beginning with "mātaraṃ." With the verse "sāhu te," the deity became joyful, paid homage to the Blessed One, made offerings with celestial flowers and scents, and returned to his celestial mansion.

## The Commentary on the Kuṭikā Sutta is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Tapodārāma Sutta

In the tenth sutta, "tapodārāme" refers to the monastery named after the hot springs called Tapoda. Below Mount Vebhāra, there is a Naga realm of five hundred leagues situated in the earth, which exists like a celestial realm.
37:
Thinking, "Does he speak knowing the meaning I wish to know, or does he speak whatever comes to his mouth without knowing?", the deity again spoke the words beginning with *kintāhaṃ*. In that verse, *kintāhaṃ* should be resolved into *kiṃ te ahaṃ* (What am I to you?). Then the Blessed One, wishing to inform the deity, spoke the words beginning with *mātaraṃ*. With the verse *sāhu te*, the deity expressed appreciation and was delighted; he paid homage to the Blessed One, made offerings with celestial flowers and scents, and returned to his own celestial abode.

## The Commentary on the Kuṭikā Sutta Ends.

## 10. Commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta

In the tenth sutta, *Tapodārāme* refers to the monastery of that name, which is based on the hot-water lake called Tapoda. It is said that beneath Mount Vebhāra, there is a Naga realm five hundred leagues in extent, belonging to the terrestrial Nagas, which is like the deva realm, complete with jeweled grounds, parks, and gardens. In the place where those Nagas play, there is a great lake. From that lake flows the river named Tapodā, which flows with boiling hot water. Why is it like this? It is said that a vast realm of hungry ghosts (*peta*) surrounds Rājagaha; the Tapodā river flows between two Great Iron Cauldron Hells (*Lohakumbhī*) located there, and therefore it flows boiling hot. 

This has also been stated: "Monks, the lake from which this Tapodā river flows is clear, cool, sweet, and pure, with excellent landing places, delightful, and full of many fish and tortoises. Lotus flowers the size of chariot wheels bloom there. However, monks, this Tapodā river flows between two great hells, and therefore the Tapodā flows boiling hot" (from the Pārājika Pali).

Because there is a large lake formed from that Tapodā river directly in front of this monastery, the monastery is called "Tapodārāma."

*Samiddhi* is the name of the elder because his physical form was perfected (*samiddha*), beautiful, and inspiring. *Gattāni parisiñcituṃ* (to bathe the limbs) refers to this elder, who was devoted to meditation; having risen at the crack of dawn and allowed his body to adjust to the season/temperature, he walked back and forth on a cloister walk (*caṅkama*) sixty cubits long outside. Thinking that the lodging he used might be soiled by his body covered in sweat from walking, he approached the water to pour it over his body and cleanse himself. *Ekacīvaro aṭṭhāsi* means he stood wearing only his inner robe, having fastened his waistband and holding his outer robe in his hand. *Gattāni sukkāpayamāno* means while drying his body...
38:
Walking back and forth on the great walkway (caṅkama), which was about sixty cubits long, he thought, "The lodging (senāsana) used by a body covered in sweat will become soiled," and so he approached the bathing place to pour water over himself and cleanse his body. Standing with only one robe, he put on his undergarment, tied his waistband, and stood holding his upper robe in his hand.

"Gattāni pubbāpayamāno" means making the body free of water droplets as it was before. A robe worn on a wet body tends to get soiled and develops a bad odor; this is not the proper practice. The Elder, however, was one accomplished in duties; therefore, remaining established in the duties, he bathed, emerged, and stood there. In this regard, this is the duty for bathing (nhānavatta): Having gone to the bathing place, one should not jump into the water immediately while standing, having placed the robes anywhere. Instead, one should look in all directions, and knowing it is secluded, note the stumps, bushes, creepers, etc. Then, having coughed three times, one should remove the upper robe while standing in a stooped position and spread it out. The waistband should be loosened and placed on top of the robe. If there is no bathing cloth (udakasāṭikā), one should sit in a squatting position near the water, remove the undergarment, and if there is a sweaty part, spread it out. If not, it should be folded and set aside. When entering the water, one should descend slowly up to the navel, without causing waves or making noise, and submerge facing the direction from which one came; in this way, the robe is protected. When emerging, one should also emerge slowly without making noise. At the end of the bath, one should sit in a squatting position near the water, wrap the undergarment around, stand up, dress neatly all around, tie the waistband, and only then stand after donning the upper robe.

The Elder also bathed in that manner, emerged, and stood looking at his body which was becoming free of water. The Elder, who was naturally inspiring, had a very radiant facial complexion after bathing with warm water at dawn, as his food had been well digested. His face was glorious like a ripe palm fruit released from its stalk, like the full moon endowed with radiance, or like a lotus blooming at that moment. His skin complexion was also exceptionally clear. At that time, a terrestrial deity (bhummadevatā) dwelling in the forest grove, looking at the inspiring monk and being unable to restrain herself, was overcome by the fever of sensual desire (kāmapariḷāha) and thought, "I will tempt the Elder," and [transforming] her body...
39:
That deity, having adorned herself with noble ornaments, made the entire monastery radiant at once, like a lamp with a thousand wicks burning or like the moon rising. Approaching the Elder, she stood in the air without paying homage and recited a verse. Therefore, it is said: "Atha kho aññatarā devatā...pe... ajjhabhāsī."

"Abhutvā" means without enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa). "Bhikkhasi" means you wander for alms. In the phrase "Mā taṃ kālo upaccagā," "kāla" (time) refers to the time of youth, which is suitable for enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure. Indeed, when one is worn out by old age, bent over, relying on a staff, trembling, and overcome by cough and asthma, it is not possible to enjoy sensual pleasures. Thus, referring to this time, the deity said, "Mā taṃ kālo upaccagā." In that phrase, "mā upaccagā" means do not let it pass.

In the phrase "Kālaṃ vohaṃ na jānāmi," the word "vo" is merely a particle without specific meaning. He says "Kālaṃ na jānāmi" (I do not know the time) referring to the time of death. Indeed, for beings—
"Life, sickness, the time [of death], the place where the body is cast down, and the destination (gati)—these five things in the world of living beings are unpredictable (animitta) and unknown."

In that verse, first of all, life is unpredictable because there is no certainty such as "It will last only this long and not beyond this." Beings die even during the stage of the embryo (kalala), and also at the stages of abbuda, pesi, ghana, at half a month, one month, two months, three months, four months, five months... up to ten months, or at the time of emerging from the mother's womb. Thereafter, they die within a hundred years or even beyond. Sickness is also unpredictable because there is no certainty such as "Beings die only of this sickness and not another." Beings die of eye disease or any other disease such as ear disease. The time of death is also unpredictable because there is no certainty such as "One must die only at this time and not another." Beings die in the morning or at any other time such as midday. The place where the body is cast down is also unpredictable because there is no certainty such as "The body must be cast down only in this place and not elsewhere." The bodies of beings born inside a village may fall outside the village; the bodies of beings born outside a village may fall inside the village. Similarly, those born on land [may die] in water, those born in water [may die] on land, and so on, which should be expanded in detail. The destination (gati) is also unpredictable because there is no certainty such as "Having passed away from here, one must be reborn here." Beings who have passed away from the deva world are also reborn among humans.
40:
Beings pass away from the human world and are reborn in various places such as the deva realms; thus, like an ox yoked to a machine, the world of beings revolves repeatedly within the five realms of existence. For such a revolving being, I do not know this time of death, thinking, 'Death will occur at such and such a time.'

'The time is hidden and not seen' means that this time of death is concealed from me and is not clearly known. Therefore, because this time is hidden and not apparent, I practice by seeking alms without enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure. In the phrase 'May the time not pass me by,' the word 'time' refers to the time for performing monastic duties. Indeed, this monastic practice cannot be performed in the final stage of life by one who has passed the three stages of age, who is bent over, who relies on a staff, who is trembling, and who is overwhelmed by cough and asthma. At that time, it is not possible to learn the word of the Buddha as desired, to undertake ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), to dwell in the forest, to enter into attainments (samāpatti) at any desired moment, or to perform verse recitation (padabhāṇa), melodic chanting (sarabhañña), Dhamma talks, or words of appreciation (anumodanā). However, in the time of tender youth, all of this can be done. Therefore, he said, 'May this time for performing monastic duties not pass me by; as long as it has not passed me, I will perform monastic duties without enjoying sensual pleasures.'

'Standing on the ground' means that the deity, thinking, 'This monk speaks of the proper and improper time for monastic practice with reason and benefit,' felt a sense of shame before the Elder. Regarding the Elder as if he were a Great Brahmā or a great mass of fire, she descended from the sky with respect and stood on the ground. This was said in reference to that action. Although she stood on the ground, she spoke the words beginning with 'You are young' based on the same desire for sensual pleasures for which she had come. In that verse, 'susu' means young and tender. 'Kāḷakeso' means having very black hair. 'Bhadrena' means auspiciously beautiful. Some people, though young, may be blind or have deformed limbs, and such a person cannot be said to be endowed with auspicious youth. But one who is handsome, attractive, pleasing, and endowed with all successes, who moves about like a son of the devas adorned with whatever ornaments he desires—such a person is called one endowed with auspicious youth. Because the Elder was endowed with excellent beauty, she spoke to him in this way.
41:
'One who has not played with sensual pleasures' means one who has never experienced the joy and play of sensual pleasures, has never enjoyed them, and has never made an effort to obtain sensual enjoyments. 'Do not abandon the sensual pleasures of the present' means that, in truth, deities who have mostly not seen the Truth, whose lust is not yet gone, and who cannot know the minds of others, see monks practicing the pure and unbroken holy life for ten, twenty... or even sixty years, and they perceive: 'These monks, having abandoned the five strands of human sensual pleasure, are performing monastic duties while longing for divine sensual pleasures.' That deity also had such a perception. Therefore, she spoke by making human sensual pleasures something visible (sandiṭṭhika) and divine sensual pleasures something delayed (kālika).

'Friend deity, I do not abandon visible sensual pleasures to run after, long for, or desire delayed sensual pleasures.' 'Friend deity, I abandon the human sensual pleasures which are called delayed (kālika) and follow the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma) which is visible (sandiṭṭhika) and can be realized by oneself.' Thus, the Elder designated both divine and human sensual pleasures as 'delayed' (kālika) because they cannot be obtained immediately after the thought arises, and he designated the supramundane Dhamma as 'visible' (sandiṭṭhika) because it can be obtained immediately after the thought arises. Even when the five strands of sensual pleasure are gathered, for a lover of pleasure who is fully endowed with them, the experience of the desired object does not occur immediately after the thought arises. For one who wishes to experience a desired object at the eye-door, one must call for painters, sculptors, or turners and say, 'Prepare such and such a thing.' In the interval of this preparation, many hundreds of thousands of millions of thought-moments arise and pass away. Only after that does one reach and experience that object. The same principle applies to the other sense-doors. However, immediately after the Path of Stream-entry, only the Fruit of Stream-entry arises; there is no turn for any other thought in between. The same principle applies to the remaining Fruits. 

The Elder, taking that very meaning, spoke the words beginning with 'Friend deity, sensual pleasures are indeed delayed.' In that context, 'kālikā' means that even when wealth and success are gathered, they must be reached and enjoyed at another time, as previously explained. 'Bahu-dukkhā' means 'having much suffering' because the suffering to be reached depending on the five strands of sensual pleasure is great. It is called 'having much despair' (bahu-upāyāsā) because the intense exhaustion arising from that cause is great. 'The danger herein is greater' (ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo) means that the danger is greater than the happiness obtained depending on the five strands of sensual pleasure; the meaning is that suffering alone is more abundant. 'This Dhamma is visible' means that this supramundane Dhamma is attained by whichever noble person; that person, abandoning the need to rely on the faith of others, through reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), personally...
42:
It is called *sandiṭṭhika* because it is to be seen by oneself (through the knowledge of reflection). It is called *akālika* because it does not depend on time in yielding its fruit; that which is not time is *akāla*, and *akāla* itself is *akālika*. Among these nine supramundane states, it means that the noble path (*ariya-magga*) yields the fruit (*phala*) immediately after its own occurrence. It is called *ehipassika* because it is worthy of the "come and see" (*ehipassividhi*) invitation, as in "Come and see this Dhamma."

It is called *opaneyyika* because it is worthy of being brought into one's own mind through the power of meditation, even by ignoring one's burning clothes or head. It is called *paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhi* because all wise people, such as those of quick intuition (*ugghaṭitaññū*), should personally know and experience in their own minds: "I have developed the path, attained the fruit, and realized cessation (Nibbāna)." This is a brief explanation here; the detailed explanation is given in the commentary on the recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*) in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Now, that deity, like a blind person who does not know the distinction of forms, did not understand the meaning of what the Elder had spoken and said, "Monk, how is it...?" and so on. In that statement, the word "how" (*kathañca*) should be understood as being connected to all the following phrases: "Monk, how is it that sensual pleasures are called *kālika* (time-bound) by the Blessed One? How are they full of suffering? How are they full of great despair?"

A monk who has not completed five years (*vassa*) is called *nava* (new); from five years onwards, he is *majjhima* (middle); from ten years onwards, he is *thera* (elder). Another method: one who has not completed ten years is *nava*; from ten years onwards, he is *majjhima*; from twenty years onwards, he is *thera*. Among those monks, he means, "I am a new monk."

Some new monks, having gone forth at the age of seven or eight, have passed twelve or thirteen years as a novice (*sāmaṇera*) and are thus "long-ordained" (*cirapabbajita*), but he means, "I am one who has not long been ordained" (*acirapabbajita*). "This Dhamma-Vinaya" refers to this Dhamma and this Vinaya. Both are names for the Dispensation (*Sāsana*). Here, the term "Dhamma" refers to two Pitakas (Sutta and Abhidhamma), and "Vinaya" refers to the Vinaya Pitaka. Thus, he means, "I have only recently come to the practice (*paṭipatti*) declared by the three Pitakas."

"By those of great power and retinue" (*mahesakkhāhi*) means those with large followings. Each celestial king may have a retinue of a billion or even a trillion; they place themselves in high positions to see the Tathāgata. In such a situation, he shows, "Where would there be an opportunity for those of little power like us, who are of the female deity class?"
43:
"We too shall come"—the deity said this, knowing that even if the entire universe were filled with a gathering, one could still approach the Teacher through the great Buddha-path. The repetition "Ask, monk; ask, monk" was made for the sake of emphasis (*āmeḍita*).

In the term "*akkheyyasaññino*," the five aggregates are called "*akkheyya*" (the expressible) because they are taught as "deity, human, householder, monk, being, person, Tissa, Phussa," etc., and because they are the basis for all expressions and all talk. They have the perception (*saññā*) of "being, man, person, woman, male"; thus they are "*saññino*." Because they have perception only in the expressible (the five aggregates), they are called "*akkheyyasaññino*." It means those who have the perception of a being or a person in the five aggregates. "*Akkheyyasmiṃ patiṭṭhitā*" means being established in the five aggregates through eight modes. Indeed, one who is lustful is established through the power of greed (*rāga*), one who is corrupt through hatred (*dosa*), one who is deluded through delusion (*moha*), one who misapprehends through wrong view (*diṭṭhi*), one who has reached firmness through underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), one who is bound through conceit (*māna*), one who is undecided through doubt (*vicikicchā*), and one who is restless through restlessness (*uddhacca*). "*Akkheyyaṃ apariññāya*" means because of not fully understanding the five aggregates through the three types of full understanding (*pariññā*). "*Yogamāyanti maccuno*" means they come under the will of Death, its instigation, its rejection, its casting down, or within its sphere of power; they go under the sway of Death. Thus, by this verse, sensual pleasures which are bound by time are explained.

"*Pariññāya*" means fully understanding through these three types of full understanding: *ñātapariññā*, *tīraṇapariññā*, and *pahānapariññā*. Among these three, what is *ñātapariññā*? It is fully understanding the five aggregates as: "This is the aggregate of form, this is the aggregate of feeling, this is the aggregate of perception, this is the aggregate of mental formations, this is the aggregate of consciousness; these are their characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes." This is *ñātapariññā*. What is *tīraṇapariññā*? Having thus known, it is investigating the five aggregates through forty-two modes such as impermanence, suffering, and disease. This is *tīraṇapariññā*. What is *pahānapariññā*? Having thus investigated, it is abandoning desire and lust (*chandarāga*) for the five aggregates through the highest path (*aggamagga*). This is *pahānapariññā*.

"*Akkhātāraṃ na maññati*" means that the Arahant monk, having thus fully understood the five aggregates through the three types of full understanding, no longer conceives of the "speaker" as a person. "*Akkhātāraṃ*" should be understood as the cause that acts through the power of kamma; it means he does not conceive or see a person who is to be expressed or spoken of.
44:
The meaning is: How should it be declared? It should be manifested by any name such as "Tissa" or "Phussa," or by clan. "That does not belong to him" means that such a cause does not exist for that Arahant (khīṇāsava). If anyone were to say of that group of five aggregates, by way of views and so on, that "he is stained by lust (rāga)," "he is corrupted by hatred (dosa)," or "he is deluded by ignorance (moha)," the cause for saying so does not exist in that Arahant.

"If you know, speak" means if you know such an Arahant, say "I know"; if you do not know, then say "I do not know." "Yakkha" is a term used by the Buddha in addressing the deity (devatā). Thus, by this verse, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara dhamma) which is visible here and now (sandiṭṭhika) is taught. The word "Sādhu" is a particle used in the sense of entreaty.

"He who thinks" means he who perceives himself as "I am equal," "I am superior," or "I am inferior." By this statement, the three types of conceit (māna) beginning with "I am superior" are included. When these three types of conceit are included, the nine types of conceit are also included. "He would dispute with him because of that" means that person, by that very conceit, would dispute with any person, saying: "In what way do you equal me? Do you equal me by birth (jāti), or by clan (gotta), or by pointing out lineage, or by beauty of complexion, or by great learning, or by the virtue of ascetic practices (dhutaguṇa)?" Thus, by this half-verse, the temporal (kālika) sensual pleasures (kāma) are taught.

"In the three modes (vidhā)" means in the three types of conceit. In texts such as "The collection of form in one mode," the portion or category is called "vidha." In texts such as "What kind (kathaṃvidhaṃ) of virtuous person do they speak of? What kind of wise person?", the manner or quality is called "vidha." In texts such as "Bhikkhus, there are these three modes (vidhā). Which three? The mode 'I am superior,' the mode 'I am equal,' and the mode 'I am inferior,'" conceit is called "vidha." Here also, it refers to conceit. Therefore, it is said, "In the three modes means in the three types of conceit." "The one who does not tremble" means that person does not tremble or waver in these three types of conceit in brief, or nine types in detail. "Equal or superior does not exist for him" shows that for that Arahant who has abandoned conceit, the thoughts "I am equal," "I am superior," or "I am inferior" do not occur. The final phrase follows the same method already mentioned. Thus, by this half-verse also, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma which is visible here and now is taught.
45:
In the phrase "pahāsi saṅkhanti," in passages such as "Reflecting wisely, he partakes of food," the word "saṅkhā" refers to wisdom (paññā). In this passage, "Is there any accountant, or mathematician, or calculator (saṅkhāyaka) who is able to count the grains of sand in the Ganges?", "saṅkhā" refers to calculation. In passages such as "Concepts of proliferation (papañca-saṅkhā) have perception as their cause," "saṅkhā" refers to a portion or aggregate (koṭṭhāsa). In this passage, "Whatever is the designation (saṅkhā) or name of those various phenomena," "saṅkhā" refers to designation (paññatti). Here also, this meaning of designation is intended. The meaning of the phrase "pahāsi saṅkhanti" is: the Arahant has abandoned or given up the designations such as "one who has lust," "one who has hatred," or "one who has delusion."

"He did not go to a mansion (vimāna)" means he no longer approaches the three types of conceit with their nine divisions. Alternatively, in the sense of a dwelling place, the mother's womb is called a "mansion" (vimāna); the meaning is that he does not approach that mother's womb again by way of rebirth in the future. A past tense verb is used in a future sense. "Acchecchi" means he has cut (cut with the sword of the Noble Path). "Chinnaganthaṃ" refers to one who stands having cut the four bonds (gantha). "Anīghaṃ" means one without suffering. "Nirāsaṃ" means one without craving. "Pariyesamanā" means (the deities) searching and looking. "Nājjhagamuṃ" means they do not find, do not see, or do not perceive. Here, a past tense verb is used in a present sense. "Whether here or elsewhere" means in this world or in the next world. "In all dwellings (sabbanivesanesu)" means that in all the dwelling places of beings—namely, the three types of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings—they do not see such an Arahant either while he is arising or after he has arisen following the breaking up of the body. By this verse, the Buddha taught only the supramundane Dhamma visible in this very life.

Having heard this verse, that deity also well understood the meaning, and for that reason, he said, "Venerable Sir, I [understand] this..." and so on. The verse beginning with "He should do no evil (pāpaṃ na kayirā)" can be explained by way of the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) or by way of the Eightfold Path (aṭṭhaṅgika-magga). To show it first by way of the ten wholesome courses of action: by the word "vacasā" (by speech), the four types of right verbal conduct are taken. By the word "manasā" (by mind), the three types of right mental conduct are taken. By the phrase "kāyena vā kiñcana sabbaloke" (or by body anywhere in the world), the three types of right bodily conduct are taken. These are the ten wholesome courses of action. By the phrase "having abandoned sensual pleasures (kāme pahāya)," the devotion to sensual pleasure (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) is rejected. By the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending (satimā sampajāno)," mindfulness and clear comprehension, which are the causes of the wholesome courses of action, are taken. By the phrase "he should not pursue suffering which is unbeneficial," the devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) is forbidden. Thus, the deity said, "I understand that the Blessed One has taught the ten wholesome courses of action together with mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding both extremes."
46:
The goddess said, "I understand, O Blessed One, the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) together with mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), which are the causes, as taught by You, having avoided the [two] extremes."

According to the Noble Eightfold Path, it should be understood in this way: It is said that a great Dhamma discourse took place at that location. At the end of the discourse, the goddess, remaining in her place, directed her knowledge according to the discourse, and being established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), she spoke thus, wishing to show the Eightfold Path she had attained. In that verse, by the word 'vacasā', Right Speech (sammā-vācā) is taken. Since the mind is not a factor of the Path, by the word 'manasā', the mind associated with the Path (magga-sampayutta citta) is taken. By the phrase 'kāyena vā kiñcana sabbaloke', Right Action (sammā-kammanta) is taken. Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva) is already included as it belongs to the same side as speech and action. By the word 'satimā', Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration are taken. By the word 'sampajāno', Right View and Right Intention are taken. By the two phrases 'kāme pahāya' and 'dukkhaṃ na sevetha', the avoidance of the two extremes is taken. Having said, "In this way, without approaching these two extremes, I understand the Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā) taught by You," she worshipped the Tathāgata with perfumes and flowers, circumambulated Him, and departed.

## The Commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta is finished.

## The Second Chapter, Nandana Vagga.

## 3. Satti Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Satti Sutta

In the first sutta of the Satti Vagga, the word 'sattiyā' is the heading of the discourse. It means with a weapon such as a single-edged sword. 'Omaṭṭha' means being struck in a downward direction. There are four types of strikes: omaṭṭha, ummaṭṭha, maṭṭha, and vimaṭṭha. Among these four, a strike delivered from above facing downwards is called omaṭṭha. A strike delivered from below facing upwards is called ummaṭṭha. A strike that pierces through like a door-bolt is called maṭṭha. All other remaining strikes are called vimaṭṭha. In this context, omaṭṭha is taken. That downward strike is the most cruel of all; it has an arrow that is difficult to extract, is hard to treat, has internal defects, and contains internal pus and blood. The pus and blood, without coming out, remain covering the mouth of the wound.
47:
Those who wish to extract the pus and blood must bind [the person] to a couch and place the head downwards; [if done so], one reaches death or suffering equivalent to death. 'Paribbaje' means one should dwell (vihareyya).

What is said by this verse? For example, just as a man struck downwards by a weapon exerts effort and strives to extract the piercing arrow and treat the wound; or for another example, just as a person whose head is on fire exerts effort and strives to extinguish that fire; in the same way, the Blessed One said that a monk, being mindful and diligent, should dwell for the purpose of abandoning sensual lust (kāmarāga).

Then the Blessed One thought: "This deity has brought a strong analogy, but holds only a small portion of the meaning. Even if he speaks repeatedly, he would only speak of the abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna) of sensual lust. As long as sensual lust is not completely eradicated by the Path, it will continue to follow." Thinking thus, He wished to reverse the discourse by the power of the First Path using that same analogy, and spoke the second verse. Its meaning should be understood in the same sequence as the previous verse. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Phusati Sutta

In the second sutta, 'nāphusantaṃ phusati' means the result (vipāka) does not reach one who does not perform the kamma (or one who is not reached), or kamma does not reach one who does not perform the kamma. Indeed, kamma is not done to one who does not do it. 'Phusantañca tato phuse' means the result reaches one who performs the kamma, or kamma reaches [him]. Indeed, kamma is done to one who does it. Therefore, 'phusantaṃ phusati appaduṭṭhapadosinaṃ' is because it does not reach one who does not perform kamma, but only reaches one who performs it; this is the nature of kamma and its result. Therefore, as it is said, "He offends against the person who is not to be offended, who is pure and stainless (an Arahant)," kamma is performed against that person who should not be offended, and thus kamma reaches that person, or the result reaches him. Whether he is able to oppress or harm others or not, by such an offense, he has already placed himself in the four woeful planes (apāya). Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Evil returns to that fool, just as fine dust thrown against the wind [returns to the thrower]." The second sutta is finished.
48:
## 3. Commentary on the Jaṭā Sutta

In the third sutta, in the verse beginning with 'Antojaṭā', the word 'jaṭā' (tangle) is a designation for craving (taṇhā), which is like a net. It is called 'jaṭā' because it arises repeatedly in sense objects such as forms, etc., in an upward and downward manner, and because of its nature of binding things together, much like the tangle of branches in a bamboo thicket. This craving is called 'internal tangle (antojaṭā)' and 'external tangle (bahijaṭā)' because it arises in one's own requisites and the requisites of others, in one's own person and the persons of others, and in the internal and external sense bases (āyatana). All beings are entangled by this tangle of craving as it arises in this way. Just as bamboo trees are entangled by the tangle of bamboo branches, so too is this entire world of beings, known as the generation of beings (pajā), entangled, bound, and tied together by this tangle of craving. Because they are thus entangled, the deity says, "O Gotama, I ask you this." "Gotama" is an address to the Blessed One by his clan name. "Who can untangle this tangle?" means who can untangle this tangle that remains entangling the three realms? Who is capable of untangling it? This is the question.

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to answer that question, spoke the verse beginning with "Sīle patiṭṭhāya." In that verse, "Sīle patiṭṭhāya" means being established in the fourfold purification virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). Here, although the Blessed One was asked about the untangling of the tangle, he began by teaching virtue; he should not be understood as "answering one thing when asked another." Virtue is taught here to show the foundation for the one who untangles the tangle.

'Naro' means a being. 'Sapañño' means a wise person endowed with rebirth wisdom resulting from kamma with three roots (kammaja-tihetuka-paṭisandhi-paññā). 'Cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ' means developing concentration and insight. Here, the eight attainments (samāpatti) are taught under the name 'citta', and insight (vipassanā) is taught under the name 'paññā'. 'Ātāpī' means one who has effort (vīriya) that burns up defilements. Effort is called 'ātāpa' in the sense of burning or scorching defilements, and one who possesses that effort is 'ātāpī'. 'Nipako' means one endowed with 'nepakka', which refers to wisdom. By this term, administrative wisdom (pārihāriya-paññā) is shown. Administrative wisdom is the wisdom that manages all affairs according to the method such as "this is the time for recitation, this is the time for inquiry." In this answer to the problem, wisdom appears three times. Among those three, the first is birth wisdom (jāti-paññā), the second is insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), and the third is administrative wisdom (pārihāriya-paññā) which manages all affairs.
49: "So imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭanti" refers to the monk endowed with these aforementioned virtues and so on. For example, just as a man, standing on the ground and lifting a very sharp weapon, would clear a large bamboo thicket; even so, the monk, standing on virtue (sīla), lifting the weapon of insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) sharpened on the stone of concentration (samādhi) with the hand of protective wisdom (pārihāriya-paññā) upheld by the power of effort (vīriya-bala), should disentangle, cut, and break through all that tangle of craving (taṇhā-jaṭā) that has fallen within his own continuity. With these words, the Teacher has spoken regarding the stage of a trainee (sekha-bhūmi). Now, wishing to show the Great Arahant (khīṇāsava) who stands having well-cut the tangle of craving, he spoke the words beginning with "Yesaṃ." After showing the Arahant who has thus cut the tangle, wishing again to show the place where the tangle of craving is cut, he spoke the words beginning with "Yattha nāmañca." In that verse, "nāmaṃ" refers to the four immaterial aggregates. In the phrase "paṭighaṃ rūpasaññā ca," the sensual realm (kāma-bhava) is included by "paṭigha-saññā," and the fine-material realm (rūpa-bhava) is included by "rūpa-saññā." By including these two realms, the immaterial realm (arūpa-bhava) is also included by way of a summary of existence. In the phrase "etthesā chijjate jaṭā," it means that this tangle of craving is cut in Nibbāna, which is the cause for the total exhaustion of the three-fold cycle of existence (vaṭṭa); it is cut and ceases upon reaching Nibbāna. The commentary on the third sutta ends. ## ၄။ မနောနိဝါရဏသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ In the fourth sutta, "yato yato" means from evil or from good. This deity, it is said, held the view: "Whatever mind there is, whether mundane or supramundane, consisting of various types such as wholesome and so on, it should only be restrained; it should not be allowed to arise." "Sa sabbato" means that person restrains the mind from everything, both good and bad. Then the Blessed One, thinking, "This deity speaks words that do not lead to liberation; as for the mind, there is that which should be restrained and that which should be developed; I will show him by distinguishing them," spoke the second verse. In that verse, "na mano saṃyatattamāgataṃ" refers to the statement "one should not restrain the mind from everything." If one asks, "Which mind is that, and what kind of mind should not be restrained in every way?" the answer is: "mano saṃyatattaṃ āgataṃ" refers to the mind that has reached the state of being well-restrained and arises in such ways as "I will give gifts, I will observe precepts," and so on. Such a mind should not be restrained; on the contrary, it should be increased and developed. "Yato yato ca pāpakaṃ" means that from whatever unwholesome state arises, from that source the mind should be restrained. The commentary on the fourth sutta ends.
50:
## 5. Arahanta Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the fifth sutta, 'katāvī' refers to one who has completed what was to be done through the four paths. Regarding the phrase 'Ahaṃ vadāmi' (I speak), this deity is one who dwells in a forest grove. Upon hearing the forest-dwelling monks using conventional parlance such as 'I eat,' 'I sit,' 'my bowl,' 'my robe,' and so on, the deity thought: 'I consider these monks to be Arahants. Do those known as Arahants have such speech based on the perception of a self, or do they not?' Thus, the deity asked this to find out.

'Sāmaññaṃ' refers to the common language or conventional parlance of the world. 'Kusalo' means one who is skilled (knowledgeable) in the aggregates and so on. 'Vohāramatta' means speaking 'I' or 'mine' while having discarded speech based on the perception of a self, without destroying conventional usage. For if one were to say, 'The aggregates eat,' 'The aggregates sit,' 'The bowl of the aggregates,' or 'The robe of the aggregates,' conventional usage would be destroyed, and no one would understand. Therefore, without speaking in that way, one speaks according to the conventional parlance of the world.

Then the deity thought: 'If he does not speak by the power of wrong view (diṭṭhi), does he perhaps speak by the power of conceit (māna)?' and asked again with 'Yo hoti' and so on. In that verse, 'mānaṃ nu kho' asks whether that monk, having approached conceit, speaks by the power of conceit. Then the Blessed One, thinking 'This deity is treating the Arahant as if he were an ordinary person,' and wishing to show that the nine types of conceit have been abandoned by the Arahant, spoke the responsive verse beginning with 'Pina manussa'. In that verse, 'vidhūpitā' means destroyed. 'Mānagantha' means that the Arahant has conceit and knots (fetters). 'Maññatā' refers to conceiving (imagining). It means that the Arahant is one who has transcended the three types of conceiving: craving, wrong view, and conceit. The remaining terms have clear meanings. The explanation of the fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Pajjota Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the sixth sutta, 'puṭṭhuṃ' means to ask. 'Kathaṃ jānemu' means 'How shall we know?' 'Divārattiṃ' means by day and by night. 'Tattha tattha' means in whatever place it shines, in that very place. 'Esā ābhā' means this is the radiance of the Buddha. If one asks what that radiance is, whether it be the light of knowledge, the light of joy, the light of confidence, or the light of Dhamma teaching, all light that arises due to the manifestation of the Buddhas is called 'Buddhābhā' (Buddha-radiance). This radiance is peerless and most excellent. The explanation of the sixth sutta is finished.
51:
## 7. Sara Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the seventh sutta, the Sara Sutta, 'kuto sarā nivattanti' means 'By what cause do these rivers of saṃsāra turn back?' or 'Depending on what do they not proceed?' 'Na gādhati' means it finds no footing. 'Ato' means from this Nibbāna. The remaining terms have clear meanings. The explanation of the seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Mahaddhana Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the eighth sutta, the Mahaddhana Sutta, they are called 'mahaddhana' (of great wealth) because they possess much wealth such as buried pearls and gems. They are called 'mahābhoga' (of great possessions) because they have many utensils such as gold and silver vessels. 'Aññamaññābhigijjanti' means they covet, long for, and delight in each other's wealth. 'Analaṅkatā' refers to those who are insatiable and whose nature is never-ending. 'Ussukkajātesu' means among those who are striving and anxious in various affairs, either to bring about sights and so on that have not yet arisen, or to enjoy those that have already arisen. 'Bhavasotānusārīsu' means among those who follow the stream of existence (vaṭṭa). 'Anussukā' means those who are free from such striving and anxiety. 'Agāraṃ' refers to a house where one lives with a woman. 'Virājiya' means having become detached (having left). The rest is clear. The explanation of the eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Catucakka Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the ninth sutta, the Catucakka Sutta, 'catucakkaṃ' refers to the four postures. In this context, the postures themselves are intended as 'wheels'. 'Navadvāraṃ' refers to the body having nine doors through nine wounds (orifices). 'Puṇṇaṃ' means the body is full of impure things. 'Lobhena saṃyuttaṃ' means the body is conjoined with craving (taṇhā). 'Kathaṃ yātrā bhavissati' asks 'How will the exit of such a body be? How will the release, the complete release, the transcending be?' 'Naddhi' refers to the binding of enmity. Anger that arises first is called 'kodha'; anger that arises later is called 'upanāha' (malice). It refers to such powerful anger. 'Varattaṃ' (thong): in the verse beginning with 'Having cut the thong and the strap,' craving is called the thong (varatta) and wrong view is called the snare (sandāna). In this context, however, excluding the defilements directly shown in the Pali, the remaining defilements should be known as 'varatta'. 'Icchā lobhaṃ': the same state is called 'icchā' (desire) in the sense of wanting, and 'lobha' (greed) in the sense of being attached. Alternatively, the weak greed that arises first is called 'icchā', and the powerful greed that arises repeatedly is called 'lobha'. Or, longing for an object not yet obtained is 'icchā', and attachment to an object already obtained is 'lobha'. 'Samūlaṃ taṇhaṃ' means craving along with its root, which is ignorance (avijjā). 'Abbuyha' means having uprooted by the path of Arahantship. The rest is clear. The explanation of the ninth sutta is finished.
52:
## 10. Eᅉijaᅅghasuttavaᅉᅉanā

In the commentary on the tenth sutta, the term 'Eᅉijaᅅgha' means one who has well-rounded calves like those of an antelope (eᅉĩ). 'Kisa' means one who has a balanced body that is not too fat. Alternatively, it also means one whose body is withered by the heat of the sun and is not enhanced by flowers, scents, or ointments. 'Vĩra' means one who is energetic. 'Appāhāra' means one who has a measured amount of food by knowing the proper limit in eating, or one who has little food by way of abstaining from afternoon and evening meals.

'Alolupa' means one who is free from greed or fickleness regarding the four requisites. Alternatively, this refers to the abandonment of craving for tastes. 'Sĩhaᅁveka-caraᅁ nāgaᅁ' means being like a lion that wanders alone, or like a noble elephant that wanders alone. Those who live in groups tend to be heedless, while those who practice alone are not heedless; therefore, it should be understood that only solitary practice is emphasized. 'Paveditā' refers to the truths that are clearly shown or spoken. 'Ettha' means in this mind-and-matter (nāma-rũpa). Indeed, form (rũpa) is taken by way of the five cords of sensual pleasure, and mind (nāma) is taken by the mind. By taking the phenomena that are inseparable from both mind and matter, the locative case (bhummaᅁ) should be applied here by way of the five aggregates and so on. The commentary on the tenth sutta ends.

## Sattivaggo Tatiyo.

## 4. Satullapakāyikavaggo

## 1. Sabbhisuttavaᅉᅉanā

In the first sutta of the Satullapakāyika Chapter, 'Satullapakāyika' refers to those who are born in heaven after speaking and teaching the Dhamma of the virtuous (sataᅁ dhammaᅁ) by way of undertaking it. In this regard, the story is as follows: It is heard that many ocean merchants set out to sea by ship. On the seventh day, while the ship was moving as fast as the speed of a launched arrow, they encountered a great disaster (uppātika) in the middle of the ocean. Great waves rose up and filled the ship with water.

While the ship was on the verge of sinking, the multitude of people cried out and performed prayers, calling upon the names of their respective deities. Among those merchants, one man reflected, "Do I have a refuge or a foundation in such a danger?" Seeing his own pure refuges and precepts, he sat down cross-legged like a yogi. The others asked him the reason for his lack of fear. He...
53:
He said to those merchants, "Friends, on the day I boarded the ship, I gave offerings to the Saᅅgha and took the refuges and the precepts. Therefore, I have no fear." When they asked, "Sir, can others also take these refuges and precepts?", he replied, "Yes, they can." They then pleaded, "If so, please give them to us as well." That man divided the people into seven groups of one hundred each and gave them the five precepts. Among them, he gave the precepts to the first hundred while they were in water up to their heels. He gave them to the second hundred at knee-depth, the third hundred at waist-depth, the fourth hundred at navel-depth, the fifth hundred at breast-depth, the sixth hundred at neck-depth, and to the seventh hundred while salt water was entering their mouths. After giving them the precepts, he exhorted them, "There is no other refuge for you; reflect only upon your virtue (sĩla)."

Those seven hundred people died right there and, due to the virtue they had undertaken near the time of death, were reborn in the Tāvatiᅁsa heaven. Mansions (vimānas) appeared for them according to their groups. In the center of all, a golden mansion of one hundred leagues (yojanas) appeared for the teacher, and the remaining mansions became his retinue, with the smallest being twelve leagues. As soon as they were reborn, they reflected on their karma and realized they had gained this prosperity because of their teacher. Thinking, "Let us go and speak of our teacher's virtues in the presence of the Buddha," they approached the Blessed One after the middle watch of the night. Those deities each spoke a verse to praise the virtues of their teacher.

In those verses, 'Sabbhireva' means only with the wise and the virtuous. The letter 'r' is a euphonic sandhi consonant. 'Samāsetha' means one should dwell together. This indicates the main point of the teaching, meaning that in all postures, one should act only together with the virtuous. 'Kubbetha' means one should do. 'Santhavaᅁ' means intimacy or friendship. Intimacy through craving should not be made with anyone, but friendship should be made with the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples. It is with this meaning in mind that 'santhavaᅁ' is said. 'Sataᅁ' means of the virtuous ones such as the Buddhas. 'Saddhammaᅁ' refers to the good Dhamma consisting of the five precepts, ten precepts, four foundations of mindfulness, and so on; however, in this context, the five precepts are intended. 'Seyyo hoti' means there is growth or progress. 'Na pāpiyo' means not even a slightly inferior or bad thing happens. 'Nāāto' means that wisdom cannot be obtained from others who are foolish, just as oil cannot be obtained from sand; but by knowing the Dhamma of the virtuous and by serving and associating with the wise, one obtains it, just as oil is obtained from sesame. 'Sokamajjhe' means not grieving even when in the midst of causes for grief or among beings who are grieving.
54:
Just like the lay devotee (Mallikā), the wife of General Bandhula Malla, and like Sāmaṇera Saṅkicca, the co-resident pupil of the Marshal of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, in the midst of five hundred robbers (one does not worry).

"Shines in the midst of relatives" means shining like Sāmaṇera Adhimuttaka, the co-resident pupil of Elder Saṅkicca, in the midst of his group of relatives. That novice was reportedly the nephew (sister's son) of the Elder. Then the Elder said to him, "Novice, you have grown in age. Go, ask about the years (of your birth) and return; I will grant you higher ordination."

The novice consented, saying "Very well," paid respects to the Elder, took his bowl and robes, and went to the village where his sister lived, located on this side of the forest inhabited by robbers, to go for alms. When the sister saw him, she paid respects, invited him into the house, and offered him food. After finishing his meal, the novice asked about his age. The sister said, "I do not know; only my mother knows."

Then the novice said, "You all stay here; I will go to my mother," and entered the forest. A robber saw him from afar and informed the other robbers. The robbers ordered, "It is said a novice has entered the forest alone; go and capture him." Some said, "Let us kill him," while others said, "Let us release him."

The novice thought, "I am a trainee (sekha) with work still to be done for the higher paths. I shall speak with these robbers to make myself safe." He then addressed the robber chief, saying, "Lay follower, I shall give you a simile," and recited these verses:

"In the past, in a vast and great forest,
A hunter set devious nets and killed a rabbit at that time.

Seeing the dead rabbit, the animals and birds were terrified,
And fled within a single night, thinking, 'A danger that should not happen has occurred here.'

In the same way, if you kill the monk Adhimutta, who is free from anxiety,
Travelers will no longer come, and there will be a loss of wealth for you."

(The robber chief replied:) "The monk Adhimutta, who is free from anxiety, has spoken the truth. Travelers will no longer come, and there will be a loss of wealth. If you meet anyone on the path ahead and do not tell them, then out of respect for your truthful word, go, Venerable Sir, as you please."
55:
When that Sāmaṇera Adhimutta was released by those robbers and went on his way, even though he met his parents and relatives, he did not tell them (about the robbers). Then, those parents and relatives, arriving in due course, were captured and harassed by the robbers. The robbers asked the novice's mother, who was beating her breast and weeping:

"How is Adhimutta related to you?
Was he a son who dwelt in your womb?
O Mother, tell us what we ask;
How are we to know him?"

(The mother replied:) "I am the biological mother of Adhimutta,
And this man is his biological father.
These are also his sisters and brothers;
Everyone here is a relative of Adhimutta.

Adhimutta is not one who acts (only) for the sake of relatives,
For even though he saw his relatives, he did not stop (us from being caught).
This indeed is the practice of monks,
Noble ones who live by the Dhamma.

Adhimutta is a speaker of truth,
For even though he saw his relatives, he did not stop (your actions).
Because of the good practice of the monk Adhimutta,
Who is a speaker of truth,
All his relatives have attained safety.
May the relatives go in peace!"

Thus, being released by the robbers, the parents and relatives went to Adhimutta and said:

"Dear son, because of the good practice of you,
A monk who is a speaker of truth,
All of us relatives have reached safety
And have returned in peace."

Those five hundred robbers also gained faith and went forth as monks in the presence of Sāmaṇera Adhimutta. Adhimutta took them to his preceptor, and after he himself attained higher ordination first, he made those five hundred his own pupils and had them ordained. All of them, established in the advice of Elder Adhimutta, attained the highest fruit, Arahantship. Based on this matter, the deity said, "Having known the True Dhamma of the virtuous, one shines in the midst of relatives."

'Sātatam' means constant happiness or lasting for a long time. 'Sabbāsaṃ vo' means of all of you. 'Pariyāyena' means by way of cause or reason. 'Sabbadukkhā pamuccati' means that one does not only become excellent, does not only gain wisdom, does not only remain without sorrow in the midst of sorrow, does not only shine in the midst of relatives, does not only arise in a happy destination, and does not only remain in happiness for a long time, but is also liberated from the entire suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha). The First Sutta (ends).
56:
## 2. Maccharisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, the phrase "maccherā ca pamādā ca" refers to stinginess (macchariya), which has the characteristic of hiding one's own wealth, and negligence (pamāda), which has the characteristic of a lack of mindfulness. Some individuals do not give gifts due to stinginess, thinking, "If I give this object, my wealth will be exhausted; there will be nothing left for me or for my family members." Others, being preoccupied with play and pleasure, do not even give rise to the thought, "A gift should be given." Thus, the Buddha explained the reason why giving—which brings followers, glory, wealth, and happiness—is not performed, starting with the words "Dānaṃ na dီyati."

"Puññaṃ ākaṅkhamānena" means by one who desires merit, which is distinguished by preliminary volition (pubba-cetanā) and so on. "Deyyaṃ hoti vijānatā" means it is said that giving should indeed be done by one who knows that there is a fruit of giving.

"Tam-eva bālaṃ phusati" means that hunger and thirst afflict and follow that fool who does not give due to stinginess, both in this world and the next; they do not leave him. "Tasmā" means because it afflicts only that fool. "Vineyya maccheraṃ" means by removing the stain of stinginess. "Dajjā dānaṃ malābhibhū" means one should give, having become one who overcomes the stain of stinginess.

"Te matesu na mīyanti" means among those who have died through death due to the habit of not giving, givers are like those who do not die. For example, just as a dead person, though surrounded by much food and drink, cannot rise and distribute it, saying, "Let this be for this person, let this be for that person," so too a non-giver does not distribute. Therefore, the wealth of a dead person and a non-giver are identical. For this reason, givers do not die among such dead ones; they are like the living. "Panthānaṃva saha vajaṃ, appasmiṃ ye pavecchanti" means, for example, just as travelers going together on a difficult journey share even the small amount of provisions they have with their companions, so too those traveling together through the beginningless wilderness of Saṃsāra share even a small gift (deyya-dhamma) with their companions. They are like the living among the dead.

"Esa dhammo sanantano" means this practice of giving and so on is an ancient law, or it is the law of the wise (sanantana). "Appasmeke" means some give even when they have only a small gift. "Bahuneke na denti" means some who are endowed with much wealth do not give. "Sahassena samaṃ mitaṃ" means it is compared to a gift of a thousand; it is equal to a gift of a thousand, and is difficult to obtain or fulfill. "Dhammaṃ care" means one should practice the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakamma-patha). "Uñchācariyaṃ" means one who seeks and collects discarded grains by gleaning in threshing floors and such. "Dāraṃ posaṃ" means while supporting a wife and children. "Appakasmiṃ" means making a distribution even of a small thing like a dish of vegetables; such a person is called a practitioner of Dhamma. "Sataṃ sahassānaṃ" means...
57:
"Pavecchanti" means they give. "Bahuneke na dicchare" means some do not give even though they possess much wealth. "Sahassena samaṃ mitaṃ" means it is measured as equal to a thousand; it is like a gift of a thousand.

"Duranvayo" means difficult to follow. "Duppūro" means difficult to fill. "Dhammaṃ care" means one practices the ten wholesome courses of action. "Yo'pi samuñjakaṃ care" means one who lives by gleaning, collecting discarded ears of grain by cleaning threshing floors and beating straw. "Dārañca posanti" means also supporting a wife and children. "Dadaṃ appakasmiṃ" means one who gives by sharing even a small thing like a dish of vegetables; such a person is said to practice Dhamma. "Sataṃ sahassānaṃ" means a hundred men counted in thousands, i.e., one hundred thousand (100,000). "Sahassayāginaṃ" means a gift given to a thousand monks or a gift performed with a thousand kahāpaṇas is a "sahassayāga." Those who have such gifts are "sahassayāgī." This refers to their gift. This shows an offering of alms-food to ten crores of monks or ten crores of kahāpaṇas. The Buddha said that those who give such large gifts do not even equal a fraction of the gift of such a Dhamma-practicing person. Even if one lives by gleaning, supports a wife, and gives only a small thing, the gifts of those "sahassayāgī" do not equal even a fraction of his gift. Even if that poor person gives only a single portion of alms or a ticket-meal (salāka-bhatta), the gifts of all those others do not equal a fraction of his gift. "Kala" means a sixteenth part, a hundredth part, or a thousandth part. Here, a hundredth part (1/100) is taken. If the gift given by that poor man is divided into a hundred parts, the ten thousand crore gifts of the others do not equal even one of those parts.

When the Tathāgata thus appraised the value of the gift, a deity standing nearby thought: "The Blessed One has, as if kicking away a great gift and throwing it into a pit of jewels, taken this small gift and raised it up as if striking the moon's disk. Why is this gift more fruitful?" and addressed him with a verse. In that verse, "kena" means for what reason. "Mahaggato" means reached greatness; it is a synonym for "vipula" (abundant). "Samena dinnassa" means of a gift given righteously. Then the Blessed One, wishing to distinguish the gifts for the deity, spoke the verse beginning with "Dadanti heke." In that verse, "visame niviṭṭhā" means established in unrighteous actions of body, speech, and mind. "Chetvā" means by harassing and striking. "Vadhitvā" means by killing. "Socayitvā" means by causing others to grieve. "Assumukhā" means with tearful faces, weeping; a gift given by making others weep is called "assumukhā-dāna." "Sadaṇḍā" means a gift given by threatening and striking with sticks and rods. "Evaṃ" means: "Because I am the Perfectly Enlightened One, I am not able to make a great gift have little fruit, nor am I able to make a small gift have great fruit. However, this great gift has little fruit because of the impurity of its origin. The other small gift has great fruit because of the purity of its origin."
58:
A gift given after making another person sorrowful, with faces full of tears (accompanied by tears), is called 'assumukhadāna' (giving with a tearful face). A gift given after threatening or striking with a stick is called 'sadaṇḍadāna' (giving with the stick).
