Regarding the word 'thus' (evaṃ): because I am the Perfectly Enlightened One, I cannot make a great gift small in result, nor can I make a small gift great in result. In truth, this great gift becomes small in result due to the impurity of its own origin; whereas that other small gift becomes great in result due to the purity of its own origin. Intending to show this meaning, He spoke the words beginning with 'evaṃ'. The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Sādhu Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'uttered an inspired utterance' (udānaṃ udānesi) means he expressed a joyful and delighted speech. Just as oil that cannot be contained in a measure overflows and goes out is called 'avasesaka', and just as water that cannot be contained in a tank overflows and flows away is called 'ogha' (a flood), even so, when a word of joy cannot be contained in the heart, becoming excessive and unable to remain within but coming outside, that speech is called an 'udāna'. The meaning is that he emitted such a speech consisting of joy.

'Giving even with faith is good' means that a gift given after believing in kamma and its results is indeed excellent and good. So they say.

How are these two (giving and fighting in war) equal? One who fears for his life cannot fight; one who fears the exhaustion of wealth cannot give. One who says, 'I will protect my life and I will also fight,' does not fight. Only one who, having abandoned attachment to life, strives saying, 'Let there be mutilation or death, I will seize this sovereignty,' can fight. One who says, 'I will protect my possessions and I will also give,' does not give. Only one who, having abandoned attachment to possessions, strives saying, 'I will give a great gift,' can give. Thus, giving and fighting are equal.

Furthermore, how are they equal? 'Though few, they conquer many' means that just as a few brave men on the battlefield conquer many cowards, even so, a person endowed with faith and other virtues, though giving a small gift, crushes much stinginess (macchera) and attains the great result of giving. In this way also, giving and fighting are equal. Therefore, it was said:

'If one gives even a little, having faith,
By that very act, he becomes happy in the hereafter.'
59:
To clarify this meaning, the story of the Brāhmaṇa Ekasāṭaka and the story of Aṅkura should be understood in detail.

'Dhammaladdhassa' refers to wealth obtained righteously and fairly, as well as to a person who has attained the Dhamma. Here, a person who has attained the Dhamma means an Ariyan (Noble One) who has realized the supramundane Dhamma. Therefore, the meaning is that giving wealth obtained righteously to an Ariyan who has attained the Dhamma is also good. In the verse 'Yo dhammaladdhassa', the meaning is the same. 'Uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatassa' means wealth acquired through initiative and energy. 'Vetaraṇiṃ' is merely the head of the discourse. In truth, it means having completely transcended King Yama's Vetaraṇī river, as well as the thirty-one great hells such as Sañjīva and Kāḷasutta.

'Viceyya dānaṃ' means a gift given after selection. In that context, there are two kinds of selection: selecting the gift (dakkhiṇā-vicinana) and selecting the recipient (dakkhiṇeyya-vicinana). Among them, removing inferior items and selecting excellent ones to give is called selecting the gift. Rejecting recipients of broken virtue or those of the ninety-five outside sects, and giving to those who have gone forth in the Dispensation (Sāsana) and are endowed with virtues such as morality, is called selecting the recipient. Thus, giving with discrimination in these two ways is 'sugata-ppasatthaṃ', praised by the Sugata (the Buddha). In that context, intending to show the selection of the recipient, He spoke the words beginning with 'ye dakkhiṇeyyā'. By the verse 'bījāni vuttāni yathā', He spoke of selecting the gift. This is because excellent gifts chosen and taken are like seeds that are not spoiled.

'Pāṇesu pi sādhu saṃyamo' means that restraint towards living beings is also good. This deity, going beyond the benefits of giving mentioned by other deities, began to speak about the benefits of virtue (sīla). 'Aheṭhayaṃ caraṃ' means living without harming. 'Parūpavādā' means due to the fear of being blamed by others. 'Bhayā' also means due to the fear of blame. 'Dānā ca kho dhammapadaṃva seyyo' means that the 'dhammapada' (the state of Dhamma), known as Nibbāna, is indeed superior to giving. 'Pubbe ca hi pubbatare ca santo' means the virtuous ones (santo) who appeared in ancient times such as the time of Kassapa Buddha, and in even earlier times such as the time of Koṇāgamana Buddha, or all those Buddhas and virtuous ones of former times. The third sutta is finished.
60:
## 4. Commentary on the Nasanti Sutta

In the fourth sutta, 'kamanīyāni' refers to desirable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa) such as visual forms and so forth. 'Apunāgamanaṃ anāgantā puriso maccudheyyā' means a person who cannot reach Nibbāna—referred to as 'non-returning' (apunāgamana)—from the realm of Death (maccudheyya), which is the round of rebirth in the three planes of existence. Indeed, beings do not return once they have reached Nibbāna; therefore, Nibbāna is called 'non-returning'. One who is bound by sensual pleasures and is negligent is called one who cannot reach Nibbāna; such a person is unable to attain Nibbāna, and thus it was said so.

'Chanda-jaṃ' means that which is born of the desire of craving (taṇhā-chanda). 'Aghaṃ' means the suffering of the five aggregates. The second term is merely a synonym (vevacana) for the first. 'Chanda-vinayā agha-vinayo' means the cessation of the five aggregates through the removal of craving. 'Agha-vinayā dukkha-vinayo' means that by the cessation of the five aggregates, the suffering of the round of rebirth is already removed.

'Citrāni' refers to varied or beautiful objects. 'Saṅkappa-rāgo' means lust born of thought (imagining something as beautiful). Thus, in this context, objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) is excluded, and only defilement sensuality (kilesa-kāma) is referred to as 'kāma'. This meaning should be clarified by the Pasūra Sutta. When the Elder Sāriputta said, "Lust born of thought is man's sensuality," the wanderer Pasūra replied thus:

Those beautiful objects in the world are not sensual pleasures,
Lust born of thought is what you call sensuality;
If one thinks unwholesome thoughts,
Then even your monks would be enjoyers of sensuality.

Then the Elder replied to that wanderer:

If those beautiful objects in the world were indeed sensual pleasures,
And you do not call lust born of thought sensuality,
Then while looking at delightful visual forms,
Your teacher too would be an enjoyer of sensuality.

While hearing sounds, smelling odors,
Tasting flavors, and touching delightful tangibles,
Your teacher too would be an enjoyer of sensuality.

'Athetta dhīrā' means that in such instances, the wise remove desire and lust (chanda-rāga) for those objects. 'Saṃyojanaṃ sabbaṃ' refers to all ten kinds of fetters. 'Akiñcanaṃ' means being free from impediments (kiñcana) such as lust. 'Nānupatanti dukkhā' means the sufferings of the round of rebirth no longer fall upon that person (who has abandoned the defilements).
61:
Having heard the verse beginning with "Pahāsi saṅkhaṃ," the Elder named Mogharāja, who was skilled in the sequence of discourse (anusandhi) in that assembly, thought, "The meaning of this verse has not yet reached its proper connection," and wishing to connect the sequence, he spoke thus. In that verse, "idha vā huraṃ vā" means either in this world or in another world, such as the realms of Nagas or Garudas. In the phrase "naruttamaṃ atthacaraṃ narānaṃ," although all Arahants are supreme among men and are those who practice for the welfare of men, the Elder said this referring specifically to the Buddha (Dasabala). "Ye taṃ namassanti pasaṃsiyā te" is a question asking: if deities and humans worship an Arahant who is thus liberated from defilements, then are those who worship the Blessed One with body, speech, or conformable practice (anupaṭipatti) praiseworthy or not praiseworthy?

"Bhikkhū" is how the Blessed One addressed the Elder Mogharāja. "Aññāya dhammaṃ" means having known the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Saṅgātigā tepi bhavanti" means those who worship the Blessed One with body, speech, and conformable practice also become those who transcend attachments (saṅga) such as lust, having understood the Four Noble Truths and abandoned doubt; they are also praiseworthy. The commentary on the fourth sutta ends.

## 5. Commentary on the Ujjhānasaññī Sutta

In the fifth sutta, "ujjhānasaññikā" does not refer to a separate celestial realm named Ujjhānasaññī. Rather, these deities came with a mind intending to criticize the Blessed One's use of the four requisites. It is said that this thought occurred to them: "The ascetic Gotama praises the limit of contentment for monks with rag-robes, alms-food, lodgings at the foot of trees, and fermented urine as medicine. However, he himself wears fine robes such as silk, linen, and fine cloth. He eats excellent food fit for a king. He dwells in a noble bed in a Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) comparable to a celestial mansion. He uses medicines such as ghee and fresh butter. He teaches the Dhamma to the great multitude all day long. His words are of one kind, but his actions are of another." Thus they came, criticizing him. Therefore, the Elders who compiled the Dhamma gave them the name "Ujjhānasaññikā" (those with a critical perception).

"Aññathā santaṃ" means that which exists in another way (i.e., falsehood). "Nikaccā" means by deceit or trickery. In the term "kitavasseva," "kitava" is said to be a bird-hunter (fowler).
62:
That bird hunter, though not a bush himself, covers himself with branches and leaves to show the appearance of a bush. He kills birds such as peacocks and partridges that come near and thus supports his wife and children. In this way, just as that bird hunter deceives with such trickery to eat bird meat, a corrupt monk also covers himself with rag-robes and wanders about deceiving the public with his skill in speech to get food. The deity, referring to the Blessed One, says that all consumption of the four requisites by such a deceptive monk is called "consumption by theft."

"The wise know" means that the wise know whether this person is one who practices well or one who does not. Thus, those deities, thinking "We alone are wiser than even the Tathāgata," spoke these words.

Then the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Nayidaṃ." In those words, "the practice that is firm" means this practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānu-dhamma-paṭipadā) is stable and firm. By which practice the wise (dhīrā), burning away defilements through the two types of meditation—meditation on the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation on the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna)—are liberated from the bonds of Māra. The meaning is that it is not possible to enter or practice that path merely by speaking or merely by hearing. "The wise do not do so" means that the wise, having known the perishing of the world, having seen the arising and passing away of the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka), and having penetrated the Four Noble Truths, are at peace through the extinguishing of defilements. Those who have crossed over the craving called visattikā in the world do not do such things; the meaning is "We do not speak such words."

"Standing on the ground" means that, feeling ashamed and thinking "We have done what is improper; we have addressed the one who does not do evil as if he were a doer of evil," they established respect for the Blessed One as if for Mahābrahmā. Seeing the Blessed One as difficult to approach like a great mass of fire, they descended from the sky and stood on the ground. "Accaya" means a transgression or fault. "Venerable Sir, a fault has overcome us" means it occurred by overwhelming and overpowering us. "Āsādetabba" means to offend or strike. It is said that those deities offended the Blessed One both by body and by speech. By not bowing to the Tathāgata and remaining in the air, they offended by body. By bringing the comparison of the bird hunter and speaking various kinds of unseemly words, they offended by speech. Therefore, they said, "We think we have offended." "Please accept" means please forgive. In the future...
63:
"For restraint" (saṃvarāya) means for the purpose of restraint in the future, so as not to commit such a transgression or fault again. "He manifested a smile" (sitaṃ pātvākāsi) means showing a joyful manner by revealing the front teeth. Why? Because those deities did not apologize with a sincere heart, and they treated the Tathāgata, the supreme individual in the world including the devas, as equal to ordinary worldly people. Then the Blessed One, intending "I will forgive after demonstrating the Buddha-power when further conversation arises," manifested a smile. "To a greater extent" (bhiyyoso mattāya) means in an exceeding measure. "Spoke this verse" (imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi) means they spoke this verse thinking, "This monk is angry with us."

"Does not accept" (na paṭiggaṇhāti) means he does not forgive or endure. "One with internal anger" (kopantaro) means one in whom anger has arisen internally. "One who values anger" (dosagarū) means one who lives holding onto anger as something important. "He binds the enmity" (sa veraṃ paṭimuñcati) means such a person binds that enmity to himself, just like fastening a knot; he keeps it and does not relinquish it. "If there were no transgression" (accayaṃ ce na vijjettha) means if there were no act of transgression committed. "If there were no offense here" (no cidha apagataṃ siyā) means if there were no such thing as an offense. "How would one be skilled here?" (kenidha kusalo siyā) means if enmities were not stilled, for what reason would there be a person of merit in this world?

In the verse "Whose transgression?" (kassaccayā), it means: Who has no transgression? Who has no offense? Who does not fall into delusion? Who is always called wise? It is said that the Blessed One's act of manifesting a smile was for the purpose of prompting this verse. Therefore, now intending to forgive after demonstrating the Buddha-power to the deities, he spoke the words beginning with "To the Tathāgata, the Buddha" (tathāgatassa buddhassa). In that verse, "to the Tathāgata" (tathāgatassa) means to the one who is called Tathāgata because of such reasons as having come in the same way as previous Buddhas. "To the Buddha" (buddhassa) means to the one who has received this name at the end of the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship due to such reasons as being the Awakened One to the Four Truths. "Of those confessing a fault" (accayaṃ desayantīnaṃ) means that what you said—"of those confessing a fault... he binds the enmity"—was well spoken; however, I do not delight in or desire that enmity. "I accept your transgression" (paṭiggaṇhāmi vo accayaṃ) means "I forgive your fault." The fifth sutta is finished.
64:
## 6. Commentary on the Saddhā Sutta

In the sixth sutta, 'Faith is the companion of a man' means that for a man going to the deva world, the human world, or Nibbāna, faith is his companion and fulfills the duties of a companion. 'If he does not stand in lack of faith' means if he does not remain in a state of faithlessness. *Yaso* means retinue. *Kitti* means the praising of virtues. 'It belongs to him' means it occurs to that person because of that faith. 'Attachments do not fall upon him' means the five types of attachments, such as the attachment of lust (*rāga-saṅga*), do not fall upon him. 'They practice negligence' means those who act with negligence or give rise to it are said to practice that negligence. 'Protects it like the best of wealth' means protecting it like excellent wealth such as pearls, emeralds, and rubies. 'One who meditates' refers to one who meditates through meditation on characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) and meditation on objects (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*). In this context, *lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna* refers to insight (*vipassanā*), the Path (*magga*), and the Fruit (*phala*). Insight is called *lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna* because it closely contemplates the three characteristics such as impermanence. The Path is called *lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna* because it fulfills the task reached through insight. The Fruit is also called *lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna* because it closely contemplates the truth of cessation (*nirodha-sacca*) which has such characteristics. The eight attainments, however, should be understood as *ārammaṇūpanijjhāna* because they closely contemplate the objects of *kasiṇa*. *Parama* refers to the bliss of the Fruit of Arahantship. The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Samaya Sutta

In the seventh sutta, *Sakkesu* refers to a certain district which is the residence of the princes named Sakya, derived from the inspired utterance, 'Indeed, sirs, the princes are capable (*sakya*).' It is called Sakka by way of conventional usage. It means 'in that Sakyan district.' *Mahāvane* means in the great forest which is self-grown, unplanted, and continuous with the Himalayas. 'With all the Arahants' means with the Arahants who reached the Fruit of Arahantship on the very day this sutta was preached.

The sequential narrative here is as follows: The Sakyans and Koliyans cultivated crops by damming the river named Rohiṇī with a single dam between the cities of Kapilavatthu and Koliya. Then, in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, when the crops began to wither, the laborers from both cities assembled. There, the residents of Koliya said, 'If this water is divided between both sides, it will not be enough for you, nor will it be enough for us. However, our crops can be brought to fruition with just this one supply of water. Give this water to us.' The residents of Kapilavatthu said, 'We cannot afford to have you fill your granaries while we wander at your doorsteps with baskets in hand, carrying red gold, blue gems, and black coins. Our crops can also be brought to fruition with just this one supply of water. Give this water to us.' When they said, 'We cannot give it,' the others replied, 'We cannot give it either.' As the argument escalated, the laborers rose up...
65:
'Taking red gold, blue gems, and black coins, and holding baskets and such in our hands, we will not be able to wander at your doorsteps. Our crops will also be brought to fruition with just this one supply of water. Give this water to us,' they said. 'We cannot give it,' they said. 'We cannot give it either,' they said. Thus, as they argued and quarreled, one rose up and struck another, and that person struck another back. Having thus beaten one another, they insulted the lineage of the royal families and increased the conflict and anger.

The Koliyan laborers said, 'You boast by relying on the Kapilavatthu residents who, like village dogs and jackals, lived together with their own sisters. What can their elephants, horses, and shields and weapons do to us?' The Sakyan laborers said, 'Now you boast by relying on the deformed and outcaste children who, being helpless and destitute like animals, lived in Kolla trees. What can their elephants, horses, and shields and weapons do to us?' They went and told the ministers appointed to that task. The ministers reported it to the royal families. Then the Sakyan kings said, 'We will show the strength and power of those who lived with their sisters,' and they set out equipped for war. The Koliyan kings also said, 'We will show the strength and power of those who lived in Kolla trees,' and they set out equipped for war.

The Blessed One, having risen from the attainment of Great Compassion (*Mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*) at the time of dawn, surveyed the world and saw these kings setting out thus prepared for war. Having seen them, he reflected, 'If I go, will this conflict be settled or not?' He decided, 'I will go there and preach three Jātakas to settle the conflict; then the conflict will be settled. After that, to demonstrate unity, I will preach two Jātakas and then the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. Having heard the teaching, the residents of both cities will each offer two hundred and fifty princes (five hundred in total). I will ordain them, and then there will be a Great Assembly (*Mahāsamāgama*).' Therefore, while those kings were setting out prepared for war, without informing anyone, he took his bowl and robes and went by himself. He sat cross-legged in the air between the two armies, emitting the six-colored rays (*chabbaṇṇaraṃsi*).

As soon as the Kapilavatthu residents saw the Blessed One, they thought, 'Our noble kinsman, the Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived. He has surely seen us engaged in conflict.' They said, 'Since the Blessed One has arrived, it is not proper for us to hurl weapons at the bodies of others. Let the Koliyans kill us if they wish, or bind us if they wish,' and they discarded their weapons and remained worshiping the Blessed One. The Koliyan residents also thought in the same way, discarded their weapons, and remained worshiping the Blessed One. The Blessed One, while staying there, asked, 'Great Kings, why have you come?' 'Venerable Sir, we have not come to play at the riverbank, nor to play on the mountain, nor to play in the river, nor to sightsee in the forest and mountains. Indeed, the battle in this place...'
66:
They did not dare to strike the bodies of others with weapons. Thinking, 'Let the residents of Koliya kill us or bind us if they wish,' they discarded their weapons, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down. The residents of Koliya thought likewise, discarded their weapons, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down.

Although the Blessed One already knew, he asked, 'Great kings, for what reason have you come?' The kings replied, 'Venerable Sir, we have not come to play at the bathing place, nor to play on the mountain, nor to play in the river, nor to view the hills. Indeed, we have come having prepared for battle in this place.' 'Great kings, on what account is your quarrel?' he asked. 'Venerable Sir, it is on account of water,' they replied. 'Great kings, how much is water worth?' he asked. 'Venerable Sir, it is of little value,' they replied. 'Great kings, how much is the earth worth?' he asked. 'Venerable Sir, it is priceless,' they replied. 'Great kings, how much are the Khattiyas worth?' he asked. 'Venerable Sir, the Khattiyas are priceless,' they replied. 'Great kings, why do you destroy priceless Khattiyas on account of water which is of little value? Great kings, there is no satisfaction in quarreling. Great kings, because of quarreling, a grudge was formed in an improper situation between a certain tree deity and a black lion, and that grudge has lasted throughout this entire eon,' he said, and then he related the Phandana Jātaka.

Then he said, 'Great kings, one should not easily believe the words of others. By believing the words of others, because of the word of a single rabbit, all the four-footed animals in the Himavanta forest, which is three thousand leagues wide, once ran into the great ocean. Therefore, one should not easily believe the words of others,' and he related the Pathavīundriya Jātaka. Then he said, 'Great kings, sometimes even a weak person sees the flaw or opening of a strong person; sometimes a strong person sees the flaw of a weak person. Even a small female laṭukika bird once killed a noble elephant,' and he related the Laṭukika Jātaka. Having thus related these three Jātakas to appease the quarrel, he related two more Jātakas to illustrate unity. How? He said, 'Great kings, no one can see a weakness in those who are united,' and he related the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka. Then he said, 'Great kings, no one could see a gap among those who were united. But when they quarreled with one another, then the son of a hunter took their lives and carried them away. Therefore, there is no satisfaction in quarreling,' and he related the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka. Having thus related these five Jātakas, he finally taught the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.

The kings were inspired and thought, 'If the Teacher had not come, we would have killed one another with our own hands and caused a river of blood to flow. Our sons and brothers...'
67:
...we would not see [our sons and brothers] at the doors of our houses, and there would be no one to bring us news or replies. We have regained our lives because of the Teacher. If the Teacher had lived the household life, the sovereignty of the four great islands with their two thousand surrounding small islands would have come into his hands, and he would have had more than a thousand sons; then he would have traveled surrounded by a host of Khattiyas. However, he renounced that prosperity, went forth, and attained Supreme Enlightenment. Now, let him travel surrounded by a retinue of Khattiyas,' they thought. Thus, the residents of both cities offered five hundred princes, two hundred and fifty from each side.

The Blessed One ordained those princes and went to the Mahāvana forest. Because they had gone forth out of respect for the Buddha and not by their own desire, dissatisfaction arose in those monks. Their former wives also sent messages, saying, 'May the young lords be weary [of the monkhood]; may the life of a householder not be established [for them],' and so forth. Those monks became exceedingly weary and bored.

When the Blessed One reflected, he knew their state of dissatisfaction and thought, 'These monks are weary even though they live together with a Buddha like me. Now, I will tell them about the beauty of Lake Kuṇāla, take them there, and dispel their dissatisfaction.' He then spoke of the virtues of Lake Kuṇāla. Those monks wished to see that lake. When he asked, 'Monks, do you wish to see Lake Kuṇāla?' they replied, 'Venerable Sir, we wish to see it.' 'If so, come, I shall go,' he said. They asked, 'Venerable Sir, how can we reach the place where those with psychic powers go?' 'If you wish to go, I will take you by my psychic power,' he said. They replied, 'Very well, Venerable Sir.'

The Blessed One took the five hundred monks, flew into the air, and standing at Lake Kuṇāla, he said, 'Monks, if you do not know the names of any fish in this Lake Kuṇāla, ask me.' The monks asked questions. The Blessed One answered everything they asked. He had them ask and then explained not only the names of the fish but also the names of the trees in that forest grove, and the two-footed and four-footed creatures and birds at the foot of the mountain.

At that time, the bird king named Kuṇāla came, sitting on a wooden stick held in the beaks of two female cuckoo birds, surrounded by a flock of birds in front, behind, and on both sides. When the monks saw that bird king, they said, 'Venerable Sir, this bird must be the king of these birds, and these birds are its retinue; so we think.' 'Monks, it is as you think. This bird king is also of my lineage, my own ancestry,' he said. 'Venerable Sir, now we have seen these birds. But as for the words...'
68:
The Blessed One said, "This king of birds is also of my lineage, my own ancestry." When the monks requested to hear about it, he asked, "Bhikkhus, do you wish to hear?" "Yes, Bhante," they replied. Then, saying, "Listen then," he related the Kunāla Jātaka, adorned with three hundred verses, and dispelled their dissatisfaction. At the conclusion of the teaching, all the monks were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Through the Path itself, psychic power (iddhi) also came to them. The Blessed One thought, "Let this much of the Path and Fruit suffice for these monks for a while," and flying into the air, he went to the Mahāvana forest. While those monks had gone there by the psychic power of the Buddha, upon their return, they descended into the Mahāvana forest surrounding the Blessed One by their own psychic power.

The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat and addressed the monks, "Come, bhikkhus, sit down. I shall teach you the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) for the defilements to be abandoned by the three higher paths." Thus he taught the meditation subject. The monks thought, "The Blessed One, knowing our dissatisfaction, took us to Lake Kunāla and dispelled it. To us who attained the fruit of Stream-entry there, he has now given the meditation subject for the three higher paths in this Dispensation. It is not proper for us to pass the time thinking, 'We are Stream-enterers'; it is only proper for us to become supreme men." They paid homage at the feet of the Ten-Powered One, rose, shook out their sitting cloths (nisīdana), and sat down individually in mountain caves and at the feet of trees.

The Blessed One reflected, "These monks are naturally those who do not abandon their meditation subject. For a monk who has obtained the proper method, there is no such thing as exhaustion. As they proceed, they will develop insight (vipassanā), reach Arahantship, and come to me, thinking, 'We shall report the qualities we have personally realized.' When they arrive, the deities from the ten thousand world-systems will gather in this single world-system; it will be a Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya). It is proper for me to sit in a secluded place." Having so reflected, he had a Buddha-seat prepared in another secluded spot and sat down.

The Elder who had taken the meditation subject and departed first of all attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Then another, and then another—all five hundred blossomed like lotuses in a lotus pond. The monk who first attained Arahantship, thinking, "I shall report this to the Blessed One," unfolded his cross-legged position, shook out his sitting cloth, rose, and faced the Ten-Powered One. In this manner, one after another, the five hundred monks [approached] as if entering the alms-hall...
69:
...they arrived in succession, just as if entering an alms-hall. The monk who arrived first paid homage, spread his sitting cloth, and sat down in a suitable place. Wishing to report the quality of Arahantship he had realized, he wondered, "Is there anyone else or not?" Turning back and looking at the path he had come, he saw another Elder, and then another. When all five hundred had arrived and sat down in a suitable place, this one, out of shyness toward that one, did not speak; and that one, out of shyness toward this one, did not speak. It is said that for those whose taints are destroyed (Arahants), two dispositions arise: the thought occurs, "Oh, would that the world with its devas quickly realize the quality I have realized!" However, like a man who has found a hidden treasure, they do not wish to report their realized state to others.

Just as those noble ones entered the presence of the Blessed One, the full moon, glorious like a silver chariot wheel held by its rim and turned, or like a great silver mirror held up in the eastern direction to see the beauty of the world adorned by the appearance of a Buddha—having been freed from the five obstructions of clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu the Asura from around the eastern Yugandhara mountains—rose and entered the path of the wind. At such a moment, second, and instant, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Mahāvana forest, together with a great community of monks, about five hundred monks, all of whom were Arahants.

At that time, the Blessed One was born in the lineage of King Mahāsammata, and those five hundred monks were also born in the family of King Mahāsammata. The Blessed One was born from a khattiya womb, and those monks were also born from khattiya wombs. The Blessed One had gone forth from royalty, and those monks had also gone forth from royalty. The Blessed One had abandoned the white parasol and renounced the universal sovereignty that was within his reach to go forth; those monks had also abandoned the white parasol and renounced the royal fortunes that were within their reach to go forth. Thus, in a pure place, at a pure time of night, the Blessed One, being pure himself, had a pure retinue. Being free from passion, he had a retinue free from passion. Being free from hatred, he had a retinue free from hatred. Being free from delusion, he had a retinue free from delusion. Being free from craving, he had a retinue free from craving. Being free from defilements, he had a retinue free from defilements. Being peaceful, he had a peaceful retinue. Being tamed, he had a tamed retinue. Being liberated, he had a liberated retinue. He shone exceedingly. This is indeed a ground for praise; one should speak as much as one is able. Thus, referring to these monks, it was said: "together with about five hundred monks, all of whom were Arahants."
70:
"Generally" means that the majority assembled. The non-percipient (asaññasatta) deities, formless (arūpāvacara) deities, and those in meditative absorption did not assemble as they were few. The order of this assembly was as follows: The deities near the Mahāvana forest stirred, shouting loudly, "Come, friends! Seeing the Buddha is of great benefit; hearing the Dhamma is of great benefit; seeing the Saṅgha is of great benefit. Come, come!" Having arrived, they paid homage to the Blessed One and the Arahants who had attained the fruit of Arahantship at that very moment, and stood to one side. In this manner, hearing the voices of those various deities, others became aware step by step—at distances of half a gāvuta, one gāvuta, half a yojana, one yojana, and so on. Thus, it should be understood that deities assembled from the ten thousand world systems: from the Himavanta mountains spanning three thousand yojanas; from the sixty-three thousand great cities; from the ninety-nine hundred thousand Doṇamukha towns; from the ninety-six billion port towns; from the fifty-six billion gem mines; from the entire Jambudīpa, Pubbavideha, Aparagoyāna, and Uttarakuru; and from the two thousand small islands. Here, "ten world elements" (dasa-lokadhātu) refers to the ten thousand world systems. Therefore, it is said, "Deities from the ten world elements generally assembled."

With the deities thus assembled, the entire interior of the world system up to the Brahma realm was as full as a needle-case packed with needles without any gap. In this regard, the height of the Brahma realm should be understood thus: If a stone slab the size of the seven-tiered pinnacle of the Lohapāsāda were dropped from the Brahma realm, it would reach the earth only after four months. In such a vast space, just as flowers or smoke thrown from below cannot go up, or mustard seeds dropped from above cannot descend because there is no gap, so too the deities were packed without any interval. However, just as the place where a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) sits is not cramped and the great powerful kings who arrive find space, while further out it becomes very crowded; even so, the place where the Blessed One sat was not cramped, and the great powerful devas and Brahmas who arrived certainly found space. Indeed, in a space as small as the tip of a hair near the Blessed One, ten or even twenty deities manifested subtle bodies and stood there. At the outermost edge, deities stood in groups of sixty each.
71:
"Suddhāvāsakāyikānaṃ" refers to those living in the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes). The Suddhāvāsa are the five Brahma realms which are the abodes of the pure ones—the Non-returners (anāgāmī) and Arahants (khīṇāsava).

"This thought occurred" — why did it occur? It is said that those Brahmas, having entered meditative absorption and emerged at the predetermined time, looked upon the Brahma realm and saw it as empty and silent as a dining hall after a meal. Then, reflecting, "Where have the Brahmas gone?" they realized the Great Assembly (Mahāsamāgama) and thought: "This assembly is magnificent; we have been left behind. For those who are left behind, an opportunity is hard to find. Therefore, let us go, but not empty-handed; let each of us compose a verse and then go. With that verse, we shall make our arrival known in the Great Assembly and also speak in praise of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala)." Thus, because they reflected after emerging from absorption, this thought occurred to them.

In the Pali phrase "They appeared before the Blessed One," it is spoken as if they descended directly into the presence of the Blessed One, but this meaning should not be taken so literally here. In fact, while still stationed in the Brahma realm, they composed the verses; then one Brahma descended at the edge of the eastern world system, one at the edge of the southern world system, one at the edge of the western world system, and one at the edge of the northern world system.

Then, the Brahma who descended at the edge of the eastern world system entered the blue kasiṇa (nīla-kasiṇa) and emitted blue rays. Making his arrival known as if covering the deities of the ten thousand world systems with a suit of emerald-blue armor, and because no one can overstep the path of the Buddhas, he approached only by the great Buddha-path (buddhavīthi), paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, he recited the verse he had composed.

The Brahma who descended at the edge of the southern world system entered the yellow kasiṇa (pīta-kasiṇa) and emitted a golden glow. Making his arrival known as if clothing the deities from the ten thousand world systems in golden garments, he acted in the same manner. The Brahma who descended at the edge of the western world system entered the red kasiṇa (lohita-kasiṇa) and emitted red rays. Making his arrival known as if wrapping the deities of the ten thousand world systems in noble red blankets, he acted in the same manner. The Brahma who descended at the edge of the northern world system entered the white kasiṇa (and emitted white rays, making his arrival known as if covering the deities from the ten thousand world systems with jasmine-patterned cloth...)
72:
Having entered (the white kasina) and emitted white rays, he made his arrival known to the deities from the ten thousand world systems, as if covering them with a cloth of jasmine flowers, and acted accordingly. In the Pali text, however, it is stated: "They appeared before the Blessed One. Then those deities, having paid homage to the Blessed One, stood to one side." Thus, their appearance before him and their standing to one side after paying homage are described as if occurring simultaneously. Although it happened in the sequence I mentioned, it is shown as a single event (in the Pali). The recitation of the verses, however, is stated separately in the Pali.

In that context, "Mahāsamaya" means a great assembly (mahāsamūha). A forest grove is called "pavana". By both terms, the Blessed One said, "In this forest grove today, there is a great assembly." Then, to show whose assembly it was, he said, "Devakāyā samāgatā" (The groups of deities have assembled). Here, "devakāyā" means groups of deities. "Āgatamha imaṃ dhammasamayaṃ" means, seeing the groups of deities thus assembled, "We too have come to this assembly of the Dhamma." Why have they come? "Dakkhitāye aparājitasanghaṃ" means they have come to see this unconquered Sangha, whom no one can defeat, and who has just today conquered the battle by crushing the three Māras. That Brahma, having recited this verse and paid homage to the Blessed One, stood at the very edge of the eastern world system.

Then the second Brahma, having arrived in the same manner as mentioned, spoke. There, "tatra bhikkhavo" refers to the monks in that place of assembly. "Samādahaṃsu" means they were endowed with (supramundane) concentration. "Cittamattano ujukaṃ akaṃsu" means they made their minds straight by removing all impurities such as crookedness and deceit. "Sārathīva nettāni gahetvā" means just as a charioteer, having laid down the goad, stands holding all the reins of the well-trained Sindhu horses without urging or restraining them, even so, these five hundred monks, endowed with six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) and with guarded sense-doors, protect their faculties. "O Blessed One, we have come to see these wise monks." That Brahma also went and stood in his usual place at the edge of the world system.

Then the third Brahma, having arrived in the same manner as mentioned, spoke. In that verse, "chetvā khīlaṃ" means having cut the stakes of lust, hatred, and delusion. "Palighaṃ" refers to the bolt of lust, hatred, and delusion. "Indakhīlaṃ" refers to the threshold pillar (city pillar) of lust, hatred, and delusion. "Ūhacca manejā" means these monks, who are without the agitation (ejā) of craving, having uprooted the threshold pillar, in the four directions...
73:
(Those monks) wander with unhindered movement in the four directions. "Suddhā" means those without the defilements that cause impurity. "Vimalā" means those without the stains of lust and so on. This word "vimalā" is a synonym (vevacana) for "suddhā". "Cakkhumanto" refers to the Buddha who possesses the five eyes (Buddha-cakkhu, dibba-cakkhu, samanta-cakkhu, pakati-cakkhu, etc.). "Sudantā" means those who are well-tamed through the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. "Susu-nāgā" means young, newly-attained Arahants. The etymological meaning in this context is: they are called "nāga" because they do not go (na gacchanti) by way of desire and so on; they are called "nāga" because they do not return (na āgacchanti) to the defilements abandoned by the respective paths; they are called "nāga" because they do not commit (na karonti) various kinds of evil (āgu). This is a summary here; the detailed explanation should be understood as stated in the Mahāniddesa.

Furthermore:
"He commits no evil (āgu) in the world,
Having abandoned all fetters and bonds;
He is unattached everywhere and liberated,
Such a person is called a Nāga (Arahant) because of his suchness."
Thus, the meaning should be understood through this verse. "Susu-nāgā" means those who have attained Arahantship while still young. "O Blessed One, we have come to see these young Arahants, who are thus tamed by the incomparable and excellent teacher of those to be tamed, who is like a skilled charioteer." That Brahma also went and stood in his usual place. The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Sakalikasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "Maddakucchismiṃ" means in the park of that name. Indeed, when Ajātasattu was in the womb, his mother, the queen, thought, "This fetus in my womb will be the enemy of the King. What benefit is there for me from this pregnancy?" and had her belly massaged (pressed) to cause an abortion. Therefore, it came to be known as "Maddakucchi" (the place where the belly was pressed). It is also called "Migadāya" (Deer Park) because it was given as a sanctuary for deer.

In the passage "Tena kho pana samayena", the sequential story is as follows: Devadatta, relying on Ajātasattu, employed archers and the elephant Dhanapāla, but failing to harm the Buddha's life, he thought, "I will kill him with my own hands." He climbed Gijjhakūṭa Mountain and, intending to crush the ascetic Gotama to pieces, hurled a large rock the size of a house-peak. That Devadatta possessed strength equal to five elephants. However, for the Buddhas, there can be no danger to life through the efforts of others; such an occurrence is impossible.
74:
Devadatta, being unable to take the life of the Tathāgata, thought, "I will kill him with my own hands." He climbed Gijjhakūṭa Hill and, having lifted a great rock the size of a house-peak, he rolled it down, thinking, "May the ascetic Gotama be crushed to pieces!" It is said that Devadatta possessed great strength, equal to that of five elephants. However, it is impossible for the life of the Buddhas to be taken by the efforts of others. As that rock was coming toward the Tathāgata's person, another rock arose from the air and intercepted it. Due to the violent collision of those two rocks, a large splinter of rock broke off and struck the edge of the Blessed One's foot. His foot became as if struck by a large axe, and with the blood flowing out, it appeared as if smeared with lac-dye. The Blessed One looked up and said to Devadatta, "O foolish man, you have produced much demerit, you who, with a corrupt and murderous mind, have caused the blood of the Tathāgata to flow." From that time on, a painful sensation arose in the Blessed One. The monks thought, "This monastery has uneven and rugged ground; it is an unsuitable place for many people such as kings and for the monastics." Those monks took the Tathāgata on a palanquin and brought him to Maddakucchi. Referring to this, it was said: "At that time, the Blessed One's foot was injured by a splinter of rock."

'Bhusa' refers to intense pains. 'Suda' is a mere particle. 'Dukkha' means the exclusion of pleasure. 'Tibba' means piercing; 'khara' means harsh; 'kaṭuka' means acute; 'asāta' means unpleasant. Because the mind does not enter into those sensations and those sensations do not cause the mind to increase, they are called 'amanāpa' (disagreeable). 'Being mindful and clearly comprehending' means being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom that can endure the sensation. 'Without being distressed' means not being oppressed, and not following the will of the sensations by tossing and turning while lying down.

In this context of 'sīhaseyyā' (the lion's sleep), there are four types of sleep: the sensualist's sleep (kāmabhogiseyyā), the petas' sleep (petaseyyā), the lion's sleep (sīhaseyyā), and the Tathāgata's sleep (tathāgataseyyā). Among these four, "Monks, for the most part, beings who enjoy sensual pleasures sleep on their left side" refers to the sensualist's sleep. Among them, there are generally none who sleep on their right side. "Monks, for the most part, petas sleep on their backs" refers to the petas' sleep. Because they have little flesh and blood and are just a mass of bones, they cannot sleep on one side and only sleep on their backs. "Monks, the lion, the king of beasts, having placed its tail between its thighs, sleeps on its right side" refers to the lion's sleep.
75:
Because of its great power and majesty, the lion, the king of beasts, places its two front paws in one place and its hind legs in another, tucks its tail between its thighs, and after noting the position of the front paws, hind legs, and tail, it sleeps with its head resting on its two front paws. Even after sleeping the whole day, when it wakes up, it wakes without being startled. It lifts its head and notes the position of its front paws and other parts. If its posture is disarranged, it becomes displeased, thinking, "This posture is not suitable for your birth, nor is it suitable for your bravery," and it sleeps again in that very place, not going out for food. However, if it remains in its position without abandoning the original posture, it becomes very joyful, thinking, "This posture is suitable for your birth and your bravery." It then gets up, performs the lion's stretch, shakes its mane, roars the lion's roar three times, and departs to seek food. Resting in the fourth jhāna is called 'tathāgataseyyā'. Among those four types of sleep, the lion's sleep (sīhaseyyā) is mentioned here. This lion's sleep is called the noble sleep because it is a posture of great power and majesty.

"Foot on foot" means placing the left foot over the right foot. "Overlapping" means placing it slightly beyond. This is because if the ankles or the knees strike each other, pain arises repeatedly, the mind does not become one-pointed, and the sleep is uncomfortable. If placed beyond so as not to strike, pain does not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, and the sleep is comfortable. Therefore, he rested in this manner. "Mindful and clearly comprehending" means being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom that governs the act of sleeping. In this context, the "perception of rising" (uṭṭhānasaññā) is not mentioned because this was the Blessed One's sleep of the sick (gilānaseyyā).

"Seven hundred deities" means that in this sutta, all those deities came to the place where the Buddha was resting in his illness to pay homage. "Uttered an inspired utterance" means that although those who come to the place of one resting in illness might feel dejected, these deities, seeing the Tathāgata's endurance of the pain, gave rise to an inspired utterance: "How wonderful is the great majesty of the Buddhas! Even while such sensations are occurring, there is not even a sign of distress; he rests with a body as motionless as a golden statue adorned on a glorious bed. Now the color of the Blessed One's face is exceedingly beautiful. His face shines like the full moon endowed with radiance, and like a newly blossomed lotus. Even the complexion of his body is now exceptionally clear, like well-polished gold."
76:
In the phrase "Nāgo vata," the word "vata" is an exhortative particle of nature. He is called "Nāga" (great elephant) in the sense of being powerful. "Nāgavatā" means by the state of being a Nāga. In the phrases such as "Sīho vata," he is called "Sīha" (lion) in the sense of being fearless. He is called "Ājānīya" (noble steed) because of his proficient and skilled conduct, or because he knows what is a cause and what is not. He is called "Nisabha" (peerless bull) in the sense of being incomparable. Indeed, the leader of a hundred cows is called "Usabha," the leader of a thousand is called "Vasabha," and the leader of a hundred thousand is called "Nisabha." The Blessed One, however, acknowledges the noble "Āsabha" (supreme) position in the sense of being peerless. It is in this sense of being peerless that he is called "Nisabha" here. He is called "Dhorayha" (burden-bearer) in the sense of carrying the burden. He is called "Danta" (tamed) because he is free from the poisons such as lust.

"Passa" (See) is an unspecified exhortation. "Samādhi" refers to the concentration associated with the fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala). "Suvimutta" (well-liberated) means well-liberated by the liberation of the fruit. A mind following lust is called "Abhinata" (inclined), and a mind following hatred is called "Apanata" (disinclined). Rejecting both, he said, "Na cābhinataṃ na cāpanataṃ" (neither inclined nor disinclined). "Na ca sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagataṃ" means it is not a practice where defilements are suppressed and restrained by effort; rather, it means a practice well-established in the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship because defilements have been completely cut off. "Atikkamitabba" means to be harassed or offended. "Adassana" means the absence of the eye of wisdom (aññāṇa). It is said, disparaging Devadatta, that only an extremely foolish person without the eye of wisdom would offend such a Blessed One.

"Pañcavedā" refers to those who can bear the five Vedas, including the Itihāsa. "Sataṃ samaṃ" means for a hundred years. "Tapassī" refers to those who practice depending on asceticism (tapa). If such brahmins practice for a hundred years, but their minds are not well-liberated from defilements, those of low nature cannot be ones who reach Nibbāna. There is also a variant reading "Hīnattharūpā," which means those who have declined from their welfare because of their low nature. "Taṇhādhipannā" means those who are overwhelmed and oppressed by craving. "Vatasilabaddhā" means those bound by vows and virtues such as the goat-vow and the dog-vow. "Lūkhaṃ tapaṃ" refers to harsh asceticism such as tormenting oneself with the five fires (pañcātapa) or sleeping on thorns. Now, the deity, wishing to state that the Dispensation (Sāsana) leads out of suffering, spoke the words beginning with "Na mānakāmassa." That has the same meaning as already stated. This concludes the commentary on the eighth sutta.

## 9. Paṭhamapajjunnadhītusutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "Pajjunnassa dhītā" refers to the daughter of the King of the rain-cloud deities named Pajjunna, of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā). "Abhivande" means...
77:
...I pay homage to your feet. "Cakkhumatā" refers to the Tathāgata who is endowed with the five eyes. In the phrase "He has fully realized the Dhamma," it means "Previously, I had only heard this from others." "Sāhaṃ dānī" means "That I, now." "Sakkhi jānāmi" means "I know directly" by way of penetration (paṭivedha). "Vigarahantā" means "criticizing," such as saying "It has inferior syllables, words, and phrases," or "It does not lead out of suffering." There are two types of Roruva hell: Dhūmaroruva and Jālaroruva. Among them, Dhūmaroruva is separate, while Jālaroruva is a name for the Avīci Great Hell itself. In that hell, beings cry out (rava) again and again in the blazing fire; therefore, it is called "Roruva." "Ghora" means terrible. "Endowed with patience and tranquility" means endowed with the patience of acceptance (gahaṇakhanti) after being pleased, and with the tranquility of lust, etc. The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10. Dutiyapajjunnadhītusutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, by the word "ca" in "Dhammañca," the Saṅgha should also be included; thus, she says she has come here paying homage to the Triple Gem. "Atthavatī" means beneficial. In the phrase "I would analyze the Dhamma spoken by that deity in many ways (pariyāya)," it is intended to show that this Dhamma of the Blessed One is of such a nature that it is suitable to be analyzed in many ways. "Lapayissāmi" means "I shall speak." "As much as I have learned with my mind" means "I will not speak the meaning of the Dhamma I have learned with my mind for the whole day, but will speak it in brief in just a moment, like squeezing a honeycomb." The rest is clear. The tenth sutta is finished.

## Satullapakāyikavagga, the Fourth.

## 5. Ādittavagga

## 1. Ādittasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Āditta Chapter, the words "By old age and death" are the head of the discourse. In reality, the world is indeed ablaze with the eleven fires, such as lust. "Dānena" means by the volition of giving. "The gift given is well-removed" means that just as goods removed from a fire are for the benefit of the householder, the volition of merit in giving is only for the benefit of the donor. Therefore, this was said. Thieves...
78:
"They carry away" means that thieves carry away wealth that has not been given, kings seize it, fire burns it, and it is lost in the places where it is kept. "By the end" (antena) means by death. "The body along with possessions" (sarīraṃ sapariggahaṃ) refers to the body and wealth that have not yet been destroyed by thieves and so on. "Goes to heaven" (saggamupeti) means being reborn in heaven like the Great King Vessantara and others. The explanation of the first sutta is finished.

## 2. Kiṃdada Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "giver of food" (annado) is said because even a very strong person cannot stand up if they do not eat for two or three meals; however, after eating, even a weak person becomes endowed with strength. Therefore, it is said, "The giver of food is the giver of strength." "Giver of clothing" (vatthado) is said because even a beautiful person looks ugly, contemptible, and unpleasant to look at if they have dirty clothes or no clothes; but when dressed in clothes, they shine like a son of the devas. Therefore, it is said, "The giver of clothing is the giver of beauty." "Giver of a vehicle" (yānado) refers to one who gives elephant vehicles and so on. Among those:

"An elephant vehicle is not suitable for a recluse, nor a horse vehicle, nor traveling by chariot. For a recluse who guards the aggregate of virtue, only this vehicle of sandals is suitable."

According to this, one who gives umbrellas, sandals, walking sticks, couches, and stools, as well as one who clears the path, makes ladders or stairways, builds bridges, or prepares boats—all these are indeed givers of vehicles. "Is a giver of happiness" (sukhado hoti) means they are called a giver of happiness because a vehicle brings happiness. "Giver of sight" (cakkhudo) means that since even those with eyes cannot see forms in the dark, a giver of a lamp is called a giver of sight; they may also attain the achievement of the divine eye like the Elder Anuruddha.

"Is a giver of everything" (sabbadado hoti) means they are a giver of all benefits such as strength. Even for one who returns after wandering for alms through two or three villages without receiving anything, when they bathe in a cool lotus pond, enter a shelter, lie on a couch for a moment, and then sit up, it is as if strength has been brought and infused into the body. For one wandering outside, the complexion (vaṇṇāyatana) of the body is scorched by wind and sun; but for one who enters a shelter, closes the door, and lies down for a moment, the disagreeable continuity subsides, the agreeable continuity (sabhāga-santati) enters, and it is as if the complexion has been brought and...
79:
...infused into the body. For one wandering outside, the complexion of the body is scorched by wind and sun. For one who enters a shelter, closes the door, and sleeps for a while, the disagreeable continuity is stilled and the agreeable continuity enters. It is as if the complexion has been brought and infused. For one wandering outside, dangers such as thorns piercing the feet, striking against stumps, snakes, scorpions, and lice, as well as the danger of thieves, arise. For one who enters a shelter, closes the door, and sleeps, all these dangers do not occur. For one who recites the Dhamma, the joy and happiness having the Dhamma as object arise. For one who attends to a meditation subject, the happiness associated with the stilling of defilements arises. Likewise, for one wandering outside, sweat is released and the eyes quiver. At the moment of entering a dwelling, it is as if one has descended into a well, and couches, stools, etc., are not visible. But for one who has sat for a moment, it is as if clarity of the eyes has been brought and infused, and door-leaves, windows, couches, stools, etc., become clear. Therefore, it was said: "And he is a giver of everything, who gives a shelter."

"And he is a giver of the deathless" (amatandado) means he gives the gift of Nibbāna, which is the cause of deathlessness, like one filling an alms-bowl with excellent food. "Who admonishes with the Dhamma" (yo dhammam anusāsati) means one who teaches the Dhamma, speaks the commentary, recites the Pali, answers questions that are asked, points out a meditation subject, or listens to the Dhamma; all these are called admonishing with the Dhamma. It should be understood that among all gifts, this gift of Dhamma is the supreme. This was also said by the Blessed One:
"The gift of Dhamma excels all gifts;
The taste of Dhamma excels all tastes;
The delight in Dhamma excels all delights;
The destruction of craving excels all suffering."
(Dhp. 354). The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Anna Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "they rejoice" (abhinandanti) means they desire. "Follows" (bhajati) means approaches; it follows behind like Citta the Householder, the Elder Sīvali, and others. "Therefore" (tasmā) means because in this world and the next, it follows only the giver of food; therefore [it is said]. The rest is clear. The third sutta is finished.

## 4. Ekamūla Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "one root" (ekamūlaṃ) means ignorance is the root of craving, and craving is the root of ignorance. In this sutta, however, craving is intended. "Two whirlpools" (dvirāvaṭṭā) means it turns by way of the two views of eternalism and annihilationism. That craving is "three stains" (timalā) because it has the three stains of lust and so on. Among those, delusion is the stain of that craving by way of the condition of conascence. The power of lust and so on is the stain of that craving by way of the condition of decisive support. The five cords of sensual pleasure are the places where that craving spreads. Because that craving spreads in those five cords of sensual pleasure, it is called "five-fold spreading" (pañcapattharā). That craving is also called the "ocean" in the sense of being impossible to fill. That ocean of craving...
80:
Delusion is the stain of that craving by way of the co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya); lust and hatred are the stains of that craving by way of the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). The five cords of sensual pleasure are the places where that craving spreads; because it spreads in those sensual pleasures, it is called 'pañcapattharā' (having the fivefold spreading of sensual pleasures). That craving is like the ocean in the sense of being insatiable. Because it revolves and turns back in the twelve internal and external sense bases (āyatana), it is called 'dvādasāvaṭṭā' (having twelve whirlpools). Because of the sense of having no standing ground, it is called 'pātāla' (the deep abyss). 'One root... the abyss, the sage crossed, ascended, transcended' means that the sage (isi/monk) has crossed, emerged from, and transcended the place called the abyss, which has no standing ground and has a single root, namely craving. The fourth sutta is finished.

## ၅။ အနောမသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the commentary on the fifth sutta, 'Anomanāma' means having a name that is not deficient, a name that is complete, because of being endowed with all virtues. 'Nipuṇatthadassī' means the Blessed One is called Nipuṇatthadassī because He sees subtle meanings such as the distinctions of the aggregates (khandha) and so on. 'Paññādada' means He is the giver of wisdom by way of teaching the practice (paṭipatti) of Samatha and Vipassanā for the attainment of supramundane wisdom. 'Kāmālaye asatta' means one who is not attached to the abode of the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Kamamāna' means the Blessed One proceeded by the Ariyan Path only at the Great Bodhi Tree; although He is not proceeding now, this is said in reference to the past. 'Mahesi' means He is called Mahesī because He seeks the great groups of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so on. The fifth sutta is finished.

## ၆။ အစ္ဆရာသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the commentary on the sixth sutta, regarding 'Accharāgaṇasaṃghuṭṭhaṃ', it is heard that: This son of a deva, having ordained in the Dispensation of the Teacher and fulfilling the duties and practices, upon reaching five vassa (years of monkhood), performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, mastered the two Mātikās by heart, learned the determination of monastic procedures (kammaviniccaya), took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of his choice, and lived a light and simple life, entering the forest. Even when the middle watch of the night (majjhimayāma), which was permitted by the Blessed One for sleep, arrived, he thought, 'I fear negligence,' and lifting his bed, he meditated on his subject day and night without taking food.

Then, sharp knife-like winds arose within that monk's belly and took his life. He passed away right at his post (while striving). Any monk who passes away while walking on the meditation path, or while standing leaning against a support post, or while sitting or lying down at the end of the meditation path with his robe on his head, or while preaching the Dhamma on an adorned Dhamma-seat in the midst of an assembly—all such monks are said to have died at their post.
81:
...is said to have passed away. Thus, this monk passed away while on the meditation path and, because he had only a slight decisive support (for liberation) and had not reached the destruction of taints (arahatta-phala), he took rebirth at the entrance of a great mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, like one waking up from sleep. At that very moment, a physical body three gāvutas in height, radiant like a golden pillar, appeared for that son of a deva.

When the thousand nymphs (accharā) within the mansion saw him, they surrounded him with musical instruments, saying, 'The lord of the mansion, the son of a deva, has arrived; let us delight him.' The son of a deva did not yet know he had passed away; still perceiving himself as a monk, he felt ashamed when he looked at the surrounding nymphs, as if seeing young women who had come to a monastery. Like a monk who observes the forest-dweller's practice (paṃsukūlika), he placed his thick upper cloth over his left shoulder, covering the shoulder's edge, lowered his faculties, and stood with his face cast down. Just by seeing the physical posture of that son of a deva, those goddesses knew, 'This is a monk-deity,' and said, 'Venerable son of a deva, this place is called the deva world; it is not a place for practicing monk-dharma, but a place for enjoying prosperity.' That son of a deva remained standing in the same way. The goddesses, thinking, 'This son of a deva does not yet realize,' began to play their musical instruments. Even when they played, the son of a deva remained standing without looking.

Then the nymphs placed a mirror that could reflect the whole body in front of him. Only when he saw his reflection did he realize he had passed away, and he became remorseful over the heavenly prosperity, thinking, 'I did not practice monk-dharma aspiring for this place; I practiced it aspiring for arahatta-phala, the supreme goal.' It was as if a warrior who descended to the battlefield thinking he would receive a golden cloth received only a handful of radishes. That son of a deva thought, 'This heavenly prosperity is easy to obtain, but the appearance of Buddhas is rare.' Without even entering the mansion, with his virtue intact, he came to the presence of the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha) surrounded by the host of nymphs, paid homage, and standing at a suitable place, spoke this verse.

In that verse, 'Accharāgaṇasaṃghuṭṭhaṃ' means resounding with the sounds of singing and music from the host of nymphs. 'Pisācagaṇasevitaṃ' is said by regarding that same host of nymphs as a group of ghosts (pisāca). The word 'Vanaṃ' refers to the Nandana Grove. This is because this son of a deva, with a mind inclined towards the Fixed Law (niyāma) and because of his own sense of gravity, did not wish to call the host of devas 'a host of devas' but called them 'a host of ghosts.' He did not call the Nandana Grove 'Nandana' (Delightful) but called it 'Mohana' (Deluding).
82:
(The deity) asked: "How will there be an exit? How will there be a crossing? O Blessed One, please teach me the Insight (Vipassanā) which is the proximate cause for Arahantship."

Then the Blessed One reflected: "This deity has the intention of greatly thinning out the defilements; what is the reason for this?" Upon reflecting, He knew that the deity had been a monk in His own dispensation. He thought: "This deity, having exerted great effort, passed away and was reborn in the celestial realm. Even until today, his individual existence (attabhāva) has come along with unbroken virtue (sīla) right from his walking meditation path (caṅkama)."

The Buddhas, like a painter who first cleans and smooths a wall, teach the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) to a disciple who has not yet practiced Insight, who is just a beginner, and who has not yet performed the preliminary tasks, saying: "First, purify your virtue; develop concentration; make your knowledge of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-paññā) straight." However, to a practitioner who is diligent and follows the Buddha's instructions, they teach only the subtle and refined Insight into Emptiness (suññatā-vipassanā), which is the proximate cause for the Path of Arahantship. This deity is also a practitioner with unbroken virtue, and since only one Path remains for him to reach, the Buddha, wishing to teach Insight into Emptiness, spoke the verse beginning with "Ujuko nāma."

In that verse, "Ujuko" (Straight) refers to the Eightfold Path, which is called the "straight path" because it is free from physical crookedness and so on. "Abhayā nāma sā disā" (That direction is called fearless) is said in reference to Nibbāna. Because there is no danger of any kind in that Nibbāna, or because there is no danger for one who has reached that Nibbāna, it is called the "fearless place." "Ratho akūjano" (The silent chariot) refers to the Eightfold Path itself. Just as an ordinary chariot creaks and rattles if the axle is not greased or if too many people ride it, the Noble Path is not like that. Even if eighty-four thousand beings ride it at once, it does not creak or rattle. Therefore, it is called the "silent chariot." "Dhammacakkehi saṃyutto" (Equipped with Dhamma-wheels) means it is equipped with the Dhamma-wheels known as physical and mental energy (viriya).

Here, by mentioning "Hiri" (Shame), "Ottappa" (Fear of wrongdoing) is also included. "Tassa apālambo" (Its leaning board) means that just as an external chariot has a wooden leaning board (handrail) to prevent the soldiers standing in the chariot from falling, so too, in this Path-chariot, Hiri and Ottappa, which arise based on internal and external factors, are the leaning boards. "Satissa parivāraṇaṃ" (Mindfulness is its enclosure) means that just as a chariot is enclosed with lion skins and so on, in this Path-chariot, the associated mindfulness (sati) is the enclosure. "Dhammaṃ" refers to...
83:
...the Supramundane Path (Lokuttara-magga). "Sammādiṭṭhipurejavo" (Having Right View as its precursor) means that Insight Right View (Vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi) is the precursor or the one that goes before that Path; thus it is "having Right View as its precursor." Just as the king's attendants first clear the road by removing the blind, the crippled, and so on, and only then does the king come out, in the same way, after Insight Right View has cleared the defilements in the aggregates (khandhas) and so on by way of impermanence and so forth, the Path Right View arises later, fully understanding the objects within the domain of Insight. Therefore, it was said: "I call the Dhamma the charioteer, which has Right View as its precursor."

Thus, the Blessed One concluded the discourse and at the end revealed the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the discourse, the deity was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). For example, when a king is eating and lifts a morsel of food proportionate to his own mouth, a young son sitting on his lap takes a small portion from that morsel proportionate to his own mouth and eats it. In the same way, even though the Blessed One teaches the discourse with Arahantship as the pinnacle, beings attain the Fruit of Stream-entry and so on according to their own potential (upanissaya). This deity also, having attained the Fruit of Stream-entry, honored the Blessed One with perfumes and so on, and then departed. The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Vanaropa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, (the deity) asked: "Who are those established in Dhamma? Who are those endowed with virtue?" The Blessed One, wishing to reveal this question by way of permanent objects (meritorious deeds of a lasting nature), spoke the verse beginning with "Ārāmaropā." In that verse, "Ārāmaropā" refers to those who plant flower gardens and fruit orchards. "Vanaropā" refers to those who enclose a boundary in a naturally grown forest and build shrines, Bodhi trees, walkways, pavilions, huts, caves, night-quarters, and day-quarters; those who plant and donate shade-giving trees are also called "Vanaropā" (forest planters). "Setukārakā" refers to those who build bridges in uneven places and those who provide boats on the water. "Papā" refers to a drinking water station. "Udapāna" refers to any kind of pond, well, and so on. "Upassaya" refers to a shelter or dwelling. There is also a variant reading "Upāsaya."

"Merit always increases" does not mean it increases for one who is thinking unwholesome thoughts or for one who is sleeping. Rather, whenever one reflects on the merit one has performed, it increases for that person. With reference to this meaning, it was said: "Merit always increases." "Dhammaṭṭhā sīlasampannā" means they are called "established in Dhamma and endowed with virtue" because they stand in that Dhamma and are endowed with that virtue. Or...
84:
Alternatively, for those who perform such meritorious deeds, the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) are fulfilled; because they are established in those wholesome qualities, they are called 'Dhammaṭṭha' (established in Dhamma). Because they are endowed with that very virtue, they are called 'Sīlasampanna' (endowed with virtue). The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Jetavanasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, the young deva Anāthapiṇḍika came to praise the virtues of the Jetavana Monastery and the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, and spoke the words beginning with "Idaṃ hi taṃ jetavanaṃ". "Isisaṅghanisevitaṃ" means frequented by the assembly of monks.

After praising the virtues of the Jetavana Monastery with the first verse, he now speaks the words beginning with "Kammaṃ vijjā" to describe the virtues of the Noble Path. Therein, "kamma" refers to the volition of the path (maggacetanā). "Vijjā" refers to the wisdom of the path (maggapaññā). "Dhamma" refers to the qualities associated with concentration (samādhipakkhikā dhammā). "Sīlaṃ jีvitamuttamaṃ" shows that the life (right livelihood) of one established in virtue is supreme. Alternatively, "vijjā" refers to right view and right intention. "Dhamma" refers to right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. "Sīla" refers to right speech, right action, and right livelihood. "Jīvitamuttamaṃ" means that the life of one established in this virtue is supreme. By this Eightfold Path, beings are purified.

"Tasmā" means because one can be purified only by the path, and not by lineage or wealth. "Yoniso vicine dhammaṃ" means one should investigate the factors of concentration with wise means. Thus, one is purified in that Noble Path. Alternatively, "yoniso vicine dhammaṃ" means one should insightfully investigate the five aggregates with appropriate means. Thus, one is purified in those Four Noble Truths.

Now, wishing to praise the virtues of the Elder Sāriputta, he speaks the words beginning with "Sāriputtova". Therein, "Sāriputtova" is an emphatic statement, meaning that Sāriputta alone is superior by way of these qualities such as wisdom. "Upasamena" means by the calming of defilements. "Pāraṃ gato" means he has reached Nibbāna. It means that any monk who has reached Nibbāna would at most be equal to him; there is no one superior to the Elder. The remaining words are clear. The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Maccharisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "maccharino" refers to those possessed of stinginess (macchariya). For instance, some people, even when a monk stretches out his hand at their own place of residence, do not even pay respect, but when they go elsewhere...
85:
...entering a monastery, they pay respect respectfully and speak pleasant words of welcome: "Venerable sir, please do not come to our place of residence; this area is well-provided (for alms), and we are capable of attending to the noble ones with gruel, rice, and so on." The monks, thinking "This lay follower is faithful," accept the support of gruel, rice, and so on. Later, an elder goes to that donor's village for alms. Seeing him, the donor either goes by another way or enters the house. Even if they meet face-to-face, he pays respect with joined palms and says, "Please give alms to the noble one; I am going on a certain business," and departs. Even after wandering through the whole village, the elder leaves the village with only an empty bowl. This is called "soft stinginess" (mudu-macchariya). One possessed of such stinginess appears like a donor even though he is not.

In this context, however, "hard stinginess" (thadda-macchariya) is intended. One possessed of such stinginess, when told "The elders are standing" as monks enter for alms, says things like "Are my feet aching?" and stands stiffly like a stone pillar or a tree stump, not even performing the proper duties. "Kadariya" is a synonym for the word "maccharino". Soft stinginess is called "macchariya", while hard stinginess is called "kadariya". "Paribhāsaka" (revilers) are those who, seeing monks standing at the door of the house, threaten them with words like "Have you come after plowing, sowing, or harvesting? We ourselves do not get enough; where would we get anything for you? Get out quickly!" "Antarāyakara" (obstructors) are those who cause obstacles: obstacles to the donor's heavenly rebirth, obstacles to the recipients' gain, and destruction to themselves.

"Samparāya" means the future world. "Rati" means delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Khiḍဍā" means the three kinds of play, such as physical play. "Diṭṭhe dhamme sa vipāko" refers to the result in the present existence of that rebirth, such as obtaining clothes and such with difficulty. "Samparāye ca duggati" means reaching a miserable destination in the future world, as stated: "They arise in the realm of Yama."

"Vadaññū" (generous) refers to those who, even though monks standing at the door are silent, understand the meaning as if they are saying "Please give alms." Then, reflecting "We cook, but these monks do not; if they do not receive when they come to where cooking is done, where will they get it?", they share and give the gifts; these are called "vadaññū". "Prakāsanti" means they shine with the radiance of their celestial mansions. "Parasambhatesu" means in things accumulated by others. "Samparāye ca suggati" means reaching a happy destination in the future world, as stated: "These are the heavens." Alternatively, it means that those who perform good or bad deeds, after passing away from that hell or heaven, again experience miserable or happy destinations in the future world. This is the end of the commentary on the ninth sutta. In the tenth sutta, "upapannāse" means having reached by the power of rebirth.
86:
"Saggā" means the happy destination (sugati) in the hereafter. Alternatively, it means that both of them, after passing away from there, will only experience the miserable and happy destinations in the next life. The commentary on the ninth sutta ends.

## 10. Ghaṭīkārasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "upappannāse" refers to those who have arrived by way of rebirth. "Vimuttā" refers to those who are liberated from defilements through the liberation of the fruition of Arahantship immediately after taking rebirth in the Aviha Brahma realm. "Mānusaṃ dehaṃ" here refers only to the five lower fetters (orambhāgiyasaṃyojana). "Dibbayogaṃ" refers to the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojana). "Upaccaguṃ" means they have transcended. "Upaka" and so forth are the names of those elders (Theras). "Kusalī bhāsasī tesaṃ" means because the word "kusala" (virtue/skill) exists in this person, he is called "kusalī." It means, "O deva, you speak of the faultless virtues of those elders, you praise them, you honor them; you are indeed wise." "Taṃ te dhammaṃ idhaññāya" means those elders, having known that Dhamma here in your Dispensation (Sāsana). "Gambhīraṃ" means having a profound meaning. "Brahmacārī nirāmiso" means a celibate free from worldly lures is an Anāgāmī (Non-returner); it means he had become an Anāgāmī. "Ahu" means he was or became. "Sagāmeyyo" means a dweller in the same village. The concluding verse was placed by the Elders who conducted the Recitation (Saṅgītikāras). The commentary on the tenth sutta ends.

## The Fifth: Ādittavagga.
## 6. Jarāvagga
## 1. Jarāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Jarāvagga, "sādhu" means excellent and beautiful.
