By the words "sīlaṃ yāva jarā" (virtue until old age), this point is shown: ornaments such as pearls, gems, and red garments are beautiful only in youth. If one wears such ornaments in old age, one becomes subject to reproach, "This person still longs for childhood even today; he must be mad." Virtue is not like that. Virtue is beautiful at all times. There is no one to reproach a person who guards virtue in youth, saying, "What is the use of virtue to him?" It is the same in middle age and old age.
87:
"Saddhā sādhu patiṭṭhitā" means that faith which has arrived through the Path and is firmly rooted in the mental continuum so that others cannot shake it—like that of Hatthaka Āḷavaka and Citta the Householder—is excellent. In the phrase "paññā narānaṃ ratanaṃ" (wisdom is the treasure of men), "treasure" (ratana) should be understood through meanings such as being revered.

Regarding this matter, it is said: If a revered thing is called a treasure, then the Blessed One, the Lion of Men, is indeed the most revered. Those who are revered in the world—kings, wise men, the Four Great Kings, Sakka, Suyāma, Mahābrahmā, and so forth—all approach the Blessed One as their refuge and show him reverence. If a thing that produces delight is called a treasure, then the Blessed One, the Lion of Men, is indeed the one who brings joy and produces delight. Those who practice according to the words of the Blessed One delight greatly in the happiness of the joy of meditation (jhāna). If an incomparable thing is called a treasure, then the Blessed One, the Lion of Men, is indeed incomparable. Since he has reached the perfection of virtues, it is impossible to measure him by those virtues. If a thing that is rare to obtain is called a treasure, then the Blessed One, the Lion of Men, is indeed rare to find. If a thing worthy of use by noble beings is called a treasure, then the Blessed One is indeed noble through virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

In this context, however, wisdom is called a "treasure" (ratana) because of the difficulty of its arising. "Puñña" refers to meritorious intention (puññacetanā). Since that meritorious intention is a mental phenomenon (nāma), others cannot take it away. The commentary on the first sutta ends.

## 2. Ajarasāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "ajarasā" means by not aging, by not perishing. Virtue is excellent only when it is not broken. Even teachers and preceptors (upajjhāya) do not support one whose virtue is broken. Such a person is only to be expelled wherever he goes. The commentary on the second sutta ends.

## 3. Mittasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "sattho" means a traveling companion, whether a pedestrian merchant or a caravan merchant. "Mittaṃ" (friend) refers to one who is beloved because they carry one to safety by a litter or another vehicle when illness arises. "Sake ghare" means in one's own home. When such an illness occurs, children, wives, and others are repulsed. A mother, however, regards even filth as if it were sandalwood. Therefore, that mother is the friend in one's own home. "Sahāyo atthajātassa" refers to one who carries out or accomplishes a task for someone who has a business or matter that has arisen. Such a person is a true friend and companion because of their state of acting together in matters. Companions such as drinking buddies, however, are not true friends. "Samparāyikaṃ" refers to a friend who brings welfare in the afterlife. The commentary on the third sutta ends.
88:
## 4. Vatthusutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "Sons are the support (vatthu)" means that because they tend to and care for their parents in old age, sons are the support and reliance. "Supreme" means that because she is the appropriate person to be told even secrets that should not be told to others, the wife is called the supreme friend. The commentary on the fourth sutta ends.

## 5-7. Paṭhamajanasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "runs about" means running here and there by going to the other side of the ocean and so forth. The commentary on the fifth sutta ends.

In the sixth sutta, "suffering" refers to the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha). The commentary on the sixth sutta ends.

In the seventh sutta, "refuge" (parāyaṇa) means the accomplishment and reliance. The commentary on the seventh sutta ends.

## 8. Uppathasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, "Lust is the wrong path" means it is a non-path, a wrong journey for one going to a happy destination (sugati) and Nibbāna. "The passing of night and day" means being consumed by or during nights and days. "Woman is an impurity" means that while other external impurities can be washed and cleaned with ash, soap, and so forth, one who is corrupted and destroyed by the impurity of women cannot be made pure; thus, woman is called "impurity." "Herein" means all beings are attached to this woman. "Asceticism (tapa)" is the name for sense restraint (indriya-saṃvara), dhutaṅga qualities, energy (vīriya), and difficult practices (dukkarakārikā). However, here, excluding difficult practices, all practices that burn away defilements (kilesa) should be taken. "Brahmacariya" means refraining from sexual intercourse. The commentary on the eighth sutta ends.

## 9. Dutiyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "In what does one delight?" is a question asking in which Dhamma one delights. "Companion (dutiyā)" means the second companion for one going to a happy destination and Nibbāna. "Wisdom rules this person" means wisdom instructs and advises that person, saying, "Do this, do not do that." The commentary on the ninth sutta ends.

## 10. Kavisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "Metre is the source" means metres such as Gāyattī are the source (nidāna) of verses (gāthā). This is because one who begins to compose a verse first considers and strives, thinking, "With what kind of metre shall it be?"
89:
He begins [the verse]. "Vyañjana" means production (janana). For a syllable (akkara) produces a word (pada), a word produces a verse (gāthā), and a verse clarifies the meaning (attha). 

"Nāmasannissitā" means depending on designations (nāma-paññatti) such as "ocean" and so on. For a teacher who begins to compose a verse starts by depending on some name, such as the ocean or the earth. 

"Āsaya" means a support (patiṭṭhā). Verses arise from a poet (kavi). That poet is the support of those verses. 

The tenth sutta [explanation] is finished.

## The Sixth Chapter: Jarā Vagga.

## 7. Addha Vagga

## 1. Nāma Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Addha Vagga, "nāmaṃ sabbaṃ addhabhavi" means the name overwhelms and dominates everything; it follows along. There is no being or formation (saṅkhāra) that is free from a name, whether it be a spontaneous (opapātika) name or a designated (kittima) name. Even for a tree or a stone where people do not know "this is its name," the name "nameless" (anāmaka) itself becomes its name. 

The first sutta [explanation] is finished.

## 2-3. Citta Sutta etc. Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "sabbeva vasamanvagū" means those things that follow the will of the mind; this is an exhaustive inclusion of only those things. 

The second sutta [explanation] is finished. 

In the third sutta, the method is the same. 

The third sutta [explanation] is finished.

## 4-5. Saṃyojana Sutta etc. Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "kiṃ su saṃyojano" asks: what is the fetter (saṃyojana), what is the bond (bandhana)? 

"Vicāraṇaṃ" refers to the feet (pāda) which are the means of going. The singular is used in place of the plural. "Vitakkassa vicāraṇaṃ" means that thoughts (vitakka) are the feet of that [verse]. 

The fourth sutta [explanation] is finished. 

In the fifth sutta, the method is the same. 

The fifth sutta [explanation] is finished.

## 6. Attahata Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "kenassubbhāhato" means by what is one struck down? The syllable "su" is merely a particle (nipāta). 

"Icchādhūpāyito" means burnt (āditta) by desire (icchā). 

The sixth sutta [explanation] is finished.
90:
## 7-9. Uḍḍitasuttādivaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "taṇhāya uḍḍito" means being entrapped (or hung up) by craving. Just as one might bind the eye-sensitivity with the rope of craving and hang it on a wall-peg (wooden post) of forms, or hang the ear-sensitivity, etc., on sounds, etc., so too the world is entrapped by craving.

"Maccunā pihito" means that although the kamma performed in the previous life and the current life are separated by only a single thought-moment, beings do not realize that kamma because they are oppressed as if by a great mountain of powerful death-bed pains; thus it is said, "The world is obstructed by death."

The seventh sutta ends.

In the eighth sutta, the deity asks the same question but in a reversed order (from top to bottom). 

The eighth sutta ends.

In the ninth sutta, everything is clear.

The ninth sutta ends.

## 10. Lokasuttavaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "In what is the world arisen?" is a question asking what must arise for the world to arise. "In six" means it is said that the world arises when the six internal sense bases (ajjhattikāyatana), such as the eye-base, arise. "Makes in six" means making intimacy or connection in those very six internal bases. "Clinging to" means it proceeds by depending on and clinging to those very internal bases. "Is afflicted" means the world is afflicted and oppressed in those very six internal bases.

Thus, although this question is presented by way of the internal bases, it should be understood by way of both internal and external bases. When the six internal bases arise, this world is said to arise; it makes intimacy in the six external bases; and depending on the six internal bases, it is afflicted in the six external bases.

The tenth sutta ends.

## Addhavaggo sattamo.

## 8. Chetvāvaggo

## 1. Chetvāsuttavaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Chetvā Vagga, "chetvā" means having killed. "Sleeps happily" means one sleeps happily because one is not burnt by the fever of anger. "Does not sorrow" means one does not sorrow because grief is vanished through the destruction of anger. "Poisonous root" means...
91:
It is called dukkhavipāka because it has suffering as its result. Madhuragga means that when one gets angry in return to an angry person, curses in return to one who curses, or strikes back at one who strikes, a kind of pleasure arises; referring to that pleasure, it is called madhuragga (sweet at the end). In this context, 'end' (pariyosāna) is meant by agga. Ariyas refers to the Noble Ones, such as the Buddha and others. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Rathasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, it is called paññāṇa because it is clearly known by this mark. The mark of a chariot is the banner; because in a great battlefield, seeing the banner from afar, the chariot becomes well-known as "This is the chariot of such-and-such a king." Therefore, it is said, "The banner is the mark of the chariot." Fire is also clearly known from afar by smoke. A kingdom is also made known by its king, such as the Coḷa kingdom or the Paṇḍu kingdom. Even the daughter of a Universal Monarch, being a woman, becomes known only upon reaching her husband as "This is the wife of such-and-such a person." Therefore, it is said, "Smoke is the mark of fire," and so on. The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Vittasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, regarding "Faith is wealth here in this world," a person of faith can obtain wealth such as pearls and rubies because of faith; they can also attain the three types of family perfection (such as royalty), the six sensual heavens, and the nine Brahma worlds, and finally attain the vision of the noble and deathless Nibbāna. Therefore, the wealth of faith is indeed the most excellent among all wealth like pearls and rubies. Dhamma refers to the ten wholesome courses of action (kusala-kammapatha). "Brings happiness" means it brings all types of happiness, both mundane (with taints) and supramundane (without taints), which are free from defilement. "Sweeter" means that in the world, Truth (Sacca) alone is sweeter and more excellent than all tastes such as salty or sour. Those established in Truth can even turn back a river with a swift current, subdue poison, ward off fire, and cause rain to fall; therefore, that Truth is said to be sweeter than all tastes. "They say the life of one living by wisdom is best" means a layperson who, established in the five precepts, gives offerings such as food-by-tickets (salāka-bhatta) and lives by wisdom; or a monk who, reflecting on the requisites obtained according to the Dhamma as "I use this for this purpose," practices meditation, develops insight, and lives by wisdom through the attainment of the Noble Fruits—such a person living by wisdom is said to live the most excellent life. The third sutta is finished.
92:
## 4. Vuṭṭhisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'bījaṃ' (seed) means that among things that emerge from the ground, the seven kinds of grain seeds are the most excellent. When those grain seeds emerge, the countryside becomes safe and food is abundant. 'Nipatataṃ' (of those that fall) means that among things that fall down, the falling of rain is the most excellent. When there is rainfall, various crops flourish, and the countrysides become prosperous, safe, and food is easily obtained. 'Pavajamanānaṃ' (of those that move) means that among creatures that travel on foot, cows are the most excellent. Depending on those cows, beings enjoy the five products of the cow (pañca-gorasa) and live happily. 'Pavadataṃ' (of those that speak) means that among those who speak in the midst of royal assemblies and so on, a son is the best. This is because such a son does not speak words that would bring harm to his parents.

Regarding the verse 'Knowledge is the best of things that arise,' it should be understood that: hearing the question asked first, a certain goddess standing nearby said, 'O goddess, why do you ask this question to the One of Ten Powers (the Buddha)? I will tell you,' and she answered the question according to her own view. Then the other goddess said, 'O goddess, you speak with a mouth that is very harsh and destructive of virtues; I am asking the Blessed Buddha. Why do you speak to me?' Rebuking her, she asked that same question again to the One of Ten Powers. Then the Teacher, answering her, spoke the verse beginning with 'Knowledge is the best of things that arise.' In that verse, 'vijjā' (knowledge) refers to the wisdom associated with the four Paths. When that Path-wisdom arises, it utterly destroys all unwholesome states. Therefore, it is said, 'Knowledge is the best of things that arise.' 'Avijjā' (ignorance) refers to the great ignorance which is the root of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra). That ignorance is the foremost among things that sink or fall down. 'Pavajamanānaṃ' means that among creatures that travel on foot, the Noble Saṅgha, who is like an incomparable field of merit, is the best. Beings who see that Noble Saṅgha in various places and have a confident heart reach well-being. 'Buddha' means that whether it be a son who speaks for the benefit of parents or anyone else, among all who speak, the Buddha is the most excellent. This is because, based on the Buddha's teaching of the Dhamma, many hundreds of thousands of beings are liberated from their bonds. The explanation of the fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Bhītāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'Why are they afraid?' is a question asking what they are afraid of. 'Maggo canekāyatanappavutto' refers to the Path taught through many reasons by way of the thirty-eight meditation objects. It means: this being so, why does this mass of beings, being afraid, take up the sixty-two types of wrong views? 'Bhūripaññā' refers to one with great wisdom or extensive wisdom. 'One should not fear the next world' means not being afraid when going from this world to the next world. 'Paṇidhāya' means having set aside (discarding).
93:
*Bahunnapānaṃ gharamāvasanto* means living in a house with plenty of food and drink, like the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and others. *Saṃvibhāgī* refers to one who has the habit of eating only after sharing with others, even dividing food taken with the fingers by using the fingernails to give to another. The meaning of the word *vadaññū* is the same as previously mentioned.

Now, the factors of the verse should be extracted and shown. By the word *vācā*, the four types of verbal good conduct are taken. By the word *manasā*, the three types of mental good conduct are taken. By the word *kāyena*, the three types of bodily good conduct are taken. Thus, these ten wholesome courses of action (*kusalakamma-patha*) are called the factors of preliminary purity. By the Pali *bahunnapānaṃ gharamāvasanto*, the requisites of sacrifice are taken. *Saddho* is one factor, *mudu* is one, *saṃvibhāgī* is one, and *vadaññū* is one. Thus, referring to these four factors, it is said, 'established in these four qualities'.

There is also another method (*pariyāya*). The three starting with *vācā* are factors. By the word *bahunnapānaṃ*, only the requisites of sacrifice are taken. *Saddho*, *mudu*, *saṃvibhāgī*, and *vadaññū* constitute a single factor. There is also another dyad method (*duka-naya*). *Vācaṃ manañca* is one factor; *kāyena pāpāni akubbamāno bahunnapānaṃ gharamāvasanto* is one factor; *saddho mudu* is one factor; *saṃvibhāgī vadaññū* is one factor. Thus, one who is established in these four virtues enumerated by the aforementioned method is called one established in the Dhamma. Such a person does not fear when going from this life to the next world. The fifth sutta ends.

## 6. Najīrati Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, *nāmagottaṃ na jīrati* means that because the names and lineages of past Buddhas are still heard today, they are said not to decay (not to vanish). Ancient teachers, however, say that while they may not be prominent as time passes, their nature is such that they do not actually decay or perish. *Ālasya* means laziness. Due to that laziness, one who is standing remains just standing, and one who is sitting remains just sitting; even when oil overflows, they cannot remain steady (content). *Pamāda* means negligence due to sleep or defilements. *Anuṭṭhāna* means the lack of effort to perform work when it is time for action. *Asaṃyama* means the lack of moral restraint, having loose conduct. *Niddā* means excessive sleepiness. Because of that excessive sleepiness, one dozes while walking, standing, or sitting, let alone when lying down. *Tandī* means temporary laziness arising from extreme hunger, etc. *Te chidde* refers to those six holes or openings mentioned.
94:
*Sabbaso* means in every way. The word *taṃ* is merely a particle (*nipāta*). *Vivajjaye* means one should avoid or abandon. The sixth sutta (ends).

## 7. Issariya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, *satthamalaṃ* refers to a weapon covered in rust. 'Whom do they prevent from taking?' is a question asking what kind of person is prevented. *Vasa* means sovereignty or the exercise of authority. *Itthī* is said to be 'the best of goods, the excellent good' because she is a treasure not to be abandoned. Alternatively, it is said 'woman is the best of goods' because all Bodhisattas and Universal Monarchs are born only in a mother's womb.

*Kodho satthamalaṃ* means anger is like a rusty weapon, or it is called *satthamala* because it is the stain on the weapon of wisdom. *Abbudam* means the cause of destruction. In the world, thieves are destroyers. *Haranto* means a monk who goes away after receiving alms-food (*salāka-bhatta*), etc., is one who is loved. This is because people have already relinquished those offerings at the time of preparation, so they love the monk who accepts those gifts. If he does not accept, they may feel uneasy, fearing a loss of merit. The seventh sutta (ends).

## 8. Kāma Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, *attānaṃ na dade* means one should not give oneself to another as a slave (this is said with the exception of all Bodhisattas). *Na pariccaje* means one should not abandon oneself to lions, tigers, etc. (this is said with the exception of all Bodhisattas). *Kalyāṇaṃ* means gentle and soft speech; *pāpikaṃ* means harsh speech. The eighth sutta (ends).

## 9. Pātheyya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, *saddhā bandhati pātheyyaṃ* is said because one gives gifts, guards morality, and performs the Uposatha observance after generating faith. *Sirī* means sovereignty. *Āsayo* means a dwelling place. If there is the glory of sovereignty, wealth comes automatically from both land and water. Therefore, this is said. *Parikassatī* means it pulls or drags. The ninth sutta (ends).

## 10. Pajjota Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, *pajjoto* means being like a lamp. *Jāgaro* means being like an awakened Brahmin (an Arahant). *Gāvo kamme sajīvānaṃ* means for those who live by work, cattle together with the work...
95:
For those who make a living, oxen are indeed the work-mates and work-companions in their labor. Along with the herds of oxen, tasks such as plowing are accomplished. "Sītassa iriyāpatho" means that for the assembly of beings who live depending on that food, the means of livelihood and existence is the ploughshare. "Sītaṃ" refers to the ploughshare. It means that if a person does not plow the field even a little with ploughshares, how can that person live? The tenth sutta is finished.

## 11. Araṇasuttavaṇṇanā
In the eleventh sutta, the Araṇa Sutta, "araṇā" refers to those who are free from defilements. "Vusitaṃ" refers to having the noble practice of the Ariyan Path that has been lived. "Bhojissiyaṃ" refers to the state of not being a slave to others. "Samaṇā" refers to the Arahants whose taints are exhausted. These Arahants are truly called "araṇa" (free from defilements). "Vusitaṃ na nassati" means that the practice of the Ariyan Path of those Arahants does not perish. "Parijānanti" means that starting from the stage of a virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana), the trainees (sekhas) fully understand through mundane and supramundane full understanding (pariññā). "Bhojissiyaṃ" refers to the state of being forever free (not a slave), which belongs only to the Arahants whose taints are exhausted. "Vandanti" means that from the day of ordination, parents and others pay homage to them. "Patiṭṭhitaṃ" means being established in virtue (sīla). "Samaṇīdha" refers to an ascetic (an Arahant) in this Dispensation. "Jātihīnaṃ" refers to one who has gone forth even if they are from a low caste like the Caṇḍālas. "Khattiyā" means that not only do kings pay homage, but even the devas pay homage to an ascetic who is endowed with virtue. The eleventh sutta is finished.

## The Eighth Chapter: Chetvā.
## Thus ends the Commentary on the Devatā Saṃyutta
## in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

## 2. Devaputtasaṃyutta
## 1. Pathamavagga
## 1. Commentary on the First Kassapa Sutta
In the first sutta of the Devaputtasaṃyutta, "devaputta" refers to males born in the laps of deities, who are called sons of gods (devaputta), while females are called daughters of gods (devadhītara). A deity who is not well-known by name is called "a certain deity" (aññatarā devatā), whereas a well-known deity is called "a son of a god named so-and-so." Therefore, while "a certain deity" was used below (in the Devatā Saṃyutta), "son of a god" (devaputta) is used here (in the Devaputtasaṃyutta). "Anusāsanti" refers to the instruction. It is said that this son of a god heard the "Description of a Monk" (Bhikkhuniddesa) in the Jhānavibhaṅga—"A monk by designation, a monk by claim"—while the Blessed One was staying in the Tāvatiṃsā heaven during the seventh rainy season after his enlightenment, having performed the Twin Miracle, and was teaching the Abhidhamma. However, he did not hear the advice and instruction given to monks such as: "Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend in this way, do not attend in that way; abandon this, attain and dwell in that." Referring to that instruction, he said: "The Blessed One has declared the monk, but not the instruction for the monk."

"Tena hi" means "Because you say that I have not declared the instruction for the monk." "Taññevettha paṭibhātu" means "Let the declaration of that instruction occur to you alone; let it be established in you." In truth, the Blessed One does not place the burden of answering a question on anyone who wishes to answer but cannot do so in comparison with the Knowledge of Omniscience, or on one who can answer but has no desire to do so, or on one who neither desires to answer nor is able to. However, this son of a god, Kassapa, both desired to answer and was able to do so. Therefore, wishing to give the burden to him alone, the Blessed One spoke thus. That son of a god then answered the question.

In that verse, "subhāsitassa sikkhetha" means one should learn well-spoken words; one should learn only the four types of right speech (vacīsucarita) based on the Four Noble Truths, the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu), and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma). "Samaṇūပါသနဿ စ" means the service of ascetics...
97:
"Samaṇūpāsana" refers to the thirty-eight subjects of meditation; the meaning is that one should learn and develop those meditation subjects. Alternatively, attending to learned monks is also called "samaṇūpāsana." One should learn to increase wisdom by attending to those monks and asking questions such as, "Venerable sir, what is wholesome?" and so forth. The phrase "cittavūpamasassa ca" means one should learn the tranquility of the mind through the power of the eight attainments (samāpatti). Thus, the deity spoke of the three trainings (sikkhā). The first phrase speaks of the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the second phrase speaks of the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā), and "cittavūpamasassa" speaks of the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā). In this way, the entire Dispensation (Sāsana) is revealed by this verse. The first sutta ends.

## 2. Dutiyakassapasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "jhāyī" refers to one who habitually meditates with the two jhānas. "Vimuttacitto" refers to a mind liberated from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by the temporary liberation (tadaṅga-vimutti) obtained through the power of meditation practice. "Hadayassānuppattiṃ" refers to the fruit of Arahantship. "Lokassa" refers to the arising and passing away of the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka). "Anissito" means one who does not rely on craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi), or one who is independent of craving and views. "Tadānisaṃso" means one who has the fruit of Arahantship as the benefit. The meaning is: a monk who has the fruit of Arahantship as his benefit should be a meditator with the two jhānas while aspiring for Arahantship; he should have a mind well-liberated from defilements, and knowing the arising and passing away of the world, he should be independent of craving and views. In this Dispensation, the Dhamma of learning (pariyatti-dhamma) is the preliminary stage of practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā). The second sutta ends.

## 3-4. Māghasutta-vaṇṇanā and Others
In the third sutta, "Māgha" is the name of Sakka, the king of devas. He is called "Vatrabhu" because he surpassed others through his own conduct and attained sovereignty over the devas, or because he conquered the asura named Vatra. The third sutta ends.

The fourth sutta has the same meaning as already stated. The fourth sutta ends.

## 5. Dāmalisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "na tenāsīsate bhavanti" means that for that reason, they do not long for any existence. This deity is named Āyatapaggaha; (he believes) there is no end to the task of an Arahant. An Arahant should initially exert effort to attain the fruit of Arahantship. Even after attaining the fruit of Arahantship, he should not remain silent, thinking "I have reached the fruit of Arahantship," but should resolve to continue making firm effort and striving just as before reaching the fruit; thus he spoke the words "na tenāsīsate bhavanti." Then the Blessed One thought, "This deity, without speaking of the completion of the Arahant's task, speaks as if my Dispensation is not leading out of suffering (niyyānika). I shall declare the completion of the task to him," and spoke the verse beginning with "natthi kiccaṃ." It is said that this verse is distinct and unmixed throughout the three Pitakas. The Blessed One never showed any fault in effort in other discourses. However, here, to restrain this deity, he said that in the earlier period, for the sake of the destruction of taints...
98:
...after reaching the fruit of Arahantship, let him not remain silent thinking "I have reached Arahantship," but let him continue to make firm effort and strive just as before. 

Then the Blessed One thought, "This deity, without speaking of the completion of the Arahant's task, speaks as if my Dispensation is not leading out of suffering. I shall declare the completion of the task to him," and spoke the verse beginning with "natthi kiccaṃ." It is said that this verse is unmixed (distinct) in the three Pitakas. It is true that the Blessed One did not show any fault in effort in other discourses. However, here, to restrain this deity, he spoke thus to show the completion of the Arahant's task: "In the earlier period, an Arahant living in the forest for the sake of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya) exerted effort by taking up a meditation subject. In the later period, if he wishes to exert effort, let him do so; if he does not wish to, let him live at ease." In that verse, "gādha" means a standing place (support). The fifth sutta ends.

## 6. Kāmadasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, "dukkaraṃ" means: this deity was a practitioner (yogāvacara) in a previous life, but due to the thickness of his defilements, he practiced the recluse's Dhamma by suppressing defilements through exertion. However, due to the weakness of his past supporting conditions (pubbūpanissaya), he passed away without reaching the stage of the Noble Ones (ariya-bhūmi) and was reborn in the deva world. He came thinking, "I will go to the presence of the Tathāgata and report the difficulty of the recluse's Dhamma," and spoke thus. In that verse, "dukkaraṃ" means that practicing the recluse's Dhamma, which is absolutely pure, for ten years... or even sixty years, is indeed difficult to do. "Sekhā" refers to the seven types of trainees (sekha-puggala). "Sīlasamāhitā" means having a mind well-established and endowed with virtue. "Ṭhitattā" means having a steadfast nature. Having answered the questions thus, he now spoke the words beginning with "anagāriyupetassa" to raise a further question.

In those words, "anagāriyupetassa" refers to one who has reached the state of homelessness. The reason is that even a monk living in a seven-storied palace, if a more senior monk arrives and says, "This place is suitable for me," he must take his bowl and robes and leave. Therefore, he is called "anagāriyupeta" (one who has entered homelessness). "Tuṭṭhi" means contentment with the four requisites. "Bhāvanā" means the meditation that brings about the tranquility of the mind.

"They, having cut the snare of Death"—those who delight in the tranquility of the senses day and night, they well-concentrate the mind which is difficult to concentrate. Those with well-concentrated minds do not grow weary while fulfilling contentment with the four requisites. Those who are content do not grow weary while fulfilling virtue.
99:
Those noble ones, the seven types of learners (sekha) who are established in virtue (sīla), go forth having cut the net of defilements (kilesa-jāla), which is called the net of Death (maccu).

"Duggamo" means: "Venerable Sir, this word is indeed true; those who delight in the calming of the faculties, they well-establish the mind which is difficult to establish ... pe ... those who are established in virtue, they go forth having cut the net of Death." This is the meaning. Why would they not go? However, he addressed the Blessed One, saying, "This journey is difficult to travel and is an uneven path." In that context, the Noble Path (ariya-magga) is actually neither difficult to travel nor uneven. However, in the practice that is the preliminary stage of that Noble Path, there are many dangers. Therefore, it was said thus.

"Avaṃsirā" means they fall head-downwards with the head of wisdom. It is also said that because they are unable to ascend to the Noble Path, they fall into the ignoble path. "Ariyānaṃ samo maggo" means that very path is the even path for the noble ones. "Visame samā" means they are equanimous even among the uneven group of beings. The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Pañcālacaṇḍasutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, regarding "sambhādhe," there are two types of confinement: the confinement of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and the confinement of the strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa). Among these two, the confinement of the hindrances is intended here. "Okāsa" is a name for jhāna. "Paṭilīnanisabho" means a noble person who has abandoned conceit. One who has abandoned conceit is called "paṭilīna." Just as the Blessed One said: "Monks, how is a monk 'paṭilīna'? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the conceit 'I am,' has cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it, so that it is no longer subject to future arising." "Paccalatthaṃsu" means they have obtained. "Sammā te" means those who have obtained mindfulness for the attainment of Nibbāna; they are well-concentrated even by supramundane concentration (lokuttara-samādhi). Thus, mixed jhāna (missaka-jjhāna) is taught. The seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Tāyanasutta Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "purāṇatitthakaro" means a teacher who established a sect in the past. Here, "tittha" refers to the sixty-two wrong views, and "titthakaro" refers to the teacher who causes those views to arise. These were Nanda, Vaccha, Kisa, and Saṅkicca. Those such as Purāṇa are called sectarians (titthiya). As for how this deity, having caused wrong views to arise, was reborn in heaven—it was because he was a proponent of action (kammavādī). It is said that he gave uposatha meals and so on, established the practice of giving to the helpless, built shelters, had ponds dug, and performed many other meritorious deeds. He was reborn in heaven as a result of those deeds.
100:
He knows the liberating nature of the Dispensation. That deity, thinking, "I shall go to the presence of the Blessed One and recite verses connected with energy that are suitable for the Dispensation," approached and spoke the verse beginning with "Chinda sotaṃ."

In that verse, "chinda" is an unrestricted command. "Sotaṃ" refers to the stream of craving. "Parakkamma" means exerting oneself with effort. "Kāme" refers to both defilement-based sensuality (kilesakāma) and objective sensuality (vatthukāma). "Panuda" means to dispel or remove. "Ekattaṃ" refers to Jhana. The meaning is this: without abandoning sensual desires, a sage cannot attain or reach Jhana.

"Kayirā ce kayirāthenaṃ" means if one is to make an effort, one should do so firmly; one should not retreat from that energy. "Daḷhamenaṃ parakkame" means one should make this effort steadfastly. "Sithilo hi paribbājo" refers to a monkhood practiced loosely. "Bhiyyo ākirate rajaṃ" means one excessively scatters the dust of defilements above. "Akataṃ dukkaṭaṃ seyyo" means it is better not to do an evil deed. "Yaṃ kiñci" means not only in doing evil, but in the practice of monkhood or in any other duty, every action done loosely is of such a nature.

"Saṅkiliṭṭhaṃ" refers to a practice performed with difficulty and impurity. In this Dispensation, the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) undertaken for the sake of the four requisites are indeed impure. "Saṅkassaraṃ" refers to actions that are suspected or doubted by others, thinking, "This monk might have done this, or he might have done that." "Ādibrahmacariyikā" means the primary effort which is the beginning of the holy life of the Path.

The eighth sutta ends.

## 9. Candimasuttavaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "Candimā" is the young deity living in the Moon Mansion. "Sabbadhī" means in all the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and so on. "Lokānukampakā" means there is the same compassionate protection for you as there is for this moon deity. "Santarāmānova" means as if in a hurry. "Pamuñcasi" is the present tense used in a past sense.

The ninth sutta ends.

## 10. Suriyasuttavaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "Suriya" is the young deity living in the Sun Mansion. "Andhakāre" refers to the darkness that causes blindness by preventing the arising of eye-consciousness. He is called "Verocana" because he has a brilliant light. He is called "Maṇḍalī" because he has a circular shape. "Mā Rāhu gilī caramantalikkhe" means, "Rāhu, do not swallow the sun moving in the sky."

As to whether that Rāhu actually swallows the Sun Mansion, it is true that it is an inauspicious omen. In detail, the person of Rāhu the Lord of Asuras (Rāhu Asurinda) is 800 yojanas in height. The breadth of his body is 4,000 yojanas. The span between his two arms is 1,200 yojanas; his neck is 600 yojanas; his head is 900 yojanas; his forehead is 300 yojanas; the space between his eyebrows is 15 yojanas. His mouth is 200 yojanas; his nose is 300 yojanas; and the open mouth cavity is 300 yojanas deep. The span of his palms and soles is 200 yojanas, and his finger joints are 50 yojanas. When that Rāhu Asurinda sees the bright moon and sun, he is severely oppressed by envy and blocks the path of the moon and sun...
101:
Does he swallow? Yes, he swallows. Indeed, the physical form (attabhāva) of Rāhu, the lord of Asuras, is immense. In height, it is four thousand eight hundred yojanas. The distance between his two arms is one thousand two hundred yojanas. Specifically, the neck is six hundred yojanas. The head is nine hundred yojanas, the forehead is three hundred yojanas, the space between the eyebrows is fifty yojanas, the mouth is two hundred yojanas, the nose is three hundred yojanas, and the opened mouth is three hundred yojanas deep. The palms of the hands and the soles of the feet are each two hundred yojanas in width. The finger joints are each fifty yojanas. When that Rāhu, the lord of Asuras, sees the shining Moon and Sun, being severely oppressed by envy, he descends into their path and stands with his mouth open. The Moon-mansion or the Sun-mansion becomes as if it were cast into a great hell three hundred yojanas deep. The deities living in the mansion, terrified by the fear of death, cry out all at once. That Rāhu, the lord of Asuras, sometimes covers the mansion with his hand, sometimes puts it under his chin, sometimes licks it with his tongue, and sometimes places it inside his cheek as if he were eating. However, he is unable to stop the momentum (of the Moon and Sun). If he were to stand holding it in his cheek to "stop" it, it would burst through the top of Rāhu's head and exit, or else it would drag him along and make him bend. Therefore, he just follows along with the mansion. "My creature (son)" means that both the young deities named Candima and Suriya attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) on the day the Mahāsamaya Sutta was preached. Therefore, the Blessed One said "my creature," meaning "this person is my son." The tenth sutta is finished.

## 2. Anāthapiṇḍika Vagga

## 1. Commentary on Candimasa Sutta

In the first sutta of the second chapter, "kaccheva" means "kacche viya" (as in a bend/recess). "Kacche" refers to a mountain recess or a river bend. "Ekodī nipakā" refers to those who have a concentrated mind and are endowed with the wisdom known as nipaka. "Satā" means those who are mindful. The meaning is: those who [attain] the jhānas...
102:
...attain the jhānas and dwell with a concentrated mind, being wise and mindful. They will go safely like deer in a mountain recess or a river bend that is free from gnats and mosquitoes. "Pāra" refers to Nibbāna. "Ambuja" refers to a fish. "Raṇañjaha" refers to one who abandons the defilements. Those who attain the jhānas and abandon the defilements without negligence will go to Nibbāna, having destroyed the net of defilements like fish [breaking a net]. The first sutta (commentary) is finished.

## 2. Commentary on Veṇḍu Sutta

In the second sutta, "Veṇḍu" is the name of that young deity. "Payirupāsiyā" means attending upon or associating with. "Anusikkhare" means learning and practicing. "Siṭṭhipade" means in the Dhamma of the virtuous, which causes the defilements to be repeatedly terrified and is to be known by practicing according to the instruction. "Kāle te appamajjantā" means that by striving in the practice of heedfulness (appamāda), namely serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), at the proper time, they do not reach the realm of Death. The second sutta (commentary) is finished.

## 3. Commentary on Dīghalaṭṭhi Sutta

In the third sutta, "Dīghalaṭṭhi": in the celestial realm, all deities are three gāvutas in height and thus equal in stature. However, while in the human world, that deity's body was so long/tall that he was given this name. Even though he was reborn in the celestial realm after performing meritorious deeds, he remained known by that same name. The third sutta (commentary) is finished.

## 4. Commentary on Nandana Sutta

In the fourth sutta, "Gotama" is an address to the Blessed One by his clan name. "Anāvaṭaṃ" means that when the Blessed One directs his omniscient knowledge, neither trees nor mountains can obstruct it; therefore, it is called "anāvaṭaṃ" (unobstructed). Having praised the Blessed One in this way, desiring to ask a question prepared in the celestial realm, he spoke the verse beginning with "kathaṃvidhaṃ". In that verse, "dukkhamaticca iriyati" means dwelling having transcended suffering. "Sīlavā" refers to an Arahant endowed with mundane and supramundane virtue. Wisdom and so forth should also be understood as a mixture of mundane and supramundane. "Pūjayanti" means they worship with incense, flowers, and so on. The fourth sutta (commentary) is finished.

## 5-6. Commentary on Candana Sutta, etc.

In the fifth sutta, "appaṭiṭṭhe anālambe" means having no standing ground below in the sense of the sensual realm (kāmabhava), and no support to cling to above in the sense of the fine-material and immaterial realms (rūpabhava and arūpabhava). "Susamāhito" means well-concentrated through both absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) and access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). "Pahitatto" means having a mind directed toward Nibbāna. "Nandirāgaparikkhīṇā" means having exhausted delight and lust (nandirāga). "Nandirāga" refers to the three types of volitional formations, such as meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra). Thus, in this verse, by taking "sensual perception" (kāmasaññā) among others, the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya saṃyojana) are included. By taking "fine-material fetters" (rūpasaṃyojana), the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya saṃyojana) are included. By "delight and lust" (nandirāga), the three types of kamma-formations—meritorious (puññābhisaṅkhāra), demeritorious (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), and imperturbable (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra)—are included. In the manner described, for whom the ten fetters and the three kamma-formations...
103:
*Samāhito* means being well-concentrated through either absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) or access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*). *Pahitatto* means having a mind sent towards Nibbāna (inclining the mind towards Nibbāna). *Nandīrāgaparikkhīṇo* means one whose delight and lust (*nandīrāga*) are exhausted. *Nandīrāga* refers to the three types of volitional formations (*kammābhisaṅkhāra*), such as meritorious formations and so on. Thus, in this verse, by taking 'perception of sensual pleasure' (*kāmasaññā*), the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) are included; by taking 'fetter of form' (*rūpasaṃyojana*), the five higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) are included; and by 'delight and lust' (*nandīrāga*), the three volitional formations are included. Thus, for whom the ten fetters and the three volitional formations are abandoned, that person no longer sinks in the deep flood (*ogha*) of the round of rebirths. Alternatively, *kāmasaññā* includes the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*), *rūpasaṃyojana* includes the form realm (*rūpabhava*), and by including these two, the formless realm (*arūpabhava*) is also included; *nandīrāga* includes the three volitional formations. Thus, it also shows that for the person who lacks the three formations in the three realms of existence, they no longer sink in the deep flood of the round of rebirths. The fifth sutta ends.

The sixth sutta has the same meaning as previously stated. The sixth sutta ends.

## 7. Subrahmasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, the Subrahma Sutta: According to what has been heard, that Subrahma Devaputta, surrounded by a group of celestial nymphs, went to the Nandana Grove to play and sat on a seat prepared at the foot of a Coral Tree (*Pāricchattaka*). Five hundred nymphs sat surrounding him, while another five hundred climbed the tree. Why did they climb the tree, given that for devas, even a tree a hundred leagues high can bend down to reach their hands by the power of their will? It was because they were intensely devoted to play. Having climbed, they sang with sweet voices and dropped flowers; the nymphs below gathered those flowers and wove them into garlands with stalks on one side and so forth. At that time, the five hundred nymphs who had climbed the tree passed away simultaneously due to the power of destructive kamma (*upacchedaka-kamma*) and were reborn in Avīci Hell, where they experienced great suffering.

Then, after some time had passed, Subrahma Devaputta thought, "The voices of these nymphs are no longer heard, nor do they drop flowers; where have they gone?" Upon reflecting, he saw their rebirth in hell and was oppressed by grief born of affection for loved ones. He then pondered, "These have gone first according to their own kamma; how much of my own life-formation (*āyusaṅkhāra*) remains?" When he saw, "On the seventh day, I too shall die along with the remaining five hundred nymphs and be reborn in that very hell," he fell into a state of extremely intense grief and anxiety. He thought, "In this world with its devas, there is no one other than the Tathāgata capable of dispelling this grief of mine," and went to the Blessed One to recite the verse beginning with "Niccaṃ utrastaṃ."
104:
In that verse, the word "idaṃ" refers to his own mind. The second word is merely a synonym of the first. Alternatively, the meaning of the word "niccaṃ" (constantly) should not be taken as starting from the time of rebirth in the deva world; rather, it should be understood as "constantly" starting from the time the grief arose. "Anuppannesu kicchesu" refers to the sufferings that will arise seven days from now. "Atho uppatitesu ca" refers to the sufferings already seen through the five hundred nymphs reborn in hell. Thus, he shows, "Because of these sufferings, both arisen and yet to arise, my mind is constantly terrified; Blessed One, I am like one being burned within."

"Nāññatra bojjhā tapasā" means he sees no safety or happiness apart from the development of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) and the virtue of austerity (*tapo*). "Sabbanissaggā" refers to Nibbāna (the relinquishing of all). In this verse, although the development of the factors of enlightenment is mentioned first and the restraint of the faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) later, in terms of meaning, the restraint of the faculties should be understood first. Indeed, when the restraint of the faculties is taken, the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) is included. A monk established in that fourfold purification of virtue, being free from dependence (*nissayamuttaka*), undertakes the virtue of austerity known as the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), enters the forest, and while developing a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), develops the factors of enlightenment along with insight (*vipassanā*). For that practitioner, the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) arises taking Nibbāna as its object; the Blessed One turned the discourse towards that Nibbāna as "sabbanissagga" (the relinquishing of all conditioned things) by way of the Four Noble Truths. At the end of the discourse, the Devaputta was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*). The commentary on the seventh sutta ends.

## 8-10. Kakudhasuttādi-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "Kakudho devaputto": This Kakudha Devaputta was the son of a lay supporter of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna in the city of Kola. While living in the presence of the Elder since his youth, he attained jhāna and, upon passing away, was reborn in the Brahma realm. Even in that Brahma world, they knew that Brahma simply as "Kakudha Brahmā." "Nandasi" is a question asking if he is delighted. "Kiṃ laddhā" (having gained what?): Delight arises from gaining even a small pleasant thing; therefore, He spoke thus. "Kiṃ jīyittha" (what is lost?): One who has even a small pleasant object such as a robe that is worn out or lost, that person grieves; therefore, He spoke thus. "Aratī nābhikīrati" means discontent does not overwhelm. "Aghajātassa" means for one born in suffering, that is, for one standing in the suffering of the round of rebirths (*vaṭṭadukkha*). "Nandījātassa" means for one in whom craving (*taṇhā*) has arisen. "Aghaṃ" means for such a person, the suffering of the round surely arrives. Indeed, it is said, "The suffering one yearns for happiness." Thus, for one fallen into the suffering of the round, delight (*nandī*) arises. Through the change and destruction of happiness, suffering surely arrives. Thus, for one with arisen craving, there is suffering (*agha*). The eighth sutta ends. The ninth sutta has the same meaning as already stated. The ninth sutta ends. In the tenth sutta, to show the power of Venerable Ānanda's inferential knowledge...
105:
It is so. Indeed, it is said, "A person in suffering yearns for happiness." Thus, for one who has fallen into the suffering of the round of rebirth, delight (nandī) arises; because suffering arrives precisely through the change and destruction of happiness, suffering arises for one who has developed craving. This is the eighth sutta.

The ninth sutta has the same meaning as already stated. This is the ninth sutta.

In the tenth sutta, the word "any" (aññatara) is used to demonstrate the power of the inferential knowledge (anumāna-paññā) of the Elder Ānanda. This is the tenth sutta.

## The Second Vagga.

## 3. Nānātitthiya Vagga.

## 1-2. Commentary on Siva Sutta and others.

The first sutta of the third vagga has the same meaning as already stated. This is the first sutta.

In the second sutta, "paṭikacceva" means even before being oppressed by old age and death. "Akkhacchinno vajhāyati" means one broods with a broken axle; one thinks with intense thoughts. In the second verse, "akkhacchinnovā" means like a carter with a broken axle. This is the second sutta.

## 3-4. Commentary on Serī Sutta and others.

In the third sutta, "dāyaka" means one who has the habit of giving. "Dānapati" (Lord of Giving) means one gives by being the master of the gift that is given; one does not give as a slave or as a friend of the gift. To explain further: a person who eats delicious food himself but gives unpalatable food to others is said to give as a slave (dānasāsa) of the gift to be given. A person who gives to others the very same food that he himself eats is said to give as a friend (dānasahāya) of the gift. However, a person who sustains himself with whatever food is available but gives delicious food to the recipients is said to give as a master, a leader, or a lord (dānapati) of the gift. He says, "I have been such a master of giving (dānasāmika)."

Regarding "catūsu dvāresu" (at the four gates): it is said that King Serī had two kingdoms, Sindhava and Sodhivāka, and the royal capital was named Roruva. At each gate of that great city of Roruva, a daily revenue of one hundred thousand arose, and another hundred thousand arose at the court of justice within the city. That King Serī, seeing the great heaps of gold and silver, developed the knowledge of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) and at the four...
106:
...gates, he had alms-halls built and appointed ministers, saying, "Give alms using the revenue received at each respective gate." Therefore, it is said, "Alms were given at the four gates."

In the phrase "samaṇabrāhmaṇakapaṇaddhikavanibbakayācakānaṃ," recluses (samaṇa) are those who have entered the monkhood. Brahmins (brāhmaṇa) are the 'bhovādins' (those who address others as 'bho'). However, this king did not encounter true recluses and brahmins who have calmed and abandoned evil. The poor (kapaṇa) refers to the destitute and impoverished, such as the blind and the crippled. Travelers (addhika) are those on a journey. Wanderers (vanibbaka) are those who travel around praising the virtues of giving, saying, "May the gift that is desired, given, pleasant, delightful, timely, and blameless gladden the mind of the giver; may the noble one reach the Brahma realm," and so on. Beggars (yācaka) are those who travel around asking for alms, saying, "Give just a handful, give just a small bowlful."

"Alms were given by the queens" means that because they received the first gate, they added other wealth to the hundred thousand revenue received at that gate, removed the king's ministers, appointed their own ministers, and gave alms that were greater and more magnificent than the alms given by the king. It is in reference to those alms that this was said. "My alms have declined" means that my alms given at that first gate have receded. The same method applies to the remaining gates. "Koci" means in a certain place. "Dīgharattaṃ" means for eighty thousand years. It means that the king's alms were given for such a long period of time. The third sutta ends.

The fourth sutta has the same meaning as already stated. The fourth sutta ends.

## 5. Commentary on Jantu Sutta

In the fifth sutta, "dwelling among the Kosalans" means they took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Blessed One and went to stay in that region. "Uddhatā" (agitated) means they were of a restless nature, perceiving what is unallowable as allowable, what is allowable as unallowable, what is blameless as blameworthy, and what is blameworthy as blameless. "Unnaḷa" (haughty) means like a reed (naḷa) that grows tall without a core; it means they possessed an uplifted and empty pride. "Capalā" (frivolous) means they were full of instability, such as being preoccupied with the ornamentation of their bowls and robes. "Mukharā" (harsh-spoken) means they had harsh mouths and spoke harsh words. "Vikiṇṇavācā" (loose-tongued) means they had unrestrained speech, spending the whole day in useless chatter and mockery. "Muṭṭhassatino" (unmindful) means those who have lost their mindfulness; they forget in one place what was done in another. "Asampajānā" means those lacking wisdom. "Asamāhitā" means those devoid of absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) and access concentration (upacāra-samādhi).
107:
They are like elephants tied in a violent current. 'Vibbhantacittā' means having a distracted mind that does not remain steady on a single object, like a young deer brought onto a path. 'Pākatindriyā' means those whose sense faculties are open, just as in their lay life, due to a lack of restraint.

'Jantu' is the name of a certain son of the devas (devaputta). 'Tadahuposathe' means on that Uposatha day. By the word 'pannarase', the fourteenth-day (cātuddasī) Uposatha and others are excluded. 'Upasaṅkamī' means approaching closely to rebuke. That son of the devas thought: "These monks left [for the forest] after taking a meditation subject from the Teacher, but now they live heedlessly. If I rebuke them while they are sitting individually, how will they take my words? I will rebuke them when they are assembled together." Knowing they were assembled on the Uposatha day, he approached. "Spoke in verses" means standing in the midst of all the monks and reciting verses.

In those words, since the faults of the virtueless become clear only when spoken alongside words of praise, he first wished to speak of their virtues and said, "Sukhajīvino pure āsuṃ," and so on. In that verse, "In the past they lived happily" means that in the past, monks were easy to support and easy to nourish; they maintained themselves with mixed alms-food obtained by wandering from house to house in order, among families of high and low status. This is the meaning. "Anicchā" means being free from craving.

Having thus spoken of the virtues of the monks of old, he now spoke of their faults, saying "Dupposā" and so on. In that verse, "Like village headmen in a village" means that just as corrupt headmen in a village oppress people in various ways, making them bring milk, curd, rice, and so on to eat, so too do you live by wrong livelihood (anesanā). This is the intended meaning. "Nipajjanti" means lying down on a bed with limbs sprawled out, having no interest in the recitation of the Pali, the commentaries, or reflection. "Parāgāresu" means in the houses of others, among the daughters-in-law of families, and so on. "Mucchitā" means sleeping while being infatuated and bewildered by defilements.

"Ekacce" refers only to those monks who deserve to be rebuked. "Apaviddhā" means those cast aside by their teachers and preceptors. "Anāthā" means those without a refuge. "Petā" means they are like corpses cast away in a cemetery. Just as various birds peck and tear at a corpse cast away in a cemetery, and relatives do not perform any protective service for those dead...
108:
(The relatives of those dead) do not perform any service of refuge, do not guard them, and do not protect them. In the same way, monks of such a nature do not receive advice and instruction from their teachers and preceptors, and thus they are cast aside and without refuge, just like corpses. The fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Rohitassasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'yattha' has the meaning of the locative case, referring to a certain place in the world-system (cakkavāḷa-loka). The words "does not pass away, is not reborn" are to be understood in terms of repeated passing away and rebirth. "By going" means by going on foot. The Teacher spoke the words "I [do not say] the end of that world" with reference to the end of the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka). In the words 'ñāteyya' and so on, the meanings are: to be known, to be seen, and to be reached.

Thus, although the son of the devas asked about the end of the world-system, the Teacher explained only the end of the world of formations. That son of the devas, thinking that the Teacher's explanation agreed with his own question, wished to praise him and said, "It is wonderful," and so on.

'Daḷhadhamma' means one who has a strong bow, one endowed with a bow of supreme power. 'Dhanuggaha' means an archery master. 'Susikkhita' means one who has trained in the art of archery for ten or twelve years. 'Katahattha' means one who has a trained hand, capable of piercing even the tip of a hair from a distance of one hundred and twenty usabhas. 'Katūpāsana' means one who is skilled in shooting arrows and has demonstrated his art in festivals. 'Asanena' means by an arrow. 'Atipāteyya' means he would surpass. He shows his own perfection of speed by saying that in the time it takes for an arrow shot by such a person to pass beyond the shadow of a palm tree, he could cross over one world-system.

"From the eastern ocean to the western ocean" means that just as the eastern and western oceans are far apart, so too was the extent of his stride. It is said that the son of the devas Rohitassa, standing on the rim of the eastern world-system, would step on the rim of the western world-system when he stretched out his leg. Then, stretching out his second leg, he would step on the rim of the next world-system. 'Icchāgata' means just the desire. By the word 'aññatreva', he shows the absence of delay. It is said that when it was time for alms-round, he would chew a nāgalatā tooth-wood, wash his face in Lake Anotatta, and then go for alms in Uttarakuru. Having sat on the rim of the world-system and eaten his meal, he would rest there for a moment and then run swiftly again. "One with a lifespan of a hundred years" refers to a time of long life. However, this person...
109:
He made an effort to go even while a hundred years of life remained. 'Vassasatajīvī' means living those hundred years without any danger. 'Antarāva kālaṅkato' means dying in the interval before reaching the end of the world-system. Even after dying there, that young deva was reborn in this very world-system. 'Appatvā' means without reaching the end of the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). 'Dukkhassa' refers to the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭadukkha). 'Antakiriyam' means making an end or a limit. 'Kaḷevare' means in the physical body (attabhāva). 'Sasaññimhi samanake' means in the body possessed of perception and mind. 'Lokaṃ' refers to the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca); 'lokasamudayaṃ' to the Truth of Origin (samudayasacca); 'lokanirodhaṃ' to the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca); and 'paṭipadaṃ' to the Truth of the Path (maggasacca). Thus, he shows: "Friend, I do not proclaim these Four Noble Truths in things like grass or wood, but I proclaim them only in this body endowed with the four great elements."

'Samitāvī' means one who has stilled unwholesome states through the Path. 'Nāsīsati' means no longer longing. The sixth sutta is finished. 108-109. The seventh and eighth suttas have the same meaning as previously stated. The seventh and eighth suttas are finished.

## 9. Susimasuttavaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "Ānanda, do you also find our Sāriputta pleasing?" The Teacher said this wishing to praise the Elder's virtues. Indeed, words of praise should not be spoken in the presence of an incompatible (visabhāga) person. If spoken in their presence, the praise does not reach its goal. For if it is said, "This monk named so-and-so is virtuous," such a person might say, "What is his virtue? He has the virtue of a cow. Have you never seen anyone else virtuous?" Or if it is said, "He is wise," they might say, "What wisdom does he have? Have you never seen anyone else wise?" and so on, creating obstacles to the talk of praise.

Venerable Ānanda, however, is compatible (sabhāga) with Venerable Sāriputta. When he receives excellent things, he offers them to the Elder. He ordains the sons of his own supporters and has them take the Elder as their preceptor (upajjhāya) and receive full ordination. Venerable Sāriputta also does the same for Venerable Ānanda. Why? Because of their mutual appreciation of each other's virtues. Venerable Ānanda, appreciating the Elder's virtues, cherishes him, thinking: "Our elder brother, having fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable period and a hundred thousand eons, and having penetrated the sixteen kinds of wisdom, stands in the position of the General of the Dhamma (dhammasenāpati)." Venerable Sāriputta also thinks of Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda performs all the duties for the Blessed One, such as offering water for washing the face, which I should do. Depending on Ānanda, I am able to enter whatever attainment (samāpatti) I desire..."
110:
Venerable Sāriputta also acts in the same way toward Venerable Ānanda. This is because they each have faith in and cherish one another's virtues. Venerable Ānanda cherishes the Elder, having faith in his virtues, thinking: "Our elder brother, Venerable Sāriputta, fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable and a hundred thousand aeons, realized the sixteen kinds of wisdom, and holds the position of the General of the Dhamma." Venerable Sāriputta also cherishes Venerable Ānanda, having faith in his virtues, thinking: "Ānanda performs the major and minor duties for the Blessed One that I should do, such as offering water for washing the face; depending on Ānanda, I am able to enter whatever attainment I desire." Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to praise the virtues of Venerable Sāriputta, began to speak in the presence of Venerable Ānanda.

In that passage, the particle 'pi' in the word 'tuyhampi' has the sense of inclusion (sampiṇḍana). This is what is meant: "Ānanda, Sāriputta's conduct (ācāra), his resort (gocara), his abiding in attainments, his going forward, his stepping back, his looking ahead, his looking aside, his bending, and his stretching are pleasing to me; they are pleasing to the eighty great elders (asītimahāthera); they are pleasing to the world with its devas. Are they pleasing to you also?"

Then Venerable Ānanda, like a powerful wrestler who has found an opportunity within the arena, became joyful in heart and thought: "The Teacher wishes to have me speak the praises of my dear friend, Venerable Sāriputta. Today, I shall hear the praise of Venerable Sāriputta, as if shaking the great Jambu tree of a hundred leagues which is like the banner of Jambudīpa, or as if bringing out and showing the moon from between the clouds." Thinking thus, first wishing to exclude worthless persons with four terms, he said: "Venerable sir, what person who is not a fool (abāla)..." and so on. For a fool, because of foolishness; a corrupt person, because of anger; a deluded person, because of delusion; and a madman with a distorted mind, because of the perversion of mind (cittavipallāsa), do not know praise as praise, or blame as blame, nor do they know "This is the Buddha, this is a disciple." Only those who are not fools, etc., can know. Therefore, he said "abālassa" and so on. "Would not find pleasing" means that only fools and the like might not find him pleasing; how could anyone else not find him pleasing?

Having thus excluded worthless persons, now wishing to praise his virtues according to reality with sixteen terms, he said: "Venerable sir, one who is wise (paṇḍita)..." and so on. In that passage, 'paṇḍita' means being endowed with wisdom; it is the name for one who stands in the four kinds of skill (kosalla). For it was said: "Ānanda, when a monk is skilled in the elements (dhātu), skilled in the sense bases (āyatana), skilled in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and skilled in what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāဋ္ဌāna). Ānanda, to this extent, a monk is fit to be called 'wise' (paṇḍita)."

In the terms such as 'mahāpañña' (of great wisdom), it means one endowed with great wisdom and so on. Herein, the distinction of great wisdom, etc., is as follows: What is great wisdom? It is called great wisdom because it discerns the great aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). It is called great wisdom because it discerns the great aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. It is called great wisdom because it discerns the great instances of the possible and impossible, the great abidings and attainments, the great Noble Truths, the great foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, and bases of power, and the great faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment...
111:
It is called Great Wisdom (Mahāpaññā) because it discerns the great Noble Path, the great fruits of recluseship, the great higher knowledges, and Nibbāna, which is the great ultimate meaning. That Great Wisdom became very manifest in the Elder Sāriputta when the Blessed One, having descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and standing at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa, asked questions to five types of persons, including worldlings, and the Elder answered those questions.

What is Wide Wisdom (Puthupaññā)? (The occurrence of knowledge) in various and diverse aggregates (is called Wide Wisdom). Knowledge that occurs in various diverse elements, in various diverse bases, in various diverse factors of dependent origination, in various diverse emptinesses that are not to be found, in various diverse meanings (attha), in dhammas, in linguistics (nirutti), and in eloquence (paṭibhāna); in various diverse groups of virtue, groups of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; in various diverse instances of possible and impossible, in meditative attainments, in the Noble Truths, in the foundations of mindfulness, in right efforts, in bases of power, in faculties, in powers, and in factors of enlightenment; in various diverse Noble Paths, fruits of recluseship, and higher knowledges; and knowledge that occurs in Nibbāna, the ultimate meaning, having transcended the various diverse dhammas common to worldlings—this is called Wide Wisdom.

What is Joyful Wisdom (Hāsapaññā)? Here, someone, being full of joy, full of zest, full of satisfaction, and full of gladness, fulfills virtue, fulfills the restraint of the faculties, practices moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, and fulfills the group of virtue, the group of concentration, the group of wisdom, the group of liberation, and the group of knowledge and vision of liberation. This is called Joyful Wisdom. Being full of joy and gladness, one penetrates the possible and the impossible; this is called Joyful Wisdom. Being full of joy, one fulfills the meditative attainments; this is called Joyful Wisdom. Being full of joy, one penetrates the Noble Truths. One develops the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Path; this is called Joyful Wisdom. Being full of joy, one realizes the fruits of recluseship and penetrates the higher knowledges; this is called Joyful Wisdom. Being full of joy, zest, and gladness, one realizes Nibbāna, the ultimate meaning. This is called Joyful Wisdom.

The Elder, having been a hermit named Sarada, made the aspiration for the position of Chief Disciple at the feet of the Blessed One Anomadassī. From that time onwards, because he fulfilled virtue and so on with great joy, he is said to be one possessed of Joyful Wisdom (Hāsapaññā).
112:
What is Swift Wisdom (Javanapaññā)? It is called Swift Wisdom because it quickly penetrates with knowledge all matter (rūpa)—whether past, future, or present... whether far or near—as impermanent. It is called Swift Wisdom because it quickly penetrates it as suffering, and quickly penetrates it as non-self. It is called Swift Wisdom because it quickly penetrates all feelings... perceptions... formations... all consciousness—whether past, future, or present... as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. It is called Swift Wisdom because it quickly penetrates dhammas from the eye... up to aging and death—whether past, future, or present—as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

Having weighed, investigated, clarified, and made manifest matter—whether past, future, or present—as impermanent in the sense of exhaustion, as suffering in the sense of fear, and as non-self in the sense of corelessness, it is called Swift Wisdom because it quickly penetrates Nibbāna, the cessation of matter. Having made manifest feelings... perceptions... formations... consciousness... the eye... up to aging and death as impermanent in the sense of exhaustion... it is called Swift Wisdom because it quickly penetrates Nibbāna, the cessation of aging and death. Having weighed, investigated, and made manifest matter... consciousness... the eye... up to aging and death as impermanent, conditioned (saṅkhata), dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna), subject to exhaustion (khayadhamma), subject to decay (vayadhamma), subject to fading away (virāgadhamma), and subject to cessation (nirodhadhamma), it is called Swift Wisdom because it quickly penetrates Nibbāna, the cessation of aging and death.

What is Sharp Wisdom (Tikkhapaññā)? It is called Sharp Wisdom because it quickly cuts off the defilements. One does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensuality, an arisen thought of ill will... an arisen thought of cruelty... whatever evil unwholesome states arise... arisen lust, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, disparaging, domineering, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, and negligence; one does not tolerate all defilements, all misconduct, all volitional formations (abhisankhāra), and all kamma leading to rebirth, but abandons them, dispels them, eliminates them, and brings them to non-existence; therefore, it is called Sharp Wisdom. It is called Sharp Wisdom because the four Noble Paths, the four fruits of recluseship, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and the six higher knowledges are attained, realized, and touched by wisdom in a single sitting.

While the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was being preached to his nephew, the wandering ascetic Dīghanakha, the Elder Sāriputta, even while standing, cut off all defilements and penetrated the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (Sāvakapāramīñāṇa); from that time on, he became known as one possessed of Sharp Wisdom (Tikkhapaññā). Therefore, it was said (by the Elder Ānanda), "Venerable Sir, the venerable Sāriputta is of sharp wisdom."
113: What is penetrative wisdom (nibbedhikapaññā)? In this Dispensation, a certain person frequently experiences a sense of urgency (saṃvega) and trepidation, fear, weariness, and successive disgust regarding all conditioned things (saṅkhāra). Not delighting in any conditioned things, they delight only in Nibbāna, which is beyond conditioned things, directing their wisdom towards it. Because it penetrates and destroys the mass of greed that was never before penetrated, broken, or destroyed, it is called penetrative wisdom. Because it penetrates and destroys the mass of hatred... the mass of delusion... the initial grudge... the deep-seated and recurring grudge... (pe)... all kamma that leads to the three realms of existence, it is called penetrative wisdom. "Appiccho" (Fewness of wishes) refers to the concealment of one's existing virtues, such as great learning (bāhusacca) or ascetic practices (dhuta-dhamma), and knowing moderation in receiving requisites. One endowed with this characteristic is called "appiccha". "Santuṭṭho" (Contentment) refers to being endowed with these three types of contentment regarding the four requisites: contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābha-santuṭṭhi), contentment according to one's strength (yathābala-santuṭṭhi), and contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppa-santuṭṭhi). "Pavivitto" (Seclusion) refers to the attainment of these three types of seclusion: physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) for those who are physically secluded and delight in renunciation; mental seclusion (citta-viveka) for those whose minds are purified and have reached supreme purity; and seclusion from substrata (upadhi-viveka) for those who have reached Nibbāna and are free from the substrata of defilements. "Asaṃsaṭṭho" (Non-association) refers to being free from these five types of association: association through seeing (dassana-saṃsagga), association through hearing (savana-saṃsagga), association through conversing (samullapana-saṃsagga), association through shared use of objects (paribhoga-saṃsagga), and association through physical contact (kāya-saṃsagga). These five types of association occur with eight types of persons: kings, royal ministers, ascetics of other sects, disciples of other sects, laymen, laywomen, monks, and nuns. Since all these associations do not exist in the Elder, he is called "asaṃsaṭṭha". "Āraddhavīriyo" (Aroused energy) refers to having energy that is exerted and perfected. In this regard, a monk with aroused energy does not allow defilements that arise while walking to persist until he stands; he does not allow those that arise while standing to persist until he sits; he does not allow those that arise while sitting to persist until he lies down. He suppresses the defilements that arise in each posture right then and there. The Elder, however, did not stretch his back on a couch for forty-four years. With reference to that fact, it is said he has "aroused energy". "Vattā" (One who speaks/admonishes) refers to one who admonishes to purify defilements. Upon seeing the transgressive behavior of monks, he does not delay by saying, "I will speak today, I will speak tomorrow," but admonishes and instructs them right at the place where he sees them. "Vacanakkhamo" (Patient of speech) refers to being patient with the words of others. Indeed, some people give advice to others but become angry when they themselves are advised by another. The Elder, however, not only advises others but...
114: ...even when he himself is admonished by others, he accepts it respectfully with his head. It is said that one day, a seven-year-old novice said to the Elder Sāriputta, "Venerable Sāriputta, the edge of your undergarment is hanging down." Without saying a single word in return, the Elder went to a suitable place, adjusted his undergarment to be neatly rounded, and upon returning, stood with palms joined and said, "Teacher (Ācariya), is it proper now?" "Even if he is one ordained on this very day, Or only seven years of age by birth, If that virtuous one should instruct me, I shall receive it respectfully upon my head." "Codako" (The accuser/instructor) refers to one who, upon seeing a transgression in conduct, whether it is evident or not, gives instruction according to the scriptures (tanti), saying, "Friend, a monk should dress his undergarment like this, wear his robe like this, walk like this, stand like this, sit like this, eat snacks like this, and eat meals like this." "Pāpagarahī" (One who censures evil) refers to the desire not to see evil persons, not to hear their words, and not to live even within the same universe as them. "May I never, in any place, meet One of evil wishes, the lazy, one of poor energy, The unlearned, or the disrespectful." In this way, he censures evil persons. "A monk should not be one who follows the power of lust, or the power of hatred and delusion; one should abandon the lust, hatred, and delusion that have arisen." In this way, he also censures evil states. For these two reasons, the Venerable Ānanda said, "Venerable Sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is one who censures evil (pāpagarahī)." When the Venerable Ānanda thus expressed the true virtues of the Elder with these sixteen terms, the Blessed One—in order to prevent any foolish person (evil person) from disparaging him by saying, "Is Ānanda not allowed to speak the praise of his dear friend? Let him speak, but is everything he says true? Is he an All-knowing Buddha?"—made that praise an unshakeable word of the Omniscient One, as if affixing the seal of a Conqueror (Jina), and said, "Ananda, it is just so," and so forth.
115:
While the Blessed One and the Elder Ānanda were thus praising the virtues of the Elder Sāriputta, the earth-dwelling deities arose and praised his virtues with these same sixteen phrases. Furthermore, the sky-dwelling deities, the deities of the cold clouds (Sītavalāhaka), the deities of the hot clouds (Uṇhavalāhaka), the deities of the Four Great Kings, and so on up to the Akanittha Brahma realm, arose and praised his virtues with these same sixteen phrases. In this manner, starting from one universe, the deities of the ten thousand world systems arose and offered praise.
