Then, the young deity Susīma, who was a co-resident disciple of the Elder Sāriputta, thought: 'These deities have abandoned their own celestial festivities and have gone to various places just to praise the virtues of my preceptor. I shall go to the Blessed One and report this praise spoken by the deities.' He did so. To show this, the passage beginning with 'Atha kho Susīmo' was spoken.

'Uccāvacā' means that although in other places 'ucca' refers to the noble and 'avaca' to the base, here it refers to various kinds of radiance. In that assembly of deities, the blue parts were intensely blue, the yellow parts were intensely yellow, the red parts were intensely red, and the white parts were intensely white; thus, four kinds of colored radiance appeared. For this reason, the four similes beginning with 'Seyyathāpi nāma' are given. Among those similes, 'subho' means beautiful. 'Jātimā' means of excellent birth (pure). 'Suparikammakato' means well-prepared through processes such as washing. 'Paṇḍukambale nikkhitto' means placed upon a crimson rug. 'Evamevaṃ' means that like a ruby on a crimson rug, all the deities began to shine and radiate simultaneously. 'Nikkhaṃ' refers to an ornament made of pure gold weighing more than five suvaṇṇas. Such gold can withstand rubbing and polishing. 'Jambonadaṃ' means gold found in the river flowing under the branches of the great Jambu tree, or it refers to an ornament made from the golden sprouts that arise where the juice of the Jambu fruit enters the earth. 'Dakkhakammāraputtaukkāmukhasukusalasampahaṭṭhaṃ' means well-beaten and crafted in a furnace by a skilled goldsmith. In the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, it refers to an unworked gold ingot, but here it should be taken as a finished ornament.

'Viddhe' means clear and remote. 'Deve' means in the sky. 'Nabhaṃ abbhussakkāmāno' means soaring and pervading the sky. By this phrase, the state of the rising sun is shown.
116:
'Sorato' means endowed with gentleness (soracca). 'Danto' means free from the impurities of defilements. 'Satthuvaṇṇābhato' means having virtues brought forth by the Teacher. Indeed, the Teacher, while seated in the midst of the eight assemblies, brought forth the virtues of the Elder Sāriputta in such ways as, 'Monks, associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna,' and thus the Elder is called 'ābatavaṇṇa' (one whose virtues are brought forth by the Teacher). 'Kālaṃ kaṅkhatī' means awaiting the time of Parinibbāna. Indeed, an Arahant neither delights in death nor yearns for life. Just as a man working for daily wages awaits the time when his work is finished, he remains looking forward only to the time of Parinibbāna. Therefore, it was said:
'I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life;
I await the time, just as a laborer awaits his wages.'
The ninth discourse is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Nānātitthiyasāvaka Sutta

In the tenth discourse, 'Nānātitthiyasāvaka' refers to those young deities who were believers in the law of kamma. Therefore, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, they were reborn in the deva realm. These deities, perceiving that 'We were reborn here due to our devotion to our own teachers,' thought, 'Let us go to the One of Ten Powers and speak of the virtues of our teachers, Pūraṇa Kassapa and others,' and having arrived, they spoke in individual verses. In those verses, 'chinditamārite' refers to the cutting of hands and feet and the killing by decapitation. 'Hatajānīsū' refers to beating and the loss of wealth. 'Puṇyaṃ vā panā' means he does not see even his own merit; in short, he says there is no result (vipāka) of merit or demerit. 'Sa ve vissāsamācikkhī' means that by saying 'There is no result for those who do evil or those who do good,' Pūraṇa Kassapa points out a basis of confidence and reliance for beings; therefore, he says he is worthy of honor, salutation, and worship.

'Tapojigucchāyā' means loathing evil through the practice of self-mortification. 'Susaṃvutatto' means being endowed with or closed off. 'Jegucchī' means one who loathes evil through ascetic practice. 'Nipako' means being wise. 'Cātuyāmasusaṃvuto' means well-restrained by the fourfold restraint (cātuyāma). The 'cātuyāma' consists of four parts: sabbavārivārito (restrained from all water), sabbavāriyutto (endowed with all restraint), sabbavāridhuto (shaken off from all evil through restraint), and sabbavārifuṭo (pervaded by all restraint). Among these, 'sabbavārivārito' means being restrained from using all cold water. This is because that Nigantha perceives that there are living beings in cold water, and thus he does not use it.
117:
"Sabbavāriphuṭo" means being touched by the restraint of all evil. These four groups are called the Cātuyāma (Fourfold Restraint). In that context, "Sabbavārivārito" means the restraint from all water or the rejection of cold water. That Nigaṇṭha (Jain ascetic) does not use cold water because he perceives that there are living beings in it. "Sabbavāriyutto" means being endowed with the restraint of all evil. "Sabbavāridhuto" means having shaken off evil through the restraint of all evil. "Sabbavāriphuṭo" means being touched by the restraint of all evil. Since he declares what is seen as "I have seen" and what is heard as "I have heard," and does not conceal anything, such a teacher cannot be a doer of evil.

"Nānātitthiye" refers to the fact that this deva was a servant of many sectarian teachers, and thus speaks with reference to them. "Pakudhako Kātyāno" refers to the teacher named Pakudha of the Kaccāyana lineage. "Nigaṇṭho" refers to Nātaputta. "Makkhali-pūraṇāse" refers to Makkhali and Pūraṇa. It is said that they have reached the summit of ascetic practice. It is said that they are not far from virtuous people and are indeed the virtuous ones in the world. "Paccabhāsī" (replied) means: "This deity Ākoṭaka is praising these inglorious naked ascetics in the presence of the Buddha; I shall speak of their faults," thus responding in opposition.

In that context, "Saha-caritena" means merely by walking together. "Chavo sigālo" means a wretched, foolish jackal. "Kotthuko" is also a synonym for that same jackal. "Saṅkassarācāro" means having a repulsive or suspicious conduct. He is not like the wise and virtuous. It means, "Why do you compare these sectarian teachers, who are like jackals, to lions?"

"Anvāvisitvā" means thinking, "This deity is speaking of the faults of such teachers; I will make him speak their praises with that very same mouth," and thus entering and possessing his body. "Āyuttā" means being greatly devoted to the loathing of evil through practices such as not wearing clothes. "Pālayam pavivekiyam" means guarding seclusion. They say, "We shall guard seclusion from hair-cutting," and they pull out their own hair. They say, "We shall guard seclusion from robes," and they wander naked. They say, "We shall guard seclusion from alms-food," and they eat like dogs, either from the ground or from their hands. They say, "We shall guard seclusion from dwellings," and they use beds of thorns and so on. "Rūpe niviṭṭhā" means being established in forms through craving and views. "Devalokābhinandino" means desiring only the deva world. "Maccā" refers to mortals. It means that these mortals give good instructions for the sake of the next world.
118:
"Iti viditvā" means "This person first spoke dispraise of these people and now speaks praise; who is he?"—having reflected and known thus. "Ye cantalikkhasmiṃ pabhāsavaṇṇā" refers to the radiant colors of the moonlight, sunlight, twilight, rainbows, and the host of stars in the sky. "Sabbeva te te" means all those are the forms praised by you (Mara). "Namuci" is an address to Mara. "Āmisaṃva macchānaṃ vadhāya khittā" means just as bait attached to a hook is thrown to kill fish, so too, these forms are thrown by you through praise to kill beings.

"Māṇavagāmiya": This young deva was an attendant of the Buddha. "Rājagahīyānaṃ" means among the mountains of Rājagaha (Mount Vipula is the best). "Seto" refers to Mount Kelasa. "Aghagāminaṃ" refers to those that travel through the sky (celestial mansions or the sun) (meaning being the most excellent). "Udadhinaṃ" refers to the reservoirs of water (oceans) (meaning being the most excellent). The meaning is this: Just as Mount Vipula is the best among the mountains of Rājagaha, Mount Kelasa is the best among the Himalayan mountains, the sun is the best among things that travel through the sky, the ocean is the best among the reservoirs of water, and the moon is the best among the stars; so too, the Buddha is the best in the world with its devas. The tenth sutta (commentary) is finished.

## III. Nānātitthiyavagga

## Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

## The Commentary on the Devaputtasaṃyutta is finished.
119:
## 3. Kosala Saṃyutta

## 1. Paṭhama Vagga

## 1. Dahara Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Kosala Saṃyutta, the phrase "exchanged friendly greetings with the Blessed One" means that when asked about his health and well-being, the Blessed One shared mutual joy with the King, just as the King shared mutual joy with the Blessed One. It was like cold water mixing with hot water to become one.

He rejoiced in harmony with such words as: "Venerable Gotama, are you healthy? Are you well? Are you and your disciples, Venerable Gotama, free from illness, free from affliction, light in body, strong, and living in comfort?" Such speech is called 'pleasurable' (sammodanīya) because it generates the joy known as pīti-pāmojja and is worthy of rejoicing. It is called 'memorable' (sāraṇīya) because it is worthy of being remembered for a long time due to the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, and is fit to be maintained continuously. It is 'pleasurable' because of the happiness felt when hearing it, and 'memorable' because of the happiness felt when recollecting it. Likewise, it is 'pleasurable' due to the purity of its phrasing and 'memorable' due to the purity of its meaning.

Having concluded the conversation that was pleasurable and memorable in these many ways, the King sat to one side, not knowing whether the Buddha's qualities were deep or shallow, as he had never seen the Tathāgata before. While sitting to one side, he spoke the words beginning with "Bhavaṃ pi no" to ask whether the Blessed One was a Sammāsambuddha, a question concerning the entry into the state of liberation from the world, which he brought like a hidden treasure of great essence.

In that text, in the word "bhavaṃ pi," the particle "pi" is used in the sense of conjunction (sampiṇḍana), and by that word, he includes the six teachers. The meaning is: "Just as Pūraṇa and others claim 'We are Sammāsambuddhas,' does the Venerable [Gotama] also claim the same?" The King did not ask this based on his own view, but based on the public claims made by the great multitude in the world. Then the Blessed One, roaring the Buddha's Lion's Roar, spoke the words beginning with "Yaṃ hi taṃ mahārāja." In that text, "Ahaṃ hi mahārāja" means: "O Great King, I have fully realized the unsurpassed, supreme Sammāsambodhi known as omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)." "Samaṇabrāhmaṇa" refers to those who are called recluses (samaṇa) merely by going forth, and those who are called brahmins (brāhmaṇa) by virtue of their birth. In the words beginning with "santi," it means that the Saṅgha, which is merely a collection of recluses, exists for those teachers like Pūraṇa who claim to be Buddhas; therefore, it is said "they exist"...
120:
They are called recluses (samaṇa) because they have approached the state of going forth, and brahmins (brāhmaṇa) by virtue of their birth. In the words beginning with 'saṅghino,' they are called 'saṅghī' because they have a Saṅgha, which is a group of recluses. They are called 'gaṇī' because they have that very group. They are called 'gaṇācariya' because they are the teachers of that group by virtue of teaching conduct and training. 'Ñātā' means they are famous and well-known. They are called 'yasassī' because they have widespread fame, such as: 'They have few wishes and are contented; because of their fewness of wishes, they do not even wear clothes.' 'Titthakarā' means they are the founders of sects. 'Sādhu-sammatā' means they are regarded as 'holy men, good men.' 'Bahujanassa' means according to the wishes of the manyfolk, the blind and foolish worldlings. Pūraṇa and the others are their names and lineages. Pūraṇa is just a name. Likewise, Makkhali is also a name. He is called Gosāla because he was born in a cow-shed. Nāṭaputta is the son of Nāṭa. Belaṭṭhaputta is the son of Belaṭṭha. Kaccāyana is the lineage of Pakudha. Ajita is called Kesakambala because he wears a blanket made of hair.

'I also know those uproars' refers to the three kinds of uproars (kolahala): the Aeon Uproar (kappa-kolahala), the Buddha Uproar (buddha-kolahala), and the Universal Monarch Uproar (cakkavatti-kolahala). Among them, the announcement that 'The destruction of the aeon will occur one hundred thousand years from now' is called the Aeon Uproar. Deities wander about the paths of men, proclaiming: 'One hundred thousand years from now, the world will perish. Friends, develop loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity.' The announcement that 'A Buddha will arise one thousand years from now' is called the Buddha Uproar. Deities proclaim: 'One thousand years from now, a Buddha will arise in the world and will wander about preaching the Dhamma, surrounded by the Jewel of the Saṅgha who have practiced the way according to the Dhamma.' The announcement that 'A Universal Monarch will appear one hundred years from now' is called the Universal Monarch Uproar. Deities proclaim: 'One hundred years from now, a Universal Monarch will appear, endowed with the seven treasures, sovereign over the four continents, surrounded by a thousand sons, and able to travel through the air.'

Among these three uproars, these six teachers heard the Buddha Uproar, attended upon teachers, learned arts such as the Cintāmaṇi-vijjā, and then made the claim 'We are Buddhas.' Surrounded by a great multitude, they wandered through the countryside and eventually arrived at Sāvatthī. Their attendants approached the King and reported: 'O Great King, it is said that Pūraṇa Kassapa... and Ajita Kesakambala are Buddhas, they are said to be omniscient.' The King then said: 'You yourselves invite them and bring them here.'
121:
The attendants of those heretics went to them and said, "The King invites you; please accept alms-food at the King's palace." However, they did not make an effort to go. When requested repeatedly, they consented for the sake of protecting the hearts of their supporters and went all together. The King had seats prepared and said, "Please be seated." The royal majesty pervaded the persons of those devoid of virtue, and they, not daring to sit on the costly seats fit for the powerful, sat on wooden planks and on the ground.

The King, thinking, "By this much behavior alone, there is no pure quality (sukka-dhamma) within them," and without giving them food, asked a question like one striking a person who has fallen from a palm tree with a club: "Are you Buddhas or not?" They thought, "If we say 'We are Buddhas,' the King will ask questions regarding the domain of a Buddha, and when we are unable to answer, he might say, 'You are wandering around deceiving the masses by saying you are Buddhas,' and have our tongues cut off or cause other harm." Thus, by their own admission, they said, "We are not Buddhas."

Then the King had them driven out of the palace. When they emerged from the palace, their supporters asked, "Teachers, did the King ask you questions and pay you honor and respect?" They replied, "The King asked, 'Are you Buddhas?' Then we, out of compassion for the King, thinking, 'If this King does not understand the answers to questions regarding the domain of a Buddha and becomes displeased with us, he will accumulate much demerit,' said, 'We are not Buddhas.' But we are indeed Buddhas; our state of being a Buddha cannot be removed even by washing with water." Thus, they said externally, "We are Buddhas," while in the presence of the King, they had said, "We are not Buddhas."

Taking this point, the King spoke thus. In that speech, he spoke taking his own admission: "How is it that the Venerable Gotama is young in birth and new in the monkhood?" In that context, the word "kiṃ" is a word of rejection. It means: "These teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa are elderly in birth and have been ordained for a long time, yet they do not claim, 'We are Buddhas.' The Venerable Gotama is young in birth and new in the monkhood; why do you claim it? Do not claim it."

"Na uññātabbā" means should not be despised. "Na paribhotabbā" means should not be treated with contempt. "Katame cattāro" is a question asked with the desire to speak. "Khattiyo" means a prince. "Urago" means a snake with potent venom. "Aggī" means fire itself. In the word "Bhikkhū," due to skill in teaching, the Buddha includes himself within it and shows a virtuous monk.
122:
In this city of Sāvatthī, one who sees a young prince and does not step aside to give way, does not remove the outer robe, does not rise from one's seat, does not descend from the back of an elephant and so on, and treats him as inferior, performing other such improper conduct (anācāra), is said to despise the prince. If one says such things as, 'This young prince is indeed handsome; he has large arms, a large neck, and a large chest; he will be able to quell any danger from thieves; he will be able to provide guidance in some place,' one is said to be treating him with contempt. One who harasses a young cobra the size of a collyrium stick at the ear-hole and so on, and lets it bite a finger or the tongue, is said to despise the snake. One who says such things as, 'This cobra is as harmless as a water snake; how could such a small thing bite or spread venom in anyone's body?' is said to be treating the snake with contempt. One who takes a fire even as small as a firefly and plays with it with the hands, or throws it into small bowls for storing goods, or places it on the head, or on beds, benches, robe-bags and so on, is said to despise the fire. One who says such things as, 'This fire is good; what kind of gruel or rice will it be able to cook? What kind of fish or meat? Whose cold will it be able to dispel?' is said to be treating the fire with contempt. Furthermore, one who sees even a young novice (sāmaṇera) and performs improper conduct as mentioned regarding the prince, such as not stepping aside to give way, is said to despise the monk. One who says such things as, 'This novice is very graceful; he has a large neck and a large belly; will he be able to learn any of the Buddha's word? Will he be able to enter and live in any forest? He will be pleasing when he becomes an elder of the Saṅgha,' is said to be treating the monk with contempt. To show that all such things should not be done, the Blessed One said, 'Should not be despised, should not be mistreated.'

'Etadavoca' means he spoke this verse composition. These verses clarify the previously mentioned meaning and also clarify a special meaning; in this case, they clarify both the previous meaning and the special meaning. In that verse, 'Khattiya' refers to the lord of the fields. For it was said: 'Vāseṭṭha, because he is the lord of the fields, the second name "Khattiya, Khattiya" arose.' 'Jātisampanna' means being endowed with birth by that very Khattiya birth. 'Abhijāta' means being born having surpassed three lineages. 'Thānaṃ hi' means there is a reason. 'Manujinda' means the chief of men. 'Rājadaṇḍena' means by the punishment meted out by the king; that punishment is not small, but is indeed ten thousand or twenty thousand in measure.
123:
"Tasmiṃ pakkamate bhusaṃ" means the king's renewed great effort against that person who showed disrespect. "Rakkhe jīvitamattano" means one who protects their own life should avoid that king and not offend him.

"Uccāvacehi" means of various and diverse kinds. "Vaṇṇehi" means by means of appearances or forms. This is because, in whatever form it moves, it obtains its prey. Whether it be in the form of a cobra, a green snake, a dhamani snake, or even at least in the form of a black squirrel, it simply moves about. "Āsajjā" means having reached or encountered. "Bālaṃ" means that fool who is offended; it would bite that foolish man or woman.

"Pahūtabhakkha" means having much food. This is because there is nothing that is not food for fire. "Jālinaṃ" means having a net of flames. "Pāvakaṃ" means fire. There is also a variant reading "pāvagaṃ". In the word "kaṇhavattanī", "vattanī" means the path. The path where fire has gone is black; therefore, it is called "kaṇhavattanī" (black-pathed).

"Mahā hutvānā" means having become great. Sometimes fire can even be as large as the Brahma realm. "Jāyanti tattha pārohā" means in that place where the fire burned, in the burnt forest, grass, trees, and so on arise. "Pārohā" refers to grass, trees, etc. Even if only the roots remain in the place burnt by fire, they grow back, arise, and increase from the roots; therefore, they are called "pārohā". Alternatively, they are called "pārohā" in the sense of growing again. "Ahorattānamaccaya" means with the passing of days and nights. Even in the summer, they grow just by the falling of rain.

"A monk burns with his power": here, a monk who scolds back one who scolds, quarrels back with one who quarrels, or strikes back at one who strikes, is not able to burn anyone with a monk's power. However, when a monk does not scold back, does not quarrel back, and does not strike back but remains patient, the one who mistreats such a monk is burned by that monk's power of virtue. Therefore, it is said: "Na tassa puttā pasavo." This means his sons and daughters, as well as his livestock such as cattle, buffaloes, chickens, and pigs, do not remain but perish. "Dāyādā vindare dhanaṃ" means his heirs do not obtain wealth. "Tālāvatthū bhavanti te" means those people, being burnt by the fire of the monk's power, become like palm trees with their heads cut off, with only the site remaining. It means they can no longer multiply through children and so on.
124:
"Therefore" means because they become like palm trees with their heads cut off, unable to grow, due to being burnt by the power of the ascetics; therefore, "one should conduct oneself properly." What should one who conducts himself properly do? One who clearly sees the benefits, such as the villages, towns, chariots, and vehicles to be obtained by depending on a king; the clothes, gold, silver, and so on to be obtained by making a snake perform by depending on it; the benefits of cooking gruel and rice, and dispelling cold to be attained by the power of fire by depending on it; and the benefits such as hearing what has not been heard, purifying what has been heard, and attaining heaven and the path and fruit to be attained by the power of a monk by depending on him—such a person should not completely abandon them, thinking, "There are dangers as previously mentioned in depending on these; what is the use of them?"

Indeed, one who desires prosperity should please the prince by such means as rising early and going to bed late, without showing the aforementioned kinds of contempt or disrespect. By doing so, he will attain prosperity from that prince. A snake charmer, without being over-familiar with the snake, should conduct himself by reciting snake-charms, grasping it by the neck with a goat-foot-shaped stick, washing the fangs with venom-removing medicinal roots, and putting it in a basket to make it perform. By doing so, he will obtain food, clothing, and so on by depending on that snake. One who wishes to cook gruel and so on should not, through over-familiarity with the fire, put it in pots and pans or touch it with hands, but should light it with cow-dung powder and so on to cook gruel. By doing so, he will obtain the benefit by depending on that fire. One who desires to hear the Dhamma that has not been heard and so on should not, through over-familiarity with the monk, employ him in medical work or construction work, but should respectfully serve him with the four requisites. By serving in this way, depending on that monk, he will hear the Buddha's word not heard before, hear the decision of questions not heard before, attain benefits in this life and the next, the three types of prosperity, the six celestial realms of the sense sphere, and the nine Brahma realms, and even attain the vision of the deathless Great Nibbāna. Intending this meaning, He said, "One should conduct oneself properly."

"He said this" means having heard the Dhamma teaching and being inspired, wishing to manifest that inspiration, he spoke these words: "Excellent!" and so on. Therein, "Abhikkantaṃ" means extremely desirable, extremely pleasing, and extremely good. Here, with one word "Abhikkantaṃ," he praises the teaching: "Venerable Sir, the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One is excellent!" With another "Abhikkantaṃ," he praises his own faith: "Venerable Sir, my faith based on the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One is excellent!" After that, he praises the teaching itself with four metaphors. Therein, "Nikkujjitaṃ" is like setting upright an object that was placed face down. "Paṭicchannaṃ" is like revealing an object that was covered with grass, leaves, and so on. "Showing the way to one who is lost" is like taking one by the hand and saying, "This is the way." "In the darkness" means in the fourfold darkness consisting of the fourteenth day of the waning moon, midnight, and thick rain clouds. This means that just as someone might set upright what was overturned, similarly, one who has fallen into the ways of the wicked is raised into the Dhamma of the virtuous; or just as one might reveal what was hidden by the views of wrong-view since the disappearance of the dispensation of the Blessed Buddha Kassapa...
125:
“Venerable Sir, this clarity that has arisen in me because of the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching is excellent indeed,” thus he praises his own clarity. After that, he praises the teaching itself with four metaphors. Among those metaphors, 'nikkujjita' refers to an object placed face down or turned downwards. 'Ukkujjeyya' means to make it face upwards. 'Paṭicchanna' refers to an object covered with grass, leaves, etc. 'Vivareyya' means to open or reveal. 'Mūḷha' is for one who is lost. 'Maggaṃ ācikkheyya' means taking one by the hand and saying, “This is the way.” 'Andhakāre' refers to the darkness of the four factors: the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, midnight, a dense forest, and a thick mass of clouds. The meaning is this: Just as someone might set upright what was overturned, similarly, by raising me up from the wrong Dhamma when I was turned away from the true Dhamma and fallen into the wrong Dhamma; just as one might reveal what was hidden, similarly, by revealing the Dispensation (Sāsana) which has been covered by the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa; just as one might show the way to one who is lost, similarly, by making clear the path to heaven and liberation for me who was following the wrong path of evil; just as one might bring an oil lamp into the darkness, similarly, by lighting the lamp of the teaching which destroys the darkness of delusion for me who was submerged in the darkness of delusion and unable to see the jewels such as the Buddha; the Blessed One has made the Dhamma clear in various ways through these methods.

Having praised the teaching in this way, with a mind clear in the Triple Gem because of that teaching, and wishing to show a gesture of devotion, he says the words beginning with “Esāhaṃ.” In those words, “Esāhaṃ” means “I.” “Bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca” means “I go for refuge to these Triple Gems: the Blessed One, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha of monks.” “Upāsakaṃ maṃ, bhante, bhagavā dhāretu” means “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One recognize me, know me, as a lay follower (upāsaka).” “Ajja-t-agge” means starting from today. There is also the reading “Ajja-d-agge”; the letter “d” is inserted for euphonic combination (sandhi), and it also means “starting from today.” “Pāṇupetaṃ” means as long as life lasts (until the end of life). In brief: May the Blessed One recognize me as a lay follower, a provider of requisites (kappiyakāraka), who has gone for refuge through the three refuges, not seeking any other teacher as long as life lasts. This is just a summary; the detailed explanation has been fully stated in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. In the Second Sutta
“Abhivādetvā” means that since he had already gone for refuge in the previous sutta, in this second assembly, he pays homage respectfully with the five limbs. “Ajjhattaṃ” refers to what arises within one's own continuity. The state characterized by attachment to greed and so forth is called greed (lobha). The state characterized by malice is called hatred (dosa). The state characterized by confusion is called delusion (moha).
126:
## 2. Purisasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'abhivādetvā' (having paid homage) means that because he had already taken refuge in the previous sutta, he pays homage in this one. 'Ajjhattaṃ' (internally) means internally related to oneself, arising within one's own continuity (santāna). Among greed and the others, greed (lobha) has the characteristic of attachment, hatred (dosa) has the characteristic of corruption, and delusion (moha) has the characteristic of bewilderment. 'Hiṃsanti' means they oppress, destroy, or cause ruin. 'Attasambhūtā' means those (states) that have arisen within one's own continuity. 'Tacasāraṃva samphalanti' means just as the fruit of a bamboo or reed, which has bark as its core, harms and destroys its own plant, so too do they harm and destroy. The second sutta ends.

## 3. Jarāmaraṇasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'aññatra jarāmaraṇā' means 'Is there anyone who is free from old age and death?' 'Khattiyamahāsālā' refers to nobles who have attained great essence of wealth. Those nobles who have at least one hundred crores of wealth buried as treasure, and have three pots of Kahāpaṇas placed in the middle of the house for daily use, are called Khattiyamahāsālā. Those Brahmins who have eighty crores of wealth buried, and have one and a half pots of Kahāpaṇas placed in the middle of the house for daily use, are called Brāhmaṇamahāsālā. Those householders who have forty crores of wealth buried, and have one pot of Kahāpaṇas placed in the middle of the house for daily use, are called Gahapatimahāsālā.

'Aḍḍhā' means lords of wealth. They are called 'mahaddhanā' (greatly wealthy) because of the greatness of their buried treasure. They are called 'mahābhogā' (having great enjoyments) because of the abundance of items for use such as gold and silver vessels. They are called 'pahūtajātarūparajatā' (having abundant gold and silver) because of the abundance of unburied gold and silver. They are called 'pahūtavittūpakaraṇā' (having abundant ornaments and equipment) because of the abundance of ornaments that bring joy. They are called 'pahūtadhanadhaññā' (having abundant wealth and grain) because of the abundance of wealth such as herds of cattle and the seven types of grain. 'Tesampi jātānaṃ natthi aunñatra jarāmaraṇā' means that for those persons such as kings who are born and possess such lordship, there is nothing other than old age and death; because of the very fact of being born, there is no escape from old age and death, and they exist only within old age and death.
127:
Among the terms beginning with *Arahanto*, they are called *Arahants* because they are far from the defilements. They are called *Khīṇāsava* because the four taints (*āsava*) are exhausted. They are called *Vusitavanto* because they have a residence where the holy life has been lived to completion. They are called *Katakaraṇīya* because they have done what was to be done through the four paths. They are called *Ohitabhāra* because they have laid down these burdens: the burden of the aggregates (*khandha*), the burden of defilements (*kilesa*), the burden of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the burden of sensual pleasures (*kāmaguṇa*). They are called *Anuppattasadattha* because they have successively attained their own goal, known as the fruition of Arahantship (*arahattaphala*). They are called *Parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojana* because the ten fetters of existence are exhausted. They are called *Sammadññāvimutta* because they are liberated by knowing the true causes well. The meaning is that they have known the Four Noble Truths through the wisdom of the path and are liberated by the liberation of fruition (*phalavimutti*).

*Bhedanadhamma* means having the nature of breaking. *Nikkhepanadhamma* means having the nature of being discarded. For an Arahant, there is also a quality that does not decay; that is Nibbāna, which is the object [of their realization], for that Nibbāna does not decay. However, in this context, wishing to show the decaying nature of that Arahant [the physical body], he spoke thus. It is said that the origin of this Sutta was due to a specific occasion. While the Blessed One was staying in the Sivikasālā (a hall for palanquins or carriages), he saw ornate chariots and such, and using those very chariots he had seen as a simile, he spoke the verse: "Royal chariots indeed wear out," and so on.

In that verse, "*jīranti*" means they reach old age and decay. "*Rājarathā*" are the chariots ridden by kings. "*Sucittā*" means well-decorated with gold, silver, and so on. If even such inanimate (*anupādinnaka*) chariots made of heartwood decay, what can be said of this internal, animate (*upādinnaka*) body made of flesh, blood, and so on? The meaning is that the body also certainly reaches old age.

"*Santo have sabbhi pavedayanti*" means that the virtuous, together with the virtuous, declare: "The Dhamma of the virtuous does not decay." The meaning is: "The Dhamma of the virtuous is Nibbāna; it does not decay, it is ageless and deathless—thus they speak." Alternatively, because the defilements, which have the nature of sinking, are broken depending on Nibbāna, that Nibbāna is called "*sabbhi*". Thus, wishing to show the reason for the preceding phrase, he said: "*Santo have sabbhi pavedayanti*". This is what is said: The Dhamma of the virtuous does not decay, therefore the virtuous declare it with the virtuous. The meaning is that they proclaim the ageless Nibbāna as the Dhamma of the virtuous. Or, "*sabbhi*" is a beautiful designation. The meaning is also: The Dhamma of the virtuous, which is Nibbāna—the *sabbhidhamma* declared and spoken of by the virtuous—does not decay. The third Sutta is finished.

In the fourth Sutta, "*rahogatassa*" means staying in a secluded place. "*Pasannindriyassa*" means dwelling alone. With the words "*Evametaṃ mahārāja*" and so on, here...
128:
## 4. Piya Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth Sutta, "*rahogatassa*" means for one who has gone to a secluded place. "*Paṭisallīnassa*" means for one who is secluded and alone. With the words "*Evametaṃ mahārāja*", the Blessed One spoke here, wishing to establish this Sutta as a discourse spoken by the Omniscient One (*sabbaññubhāsita*). "*Antakenādhipannassa*" means for one who is overwhelmed and oppressed by the Ender (Death). The fourth Sutta ends.

## 5. Attarakkhita Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth Sutta, "*hatthikāyo*" is a group of elephants. The same method applies to the remaining terms like *kāyo*. "*Saṃvaro*" means closing, forbidding, or restraining. By the words "*Sādhu sabbattha saṃvaro*", he shows the restraint of an action (*kamma*) that has not yet reached the specific 'path of action' (*kammapatha*). "*Lajjī*" is one who possesses the sense of shame (*hiri*). By taking the word "*lajjī*", moral dread (*ottappa*) is also included here. The fifth Sutta ends.

## 6. Appaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the sixth Sutta, "*uḷāre uḷāre*" means both noble and abundant. "*Majjanti*" means they are intoxicated with the intoxication of conceit (*māna*). "*Atisāraṃ*" means transgression or going to excess. "*Kūṭaṃ*" is a snare or a trap. "*Pacchāsaṃ*" means in their future time. The sixth Sutta ends.

## 7. Aḍḍakaraṇa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the seventh Sutta, "*kāmahetū*" means having sensual desire as the cause; "*kāmanidānaṃ*" means having sensual desire as the source; "*kāmādhikaraṇaṃ*" means having sensual desire as the basis. All these terms are merely synonyms for one another. "*Bhadramukho*" means one with a handsome face.

One day, the King was in the hall of justice (*aḍḍakaraṇa*). In that hall, the ministers, having first taken bribes, made those who were not the owners into owners. The King, knowing this, thought: "Even in the presence of me, the lord of the earth, they do such things; what then will they not do in my absence? Now General Viṭaṭūbha will become known by his own kingship; what benefit is there for me in sitting in the same place with such bribe-eaters and liars?" Therefore, he spoke thus. "*Khippaṃva oḍḍitaṃ*" means like a fish-trap (*kumina*) that has been set. Just as fish do not know when they enter a set trap, so too beings do not know when they transgress against the objects of sensual pleasure (*vatthukāma*) through the defilement of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*). The seventh Sutta ends.
129:
## 8. Commentary on the Mallikā Sutta

In the eighth sutta (Mallikā Sutta), why is it asked, "Mallikā, is there anyone (dearer to you than yourself)?"

It is said that this Mallikā was the daughter of a poor garland-maker. One day, while she was carrying a cake from the market, thinking, "I will go to the flower garden and eat it," she saw the Blessed One entering for alms, surrounded by the community of monks. With a heart full of faith, she offered that cake to the Blessed One. The Blessed One indicated his desire to sit. The Venerable Ānanda spread out a robe and offered it. The Blessed One sat there, consumed the cake, washed his mouth, and manifested a smile.

Venerable Ānanda asked, "Venerable Sir, what will be the benefit for this woman?" The Buddha replied, "Ānanda, this woman has offered the first meal to the Tathāgata this very day; this very day she will become the chief queen of the King of Kosala."

On that same day, the King of Kosala, having been defeated in battle by his nephew in the village of Kāsi, was fleeing and entered the flower garden while entering the city, waiting for the arrival of his troops. That Mallikā attended to the King's needs. The King, pleased with her service, had her taken to the palace and established her in the position of chief queen.

Then one day, the King thought: "I have given great sovereignty to this daughter of a poor family. What if I were to ask her, 'Who is dear to you?' She will say, 'Great King, you are dear to me,' and then she will ask me back. Then I will tell her, 'You alone are dear to me as well.'" Thus, he asked her while speaking pleasant words to create mutual intimacy. However, that queen was wise, a devotee of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and possessed great wisdom. Therefore, she thought: "This is not a question to be answered by merely looking at the King's face (to please him)." Speaking according to her own true nature, she answered and then questioned the King in return. Because she spoke the truth, the King was unable to avoid it and spoke the truth himself. Then, thinking, "This matter is based on a reason; I will report it to the Tathāgata," he went and reported it to the Blessed One.

"Nevajjhagā" means did not find (did not attain). "Evaṃ piyo puthu attā paresaṃ" means that just as one's own self is dear to oneself, so too is the self dear to many others. 

The eighth sutta ends.
130:
## 9. Commentary on the Yañña Sutta

In the ninth sutta, the Yañña Sutta: "Thūṇūpanītāni" means those beings brought to the sacrificial post, those tied to the sacrificial post. By the words "parikammāni karonti," it is meant that those monks reported to the Blessed One about the sacrifice undertaken by the King of Kosala. 

Why did the King undertake this sacrifice? It was to ward off the effects of an evil dream. It is said that one day, the King, adorned with all ornaments and mounted on a noble elephant, was touring the city. He saw a woman looking out through a window and became infatuated with her. Returning from that spot, he entered the palace, told the matter to a royal servant, and sent him, saying, "Go and find out whether that woman has a husband or not."

The servant went and inquired, and the woman pointed out, "That man sitting in the market is my husband." The servant reported this to the King. The King summoned the man and said, "Serve me." Although the man replied, "Great King, I do not know how to serve," the King said, "Service is not something to be learned from a teacher," and by force made him take up a weapon and shield, appointing him as an attendant. 

As soon as the man reached home after serving the King, the King summoned him again and said, "An attendant must obey the King's word. Go; at a distance of about one yojana from here, there is our royal head-washing pond. Bring back from that pond the dawn-colored clay (aruṇa-mattikā) and a garland of red lotuses. If you do not return this very day, I will impose royal punishment." He then sent him away. The man departed, fearing the King's punishment.

After the man had left, the King summoned the gatekeeper and instructed him, "Close the gate this very evening. Even if someone says, 'I am a royal messenger' or 'I am the viceroy's messenger,' do not open it."

The man took the clay and the lotuses and arrived just as the gate was closed. Although he spoke much, he was not allowed entry. Fearing danger, he went to the Jetavana monastery. The King, oppressed by the fever of lust, sometimes sat, sometimes stood, and sometimes lay down. Unable to reach a firm decision (about getting the woman), he fell into a fitful sleep, like a monkey's sleep, while sitting wherever he happened to be.
131:
In the past, in that very city of Sāvatthī, four sons of wealthy merchants committed the act of adultery (paradārika-kamma) and were reborn in the Lohakumbhī iron cauldron hell named Nandopananda. While being cooked and bubbling with foam, those merchant sons sank downwards for thirty thousand years until they reached the bottom of the cauldron. Then, for another thirty thousand years, they rose upwards until they reached the rim of the cauldron. On the day the King of Kosala had his dream, they reached the rim of the cauldron and, seeing the light, each wished to recite a verse due to the fear of their past misdeeds. However, being unable to speak, they could only utter a single syllable each. One said the syllable 'Sa', one said 'So', one said 'Na', and one said 'Du'. From the moment the King heard the sounds of those hell-beings, he could not find any peaceful sleep and spent the remainder of the night in distress.

At dawn, the royal chaplain came and asked the King if he had slept well. The King replied, "Teacher, how could I have slept well?" and explained, "I heard such sounds in my dream." The Brahmin thought, "This dream will bring neither prosperity nor ruin to this King. However, all the wealth in this King's house is going only to the ascetic Gotama and his disciples; we Brahmins receive nothing. I will create an opportunity for the Brahmins to receive alms." He then said, "Great King, this dream is very grave. One of the three types of losses is indicated: there will be danger to the kingdom, danger to your life, or there will be no rain."

When asked, "Teacher, how can there be safety and well-being?" he replied, "It can be known after consultation, Great King." The King said, "Go, consult with the other teachers and ensure our safety."

The chaplain gathered the Brahmins in the palanquin hall, explained the matter, and divided them into three groups, saying, "Go separately and speak thus." The Brahmins entered the palace and asked the King if he had slept well. The King told them exactly what he had told the chaplain and asked, "How can there be safety and well-being?" The great Brahmins replied, "Great King, by performing a sacrifice of five hundred of each kind of animal, you can be safe from the danger of this dream. This is what the teachers say." Although the King heard their words, he neither welcomed nor rejected them, but remained silent. Then the second group of Brahmins came and spoke in the same way. Likewise, the third group of Brahmins spoke. Then the King commanded, "Perform the sacrifice." From that time on, the Brahmins began to have animals such as bulls brought in. In the city, a great sound...
132:
...arose. Knowing of this matter, Queen Mallikā sent the King to the presence of the Blessed One. The King went, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat in a suitable place. Then the Blessed One said to him, "Well, Great King, from where have you come at this time of day?" The King replied, "Venerable Sir, today I heard four sounds in a dream. I asked the Brahmins about it, and they said, 'Great King, this dream is very grave. We must remedy it by performing a sacrifice of five hundred of each kind of animal,' and they have begun their efforts." When asked, "Great King, what kind of sounds did you hear?" the King reported them as he had heard them.

Then the Blessed One said: "Great King, in the past, in this very city of Sāvatthī, four sons of wealthy merchants committed adultery and fell into the Lohakumbhī hell named Nandopananda. After sixty thousand years had passed, they rose to the top of the cauldron.

Among them, one wished to say this verse:
'Sixty thousand years have been completed in every way;
for us who are being cooked in hell, when will there be an end?'
But he could not say it.

The second one wished to say this verse:
'If I, having surely gone from here, obtain a human birth,
I will be one who knows the wishes of those who ask, endowed with virtue, and I will perform many meritorious deeds.'
But he could not say it.

The third one wished to say this verse:
'There is no end. From where could there be an end? No end is in sight.
For then, evil was committed by me and by you, dear friends.'
But he could not say it.

The fourth one wished to say this verse:
'We lived a miserable life, we who did not give to those who were present;
though wealth existed, we did not make a refuge for ourselves.'
But he could not say it.

Being unable to say these verses to the end, they uttered only one syllable each and sank back into that very hell. Thus, Great King, those hell-beings cried out according to the karma they had committed. Because of hearing those sounds, there will be neither ruin nor prosperity for you. However, the act of killing so many living beings is a very grave matter." Thus, the Buddha taught the Dhamma, threatening him with the fear of hell.
133:
The Blessed One preached the Dhamma. The King, having gained confidence in the Blessed One, said, "I release these beings, I give them their lives. Let them eat green grass, let them drink cool water, and let a cool breeze blow upon them." He then commanded the people, "Go and release them." Those people went, drove away the Brahmins, released the multitude of beings from their bonds, and beat the Dhamma-drum in the city, proclaiming, "Do not kill or harm living beings." Then the King, sitting near the Blessed One, said, "Venerable Sir, a night consists of three watches, but to me today, it was as if two nights were joined together." That man, also sitting there, said, "Venerable Sir, a league (yojana) consists of four gāvutas, but to me today, it was as if two leagues were made into one." Then the Blessed One, considering, "To the wakeful, the length of the night is evident; to the weary, the length of the league is evident; but to the foolish worldlings wandering in the cycle of existence, the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra is indeed long," spoke this verse in the Dhammapada concerning the King, the man, and the beings in hell:

Long is the night to the wakeful;
Long is the league to the weary;
Long is saṃsāra to the foolish
Who do not know the True Dhamma. (Dhp. 60)

At the end of the verse, that man, the husband of the beautiful woman, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). "Knowing this matter" (Etamatthaṃ viditvā) means having known this reason.

Regarding the terms "Sassamedha" and so on—it is said that in the time of ancient kings, there were four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) by which kings favored the world: Sassamedha, Purisamedha, Sammāpāsa, and Vācāpeyya. Among them, taking a tenth part of the harvested crops is called Sassamedha; it means wisdom in ensuring the abundance of crops. Giving rations and wages every six months to great warriors is called Purisamedha; it means wisdom in winning over men. Taking a written bond from poor people and providing them with a thousand or two thousand pieces of wealth for three years without interest is called Sammāpāsa. Because this basis of sympathy binds people well as if with a noose around the heart, it is called Sammāpāsa. Speaking gentle words such as "Father" or "Uncle" is called Vācāpeyya; it means pleasant speech (piyavācā). A country favored by these four bases of sympathy is prosperous, wealthy, and abundant in food and drink, peaceful, and free from the thorns of thieves. People live rejoicing with one another, making their children dance in their laps, and leaving their house doors open. Because there are no door-bolts, it is called "Niraggala" (unbolted). This was the tradition from ancient times. However, in later times, during the reign of King Okkāka, the Brahmins altered these four bases of sympathy and the prosperity of the country, turning things upside down, and performed five sacrifices such as Assamedha and Purisamedha. In those sacrifices, in the Assamedha sacrifice, they killed horses...
134:
Such a country is prosperous, wealthy, and abundant in food and drink, safe and peaceful. People live rejoicing, making their children dance in their laps, and staying with their house doors open. This is called "Niraggala" because there are no bolts on the house doors. This is the ancient tradition.

In later times, during the reign of King Okkāka, the Brahmins altered these four bases of sympathy and the prosperity of the country, turning them upside down, and performed five sacrifices such as Assamedha and Purisamedha. Among those sacrifices, it is called "Assamedha" because horses are killed in this sacrifice. It is the name of a sacrifice that is performed with two subsidiary sacrifices, has twenty-one sacrificial posts, and is terrifying due to the slaughter of ninety-seven hundred and five hundred (97,500) animals on the middle day alone; it involves giving away all remaining wealth as a gift, excluding the land and the people. It is called "Purisamedha" because men are killed in this sacrifice. It is the name of a sacrifice performed with four subsidiary sacrifices, where wealth as mentioned in the Assamedha is given along with the land. It is called "Sammāpāsa" because a yoke-pin (samma) is thrown in this sacrifice. It is the name of a Sattrayāga sacrifice performed by throwing a yoke-pin daily, preparing an altar at the spot where it falls, and proceeding upstream from the place where the Sarasvatī River disappears, using portable sacrificial posts and so on. It is called "Vājapeyya" because they drink "vāja" (bamboo juice) in this sacrifice. It is the name of a sacrifice performed with one subsidiary sacrifice and seventeen animals, having a sacrificial post made of bamboo (beluva), and having seventeen items of donation. It is called "Niraggala" because there are no bolts in this sacrifice. It is the name of a variation of the Assamedha sacrifice, also known as Sabbamedhapariyāya, performed with nine subsidiary sacrifices, where all wealth as mentioned in the Assamedha is given along with the land and the people. "Mahārambha" refers to sacrifices involving great slaughter and great undertakings. "Sammaggata" refers to the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas, who have practiced rightly. "Nirārambha" refers to sacrifices that do not involve slaughter. "Yajanti anukulaṃ" means they sacrifice in suitable families; it means people give the regular alms (niccabhatta) and so on established by their ancestors without interruption through successive generations. The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10. Bandhanasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "Venerable Sir, here by the King" and so on—these words were spoken by the monks to inform the Elder Ānanda of the good deed done for those people. It is said that an eight-faceted gem given by Sakka to King Kusa had come down through the royal lineage. When the King wished to adorn himself, he said, "Bring that gem." The people...
