## 2. Second Chapter (Dutiya Vaggo)
## 1. Commentary on the Satta Jaṭila Sutta
In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'Pubbārāme Migāramātupāsāde' means in the monastery known as Pubbārāma, in the palace of the lay devotee Visākhā, who was known as Migāra's Mother. In this regard, this is the chronological account: One hundred thousand aeons ago, a certain laywoman invited the Blessed One Padumuttara, gave gifts for seven days to the Saṅgha of one hundred thousand monks with the Buddha at their head, and prostrating at the feet of the Blessed One, made a wish: "In the future, may I be the chief female attendant of a Buddha like you."

After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she took rebirth in the womb of Sumanadevī in the house of Dhanañjaya Seṭṭhī, the son of Meṇḍaka Seṭṭhī, in the city of Bhaddiya during the time of our Blessed One. At the time of her birth, they gave her the name Visākhā. When the Blessed One went to the city of Bhaddiya, she went with five hundred young maidens to welcome the Blessed One, and upon her first sight of Him, she became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). Later, she went to the house of the youth Puṇṇavaddhana, the son of Migāra Seṭṭhī in Sāvatthī. There, Migāra Seṭṭhī placed her in the position of a mother; therefore, she is called Migāra's Mother. [The Buddha stayed] in the palace built and offered by her.

'Bahi dvārakoṭṭhake' means outside the gate-tower of the palace, not outside the gate-tower of the monastery. That palace was surrounded by a wall with four gate-towers, like the Lohapāsāda. Among those four gate-towers, the Buddha sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the shade of the palace outside the eastern gate-tower, looking towards the eastern world-system.

'Parūḷhakacchanakhalomā' refers to having overgrown armpit hair, fingernails, and body hair. It means having long hair in the armpits and so on, and long nails. 'Khārivividhaṃ' refers to the various requisites and belongings of the ascetics, such as baskets, earthen pots, and fire-drills. 'Avidūre atikkamanti' means they entered the city by a path not far away. 'Rājāhaṃ bhante' means, "Venerable sirs, I am King Pasenadi of Kosala; please know my name."

The point to be examined is: why did the King, while sitting in the presence of the Supreme Individual in the world, pay respect to such naked, deformed, and lusterless people? It was for the sake of winning them over (favoring them). For the King thought: "If I do not show even this much respect to them..."
137:
[The king thought,] "I will perform [the salutation]. [Otherwise, they might think,] 'We have abandoned our wives and children and endured the hardships of poor food and uncomfortable beds for the sake of this king, yet he does not even offer us a simple salutation.' Thus, [out of dissatisfaction,] they might conceal what they have seen and heard. However, if I show them [this honor], they will speak without concealment." Therefore, he acted in that way. Furthermore, he did so to understand the Buddha's intention.

'Kāsikacandana' refers to fine sandalwood. 'Mālāgandhavilepana' means by wearing flowers for the sake of color and scent, perfumes for the sake of fragrance, and ointments for the sake of color and scent.

'Saṃvāsena' means by living together. 'Sīlaṃ veditabbaṃ' means that whether a person is virtuous or immoral is to be known by associating and approaching them while living together. Furthermore, that virtue must be known over a long period, not a short one. This is because it is impossible to truly demonstrate the manner of restraint in body and speech and the manner of guarding the sense faculties in just two or three days. 'Manasikarotā' means it can only be known by one who reflects and investigates with the thought, "I will examine his virtue," and not by anyone else. 'Paññavatā' means that virtue can only be known by a wise person. This is because a fool, even if he reflects, is unable to know.

'Saṃvohārena' means by communication. In the passage, "Vāseṭṭha, know that among humans, whoever lives by trade is a trader, not a brahmin," the term 'byavahāra' is called 'vohāra' [meaning trade]. In the passage, "Four noble usages (ariya-vohāra), four ignoble usages (anariya-vohāra)," volition (cetanā) is called 'vohāra'. In the passage, "Designation (saṅkhā), term (samaññā), concept (paññatti), usage (vohāra)," concept is called 'vohāra'. In the passage, "He should speak by means of mere usage (vohāra)," speech is called 'vohāra'. Here also, only speech is intended. The speech of some people in their presence does not match their speech behind their back, and their speech behind their back does not match their speech in their presence. Likewise, their earlier speech does not match their later speech, and their later speech does not match their earlier speech. Such a person can be known as an "impure person" through their speech alone. For one of pure virtue, however, the earlier speech matches the later, and the later matches the earlier; the speech in person matches the speech behind the back, and the speech behind the back matches the speech in person. Therefore, desiring to show that purity can be known through communication, the Buddha spoke in this way.
138:
'Thāma' refers to the strength of wisdom (ñāṇathāma). One who lacks the strength of wisdom, when dangers arise, cannot see what should be taken or what should be done, and thus wanders like someone who has entered a house without a door. Therefore, the Buddha said, "Great King, strength is to be known in times of adversity."

'Sākacchā' means discussion. The speech of an unwise person moves like a fish in water. When a wise person speaks, however, the fluency of wisdom (paṭibhāna) arises profoundly and without limit. Just as a fish is known to be small or large by the movement of the water.

'Ocaraka' refers to those who move about below (spies). Even if spies move about on a mountain top, they are still considered "low-movers." 'Ocaritvā' means having investigated and known various circumstances. 'Rajojalla' refers to dust and dirt. 'Vaṇṇarūpena' means by way of physical appearance. 'Ittaradassanena' means by a brief sighting. 'Viyañjanena' means by external requisites and belongings. 'Patirūpako mattikākuṇဍalo vā' means like a clay earring that is a counterfeit of a gold earring. 'Lohaဍ္ဎmāsa' is a coin worth half a copper māsaka. The first discourse ends.

## 2. Pañcarājasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second discourse, 'rūpā' refers to visual objects categorized by blue, yellow, etc. "Kāmānaṃ aggaṃ" (the best of sensual pleasures) is said by one who values visual forms. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Yato' means when. 'Manāpapariyantaṃ' refers to sensual pleasures that reach the limit of what is pleasing or are bounded by what is pleasing. In this context, there are two types of pleasing objects: individually pleasing (puggalamanāpa) and conventionally pleasing (sammutimanāpa).

'Individually pleasing' means that a sensual object which is desired, loved, and pleasing to one person may be undesired and unloved by another. For those living in border regions, even earthworms are desired, loved, and pleasing, whereas for those living in the Middle Country, they are extremely loathsome. For those in the Middle Country, peacock meat and such are desired, while for others in border regions, those things are extremely loathsome. This is called 'individually pleasing.' The other is called 'conventionally pleasing.'

There is no fixed division of desirable and undesirable objects in the world; rather, they should be shown by analysis. In analyzing, one should not analyze according to the standards of extremely powerful rulers like King Mahāsammata, King Mahāsudassana, or King Dhammāsoka. For them, even an object similar to a divine luxury might appear unpleasant. Nor should one analyze according to the standards of the extremely poor who find it difficult to obtain food and drink. For them, even broken rice grains or the juice of rotten meat seems extremely sweet, like nectar. Rather, [one should analyze] according to the standards of middle-class people such as accountants, high ministers, treasurers, householders, and merchants...
139:
Distinction should be made by way of neutral persons who receive pleasant objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa) at times and unpleasant objects (aniṭṭhārammaṇa) at times. Moreover, that object cannot be determined by the impulsion (javana). For impulsion is attached to both pleasant and unpleasant objects, and is averse to both pleasant and unpleasant objects. In reality, however, only the resultant consciousness (vipāka-citta) determines the pleasant and the unpleasant. Even if those with wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi), upon seeing the Buddha, the Saṅgha, or noble objects such as the Great Stūpa, close their eyes and fall into displeasure, or upon hearing the sound of the Dhamma, plug their ears, the eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness that arise in them are nonetheless wholesome resultants (kusala-vipāka). Even if creatures such as village pigs, smelling the scent of dung, become joyful thinking 'We shall get to eat,' their eye-consciousness in seeing the dung, their nose-consciousness in smelling its scent, and their tongue-consciousness in tasting it are nonetheless unwholesome resultants (akusala-vipāka). The Blessed One, referring to personal preference (puggalamanāpa), said, 'Great King, those forms...' and so forth.

'Candanaṅgalika' is the name of that lay follower. 'Paṭibhāti maṃ bhagavā' means 'The Blessed One makes a certain matter clear to my intellect.' Although those five kings came with great royal majesty and supreme sovereign wealth, wearing jeweled earrings and seated in a prepared drinking area, from the moment they stood in the presence of the Ten-Powered One, their radiance and beauty vanished like a lamp in the daytime, like embers sprinkled with water, or like fireflies at sunrise. Seeing the Tathāgata shining a hundredfold or a thousandfold more than them, the inspiration arose in that lay follower's intellect: 'Truly, those called Buddhas are great!' Therefore, he spoke thus.

'Kokanada' is a synonym for the Paduma lotus. 'Pāto' means early in the morning. 'Siyā' means 'would be.' 'Avītagandha' means not devoid of scent (fragrant). 'Aṅgīrasa' refers to the Blessed One. Because rays of light emit from the Blessed One's limbs (aṅga), he is called 'Aṅgīrasa.' The brief meaning here is: 'I see the Blessed One, Aṅgīrasa, shining like the sun in the sky, just as a Paduma lotus called Kokanada would be blooming and fragrant early in the morning.' 'Bhagavantaṃ acchādesi' means he gave to the Blessed One. Such an expression is used according to worldly usage. That lay follower, thinking, 'These five kings, having gained confidence in the qualities of the Tathāgata, [gave] me five...'
140:
(Those five kings) gave their upper robes (uttarāsaṅga). Thinking, 'I too will give these to the Blessed One,' he gave them. The second sutta ends.

## 3. Doṇapākasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'doṇapākakuraṃ' means he eats a bucket-measure (doṇa) of rice and curries suitable for that rice. 'Bhuttāvī' (having eaten) means that while previously he would dispel the drowsiness caused by the meal and rest for a moment before going to attend on the Buddha, on that day, even while eating, he remembered the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala), washed his hands, and went immediately. 'Mahassāsī' (breathing heavily) refers to the heavy breathing of the King as he went, due to the intense heat arising from the meal. Sweat drops fell from his body, and although people standing on both sides fanned him with pairs of palm-leaf fans, he did not dare to lie down out of respect for the Buddha; it is with reference to this that 'mahassāsī' was said.

'Imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi' (spoke this verse) means the Buddha spoke this verse thinking, 'The King is suffering because he does not know moderation in eating; I will now act so that he may live comfortably.' 'Manujassa' means to a being. 'Kahāpaṇasataṃ' (a hundred Kahāpaṇas) means a hundred Kahāpaṇas (to be given to the youth), fifty for the morning meal and fifty for the evening meal.

'Pariyāpuṇitvā' (having mastered) means that after following the King for a short distance, he asked, 'Great King, to whom shall I give this auspicious sword?' The King replied, 'Give it to such-and-such a person.' Having delivered the sword, he returned to the Blessed One, paid homage, and while standing, said, 'Speak the verse, O Gotama,' thus learning the verse spoken by the Blessed One.

'Bhattābhihāre sudaṃ bhāsati' (recites at the time of serving food) means how he recites it; he recites it according to the Buddha's instruction. The Blessed One instructed the youth thus: 'Young man, do not recite this verse everywhere like an actor. Stand where the King eats. Do not recite it while he is eating the first morsels, but recite it when he takes the final morsel. Upon hearing it, the King will discard that morsel. Then, after the King washes his hands and the table is cleared, count the grains of rice, note the suitable curries, and the next day, have only that many grains of rice cooked. Recite it only at the morning meal, and do not recite it at the evening meal.'

The youth agreed, saying 'Very well.' Since he had gone to the Buddha after the King's morning meal that day, he recited the verse at the evening meal according to the Buddha's instruction. The King, remembering the Buddha's words, discarded the morsel even in the golden bowl, washed his hands, had the grains counted, and from the next day, had only that much rice cooked. By remaining within the measure of one nāḷika of rice (nāḷikodana), the youth visited the Buddha daily and became familiar. One day the Buddha asked, 'How much does the King eat?' He replied, 'Venerable Sir, the King eats only one nāḷika of rice.' The Buddha said, 'Young man, this measure is sufficient; this is the amount a middle-sized man should eat. From today, do not recite the verse anymore.' The King remained within that measure and was endowed with benefits in both this life and the hereafter.
141:
It was said. The King, remembering the words of the Buddha, discarded the morsel of food right into the golden bowl. After the King had washed his hands, he set aside the golden bowl, counted the grains of rice, and having determined the appropriate amount of curry, he had only that much rice cooked on the following day.

He remained established in the measure of food cooked from one nāḷika of rice. That youth Sudassana used to go to the presence of the Buddha daily and became an intimate of the Buddha. Then one day, the Buddha asked, "How much does the King eat?" The youth replied, "He eats food cooked from one nāḷika of rice." The Buddha said, "With this measure, a man's portion is sufficient; from this day forward, do not recite the verse." Thus, the King remained established in that very measure. In the phrase "benefit in the present life and benefit in the future life," the state of the body being lean and fit, free from fatness, is called the benefit in the present life (diṭṭhadhammikattha), and virtue (sīla) is called the benefit in the future life (samparāyikattha). This is because moderation in eating is a factor of virtue. The third sutta is finished.

## 4. Paṭhamasaṅgāmasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "Vedehiputto" means that Vedehī is a name for a wise person, thus it means the son of a wise mother. "Caturaṅginiṃ" refers to an army endowed with the four factors: elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. "Sannayhitvā" means having donned armor and accoutrements. "Saṅgāmesuṃ" means they fought a battle. For what reason did they fight? It is heard that when King Mahākosala gave his daughter to King Bimbisāra, he gave the village of Kāsī, which yields a revenue of one hundred thousand, as a gift to his daughter, situated between the two kingdoms. When King Ajātasattu killed his father, the mother also died not long after due to the sorrow of separation from the King. Then King Pasenadi Kosala, saying, "Ajātasattu has killed his parents; this village belongs to my father," made a claim for that village. Ajātasattu also said, "It belongs to my mother," and thus the two kings, uncle and nephew, fought for that village.

Because he has evil persons such as Devadatta as friends, he is called "pāpamitta" (one with evil friends). Because those very persons are his companions, he is "pāpasahāyo." Because his mind is inclined and bent towards them, he is "pāpasampavaṅko." In the case of King Pasenadi, his state of having good friends (kalyāṇamitta) through the influence of the Elder Sāriputta and others should be understood. "Dukkhaṃ seti" means he will sleep in suffering, repeatedly grieving over the lost elephants, horses, and so on. The Buddha said this after seeing again the cause of that King's victory. "Jayaṃ veraṃ pasavati" means the victor breeds hatred and acquires an enemy. The fourth sutta is finished.
142:
## 5. Dutiyasaṅgāmasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "Abbhuyyāsī" means that having lost the battle and being subject to reproach, he went to the monastery and while listening to the conversation of the monks, he heard the reason for victory spoken by an elderly monk named Buddharakkhita to another elderly monk named Dhammarakkhita during the night: "If the King were to go using this strategy, he would win again." Having heard this, he set out for battle.

"Yāvassa upakappati" means as long as it is convenient for him and he is able to plunder. "Yadā caññe" means when others plunder. "Vilumpantī" means they plunder that person who remains after plundering. "Vilumpati" means he is plundered. "Ṭhānaṃ hi maññati" means he considers it a reason. "Yadā" means at which time. "Jetāraṃ labhate jayaṃ" means the person who conquers later meets one who will conquer him. "Rosetāraṃ" refers to one who harms or oppresses. "Rosako" means an oppressor. "Kammavivaṭṭena" means by the turn of kamma, or by the ripening of the result of that act of plundering. "So vilutto viluppati" means that plunderer is plundered in return. The fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Mallikāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "Upasaṅkami" means that at the time Queen Mallikā was about to give birth, the King had the delivery room prepared and provided protection, and then he approached. "Anattamano ahosi" means he became displeased, thinking, "I gave great sovereignty to my daughter who came from a poor family; if she had a son, he would have attained great honor, but now she has fallen away from that." "Seyyā" means a certain woman is indeed better than a son of dull wisdom or one who is mute. "Posā" means than men. By the word "Janādhipā," he addresses the King, the lord of people. "Sassudevā" means one who honors her parents-in-law like gods. "Disampati" means the King, the lord of the directions. "Tādisā subhariyā" means a son born of such a good wife, endowed with virtue and wisdom, can discipline and rule the country. The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Appamādasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "Samadhiggayha" means having taken up or having acquired. "Appamādo" refers to the heedfulness that causes wholesome states to be performed. "Samodhānaṃ" means gathering together or inclusion. "Evameva kho" means that just as the elephant's footprint is the chief, so is heedfulness that causes actions, while the remaining wholesome states of the four planes are like the other footprints. Just as all those footprints are included within the elephant's footprint, all wholesome states are included within heedfulness. they revolve only within heedfulness. Alternatively, just as the elephant's footprint is said to be the best among all footprints, the Buddha shows that heedfulness is the best among the remaining states. Because this heedfulness is the cause for attaining the supramundane states, even though it is a state of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), it is superior even to the lofty (mahaggata) and supramundane states.
143:
Just as the footprints of all other living beings are contained within the footprint of an elephant, so too the wholesome states belonging to the four planes are contained within heedfulness (appamāda); they revolve only within heedfulness. Just as the elephant's footprint is the foremost and best among all footprints, so too heedfulness is the foremost among all other states—this is the meaning shown. This heedfulness, though being a mundane (lokiya) state, is indeed superior even to the sublime (mahaggata) and supramundane (lokuttara) states in the sense of being the means for their attainment.

'They praise heedfulness' (appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti) means that the wise praise heedfulness alone, saying, 'One who desires such benefits as long life and so forth should practice only heedfulness.' Alternatively, because the wise praise heedfulness in the grounds for making merit (puṇya-kiriya-vatthu), therefore one who desires benefits such as long life should practice only heedfulness—this is the meaning. 'Through the attainment of the goal' (atthābhisamayā) means one is called wise because of obtaining the benefit. The seventh sutta (ends).

## 8. Commentary on the Kalyāṇamittasutta

In the eighth sutta, 'And that [Dhamma] is for one with a good friend' (so ca kho kalyāṇamittassa) means that this well-expounded Dhamma is indeed called 'well-expounded' for one who has a good friend, not for one with an evil friend. For although the Dhamma is well-expounded for everyone, it fulfills the purpose in accordance with virtue and so forth only for one with a good friend who listens attentively and has faith, just like medicine fulfills the purpose of curing disease only for one who uses it, not for one who does not. Because of this fulfillment of purpose, this was said. Here, 'Dhamma' should be understood as the Dhamma of teaching (desanā-dhamma).

'This is half' (upaḍḍhamidaṃ): It is said that the Elder Ānanda, while in seclusion, reflected: 'This so-called ascetic practice (samaṇa-dhamma) is perfected for one who has a good friend as a mentor and instructor, and who stands firm in his own personal effort. Half of the benefit comes from the good friend, and half from personal effort.' Then it occurred to the Elder: 'Standing in limited knowledge (padesa-ñāṇa), I cannot reflect without limitation (nippadesaṃ). I shall ask the Teacher and become free from doubt.' Therefore, he approached the Teacher and spoke thus. 'Of the holy life' (brahmacariyassa) means of the Noble Path. 'That is, good friendship' (yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatā) means that which is called good friendship is half; the meaning is that the other half of the benefit comes from [one's own effort]. Thus, the Elder said, 'Half and half of the factors such as right view come from a good friend, and half and half come from personal effort.' However, this was merely the Elder's wishful thought. For example, when many people set up stone pillars, it is impossible to distinguish, 'This much space was set up by so-and-so, and that much by so-and-so'; and just as with children born depending on parents, it is impossible to distinguish, 'This much part is from the mother, and that much from the father'; in the same way, this matter also has a nature that cannot be distinguished. 'This much...
144:
...among the states such as right view, it is impossible to obtain a distinction like 'This much of the state arose from the good friend, and this much from personal effort.' However, because half of the virtue is obtained through having a good friend, it became known as 'half' according to the Elder Ānanda's inclination. Because the entire virtue is obtained [through the friend as the root], it became known as 'the whole' according to the Blessed One's inclination. This 'good friendship' (kalyāṇamittatā) is taken as the factor for the attainment of the preliminary stage. In terms of meaning, it refers to the four aggregates [of the path] consisting of virtue, concentration, and insight, obtained by depending on a good friend. Teachers also call it the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).

'Do not say so, Ānanda' means 'Ānanda, do not speak thus. You are one of great learning, one who has attained the analytical knowledges of a trainee (sekha-paṭisambhidā), you serve me having accepted the eight boons, and you are endowed with four wonderful and marvelous qualities. It is not proper for such a person to speak in this way.' 'Ānanda, this good friendship is indeed the entire holy life (sakala-brahmacariya)'—the Blessed One said this referring to the fact that the four paths, the four fruits, the three true knowledges, and the six direct knowledges are all rooted in good friendship. Now, wishing to show the reason through verbal explanation, he said 'This is for one with a good friend' (kalyāṇamittasse'taṃ) and so forth. In that Pali, 'is to be expected' (pāṭikaṅkhaṃ) means it should be desired, it is inevitable.

'Here' (idha) means in this Dispensation. In 'develops right view' (sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāveti) and so forth, this is the brief commentary on the first eight terms: Right view has the characteristic of right seeing. Right intention has the characteristic of right application. Right speech has the characteristic of right grasping. Right action has the characteristic of right originating. Right livelihood has the characteristic of right purification. Right effort has the characteristic of right exertion. Right mindfulness has the characteristic of right establishment. Right concentration has the characteristic of right composure.

Among them, each has three functions. Namely: First, right view abandons wrong view along with its own opposing defilements, takes Nibbāna as its object, and sees the associated states without delusion by dispelling the delusion that covers them. Right intention and the others likewise abandon wrong intention and so forth, and take Nibbāna as their object. Specifically, here, right view shows the co-nascent states rightly. Right intention applies the co-nascent states rightly. Right speech grasps them rightly. Right action...
145:
Right Action (sammākammanta) causes the conascent states (sahajāta-dhammā) to arise well. Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva) purifies the conascent states well. Right Effort (sammāvāyāma) exerts the conascent states well. Right Mindfulness (sammāsati) establishes the conascent states well. Right Concentration (sammāsamādhi) places the conascent states well in equilibrium.

Alternatively, this Right View (sammādiṭṭhi), in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga), has various moments due to repeated occurrences and has various objects such as impermanent form, etc. However, at the time of the Path (maggakāla), it has a single moment and a single object, which is Nibbāna. In terms of function, Right View receives four names such as 'knowledge of suffering' (dukkhe ñāṇaṃ), etc. Right Intention (sammāsaṅkappa) and the other factors also have various moments and various objects in the preliminary stage. At the time of the Path, they have a single moment and a single object, which is Nibbāna. Among them, Right Intention receives three names in terms of function, such as 'intention of renunciation' (nekkhamma-saṅkappa), etc. The three factors starting with Right Speech (sammāvācā) can be both abstinences (virati) and volitions (cetanā). But at the moment of the Path, they are only abstinences. This pair, Right Effort and Right Mindfulness, also receives four names in terms of function by way of the right efforts (sammappadhāna) and the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Right Concentration, however, remains only Right Concentration both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the Path.

Having thus first understood the explanation of the meanings of the eight initial terms mentioned by the method starting with 'Right View', one should now understand the terms starting with 'develops based on seclusion' (bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ) as follows: 'Develops' (bhāveti) means to increase, to cause to arise repeatedly in one's own mental continuum, to bring into existence. 'Based on seclusion' (vivekanissitaṃ) means depending on seclusion or situated in seclusion. Seclusion (viveka) is the state of being secluded. This seclusion is fivefold: seclusion by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-viveka), seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka), seclusion by eradication (samuccheda-viveka), seclusion by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-viveka), and seclusion by escape (nissaraṇa-viveka). Among these five types of seclusion, it should be understood that one develops Right View based on seclusion by substitution of opposites, based on seclusion by eradication, and based on seclusion by escape. For instance, this practitioner (yogī) devoted to the development of the Noble Path develops Right View which, at the moment of insight (vipassanā), is based on seclusion by substitution of opposites in terms of function, and based on seclusion by escape in terms of inclination (with the desire to realize Nibbāna); but at the time of the Path, it is based on seclusion by eradication in terms of function, and based on seclusion by escape in terms of object. This same method applies to 'based on dispassion' (virāganissitaṃ), etc., because dispassion, etc., have the same meaning as seclusion.

In fact, here, relinquishment (vossagga) is of two kinds: relinquishment as giving up (pariccāga-vossagga) and relinquishment as entering into (pakkhandana-vossagga). Among them, 'relinquishment as giving up' is the abandoning of defilements by way of substitution of opposites at the moment of insight, and by way of eradication at the moment of the Path. 'Relinquishment as entering into' is the entering into Nibbāna by way of being inclined towards it at the moment of insight, and by way of making it the object at the moment of the Path. Both of these in this mundane...
146: It is appropriate in the method of explaining the meaning mixed with the supramundane. For this Right View (Sammādiṭṭhi) abandons the defilements (kilesas) according to the aforementioned method and plunges into Nibbāna. By the entire phrase "vossaggapariṇāmi" (leading to relinquishment), it means the sense of being inclined toward, having inclined toward, maturing toward, and having matured toward the benefit of relinquishment. This bhikkhu, devoted to the development of the Noble Path (ariyamaɡɡa), develops Right View so that it matures and has matured for the benefit of relinquishment, which is the abandoning of defilements, and for the benefit of relinquishment, which is the plunging into Nibbāna. The same method applies to the remaining path factors. "Āɡamma" means having based on, having aimed at, or depending on. "Jātidhammā" refers to (beings) who have the nature of being born or the character of being born. "Tasmā" (therefore) is because even the entire Noble Path is obtained by depending on a noble friend (kalyāṇamitta). "Handa" is an exclamation in the sense of determination. "Appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti" means they praise heedfulness (appamāda); therefore, heedfulness should be practiced. "Atthābhisamayā" is because of the attainment of the benefit. The eighth sutta (ends). ## 9. Commentary on the First Aputtaka Sutta. In the ninth sutta, "divā divassa" means the day of the day, meaning at the time of midday. "Sāpateyya" is wealth. Regarding gold and silver treasures—consisting of gold, silver, copper, iron, plowshares, tortoise-shaped items, etc., whether made into solid blocks or into utensils such as plates and bowls—there is no need to speak further. It means there is no way even to define it by saying, "It is this much." "Kaṇājaka" is rice cooked with rice bran. "Bilaṅgadutiya" is rice with sour gruel as the second (side dish). "Sāṇa" is clothing made of hemp. "Tipakkhavasana" is a garment made by sewing three pieces in two places. "Asappurisa" is a bad man. In the terms beginning with "uddhaggika," it is called "uddhaggika" because it has a superior (uddha) result (agga) by way of giving fruit in higher and higher planes. It is called "sovaggika" because it is for the benefit of heaven by producing rebirth there. It is called "sukhavipāka" because it has a happy result in the places of rebirth. It is called "saggasaṃvattanika" because it produces the noble distinctions of celestial appearance and so on. One does not establish (give) such a noble gift. "Sātodakā" refers to (a lake) with sweet water. "Setodakā" refers to having white water because of the whiteness of the water where waves break. "Supatitthā" means having good landing places. People do not take that water with pots and vessels. They do not perform any of the tasks that should be done with that water. Just as that water remains without being drunk or used by anyone (so too is that person's wealth useless). "Kiccākaro ca hoti" means being one who performs his own duties and performs meritorious deeds; he eats, manages affairs, and gives gifts.
147:
A person should not carry away that sweet water after filling it in vessels. "Na yathāpaccayaṃ vā kareyya" means that one should not perform any of the various tasks that ought to be done with water. "Tadapeyyamānaṃ" means that the water remains in a state where not even a single person should drink or use it. "Kiccakaro ca hotī" means being one who performs one's own duties as well as meritorious deeds; he eats, engages in various works, and gives gifts. The ninth sutta ends.

## 10. Dutiya-aputtakasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "piṇဍapātena paṭipādesi" means he provided alms-food; it means he gave alms-food. "Pakkāmi" means he went away for some business, such as attending to the king. The meaning of the phrase "pacchā vippaṭisārī ahosi" should be understood as follows: The merchant had seen that Paccekabuddha on other days as well, but the thought of giving had never arisen in him. On that day, however, this Paccekabuddha named Taggarasikhī, the third son of Queen Padumavatī, having spent time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) on Mount Gandhamādana, arose from the attainment in the morning, washed his face in Lake Anotatta, dressed in his lower robe on the Manosilātala stone slab, fastened his girdle, took his bowl and robes, entered the fourth jhāna which is the basis for direct knowledge, flew into the air by psychic power, descended near the city gate, donned his robes, took his bowl, and reached the merchant's door in due order with an inspiring gait, as if placing a bundle of a thousand coins at the doors of the city dwellers.

On that day, the merchant had risen early, eaten choice food, and was sitting at the entrance of his house, cleaning his teeth, after having a seat prepared. Seeing the Paccekabuddha, and because he was sitting there having already eaten in the morning, a mind of giving arose. He called his wife and said, "Give alms-food to this recluse," and then departed.

The merchant's wife thought: "For so long a time, I have never heard this man say 'Give.' Even when he asks to give today, he is not asking to give to just anyone, but to a Paccekabuddha who is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, who has discarded defilements, and who has laid down the burden. I will not give just any food, but will offer choice alms-food." She went out of the house, paid homage to the Paccekabuddha with the fivefold prostration, took his bowl, invited him to sit on a prepared seat inside the house, prepared alms-food with very pure Sāli rice, and having noted the appropriate snacks, curries, and soups, filled the bowl, decorated it externally with perfumes, and offered it to the Paccekabuddha.
148:
(The merchant's wife) placed the bowl in his hands and paid homage. The Paccekabuddha, thinking "I will also support other Paccekabuddhas," departed after giving a blessing (anumodanā) without eating yet. The merchant, returning from outside, saw the Paccekabuddha and asked, "We departed after saying 'Give alms-food to the Venerable One'; did you receive alms-food?" "Yes, merchant, I received it," (he replied). "Let me see," he said, lifting his neck to look. Then the aroma of the alms-food arose and struck his nostrils. Being unable to restrain his mind, he later felt remorse (vippaṭisāra).

The words beginning with "Varametaṃ" show the manner in which the remorse arose. Regarding the phrase "He deprived his brother's only son of life for the sake of wealth": At that time, it is said, his parents and elder brother died before the family estate was divided. He lived together with his brother's wife. His brother had one son. People would say to the boy playing in the street, "This male slave, this female slave, this vehicle, this wealth—these belong to you." The boy, taking their words to heart, would say, "This slave belongs to me," and so on.

Then his uncle thought, "This boy is speaking like this even now; when he grows up, he will have the estate divided in the middle. I will do what should be done to him right now." One day, taking an axe, he said, "Come, son, let's go to the forest." He took him to the forest and, while the boy was crying and lamenting, killed him, threw him into a pit, and covered him with earth. This was said in reference to this incident. "Seven times" means occurring for seven times. Here, the meaning should be understood by the power of the preceding and succeeding volitions (cetanā). For in a single offering of alms-food, a single volition cannot give two rebirths. It is only because of the preceding and succeeding volitions that he was reborn seven times in heaven and seven times in a merchant's family. "Old" refers to the kamma of the volition of the alms-food given to the Paccekabuddha.

"Possessions" (pariggaha) means the things that were possessed. "Dependents" (anujīvino) refers to the people, such as fifty or sixty families, who live depending on one great family. "One must go without taking everything" means one must depart without taking all these riches. "Everything is of the nature of being left behind" means all these things are of the nature of being deposited, of the nature of being abandoned. The tenth sutta ends.

## Chapter Two.

## 3. Tatiya Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Puggala Sutta

In the first sutta of the third vagga, the word "tama" (darkness) refers to being associated with darkness through the phrase "nīce kule paccājāto" (born into a low family) and so on. One is called "tamaparāyana" (bound for darkness) because one again approaches the darkness of hell through bodily misconduct and so forth. In both these ways, it refers only to the darkness of the aggregates (khandha). Through the phrase "ucce kule paccājāto" (born into a high family) and so on, one is called "joti" (light) because of being associated with light; it means one who has become enlightened. One is called "jotiparāyana" (bound for light) because one again approaches the state of light, which is rebirth in the celestial realm, through bodily good conduct and so forth. In this manner, the other two types of persons should also be understood.

"Veṇakula" refers to the family of bamboo-weavers. "Nesādakula" refers to the family of hunters and the like. "Rathakārakula" refers to the family of chariot-makers (leather-workers). "Pukkusakula" refers to the family of flower-scavengers. "Kasiravutti" refers to one who lives a life of hardship. "Dubbaṇṇa" refers to one who has a complexion like a burnt stump, similar to an earth-spirit (paṃsupisāca). "Duddasika" refers to one whose appearance is unpleasant even to the mother who just gave birth. "Okoṭimaka" refers to one who is dwarfish and short in stature. "Kāṇa" refers to one who is blind in one eye or both eyes. "Kuṇī" refers to one who has one crooked hand or both hands crooked. "Khañja" refers to one who is lame in one foot or both feet. "Pakkhahata" refers to one who is paralyzed on one side and moves on a stool (pīṭhasappī). "Padīpeyya" refers to lighting requisites such as oil lamps and bowls. In the phrase "evaṃ kho mahārāja," a certain person, without seeing light externally, dies within the mother's womb and, being reborn in the states of deprivation (apāya), wanders through saṃsāra for an entire aeon; such a person is also "tamotamaparāyana" (bound for the deepest darkness). That person would be a deceitful person (kuhaka). It is said that such a birth occurs for a deceitful person.

Here also, through the words "nīce kule paccājāto hoti caṇḍālakule vā" and so on, the failure of arrival (āgamanavipatti) and the failure of past causes (pubbuppannapaccayavipatti) are shown. Through the words "dalidde" and so on, the failure of current conditions (pavattapaccayavipatti) is shown. Through the words "kasiravuttike" and so on, the failure of the means of livelihood (ājīvūpāyavipatti) is shown.
150:
Through the words "dubbaṇṇa" and so on, the failure of the physical form (attabhāvavipatti) is shown. Through the words "bavhābādha" and so on, the combination of the causes of suffering is shown. Through the words "na lābhī" and so on, both the failure of the causes of happiness and the failure of the enjoyment of wealth are shown. Through the words "kāyena duccaritaṃ" and so on, the combination of causes for being bound for darkness in the future life is shown. Through the words "kāyassa bhedā" and so on, the arrival at the darkness of hell in the future life is shown. The bright side (sukkapakka) should be understood by the opposite method of what has been stated.

"Akkosati" means reviling by way of the ten grounds for reviling. "Paribhāsati" means scolding with threatening words such as, "Why are you standing there? Have you done our plowing work and so on?" "Rosaka" refers to one who is offensive and irritable. "Abyaggamanasa" refers to one who has an undistracted and concentrated mind. The first sutta ends.

## 2. Commentary on the Ayyikā Sutta

In the second sutta, "jiṇṇā" means decayed by old age. "Vuḍḍhā" means advanced in age. "Mahallikā" means elderly by birth. "Addhagatā" means having passed through a long period of time. "Vayoanuppattā" means having reached the final stage of life. Regarding "piyā manāpā," it is said that when the King's mother died, the grandmother took the mother's place and cared for him; therefore, the King developed a powerful love for his grandmother. That is why he spoke thus. "Hatthirataneṇa" refers to an elephant treasure worth one hundred thousand, adorned with ornaments worth one hundred thousand. The same method applies to the horse treasure. "Gāmavaro" also refers to an excellent village yielding a revenue of one hundred thousand. "Sabbāni tāni bhedanadhammāni" means that among the pots made by potters, some break while being made, some break after being made but before being removed from the wheel, some break just as they are removed and placed on the ground, and some break after that. Similarly, among beings, some die at the moment of conception, some die in the mother's womb while the fetus is confused and before coming out, some die just as they are born, and some die after that. Therefore, he spoke thus. The second sutta ends.

In the third sutta, the entire meaning is clear. The third sutta ends.

## 4. Commentary on the Issatta Sutta

The composition of the fourth sutta should be understood by its origin (aṭṭhuppatti). It is said that during the early Enlightenment of the Blessed One, great gain and honor arose for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks. The ascetics of other sects (titthiyas), having lost their gain and honor, wandered among the families complaining: "The ascetic Gotama says, 'Gifts should be given only to me, not to others; they should be given only to my disciples, not to the disciples of others. Only gifts given to me are of great fruit, not those given to others; only gifts given to my disciples are of great fruit, not those given to the disciples of others.' While he himself lives depending on alms-gathering, it is improper for him to create obstacles to the requisites and gains of others who also live by alms-gathering, yet he does so." Thus they wandered about disparaging him. That talk spread and reached the King's palace. When the King heard it, he thought, "This statement that the Tathāgata creates obstacles to the gains of others cannot be logical."
151:
The ascetic Gotama says, "Gifts should be given only to me, not to others. Gifts should be given only to my disciples, not to others' disciples. Only what is given to me is of great fruit, not what is given to others. Only what is given to my disciples is of great fruit, not what is given to others' disciples." Is it appropriate for one who himself relies on alms-gathering to cause an obstacle to the four requisites of others who also rely on alms-gathering? He does what is inappropriate; he does what is unsuitable. This talk spread and reached the royal palace. When the King heard it, he thought, "It is impossible that the Tathāgata would cause an obstacle to the gains of others. These people are striving for the Tathāgata's loss of gain and ill-repute. If I, staying here in the palace, were to say, 'Do not speak thus; the Teacher does not say so,' this talk would not reach a resolution. I will clarify it only when this great multitude has assembled." Thus, he remained silent, waiting for a certain festival day.

Later, when the great festival day arrived, thinking, "This is the time to make this known," he had the drum sounded throughout the city: "Whether one has faith or no faith, whether one holds right view or wrong view, except for those staying to guard the house, children, and women, if the rest do not come to the monastery, they shall be fined fifty [units]." He himself bathed early in the morning, had his breakfast, and, adorned with all ornaments, went to the monastery with a great army. While going, he thought, "It is not appropriate to ask directly, 'Venerable Sir, do you say, "Gifts should be given only to me... (pe)... giving to others' disciples is not of great fruit"?' I will only ask a question. When the Blessed One answers the question, he will break the doctrine of the heretics at the end." Desiring to ask a question, the King said, "Venerable Sir, where should a gift be given?" "Yattha" means in whichever person the heart feels confidence, to that person it should be given; this is the meaning.

When this was said, the King looked at those people who had come to report the words of the heretics. As soon as they were looked at by the King, they became crestfallen, with downcast faces, and stood scratching the ground with their big toes. The King, wishing to let the great multitude hear, spoke with a loud voice, "Venerable Sir, the heretics are defeated by just a single word." Having spoken thus, he said, "Venerable Sir, as for the heart, in whichever person among the Nigaṇṭhas, Acelakas, Paribbājakas, and so on..."
152:
"Venerable Sir, where does a gift given bear great fruit?" he asked. The Blessed One said, "Great King, the question you asked first and the question you asked later are different. Note this meaning well; however, the responsibility of explaining the problem is mine," and he spoke the verse beginning with "Sīlavato kho."

In that Pali, "tyassā" means it would be to you in this world. "Samupabyūḷha" means being gathered in a mass. "Asikkhita" means not yet trained in the art of archery. "Akatahattha" means the hand has not yet been trained in such things as gripping the bow. "Akatayogga" means practice has not yet been performed on heaps of grass, heaps of clay, and so on. "Akatūpāsana" means the skill of shooting arrows has not yet been demonstrated to kings and great ministers. "Chambhī" means having a trembling body.

In the phrases such as "kāmacchando pahīno," sensual desire is abandoned by the path of Arahantship; ill-will is abandoned by the path of Non-returning; sloth and torpor and restlessness are abandoned only by the path of Arahantship; remorse is abandoned only by the path of Non-returning; and doubt is abandoned by the path of Stream-entry. "Asekhena sīlakkhandhena" refers to the aggregate of virtue of an Arahant, which is called the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekha). This method applies to all the terms. Here, by the first four terms, mundane and supramundane virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation are taught. "Vimuttiñāṇadassana" (knowledge and vision of liberation) is reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), and it is purely mundane.

"Issattaṃ" means the art of archery. In the term "balavīriyaṃ," "bala" (power) is the wind element, and "vīriya" (effort) is just physical and mental energy. "Bhare" means one should support. "Nāsuaraṃ jātipaccayā" means one should not support (or honor) a coward simply because he is of noble birth.

In the term "khantisoraccaṃ," "khanti" is patience as endurance (adhivāsana-khanti), and "soracca" (gentleness) is the state of Arahantship. "Dhammā" refers to these two qualities. "Assame" means in hermitages. "Vivane" means in forest areas; it means one should construct square ponds and so on in waterless forests. "Dugge" means in uneven places. "Saṅkamanāni" means one should construct walkways fifty or sixty cubits long, spread with pure white sand.

Now, wishing to show the alms-gathering duties of the monks living in those forest dwellings, he spoke the words beginning with "annaṃ pānaṃ." There, "senāsanāni" means beds, stools, and so on. "Vippasannena" means that even when giving to an Arahant, one should not give with a mind defiled by the defilement of doubt, but should give only with an especially clear and confident heart. "Thanayaṃ" means thundering. "Satakkakū" means having countless peaks (many peaks). "Abhisaṅkhacca" means having prepared, gathered together, and made into a heap.
153:
Āmodamāno means having a joyful mind. Pakireti means scattering in the context of giving, or giving a gift as if distributing it. Puññadhārā refers to the streams of merit consisting of many intentions of giving. Dātāraṃ abhivassati means that just as streams of water coming from rain clouds in the sky rain down, moistening, softening, and soaking the earth, in the same way, the stream of merit arising within the donor moistens, fills, and overflows that very donor. Thus it is said, "it rains upon the giver." The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Pabbatūpamasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, muddhāvasittānaṃ refers to kings who have had the consecration poured upon their heads through the royal consecration. Kāmagedhapariyuṭṭhitānaṃ refers to those who are surrounded and oppressed by greed for sensual pleasures. Janapadatthāvariyappattānaṃ refers to those who have attained stability in the realm. Rājakaraṇīyāni refers to royal duties and affairs to be performed by kings. Tesu khvāhaṃ means "In those [royal duties], I..." Ussukkamāpanno means having reached the state of exertion. It is heard that this king used to go to attend upon the Blessed One three times a day, and there were also many travels in between. The military force of the king who went thus regularly was sometimes large and sometimes small. Then one day, five hundred robbers thought, "This king goes to attend upon the ascetic Gotama at an unusual time with a small force; let us capture him on the way and take over the kingdom." Those robbers hid in the Andhavana forest. Kings are indeed of great merit. Then, one man from among those robbers came out and informed the king. The king took a large military force, surrounded the Andhavana forest, and captured all those robbers. From the Andhavana forest to the city gate, on both sides of the road, he had stakes planted close together and had them impaled on the stakes, as if they were looking into each other's eyes. Referring to this incident, he spoke thus.

Then the Teacher thought, "If I say, 'Great King, while a Samma Sambuddha like me is residing in a nearby monastery, you have committed such a cruel deed; what you have done is improper,' then this king might become dejected and unable to remain steady. Only if I teach the Dhamma by a figurative method will he be able to take my words to heart." Thinking thus, [he gave] the Dhamma teaching...
154: While the Buddha was preaching the Dhamma, considering that [the King] would remember, He spoke the words beginning with "Taṃ kiṃ maññasi" (What do you think?). In that text, "saddhāyika" means one who should be believed, one whose words you, O King, believe. "Paccayika" is a synonym for that same "saddhāyika," meaning one whose words are trusted. "Abbhasama" means like the sky. "Nippothento āɡacchati" means he comes crushing and grinding all beings from the surface of the earth up to the Akanittha Brahma realm, like grass powder that has been finely ground. "Aññatra dhammacariyāya" means there is no other duty to be done except the practice of Dhamma; it is said that only the practice of Dhamma, known as the ten courses of wholesome action (kusalakamma-patha), should be performed. Terms such as "samacariyā" are merely synonyms for that "dhammacariyā." "Ārocemi" means I inform; "paṭivedayāmi" means I make known. "Adhivattati" means it overwhelms or oppresses. "Hatthiyuddhāni" are battles fought by mounting elephants adorned with gold ornaments, like the elephant Nāḷāgiri. "Gati" means the accomplishment (result) through military means. "Visayo" means opportunity (place) or capability. It is not possible to ward off old age and death with those fourfold armies of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. "Mantino mahāmattā" are great ministers endowed with counsel, like the wise Mahosadha and Vidhura. "Bhūmiɡataṃ" is wealth placed in large bronze pots and buried in the ground. "Vehāsaṭṭhaṃ" is wealth placed in leather bags and hung from rafters or placed in the upper chambers of palaces. "Upalāpetuṃ" means to cause division among one another. It means one cannot entice (the enemy) as one might act to prevent two people from traveling the same path. "Nabhaṃ āhacca" means filling up to the sky. In this sutta, "evaṃ jarā ca maccu ca," although only two mountains are taken, in the Rājovāda it is stated that four great mountains—old age (jarā), death (maraṇa), sickness (byādhi), and failure (vipatti)—come, as it is said, "Old age comes plundering all youth." "Tasmā" is because old age and death cannot be conquered by elephant battles and so on. "Saddhaṃ nivesaye" means one should instill or establish faith in the Triple Gem. This is the fifth sutta. ## The Third Chapter (Tatiyo Vaggo). ## Thus the Commentary on the Kosala Saṃyutta in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya, is finished.
155:
## 4. Māra Saṃyutta ## 1. Paṭhama Vagga ## 1. Tapokamma Sutta Commentary

In the first sutta of the Māra Saṃyutta, the phrase "Uruvelāyaṃ viharati" means that the Buddha, possessing the penetrated knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa), was staying in dependence on the village of Uruvelā. "Paṭhamābhisambuddho" means having just attained Enlightenment, specifically within the first seven days. "Dukkarakārikāya" refers to the performance of austerities that are difficult for others to perform, which he carried out for six full years. "Māro pāpimā": he is called "Māra" because he oppresses or kills beings who strive to transcend his domain, the sensual realm (kāma-bhūmi). He is called "Pāpimā" (the Evil One) because he incites others to evil, or because he himself is devoted to evil. Although he has many other names such as Kaṇha, Adhipati, Vasavattī, Antaka, Namuci, and Pamattabandhu, only these two names are used in this text. "Upasaṅkami" means he approached after thinking, "This ascetic Gotama thinks he is liberated from the defilements; I will tell him that he is not yet liberated."

"Tapokammā apakkammā" means having departed from the practice of austerities. "Aparaddho" means "You are far from the path of purity." "Amaraṃ tapaṃ" refers to the harsh asceticism performed for the sake of attaining immortality (amarabhāva); it is the devotion to self-mortification. "Sabbānatthāvahaṃ hoti" means he realized that "All these austerities do not bring about my welfare." "Phiyārittaṃva dhammani" means like an oar or a rudder on dry land in a forest. This is the meaning: for example, if people were to place a boat on dry land in a forest, fill it with goods, and then many people were to board it and try to pull or push it using oars and rudders, the effort of those people would be useless as it would not cause the boat to move even an inch or two; however, it does not necessarily bring about active harm. Similarly, I (the Buddha) realized that "All these ascetic practices for immortality bring no benefit," and thus I abandoned them.
156: Now, wishing to show the path by which the Buddha arose, having abandoned that amara-tapa (ascetic practice), he said 'Sīlaṃ' and so forth. In that statement, by the word 'Sīla', Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood are taken. By 'Samādhi', Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration are taken. By 'Paññā', Right View and Right Thought are taken. 'Maggaṃ bodhāya bhāvayanti' means developing this very Noble Eightfold Path for the sake of the benefit of knowledge (the Path). Here, 'bodhāya' means for the sake of the Path. Just as one cooks gruel only for the sake of gruel, or cooks cake only for the sake of cake, and does nothing else, so one develops the Path only for the sake of the Path. Therefore, he said 'Maggaṃ bodhāya bhāvayanti'. 'Paramaṃ suddhiṃ' refers to the Fruit of Arahantship. 'Nihato' means 'I have conquered you, Māra; I have made you lose.' The first sutta (commentary) ends. ## 2. Hatthirājavaṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā In the second sutta, 'rattandhakāratimisāyaṃ' means in the great darkness consisting of four factors that causes blindness at night. 'Abbhokāse nisinno hoti' means having come out from the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), he was sitting on a stone slab at the edge of the cloister walk, placing the great robe over his head, and undertaking the practice of supreme effort. Indeed, for the Tathāgata, there is no path undeveloped, no defilements unabandoned, no unshakable fruit (of Arahantship) unpenetrated, and no Nibbāna unrealized; so why did he do this? He did it to serve as an example (aṅkusatthaṃ) for sons of good family in the future. The Teacher did this, seeing clearly: 'In the future, sons of good family, reflecting on the path I have traveled, will think that living in the open air is truly worthy, and will perform the work of supreme effort.' 'Mahā' means great. 'Ariṭṭhako' means black. 'Maṇိ' means stone. 'Evamassa sīsaṃ hoti' means that the head of that Māra has such a form; it is black in color and resembles a large stone slab the size of a peaked house. 'Subhāsubhaṃ' means he says that while wandering in Saṃsāra for a long time, he has come after creating beautiful and ugly appearances. Alternatively, 'saṃsaranti' means while coming along wandering. 'Dīghamaddhānaṃ' means either the long journey from the Vasavatti heaven to Uruvelā, or the long time known as the period of difficult practices (dukkara-cariyā) for six years before Enlightenment. 'Vaṇṇāṃ katvā subhāsubhaṃ' means the meaning is that he has come to the presence of the Buddha many times, creating various beautiful and unbeautiful appearances. That appearance, however, does not truly exist.
157: Māra had never before come to the presence of the Blessed One with such an appearance for the purpose of causing terror. Therefore, the Blessed One said to that Māra, 'Alaṃ te tena'. The meaning of those words is: 'Even though you are making an effort by showing such a terrifying manner, it is of no use to you anymore.' The second sutta (Hatthirājavaṇṇasutta) ends. ## 3. Subhasuttavaṇṇanā In the third sutta, 'susaṃvutā' means those who are well-closed (by the Path). 'Na te māravasānugā' means 'Māra, those people do not follow your will.' 'Na te mārassa baddhagū' means those people are not your disciples who are constantly bound to you, Māra. The third sutta ends. ## 4. Paṭhamamārapāsasuttavaṇṇanā In the fourth sutta, 'yoniso manasikārā' means because of attending to the mind with proper means. 'Yoniso sammappadhānā' means because of appropriate effort, effort that is the cause of the result. 'Vimutti' refers to the liberation of the Fruit of Arahantship. 'Ajjhabhāsi' means Māra spoke after thinking: 'This ascetic Gotama, though he has reached Arahantship by making effort himself, is not yet satisfied and is now encouraging others also, saying "Reach it!"; I will hinder him.' 'Mārapāsena' means by the snare of defilements. 'Ye dibbā ye ca mānusā' means there are Māra's snares called divine sensual pleasures and human sensual pleasures; it means 'you are bound by all those snares.' 'Mārabandhanabaddho' means bound by Māra's bond, or bound in Māra's bond. 'Na me samaṇa mokkhasi' means 'Ascetic, you will not be free from my domain.' The fourth sutta ends. ## 5. Dutiyamārapāsasuttavaṇṇanā In the fifth sutta, 'muttāhaṃ' means 'I am liberated (from all bonds).' The previous sutta was preached during the rains retreat, but this sutta was preached at the time of emerging from the retreat (after Pavāraṇā). 'Cārikaṃ' means wandering on a journey in due order. He said, 'Wander, going no more than one league (yojana) each day after the retreat.' 'Mā ekena dve' means do not two people go by a single path. This was said because if they go together like this, when one preaches the Dhamma, the other must remain silent. 'Ādikalyāṇaṃ' means beautiful or good in the beginning. Likewise in the middle and the end. This goodness in the beginning, middle, and end is twofold: by way of the Dispensation (Sāsana) and by way of the Teaching (Desanā). Therein, in the Dispensation, virtue (sīla) is the beginning; tranquility (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and the Path (magga) are the middle; the Fruit (phala) and Nibbāna are the end. Or, virtue and concentration are the beginning; insight and the Path are the middle; the Fruit and Nibbāna are the end. Or, virtue, concentration, and insight are the beginning; the Path is the middle; the Fruit and Nibbāna are the end. In the Teaching, however, in a four-line verse, the first line is the beginning; the second and third lines are the middle; the fourth line is the end. In verses of five or six lines, the first line is the beginning; the last line is the end; the remaining lines are the middle. In a sutta with a single introduction (nidāna), the introduction is the beginning; the words starting with 'idamavoca' are the end; the remaining words are the middle. In a sutta with many introductions, the many words in the middle are just the middle. The introduction is the beginning; the words of the Blessed One starting with 'idamavoca' are the end. 'Sātthaṃ' means preach making it complete with meaning. 'Sabyañjanaṃ' means preach making it complete with sounds and words.
158:
That beginning, middle, and end are twofold: by way of the Dispensation (sāsana) and by way of the Teaching (desanā). Among those two, the beginning of the Dispensation is virtue (sīla); the middle is serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and the Path (magga); and the end is the Fruition (phala) and Nibbāna. Alternatively, virtue and concentration (samādhi) are the beginning; insight and the Path are the middle; and the Fruition and Nibbāna are the end. Or, virtue, concentration, and insight are the beginning; the Path is the middle; and the Fruition and Nibbāna are the end.

In the Teaching, in a verse of four lines (pādas), the first line is the beginning; the second and third lines are the middle; and the fourth line is the end. In verses of five or six lines, the first line is the beginning; the last line is the end; and the remaining lines are the middle. In a sutta with a single sequence (anusandhi), the introduction (nidāna) is the beginning; the words "idamavoca" are the end; and the remaining words are the middle. In a sutta with many sequences, the many sequences in the middle are simply the middle; the introduction is the beginning; and the words "idamavoca" are the end.

"Sātthaṃ" means preach it making it complete with the meaning. "Sabyañjanaṃ" means preach it making it complete with the sounds and words. "Kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ" means entirely complete. "Parisuddhaṃ" means without the impurities of defilements. "Brahmacariyaṃ" means the holy life of the Dispensation, which is comprised of the threefold training (sikkhā). "Pakāsetha" means make it clear.

"Apparajakkhajātika" means those who by nature have little dust of defilements in their eye of wisdom; it means there are those capable of reaching Arahantship at the end of a four-line verse, as if being uncovered from a white cloth screen. "Assavanatā" means because of not hearing. "Parihāyantī" means they decline from the Dhamma through non-attainment and loss. "Senānigama" is either a village established at the place where the army of the first people of the aeon stayed, or it is the market town named Senānī, the father of Sujātā. "Tenupasaṅkamissāmi" means "I will not stay here sending you away and having monasteries and such built to be attended to by supporters; instead, I will approach the three matted-hair ascetics (jaṭilas) to preach the Dhamma after showing them three and a half thousand miracles." "Tenupasaṅkami" means Māra approached, thinking: "This ascetic Gotama, like a general directing a great battle, sends out sixty people saying, 'Let not two go by one way, preach the Dhamma'; I have no pleasure in my mind even when this one person is preaching the Dhamma, so how will it be when so many are preaching? I will stop him." The fifth sutta ends.

## 6. Commentary on the Sappa Sutta
In the sixth sutta, "soṇḍikākilañjaṃ" is the mat used by brewers for spreading flour. "Kosalikā kaṃsapātī" is the bronze bowl used by the King of Kosala, which is the size of a chariot wheel.
159:
It is a bronze bowl used as a utensil. 'Gaḷagaḷāyanta' means roaring or thundering. 'Kammāragaggariyā' refers to the nozzle of a blacksmith's bellows. 'Dhamamānāya' means being filled with air from the bellows. The phrase 'knowing thus' refers to understanding that 'The ascetic Gotama is seated comfortably, exerting himself in meditation; I will disturb him,' and then seeing Mara, who had created a manifold physical form as described and was wandering here and there on the ground, by the light of a flash of lightning, and reflecting, 'Who is this being?' and thus knowing, 'This is Mara.'

'Suññagehāni' means empty or secluded places. 'Seyyā' is for the purpose of resting. It means that a sage frequents secluded places for the purpose of 'I shall stand, I shall walk, I shall sit, I shall lie down.' 'That sage is self-restrained' means that the Buddha-sage has a self-restrained physical form, being free from restlessness of hands and feet. 'He should wander there having relinquished' means he should wander having relinquished and abandoned attachment and longing for that physical body. Indeed, for such a Buddha-sage of that nature, it is fitting, proper, and appropriate to wander having relinquished attachment to the physical body.

'Carakā' refers to wandering creatures such as lions and tigers. 'Bheravā' refers to both animate and inanimate terrors. Among them, animate terrors are lions, tigers, and so on; inanimate terrors are tree stumps, anthills, and so on, which appear like ogres at night. Even those stumps and anthills appear like ogres at that time, and all things like ropes and creepers appear like snakes. In the presence of such terrifying objects, the Buddha-sage who has reached a secluded place does not show even a slight tremor of his body hairs.

Now, to show the contemplation of the impossible, he said 'The sky might split,' and so on. In that verse, 'phaleyya' means it might split into shreds like a crow's foot. 'Caleyya' means it might tremble like a drop of water on a lotus leaf struck by the wind. 'Even if they should pierce the chest with an arrow' means even if they should cause a sharp sword-like arrow to pierce the chest (to torment). 'Upadhīsu' means in the acquisitions (upadhi) of the aggregates. 'They do not seek protection' means that when the chest is being pierced by a sharp arrow, ordinary people seek protection by entering thickets or caves out of fear. The Buddhas, however, having completely cut off all fear, do not seek such protection. The sixth sutta is finished.
160:
## 7. Supatisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, 'pāde pakkhāletvā' means having washed the feet for the purpose of obtaining coolness. On the bodies of the Buddhas, however, dust and dirt do not adhere; even water rolls off like a drop of water poured onto a lotus leaf. Nevertheless, washing the feet before entering a house is a duty (vatta) of the monks. In performing that duty, although there is no such thing as a breach of duty for the Buddhas, they wash their feet as a primary part of the duty. If the Tathāgata were to remain without bathing or washing his feet, people would say, 'This is not a human being.' Therefore, without abandoning human customs, he washes his feet. 'Sato sampajāno' means being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension that can control sleep. 'Upasaṅkami' means that Mara approached, thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama, having walked in the open air all night, has entered the Gandhakuṭi and is sleeping; he must be sleeping very comfortably, I will disturb him.'

'Kiṃ soppasi' means 'Why do you sleep?' or 'What is this sleeping to you?' 'Kiṃ nu soppasi' is a question: 'Why do you sleep?' 'Dubbhago viya' means sleeping like an unfortunate person, or like a dead person, or like one without mindfulness. 'Suññamagāraṃ' means he says, 'Do you sleep because you have found an empty house?' 'Suriye uggate' means when the sun has risen. At this time, other monks are sweeping, setting out drinking and washing water, and preparing to go for alms; why do you just keep sleeping?

'Jālinī' (the ensnarer) is so called because it is like a net, consisting of the eighteen explorations of craving starting with the internal, which stands overwhelming the three realms of existence. 'Visattikā' is so called because of its particular clinging to forms and so on, because it is the root of poison, and because it consumes suffering. 'Kuhiñci netawe' means to lead to any state of existence. 'Sabbūpadhi parikkhayā' means due to the total destruction of all acquisitions (upadhi) consisting of the aggregates, defilements, volitional formations, and sensual pleasures. The Buddha said, 'Mara, what interest do you have in this? Why do you wander around just criticizing from the side, like a small fly that is unable to land on hot gruel?' The seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Nandatisutta-vaṇṇanā

The eighth sutta has the same meaning as already stated in the Devatā-saṃyutta. The eighth sutta is finished.
161:
## 9. Paṭhamaāyusutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth discourse, 'Appaṃ vā bhiyyo' means that one who lives beyond a hundred years is not able to live for another full hundred years; they live for only fifty or sixty years. 'Ajjhabhāsī' means the ascetic Gotama says, 'The life of humans is short'; [Mara] spoke with a contrary nature, intending to overwhelm [him] by saying, 'I will speak of the length of life.'

'Na naṃ hīḷeti' means one should not despise that life, saying, 'This life is very short.' 'Khīramatto vā' means just as a very young infant who cannot yet turn [left or right] and must lie only on their back, drinks milk and sleeps on a cloth wrap (dukūla-cumbataka) as if unconscious, not thinking whether someone's life is short or long; so is the virtuous person. 'Careyyādittasīso vā' means knowing life is very short, one should practice [diligently] like one whose head is on fire. The explanation of the ninth discourse ends.

## 10. Dutiyaāyusutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth discourse, 'Nemīva rathakubbaraṃ' means just as the rim of a wheel follows the axle-box of a chariot that is moving all day and does not leave it, likewise the life of beings follows [them]. The explanation of the tenth discourse ends.

## Paṭhamo Vaggo.

## 2. Dutiyavaggo

## 1. Pāsāṇasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first discourse of the second chapter, 'Nisinno' means he was sitting, having fully undertaken the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) in the manner previously mentioned. Mara, knowing the state of the Blessed One sitting comfortably, approached thinking, 'I will disturb and destroy [his peace].' 'Padālesi' means standing on the mountain plateau, he hurled rocks. The rocks fell, striking each other without interval. 'Kevalaṃ' means the entire sense. The word 'Sabbaṃ' is a synonym for that word 'Kevalaṃ'. The explanation of the first discourse ends.

## 2. Kinnusīhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second discourse, 'Vicakkhukammāya' means because of the desire to destroy the wisdom-eye (paññācakkhu) of the assembly. In truth, this Mara is unable to destroy the wisdom-eye of the Buddhas; to the assembly...
162:
[Mara] is able to destroy [the wisdom-eye of the assembly] by making them hear or see terrifying objects. 'Vijitāvī nu maññasi' is a question: 'Why do you think, "I am one who has won the victory"?' Do not think so; there is no victory for you. 'Parisāsu' means among the eight assemblies. 'Balappattā' means because of being endowed with the ten powers (dasabala). The explanation of the second discourse ends.

## 3. Sakalikasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third discourse, 'Mandiyā nu' means do you sleep out of foolishness, out of extreme delusion? 'Udāhu kāveyyamatto' means or else, just as a poet, while contemplating a poem, sleeps intoxicated and heedless by that poetic composition, do you sleep thus? 'Sampacurā' means many people. 'Kimidaṃ soppase vā' is said oppressively: 'Why do you sleep this sleep?' 'Atthaṃ samecca' means having well attained the goal, which is the noble Nibbāna. For me, the Buddha, there is no goal of Nibbāna that is unattained or deficient in its attainment (saṅgahavipanna). 'Sallaṃ' refers to a very sharp spear-point. 'Jaggaṃ na saṅke' means just as some people, while awake and clearing [the path] where lions, leopards, or tigers roam, are anxious about dangers; likewise, though I am awake and clearing [the path], I am not anxious about dangers. 'Napi bhemi sottuṃ' means just as some are afraid to sleep in places where lions, leopards, or tigers roam; likewise, I am not afraid to sleep. 'Nānutapanti maṃ' means just as when a teacher or a resident pupil is unwell, and because they are engaged in the instruction and inquiry (uddesa-paripucchā) [of the Pali and Commentary], the passing of days and nights causes repeated worry for the resident pupil; likewise, [the passing of days and nights] does not cause worry for me. For me, there is no task that has not reached completion. Therefore, he said: 'I see no loss anywhere in the world.' The third discourse ends.

## 4. Patirūpasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth discourse, 'Anurodhavirodhesu' means in compliance and opposition, which are greed (rāga) and aversion (paṭigha). 'Mā sajjittho tadācaraṃ' means do not be attached while performing this act of teaching the Dhamma. For some people give applause and say 'Sādhu' to the teacher, and greed may arise towards them. Some listen disrespectfully, and aversion (paṭigha) may arise towards them. Thus, a Dhamma-teacher is said to be attached to compliance and opposition. It means: 'Do not be attached in this way.' 'Yadaññamanusāsati' refers to that which he instructs another. The Buddha, being compassionate for the welfare [of others], protects them with welfare. And because...
163:
The Blessed One is one who constantly looks after the welfare [of beings]; therefore, the Tathāgata is free from attraction and repulsion. The fourth sutta ends.

## 5. Commentary on the Mānasa Sutta

In the fifth sutta, he is called "antalikkhacara" (roaming in the air) because he binds even those traveling in the sky. "Pāsa" refers to the snare of lust (rāga). "Mānasa" refers to the snare associated with the mind. The fifth sutta ends.

## 6. Commentary on the Patta Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "clinging to the five aggregates of clinging" means taking the five aggregates of clinging and showing them by dividing them in various ways through the power of their individual and common characteristics. "Sandasseti" means he shows the individual characteristics, etc., of the aggregates. "Samādapeti" means he makes [them] take [the Dhamma]. "Samuttejeti" means he rouses effort in undertaking [the practice]. "Sampahaṃseti" means he purifies and illuminates with the quality of penetration.

"Aṭṭhiṃ katvā" means making it a goal, noting "this is the benefit we should attain," and thus desiring that teaching. "Manasi katvā" means keeping it in mind. "Sabbacetaso samannāharitvā" means attending well with the whole of that active mind. "Ohitasotā" means having ears pricked [to listen to the Dhamma]. "Abbhokāse nikkhittā" means being placed in the open to be dried in the sun.

"Rūpaṃ vedayitaṃ saññā" refers to these three aggregates: form, feeling, and perception. By the phrase "yañca saṅkhataṃ", the aggregate of mental formations is taken. "Thus he is dispassionate therein" means seeing "this is not I, this is not mine," and thus becoming dispassionate towards those five aggregates. "Khemattā" refers to the safe state of self (attabhāva). By this word, the characteristic of the fruit (phala) is shown. "Anvesaṃ" means while searching in all places known as existence (bhava), origin (yoni), destination (gati), station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and abode of beings (sattāvāsa). "Nājjhagā" means he did not see (did not find). The sixth sutta ends.

## 7. Commentary on the Chaphassāyatana Sutta

In the seventh sutta, "phassāyatanānaṃ" refers to the bases of contact occurring at the six doors, in the sense of origin and convergence. "Bhayabheravaṃ saddaṃ" refers to a terrifying sound similar to the sound of thunder, drums, or a thunderbolt. "Pathavī maññe undrīyati" means this great earth...
164:
...was as if making a "paṭapaṭa" sound. "Herein the world is infatuated" means the world of beings is excessively attached and infatuated with these six sense objects. "Māradheyya" refers to the round of suffering in the three realms, which is the domain of Māra. The seventh sutta ends.

## 8. Commentary on the Piṇḍa Sutta

In the eighth sutta, "pāhunakāni bhavanti" means they are gifts to be sent here and there on such a festival day, or they are gifts to be given to arriving guests. On the day of Sayam-carana (the day of roaming at will), young men of similar age, caste, and lineage gather from various places. Young women also wander here and there, adorned according to their wealth. Then, the young women send gifts to the young men they like, and the young men, if they have nothing else to give, throw at least a handful of flowers at the young women. "Anvāvittā" means being possessed or entered into. It is heard that on that day, five hundred young women, while going to play in the park, saw the Teacher on the way and would have offered festival cakes. The Teacher would have delivered a miscellaneous Dhamma discourse to them to express appreciation for their dana, and at the end of the discourse, all the young women would have been established in the fruit of Stream-entry. Māra, intending to obstruct their welfare, possessed [the villagers]. In the Pali text, however, it is only said: "Let not the recluse Gotama receive alms."

Did the Teacher enter the village without knowing Māra's trickery? Yes, he entered without knowing. Why? Because of not reflecting. For the Buddhas, it is not that reflecting beforehand, "I will receive alms in such a place, or I will not," is inappropriate (it is appropriate).
