However, after entering the village and seeing the change in people's behavior, he reflected, "What is this?" and then knew. Thinking, "It is not appropriate to destroy Māra's trickery for the sake of material things (alms)," he departed without destroying it.

"Upasaṅkami" means he approached the Blessed One, who was leaving the village without receiving even a spoonful of rice in the whole village, in the guise of a villager, feeling joyful like a conqueror of enemies.

"I will do so"—this statement was spoken falsely by Māra.

Māra had this thought: "If I speak thus, the Teacher will enter again. Then the village children will say, 'Having wandered through the whole village and not receiving even a spoonful of alms, he left the village and then again...'"
165:
"He has left the village and entered it again," and so on—thinking that they would mock him thus (Māra planned). But the Blessed One, thinking, "If this Māra harasses me thus, his head will split into seven pieces," out of compassion for that Māra, did not enter the village again and spoke two verses.

In those verses, 'pasavi' means produces or accomplishes (evil). 'Āsajja' means by striking or impinging. "Why do you think, 'My evil does not ripen, this deed is fruitless'?" Do not think that it does not ripen; it shows that there is indeed a fruit of the evil done by you. 'Kiñcana' refers to the mass of defilements such as the attachment of lust (rāga-kiñcana) which is capable of oppressing. 'Ābhassarā yathā' means just as the Brahmās born in the Ābhassara realm subsist on the jhāna of joy and are called 'feeders on joy' (pītibhakkhā), so shall we be. The eighth sutta ends.

## 9. Kassakasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, 'nibbānapaṭisaṃyuttāya' means (a discourse) that occurs based on Nibbāna. 'Haṭahaṭakeso' refers to one with disheveled hair, having spread the front hair to the back, the back hair to the front, the left hair to the right, and the right hair to the left. 'Mama cakkhusamphassaviññāṇāyatanaṃ' means that the eye-contact associated with eye-consciousness and the consciousness-base belong only to me. Here, by 'eye-contact' (cakkhusamphassa), the states associated with eye-consciousness such as contact (phassa) are taken. By 'consciousness-base' (viññāṇāyatana), all consciousnesses such as adverting (āvajjana) that arise at the eye-door are taken. The same method applies to the ear-door and so on. In the mind-door, however, 'mano' refers to the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅgacitta) together with adverting. 'Dhammā' refers to the mental objects. 'Manosamphassa' refers to the contact associated with the life-continuum together with adverting. 'Viññāṇāyatana' refers to the impulsion (javana) and registration (tadārammaṇa) minds.

"Evil Māra, whatever eye in the world is afflicted by cataracts (timira) or glaucoma (kāca), which is the site of various diseases, surrounded by ailments and burning, even if it be a blind eye—let all that eye be yours alone." The same method applies to forms (rūpa) and so on.

'Yaṃ vadanti' refers to things such as gold, silver, fields, buildings, alms-bowls, and robes about which people say, "This is mine." 'Ye vadanti mamanti ca' refers to those persons who say, "It is my self." If your mind exists in these possessed things and the persons who possess them, then you say, "Ascetic, you will not escape from my realm." 'Yaṃ vadanti' means that in the world, many people say of things like gold, silver, alms-bowls, and robes, "This is mine," but those things are not mine. 'Ye vadanti' means those persons who say "mine" in this way are not I. 'Na me maggampi dakkhasī' means you will not even see the path I travel through existence (bhava), origin (yoni), and destiny (gati). The ninth sutta ends.
166:
## 10. Rajjasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, 'ahanaṃ aghātayaṃ' means by not killing oneself and not causing others to kill. 'Ajinaṃ ajāpayaṃ' means by not causing the loss of others' property oneself and not causing others to do so. 'Asocaṃ asocāpayaṃ' means by not grieving oneself and not causing others to grieve. Thus, the Blessed One, seeing people oppressed by punishment and taxes within the kingdoms of unrighteous kings, thought thus out of the power of compassion.

'Upasaṅkami' means Māra approached, thinking: "The ascetic Gotama is thinking, 'Is it possible to exercise sovereignty?' He must have a desire to rule. Sovereignty is a ground for negligence. While he is ruling, I might get an opportunity. I will go and arouse his effort." 'Iddhipādā' means the components of success. 'Bhāvitā' means developed. 'Bahulīkatā' means practiced frequently. 'Yānīkatā' means made like a well-hitched vehicle. 'Vatthukatā' means made like a foundation in the sense of a basis. 'Anuṭṭhitā' means not abandoned, constantly followed. 'Paricitā' means well-practiced by constant repetition, like the hand of an archer who shoots without missing. 'Susamāraddhā' means very well undertaken, having complete development. 'Adhimucceyya' means one should think.

'Pabbatassā' means it would be a mountain. 'Dvittā vā' means let one golden mountain stand; even a golden mountain twice that size would not be enough or sufficient for a single person. 'Iti vidvā samañcare' means knowing thus (the insatiable nature of craving), one should live evenly. 'Yatonidānaṃ' means what is called suffering (dukkha) has the five cords of sensual pleasure as its cause; that suffering arises because of that cause; thus a being sees. 'Kathaṃ nameyya' means for what reason would that being incline towards those sensual pleasures which are the cause of suffering? 'Upadhiṃ viditvā' means knowing the acquisition (upadhi) of the cords of sensual pleasure as "this is an attachment, this is a clinging." 'Tasseva jantu vinayāya sikkhe' means one should train for the removal of that very acquisition. The tenth sutta ends.

## Dutiyo Vaggo

## 3. Tatiyavaggo

## 1. Sambahulasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'jaṭaṇḍuvena' means having matted hair wound upon the head. 'Ajinakkhipanivattho' means wearing one antelope skin with claws and hooves and wrapping another around oneself.
167:
"Udumbaradaṇḍaṃ" means having taken a slightly crooked staff made of fig wood to demonstrate a state of fewness of desires. "Said these words" means that, considering that in the world people usually listen to the words of many, and among brahmins, to the words of one who has gone forth, and among those who have gone forth, to the words of one who is elderly, [Māra] took the form of an elderly brahmin ascetic. He approached those monks who were practicing meditation in the place of exertion, raised his hand, and said these words: "Venerable sirs, you are young," and so on. "Okampetvā" means making the head bend downwards so that the chin touches the chest. "Jivhaṃ nillāletvā" means sticking out a large, variegated tongue and moving it up and down and to both sides. "Tivisākhaṃ" means having a three-pronged appearance. "Nalāṭikaṃ" means frowning, which results in three wrinkles appearing on the forehead. "Pakkāmi" means that he departed by a certain path after saying, "Without following the words of those who know, you will only experience the results of your own unwholesome kamma (it will be like being fried in your own oil)." The first sutta ends.

## 2. Samiddhisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "It is a gain for me, it is well-gained by me" means "It is a great gain for me, it is well-gained, because of obtaining such a Teacher, the Dhamma, and fellow celibates." Later, that Venerable Samiddhi, reflecting on his own suitable primary meditation subject (mūlakammaṭṭhāna) and thinking, "I shall attain the fruit of Arahantship," first took up an inspiring meditation subject. He sat reflecting on the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, making his mind healthy, joyful, and delighted. Therefore, such a thought arose in him. "Upasaṅkami" (approached) means that [Māra] approached thinking, "This monk Samiddhi appears to be sitting having taken up an inspiring meditation subject; I will create an obstacle for him before he takes up his primary meditation subject and attains the fruit of Arahantship." "Gaccha tvaṃ" (Go you) means that when the Blessed One looked over the whole of Jambudīpa, He saw that that very place would be suitable for that elder to practice meditation; therefore, He said, "Go." "Satipaññā ca me buddhā" means "I have known mindfulness and wisdom through the Noble Path." "Karassu rūpāni" means "You may create many terrifying forms." "Neva maṃ byādhayissasī" means "You will not be able to make me tremble." The second sutta ends.
168:
## 3. Godhikasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "Isigili-passe" means on the side of the mountain named Isigili. "Kāḷasilāyaṃ" means on a black-colored stone slab. "Sāmayikaṃ cetovimutti" (temporary liberation of mind) refers to mundane attainment (lokiya-samāpatti), so called because of the liberation from opposing hindrances (nīvaraṇa) at the moment of entering jhāna and the mind's commitment to the object. "Phusi" means he attained or obtained. "Parihāyi" (he fell away): why did he fall away as many as six times? It was because of a painful affliction. Venerable Godhika had a recurring illness caused by the combined disturbance of wind, bile, and phlegm. For that reason, he was unable to fulfill the factors conducive to the suitability of concentration, and thus he fell away from the attainment he had reached.

"Yannūnāhaṃ satthaṃ āhareyyaṃ" (What if I were to use the knife?)—thus the monk Godhika thought. This was because if one who has fallen away from jhāna dies, his destination is uncertain, but if one who has not fallen away from jhāna dies, his destination is certain and he is reborn in the Brahma world; therefore, he wished to use the knife (to take his own life). [Māra thought,] "This monk wishes to use the knife. Using the knife occurs to one who has no regard for body or life. One who has no regard for body or life in this way is capable of attaining even the fruit of Arahantship by contemplating the primary meditation subject. Even if I forbid him, he will not stop; he will only stop if the Buddha forbids him." Thus, pretending to desire the elder's welfare, [Māra] approached the Blessed One.

"Jalā" means shining or radiant. "Pāde vandāmi cakkhumā" means "I pay homage to the feet of the One who possesses the five kinds of eyes." "Jutindharā" means endowed with power and majesty. "Appattamānaso" means one who has not yet reached the fruit of Arahantship. "Sekho" (a trainee) means one who is still training in virtue and so on, and who still has work to do. "Jane sutā" means famous or well-known among the people. "Satthaṃ āharitaṃ hoti" (the knife was used): the elder decided, "What is the use of this life to me?" and lying on his back, he cut his throat with the knife, and painful feelings arose. The elder, having dispelled the pain and then grasping that very pain, established mindfulness and contemplated the primary meditation subject. He attained the fruit of Arahantship, became a "Samasīsī" (one who attains the end of defilements and the end of life simultaneously), and attained Parinibbāna. There are three kinds of Samasīsī: Irīyāpatha-samasīsī, Roga-samasīsī, and Jīvita-samasīsī.
169:
Among those three types of samasīsī individuals, one undertakes a certain posture among the postures such as standing, etc., and develops insight (vipassanā) thinking, 'I shall reach the fruit of Arahatship without disturbing this posture.' At that time, for that person, the attainment of the fruit of Arahatship and the disturbance of the posture occur simultaneously. This person is called an iriyāpathasamasīsī.

One who, while suffering from a certain disease such as eye disease, develops insight thinking, 'I shall reach the fruit of Arahatship before rising from this disease.' At that time, for that person, the attainment of the fruit of Arahatship and the recovery from the disease occur simultaneously. This person is called a rogasamasīsī.

Some teachers designate the state of samasīsī here by way of attaining parinibbāna in that very posture and in that very disease. For the person for whom the destruction of the taints (āsavas) and the end of life occur simultaneously, this person is called a jīvitasamasīsī. This was also said: 'For which person the exhaustion of taints and the exhaustion of life occur neither before nor after but simultaneously, this person is called a samasīsī' (in the Puggalapaññatti).

In this context, there are two types of 'heads' (sīsa): the head of occurrence (pavattisīsa) and the head of defilement (kilesasīsa). Therein, the head of occurrence is the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), and the head of defilement is ignorance (avijjā). Between these two, the life-faculty exhausts the death-consciousness (cuti-citta), and ignorance exhausts the path-consciousness (magga-citta). There is no simultaneous arising of two consciousnesses. Immediately after the Path is the Fruit; immediately after the Fruit is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); emerging from the life-continuum, reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) occurs. That reviewing may be complete or incomplete. Even while the head is being severed by a sharp sword, one or two cycles of reviewing certainly arise. Because of the rapid transformation of consciousness, the destruction of taints and the end of life appear as if they occur in a single moment.

'Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha' means having uprooted craving along with its root, which is ignorance, by the Path of Arahatship. 'Parinibbuto' means having attained parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna).

'Vivattakkhandha' means having the aggregates turned over. 'Semānaṃ' means lying down on one's back. Although the Elder was lying on his back, because of his habit of sleeping on his right side, his head remained turned toward the right. 'Dhūmāyitattaṃ' means the state of smoking. At that moment, something like a cloud of smoke or a cloud of darkness appeared. 'Viññāṇaṃ samanvesati' means searching for the rebirth-consciousness. 'Appatiṭṭhitena' means by way of the rebirth-consciousness being unestablished; this is the meaning. 'Beluvapaṇḍuvīṇā' is a great golden lute with a yellowish color like a ripe wood-apple. 'Ādāya' means placing it under the armpit. 'Upasaṅkami' means 'the place where the Elder Godhika was reborn...'
170:
"I do not know; I shall become one free from doubt by questioning the Ascetic Gotama," so saying, he approached, having assumed the appearance of a young child. "Nādhigacchāmi" means "I do not see." "Sokaparetassa" means "of one afflicted by grief." "Abhassatha" means "fell at the top of the foot." The third sutta is finished.

## 4. Sattavassānubandhasutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "satta vassāni" refers to the six years before Enlightenment and one year after Enlightenment. "Otārāpekkho" means one who is looking for a flaw, thinking, "If I see even a slight impropriety in the bodily door, etc., of the Ascetic Gotama, I will rebuke him." "Alabhamāno" means one who does not see even a slip as small as a speck of chariot dust. Therefore, it is said: "For seven years I followed the Blessed One step by step, seeking a flaw in the mindful Sambuddha, but I did not find any flaw."

"Upasaṅkami" means he approached, thinking, "Today I will go having overcome the Ascetic Gotama."

"Jhāyasi" means "Are you sitting there meditating and reflecting?" "Vittaṃ nu jīno" means "Have you lost a hundred or a thousand?" "Āguṃ nu gāmasmiṃ" means "Have you committed a transgression beyond measure in the village? Why do you wander in the forest, unable to look others in the face?" "Sakkhiṃ" refers to friendship.

"Palikhāya" means having dug out and cut off. "Bhavalobhajappaṃ" means craving, which is called attachment to existence. "Anāsavo jhāyāmi" means "Being free from craving, I meditate with the two types of meditation." He addresses Māra as "Pamattabandhu" (Kinsman of the Heedless). This is because Māra is the friend of those who are heedless in the world.

"Sace maggaṃ anubuddhaṃ" means "If you have understood the Path." "Apehi" means "Go away." "Amaccudheyyaṃ" means Nibbāna, which is not the realm of Death. "Pāragāmino" refers to those who have reached the further shore, those who will reach it, and those who wish to reach it.
171:
Visūkāyikāni means the opposing factors of Māra. Visevitāni means things practiced in opposition. In the statement, "The life of humans is short, days and nights pass by," the opposing reasons (vippaṭinīka) such as "The life of humans is long, days and nights do not pass by," are meant. Vipphanditāni refers to the manifestations of the forms of a king elephant, a king snake, and so forth at various times. Nibbejanīyā means things that cause dread or weariness.

In the words beginning with anupariyagā, although a past tense verb is used, the meaning should be understood through the consideration of a simile. This is what is meant: Just as a crow, seeing a stone with the appearance of a lump of fat, might circle around it thinking, "Perhaps I may find something soft here, perhaps there may be something delicious," but upon finding no taste in that stone, that crow would depart from there and leave that stone; in the same way, we, like that crow, having approached the mountain-like Gotama and finding neither pleasure nor friendship, will depart from Gotama in weariness. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Māradhītusutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, in the word "abhāsitvā," the letter "a" is merely a particle, and it carries the meaning of "bhāsitvā" (having spoken). There is also a variant reading "abhāsayitvā." Upasaṅkamiṃsu means—they approached Māra who was sitting very dejectedly, scratching lines on the ground with a stick like a young cowherd boy, thinking, "For what reason is this?" and intending to find out by asking.

Socasī means he thought with sorrow. Āraññamiva kuñjaraṃ means—just as female elephants sent from the forest lure a wild forest elephant by displaying feminine gestures and then bind and bring him away, so shall we bring him. Māradheyyaṃ refers to the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) occurring in the three realms.

Upasaṅkamiṃsu means—having comforted their father, saying, "You please wait for a while, we shall bring that Gotama," they approached. Uccāvacā means of various and diverse kinds. Ekasataṃ ekasataṃ means making one hundred each. Kumārivaṇṇasataṃ means, by this method, a hundred forms of young girls.
172:
By both these terms, "atthassa pattiṃ hadayassa santiṃ," only the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) is preached. Senaṃ refers to the army of defilements. That army of defilements is indeed called that which is attractive and pleasant in nature. Ekāhaṃ jhāyāṃ means I am meditating alone. Sukhamanubodhiṃ means I have penetrated and realized the bliss of Arahantship. This is what is meant: Having conquered the attractive and pleasant army of defilements, I, meditating alone, have penetrated and realized the bliss of Arahantship known as "the attainment of the goal, the peace of the heart." Therefore, I do not make friends or intimacy with people, and for that very reason, I have no friendship with anyone.

Kathaṃvihārībahulo means living mostly in what kind of dwelling? Aladdhā means without obtaining. Yo is merely a particle. This is what is meant: By what kind of jhāna does that person live, meditating much, so that sensual perceptions (kāmasaññā), finding no opportunity, remain only outside?

Passaddhakāyo means one who has a tranquil body because the body of inhalation and exhalation is stilled by the fourth jhāna. Suvimuttacitto means one whose mind is well-liberated by the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship. Asaṅkharāno means one who does not perform the three types of karmic formations (kammābhisaṅkhāra). Anoko means one who is without attachment (anālaya). Aññāya dhammaṃ means having known the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. Avitakkajhāyī means one who meditates with the fourth jhāna which is without thought-conception (vitakka). In the words beginning with "na kuppati," it means he does not get angry through hatred, does not remember with lust, and has no sloth through delusion. When these three root defilements are taken, the one thousand five hundred defilements are already included. Alternatively, by the first term, the hindrance of ill-will (byāpāda-nīvaraṇa) is taken; by the second, the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa); and by the third, the remaining hindrances starting with sloth and torpor (thina-middha). Thus, by this abandonment of the hindrances, the state of an Arahant (khīṇāsava) is shown.

Pañcoghatiṇṇo means one who has crossed the flood of defilements occurring in the five doors. Chaṭṭhaṃ means he has also crossed the sixth flood of defilements occurring in the mind door. Alternatively, by the expression "pañcogha," the five lower fetters (saṃyojana) should be understood, and by the expression "chaṭṭha," the five higher fetters. Gaṇasaṅghacārī means the Teacher is called gaṇasaṅghacārī because he moves among groups and the Saṅgha. Addhā carissanti means other faithful people will certainly practice. Ayaṃ refers to this Blessed One. Anoko means one who is without attachment.
173:
"Acchejja nessati" means he will lead away by force; it means he will snatch from the hands of the King of Death and lead to the other shore, which is Nibbāna. "Nayamānānaṃ" carries the meaning "among those being led."

"Selaṃva sirasūhacca, pātāle gādhamesatha" means it is like placing a stone the size of a great palace pinnacle on one's head and searching for a footing in the abyss. "Khāṇuṃva urasāsajja" means it is like striking a stump with one's chest. "Apetha" means go away. At this point, the Elders who performed the Recitation (Saṅgītikāras), having concluded the teaching with the words "Idamavoca," spoke the verse beginning with "Daddallamānā." Therein, "daddallamānā" means exceedingly shining and beautiful. "Āgañchu" means they have come. "Panudi" means he dispelled or drove away. "Tūlaṃ bhaṭṭhaṃva māluto" means just as the wind blows away silk-cotton or grass-cotton that has fallen from the fruit, so he dispelled them. The fifth sutta is finished.

## Third Vagga.

## Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

## The Commentary on the Māra Saṃyutta is concluded.
174:
## 5. Bhikkhunī Saṃyutta

## 1. Commentary on the Āḷavikā Sutta

In the first sutta of the Bhikkhunī Saṃyutta, "Āḷavikā" refers to one who was born in the country of Āḷavī and went forth as a nun after leaving from the city of Āḷavī itself. "Andhavana" (Blind Men's Grove) is a forest that came to be known by that name from the time when five hundred thieves, who had their eyes plucked out and became blind in that very place, lived there; they had plucked out the eyes of an Ariya person, a Dhamma preacher named Yasodhara, who was returning after collecting funds for new construction at the shrine of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha. That forest is located about one gāvuta to the right of the city of Sāvatthī and is a forest protected by kings. Monks and nuns who desire seclusion often go to that forest. Therefore, this nun also, desiring physical seclusion (kāyaviveka), approached that forest.

"Nissaraṇa" means Nibbāna. "Paññāya" means by reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa). "Na tvaṃ jānāsi taṃ padaṃ" means "You, Māra, do not know this state of Nibbāna, nor do you know the state of the path leading to Nibbāna."

"Sattisūlūpamā" means they are like spears and stakes because of their piercing nature. "Khandhāsaṃ adhikuṭṭanā" means the aggregates of those beings are like a chopping block. The first sutta ends.

## 2. Commentary on the Somā Sutta

In the second sutta, "ṭhāna" refers to the fruition of Arahatship. "Durabhisambhava" means a state that is very difficult to attain. "Dvanguḷapaññāya" (with two-finger wisdom) is said of women either because they have weak wisdom, or because they are known to spin thread by holding a roll of cotton with two fingers. "Ñāṇamhi vattamānamhi" means while the knowledge of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) is occurring. "Dhammaṃ vipassato" means for one who sees the Four Noble Truths, or for one who sees only the group of five aggregates which is the object of insight (vipassanā) in the preliminary stage. "Kiñci vā pana aññasmī" means in any other object, the thought "I am" might occur to someone through the power of craving, conceit, and views. The second sutta ends.

## 3. Commentary on the Kisāgotamī Sutta

In the third sutta, "Kisāgotamī" is so called because she was lean (kisā) due to having little flesh and blood; "Gotamī" was her name. Formerly, in the city of Sāvatthī, all the wealth of eighty crores in a certain family turned into nothing but charcoal. The householder, seeing the things that had become charcoal...
175:
Without removing the wealth that had turned into charcoal, he thought, "Surely some person of merit will appear; by that person's merit, these will turn back into gold and silver as before." He filled pots with the gold and silver (charcoal), placed them in the market, and sat nearby. While he was sitting there, a woman born into a poor family went to the street thinking, "I will take a half-māsaka and bring firewood and vegetables." Seeing those items, she said to the householder, "If there is this much wealth even in the market, how much must there be in the house?" He asked, "Dear daughter, what did you see to say this?" She replied, "I say this because I see this gold and silver."

That householder thought, "This young woman must be a person of merit." He asked for her place of residence, put away the goods in the market, and then approached her parents, saying, "In our house, there is a son who has reached the proper age; give this young woman to that son." They replied, "Sir, why do you make fun of poor people?" He said, "What is called friendship and intimacy can also happen with poor people; give her to him, she will become the mistress of the household." So he took her and brought her to his home.

In due course, through their union, she gave birth to a son. That son passed away at the age when he could wander about on foot. Although she had come from a poor family to a noble family, when intense grief arose thinking, "I have come to the destruction of my son," she prevented the funeral rites of the son and, carrying the dead body, wandered about the city lamenting.

One day, she went to the presence of the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha) on the great Buddha-road and said, "Blessed One, give me medicine for the health of my son." He said, "Go and wander through Sāvatthī; in whatever house no one has ever died, bring mustard seeds from that house; that will be the medicine for your son." She entered the city and, starting from the first house, asked for mustard seeds at every house according to the method told by the Blessed One. Being told, "Where will you find such a house?", she wandered through a few houses and then reflected, "This nature of death is indeed the norm for all people; it is not for my son alone." She discarded the corpse at a rest house and requested ordination.

The Teacher sent her to the nuns' quarters, saying, "Let this woman be ordained." She attained Arahatship at the very end of the hair-shaving ceremony. In reference to this Elder Nun, it was said: "Atha kho Kisāgotamī."

"Ekamāsī" means she was alone. "Rudammukhī" means as if having a crying face. In the phrase "accantaṃ mataputtāmhi," "antaṃ" means passing the end; this word 'anta' is a neuter abstract noun (bhāvanapuṃsaka). The meaning is this: Just as the death of a son is an end that has been passed, so too am I one whose son has died; now for me, there is no more such a thing as the death of a son again. "Purisā etadantikā" means men also to me...
176:
The meaning is this—just as the end which is the death of a son has been transcended, likewise for me, whose son has died, there is no longer such a thing as the death of a son. Men also have such an end for me. Whatever end of death there is, that very end is the end for me and for men. It means that now I am no longer fit to seek a man.

'Sabbattha vihatā nandī' (Delight is destroyed everywhere) means that my delight in craving for all aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), existences (bhava), modes of birth (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness (ṭhiti), and abodes (nivāsa) has vanished. 'Tamokkhandho' (Mass of darkness) refers to the mass of ignorance (avijjā). 'Padālito' (Burst asunder) means shattered by the knowledge of vision (vijjā-ñāṇa). The commentary on the third sutta ends.

## 4. Vijayāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'pañcaṅgikena' (with five-fold) means with a musical instrument endowed with five factors, such as a drum covered on one side, a drum covered on both sides, a drum covered on both sides and tied with strings, a solid instrument, and a hollow instrument. 'Niyyātayāmi tuyheva' means I give all sense objects to you alone. 'Nāhaṃ tenatthikā' means I have no need for those five sense objects. 'Pūtikāyena' (with a foul body) means that even though the body has a golden complexion, it is indeed a foul body because of the nature of constantly oozing from above and below; therefore, it is said 'pūtikāyena'. 'Bhindanena' means by the nature of breaking. 'Pabhaṅgunā' means by the nature of reaching a state of being crushed into pieces. 'Aṭṭīyāmi' means I am oppressed and thus weary. 'Harāyāmi' means I am very ashamed. 'Santā samāpattī' (Peaceful attainments) means the eight mundane attainments are called peaceful because of the tranquility of the object and the tranquility of the factors. 'Sabbattha' (Everywhere) means in all fine-material existences and immaterial existences; and since by taking these two existences, the sensual existence is also taken, it means that in all these eight attainments and places, my darkness of ignorance has vanished. The commentary on the fourth sutta ends.

## 5. Uppalavaṇṇāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'supupphitaggaṃ' refers to a Sāla tree that is well-flowered from the top. 'Na catthi te dutiyā vaṇṇadhātu' means there is no second complexion-element similar to your complexion; it means there is no other bhikkhunī similar to you. 'Idhāgatā tādisikā bhaveyyunti' means just as you, having come here, do not find any companionship or affection, likewise, they too should be just like you. 'Pakhumantarikāyaṃ' means you cannot see me even as I stand on the bridge of the nose between the two eyes. 'Vasībhūtamhi' means I am one who has attained mastery (vasībhāva). The commentary on the fifth sutta ends.

## 6. Cālāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'ko nu taṃ idamādapayi' means what dull-witted fool prompted you to take up this view? 'Pariklesaṃ' means other various kinds of danger or suffering. Now, Māra
177:
Māra said, 'Who prompted you to take up this view?' Desiring to refute those words of Māra, and to show that 'The blind fool Māra did not prompt me, but in the world, the Teacher, the Supreme Person, taught the Dhamma,' she spoke the words beginning with 'Buddho'. In those words, 'sacce nivesayi' means he established and placed me in Nibbāna, which is called the ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca). 'Nirodhaṃ appajānantā' means because they do not know the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca). The commentary on the sixth sutta ends.

## 7. Upacālāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'enti māravasaṃ punā' means they repeatedly come under the power of the Māra of death, the Māra of defilements, and the Māra as a deity. 'Padhūpito' means burnt or oppressed. 'Agati yattha mārassa' means the place which is not the range of you, Māra. 'Tattha' means in that Nibbāna. The commentary on the seventh sutta ends.

## 8. Sīsupacālāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, 'samaṇī viya dissasi' means you appear similar to a bhikkhunī. 'Kimiwa carasi momūhā' is a question: for what reason do you wander like a deluded person? 'Ito bahiddhā' means outside of this Dispensation (Sāsana). They are called 'pāsaṇḍa' (sectarians) because they throw (khipanti) the snare (pāsa) of views into the minds of beings. The Sāsana, however, releases one from snares; therefore, the Sāsana is not called 'pāsaṇḍa'. Only outside of this Sāsana do sectarians exist. 'Pasīdanti' means they are attached or they sink in.

Now, desiring to answer the question 'On account of whom have you become shaven-headed?', she spoke the words beginning with 'Atthi sakyakule jāto'. In those words, 'sabbābhibhū' means one who stands having overcome all aggregates, sense bases, elements, existences, modes of birth, destinations, and so forth. He is called 'māranuda' because he removes the Māra of death and so forth. 'Sabbatthamaparājito' means one who is undefeated in all things such as lust, or in the battle with Māra. 'Sabbattha mutto' means one who is liberated from all aggregates and so forth. 'Asito' means one who is unsupported by the dependencies of craving and views. 'Sabbakammakkhayaṃ patto' means one who has reached the fruit of Arahantship, which is the destruction of all kamma. 'Upadhisaṅkhaye' means one who is liberated by taking Nibbāna, the destruction of acquisitions (upadhi), as an object. The commentary on the eighth sutta ends.

## 9. Selāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'kenidaṃ pakataṃ' means by whom was this mass of suffering (this person) made? 'Bimba' is said in reference to the physical body (attabhāva). 'Aghaṃ' refers to the physical body itself because it is the site of suffering. 'Hetubhaṅgā' means due to the cessation of causes, or due to the deficiency of conditions. The commentary on the ninth sutta ends.
178:
## 10. Vajirāsuttavaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the tenth sutta, the Vajirā Sutta, "no being is found here" means that in this mere heap of formations (saṅkhārapuñja), in the ultimate sense (paramatthato), what is called a "being" (satta) is not found. "When the aggregates exist" means when the five aggregates are present, being defined in various ways. "Convention" (sammuti) means it is just a mere name, "being". "Suffering" (dukkha) means the suffering of the five aggregates themselves. "Nothing other than suffering" means that apart from suffering, no other thing arises, nor does anything else cease. The tenth sutta is finished.

## Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,
## the commentary on the Bhikkhunī Saṃyutta is concluded.
179:
## 6. Brahmasamyutta
## 1. Paṭhamavagga
## 1. Brahmāyācanasuttavaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Brahmasamyutta, "a reflection arose" (parivitakko udapādi) refers to this thought of the mind that is habitually practiced by all Buddhas. When did it arise? After becoming a Buddha, during the eighth week, at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, having eaten the tooth-stick and the medicinal myrobalan (harītakī) brought and offered by Sakka, Lord of the Devas, and having washed his face, he partook of the alms-food of the merchants Tapussa and Bhallika in the precious stone bowl brought by the four Great Kings (Lokapālas). Then, having returned and just sat down at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, this reflection of the mind arose.

"Attained" (adhigato) means penetrated [by the path-knowledge]. "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Deep" (gambhīro) is a word that rejects shallowness. "Hard to see" (duddaso) means it is hard to see precisely because it is deep; it is seen with difficulty, it cannot be seen easily. Because it is hard to see, it is "hard to understand" (duranubodho); it is understood with difficulty, it cannot be understood easily. "Peaceful" (santo) means the stilling of the heat of defilements. "Sublime" (paṇīto) has the meaning of being extremely noble (not causing dissatisfaction). These two terms are spoken with reference only to the supramundane (lokuttara) Dhamma. "Beyond the sphere of reasoning" (atakkāvacaro) means it is not to be explored or entered into by reasoning, but is to be explored only by wisdom (ñāṇa). "Subtle" (nipuṇo) has the meaning of being fine and delicate. "To be experienced by the wise" (paṇḍitavedanīyo) means it is a Dhamma to be known only by the wise who have practiced the right path.

"Delighting in attachment" (ālayārāmā): beings cling to the five cords of sensual pleasure; therefore, those sensual pleasures are called "attachments" (ālaya). Or, they cling to the 108 varieties of craving; therefore, they are also called "attachments". Because they delight in these attachments, they are "delighting in attachment" (ālayārāmā). Because they take pleasure in attachments, they are "rejoicing in attachment" (ālayaratā). Because they are well-pleased in attachments, they are "gladdening in attachment" (ālayasammuditā).

For example: just as a king who enters a well-prepared garden filled with trees laden with flowers and fruits delights in the excellence of those various things, being greatly gladdened, repeatedly pleased, and not becoming weary, not even wishing to leave in the evening; in the same way, beings delight in these attachments to sensuality and attachments to craving, living gladdened and without weariness in the round of saṃsāra. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show them the two kinds of attachment like a garden, spoke the words beginning with "ālayārāmā".

In that text, "yadidaṃ" is an indeclinable (nipāta). With reference to its place, it should be understood as "yaṃ idaṃ". With reference to dependent origination, it should be understood as "yo ayaṃ". The partial meaning of the term "idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo" should be known. It refers to ignorance (avijjā) etc., which are the causes of these formations (saṅkhāra) etc...
180:
Because of ignorance and so forth, which are the causes of these formations, it is called 'Idappaccaya' (this conditionality). The word 'Idappaccaya' itself is called 'Idappaccayatā'. Because it is both Idappaccayatā and Dependent Origination, it is called 'Idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppāda'. This is a designation for ignorance and so forth, which are the causes of formations.

All terms such as 'Sabbasaṅkhārasamatha' (the stilling of all formations) refer only to Nibbāna. This is because, depending on that Nibbāna, all the vibrations of formations are stilled and ceased; therefore, it is called 'Sabbasaṅkhārasamatha'. Because, depending on that Nibbāna, all acquisitions (upadhi) are relinquished, all cravings are exhausted, all passion of defilements fades away, and all suffering ceases; therefore, it is called 'Sabbūpadhipaṭinissagga' (the relinquishment of all acquisitions), 'Taṇhākkhaya' (the destruction of craving), 'Virāga' (dispassion), and 'Nirodha' (cessation).

That craving which binds one existence to another, or action to its fruit, is called 'vāna' (weaving/binding). The escape from that 'vāna' is called 'Nibbāna'.

'That teaching would be wearying to me' means that teaching the Dhamma to those who do not understand would be merely physical weariness for me; such teaching would be a vexation to me. It means it would result in physical weariness and physical vexation. However, in the mind, both weariness and vexation do not exist for the Buddhas. The word 'apissu' is a particle used for emphasis. It shows that 'not only did this thought arise, but these verses also became clear.' 'Anacchariyā' means repeatedly wonderful. 'Paṭibhaṃsu' means they became the object of the knowledge of intuition; they reached the state of being reflected upon.

'Kicchena' means with difficulty, but not through a painful practice (dukkhā paṭipadā). For the Buddhas, all four paths are indeed a pleasant practice (sukhā paṭipadā). However, this was said in reference to the practice leading to the attainment (āgamanīya-paṭipadā) during the time of fulfilling the perfections, when, despite having passion, hatred, and delusion, he cut off his adorned head, drew out his throat's blood, plucked out his well-anointed eyes, and gave away his son, the light of the lineage, and his beloved wife to whoever came to ask, and underwent cutting and breaking of his body in existences such as that of the Preacher of Patience (Khantivādī).

In the word 'halaṃ', the letter 'ha' is a mere particle, and it means 'alaṃ' (enough/sufficient). 'Pakāsituṃ' means to teach. It means: 'It is not suitable to teach this Dhamma attained with such difficulty; I am not able; what benefit would there be in teaching it?' 'Rāgadousaparetehi' means those touched by lust and hatred, or those who follow after lust and hatred.

'Paṭisotagāmi' (going against the stream) refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths understood as 'impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness,' which is like the upstream against the perversions (vipallāsa) such as permanence, etc. 'Rāgarattā' means those infatuated with sensual lust, lust for existence, and lust for views. 'They will not see' means they cannot see through this nature of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness...
181:
(Those beings) cannot see with this nature of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness. If they cannot see thus, who would be able to make them see and understand in this way? 'Tamokhandhena āvuṭā' means they are covered by the mass of delusion called ignorance and thus cannot see.

'Appossukkatāya' means with a state of being effortless, meaning not desiring to teach the Dhamma. Why did the mind of the Blessed One incline towards not teaching the Dhamma? Did he not fulfill the perfections and reach omniscience after making the aspiration: 'When I am liberated (from Saṃsāra), I will liberate others; when I have crossed over, I will cross others over. What is the use of realizing the Truth in this world in an obscure form as a disciple? Having reached omniscience, I will save the world of men and devas'?

This statement is true. However, the mind of the Blessed One inclined in this way through the power of such reflection (paccavekkhaṇā). To the Blessed One who had reached omniscience and reflected on the thickness of the defilements of beings and the depth of the Dhamma, the thickness of beings' defilements and the depth of the Dhamma became manifest in every aspect. Then, he thought: 'These beings are filled with defilements and are extremely soiled, like a gourd filled with sour gruel, like a jar filled with buttermilk, like a cloth soaked in fat and oil, or like a hand smeared with eye-ointment. They are infatuated by lust, corrupted by hatred, and blinded by delusion. How indeed will they penetrate (the Dhamma)?' Thus, his mind inclined in this way also through the power of reflecting on the thickness of defilements.

'And this Dhamma is deep like the mass of water that supports the great earth. It is difficult to see like a mustard seed covered by Mount Meru. It is difficult to understand like making the tips of a hair split into a hundred pieces meet tip to tip. While I was striving to penetrate this Dhamma, there was no gift I did not give, no virtue I did not keep, and no perfection I did not fulfill. Yet, for me, the earth did not shake even when I was destroying the army of Māra as if without effort; it did not shake when I was recollecting past lives in the first watch; it did not shake when I was purifying the divine eye in the middle watch. But only when I was penetrating the Law of Dependent Origination in the last watch did my ten-thousandfold world system shake. How will the ordinary people of the world penetrate this Dhamma which was penetrated with difficulty even by one with sharp wisdom like me?' Thus, it should be understood that his mind inclined in this way also through the power of reflecting on the depth of the Dhamma.

Furthermore, his mind inclined in this way because he desired to teach only when requested by the Brahmā. For the Blessed One knew: 'If my mind inclines towards inaction regarding teaching the Dhamma, the Great Brahmā will request me to teach. Beings also respect and revere the Brahmā. That...'
182:
The Great Brahmā will request the Dhamma teaching; these beings also hold the Brahmā in high regard. He [the Buddha] knew: 'They will think, "The Teacher was indeed disinclined to teach the Dhamma, but then the Great Brahmā requested him to teach. Truly, the Dhamma is peaceful; truly, it is noble," and they will listen respectfully.' It should be understood that it was also based on this reason that the Buddha's mind inclined toward inaction (appossukkata) rather than toward teaching the Dhamma.

'Sahampatissa' means that this Brahmā was a thera named Sahaka during the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa; having attained the first jhāna, he was reborn as a Brahmā with a lifespan of one kappa in the first jhāna realm. There, he was known as 'Sahampati Brahmā.' It is in reference to him that it was said 'Brahmuno Sahampatissa.' 'Nassati vata bho' means that Sahampati Brahmā uttered this cry so loudly that the Brahmās of the ten thousand world systems heard it and assembled together. 'Yatra hi nāma' means 'in which world.' 'Purato pāturahosi' means he appeared together with those ten thousand Brahmās. 'Apparajakkhajātika' refers to those whose nature is to have only a little dust of greed, hatred, and delusion in their eye of wisdom. 'Assavanatā' means due to not hearing. 'Bhavissanti' indicates that there will be not just one or two, but hundreds of thousands of beings who will understand the Dhamma—those who have matured their perfections (pāramī) by performing ten kinds of meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, who are like lotuses awaiting the touch of sunlight, longing only for the Dhamma teaching, and who are capable of entering the stage of the Noble Ones (ariya) at the end of even a single four-line verse.

'Pāturahosi' means he appeared. 'Samalehi cintito' refers to the doctrine thought out by the six teachers, such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, who were possessed of the stains of greed and so forth. These teachers, having arisen earlier, taught the defiled Dhamma of wrong view throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, as if spreading thorns or pouring out poison. 'Apāpuretaṃ' means 'Please open this door to Nibbāna.' 'Amatassa dvāraṃ' refers to the Noble Path, which is like the door to Nibbāna. 'Suṇantu dhammaṃ vimalenānubuddhaṃ' is a request: 'May these beings hear the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths realized by the Buddha, who is stainless (vimala) due to the absence of the stains of greed and so forth.'

'Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito' means just like one standing on a solid rocky mountain peak. For such a person, there is no need for efforts like craning or stretching the neck to see in all directions. 'Tathūpamaṃ' means having a similar metaphor to that mountain. The summary of the meaning here is: Just as a man with sight standing on a rocky mountain peak can see the people all around, so too the Buddha, who possesses excellent wisdom and is endowed with the All-Seeing Eye (Samanta-cakkhu) that can see everything through the knowledge of omniscience, should ascend the Palace of Dhamma (Dhammamaya Pāsāda) made of supramundane wisdom. Being himself free from sorrow, he should look down upon the multitude of people who are immersed in sorrow and oppressed by birth and aging...
183:
...should see. O Lord, who possesses excellent wisdom and is endowed with the All-Seeing Eye of Omniscience, likewise, may You ascend the Palace of Dhamma. Being Yourself free from sorrow, please look upon, investigate, and examine the multitude of people who are immersed in sorrow and oppressed by birth and aging. The meaning here is this: For example, if people were to make a large field around the foot of a mountain, build small huts on the embankments of those fields, and light fires at night, even if the darkness were fourfold in its density, a man with sight standing on the peak of that mountain looking down at the ground would not be able to see the fields, the embankments, the huts, or the people sleeping in those huts. He would only be able to see the flames of the fires in the huts. In the same way, for the Tathāgata who has ascended the Palace of Dhamma and is looking at the multitude of beings, those beings who have not performed meritorious deeds do not come into the range of the Buddha-eye (Buddha-cakkhu), even if they are sitting in the same monastery near His right knee; they are like arrows shot in the night. However, those veneyya persons (beings to be tamed) who have performed meritorious deeds come into the range of the Buddha-eye even if they are far away; they are prominent like a fire or like the Himalaya, the king of mountains. Thus it was said:

'The good shine from afar, like the Himalaya mountain;
The wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot in the night.' (Dhp. 304)

'Ajjhesana' means request. 'Buddha-cakkhuna' refers to the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of their latent tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa). These two knowledges are called the 'Buddha-eye' (Buddha-cakkhu); the knowledge of omniscience is called the 'All-Seeing Eye' (Samanta-cakkhu); and the three lower path-knowledges are called the 'Dhamma-eye' (Dhamma-cakkhu). In the terms beginning with 'Apparajakkha,' according to the method already mentioned, those who have little dust of greed and so forth in their eye of wisdom are called 'Apparajakkha.' Those who have much of that dust are called 'Mahārajakkha.' Those whose faculties such as faith are sharp are called 'Tikkhindriya.' Those whose faculties are dull are called 'Mudindriya.' Those whose dispositions of faith and so forth are good are called 'Svākāra.' Those who can note the reasons taught and can be easily made to understand are called 'Suviññāpaya.' Those who see the next world and faults as a danger are called 'Paralokavajjabhayadassāvī.'

In this context, the Pali text is: 'A person with faith is Apparajakkha; a person without faith is Mahārajakkha. One who has aroused energy is Apparajakkha; one who is lazy is Mahārajakkha. One who has established mindfulness is Apparajakkha; one who is forgetful is Mahārajakkha.'
184: A person who is composed is called one with little dust (apparajakkha); a person who is not composed is called one with much dust (mahārajakkha). A wise person has little dust; one lacking wisdom has much dust. Likewise, a person with faith has sharp faculties... A wise person is one who sees the danger in faults regarding the next world; one lacking wisdom does not see the danger in faults regarding the next world. The 'world' (loka) refers to the world of aggregates (khandhaloka), the world of bases (āyatanaloka), the world of elements (dhātuloka), the world of the existence of success (sampattibhavaloka), the world of the origin of success (sampattisambhavaloka), the world of the existence of failure (vipattibhavaloka), and the world of the origin of failure (vipattisambhavaloka). One world: all beings subsist on nutriment. Two worlds: mind and matter. Three worlds: the three feelings. Four worlds: the four nutriments. Five worlds: the five aggregates of clinging. Six worlds: the six internal bases. Seven worlds: the seven stations of consciousness. Eight worlds: the eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds: the nine abodes of beings. Ten worlds: the ten bases. Twelve worlds: the twelve bases. Eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements. 'Fault' (vajja) means: all defilements are faults, all misconducts are faults, all volitional formations are faults, and all kamma leading to rebirth are faults. Thus, in this world and in this fault, a strong perception of fear is established, just as if an executioner were raising a sword. Through these fifty modes, He knows, sees, understands, and penetrates these five faculties. This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the proficiency of the faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa). 'Uppaliniyaṃ' means in a grove of blue and white lotuses. The same method applies to the other terms. 'Antonimuggaposīnī' refers to lotuses that grow while remaining submerged in the water. 'Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitānī' refers to lotuses that stand having risen above the water. Among them, those that stand having risen above the water are lotuses that will bloom today, awaiting the touch of the sun's rays. Those that stand level with the water are lotuses that will bloom tomorrow. Those that have not yet emerged from the water but grow while submerged are lotuses that will bloom on the third day. There are also other blue and red lotuses that do not emerge from the water and are diseased; these will not bloom but will only become food for fish and tortoises. Although these are not mentioned in the Pāḷi text, the commentator included them for comparison. Just like these four types of lotuses, there are four types of persons: the one who understands through a brief instruction (ugghaṭitaññū), the one who understands through a detailed explanation (vipañcitaññū), the one who is guidable (neyya), and the one for whom the word is the maximum (padaparama). Among these four types of persons, the person for whom the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurs at the very time a teaching is uttered is called an 'ugghaṭitaññū' person. For the person who, when...
185: ...is called an 'ugghaṭitaññū' person. For the person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs when the meaning of a briefly stated Pāḷi text is analyzed in detail, this person is called a 'vipañcitaññū' person. For the person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs gradually through learning the Pāḷi, questioning the commentary, proper attention (yoniso manasikāra), and associating with, following, and attending upon good friends, this person is called a 'neyya' person. For the person who, although having learned much of the Pāḷi and commentary, having memorized much of the Pāḷi, and having taught many scriptures, does not attain the realization of the Dhamma in that very life, this person is called a 'padaparama' person. Then, the Blessed One, surveying the ten thousand world systems which are like a lotus grove, saw: 'Ugghaṭitaññū persons like the lotuses blooming today, vipañcitaññū persons like the lotuses blooming tomorrow, neyya persons like the lotuses blooming on the third day, and padaparama persons like the lotuses that do not bloom and are eaten by fish and tortoises.' While seeing this, He saw in every aspect: 'This many beings have little dust in their eyes of wisdom, this many beings have much dust in their eyes of wisdom; among them, this many are ugghaṭitaññū persons.' Among those four types of persons, for the three types beginning with the ugghaṭitaññū, the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One brings about the benefit in this very life. For the padaparama persons, it becomes a latent tendency (vāsanā) for the sake of attaining the Path in the future. Having seen this, the Blessed One, knowing the Dhamma teaching that brings benefit to these four types of persons, aroused the desire to teach. Then, He again divided all beings in the three realms of existence into two groups based on whether they were capable or incapable of liberation. Regarding those beings, it was said: 'Which beings are incapable (abhabba)? Those beings who are possessed of the obstruction of kamma (kammāvaraṇa), possessed of the obstruction of defilement (kilesāvaraṇa), possessed of the obstruction of result (vipākāvaraṇa), who lack faith, lack desire, and lack wisdom—these are incapable of entering the certain path of rightness (sammattaniyāma) in wholesome states. These are called incapable beings. Which beings are capable (bhabba)? Those beings who are not possessed of the obstruction of kamma... (pe)... these are called capable beings.' Among those aforementioned persons, setting aside all incapable persons and encompassing only the capable persons with His knowledge, He made six divisions: 'This many have a lustful temperament (rāgacarita), this many have a hateful temperament (dosacarita), a deluded temperament (mohacarita), a discursive temperament (vitakkacarita), a faithful temperament (saddhācarita), and a wise temperament (paññācarita).' Having done so, He reflected, 'I shall teach the Dhamma.' 'Paccabhāsī' means He replied. 'Apārutā' means they are opened. 'Amatassa dvārā' means the Noble Path (ariyamagga). For that Noble Path is like the entrance door to Nibbāna, which is called the Deathless. He shows: 'That Noble Path, which is like the door to Nibbāna, has been opened by Me.' 'Pamuñcantu saddhaṃ' means let all people release their faith. In the combination of the two words 'I have opened' and so on, the following is the meaning. Therein, one's own person...
186:
"Let them release (their faith); let them give it up." In the last two feet, this is the meaning: "Indeed, I did not speak this sublime and supreme Dhamma, which I have well-mastered and well-practiced, thinking that it would be a weariness to my body and speech. But now, let all people bring the vessel of faith; I shall fulfill their aspirations."

"Antaradhāyī" means having honored the Teacher with flowers, perfumes, and so forth, he disappeared from before Him and went to his own place. After that Brahma had left, the Blessed One reflected, "To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?" Knowing that Āḷāra and Uddaka had passed away, and knowing the great helpfulness of the group of five (pañcavaggiya), He wished to teach them. He went to Isipatana in Bārāṇasī and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana). The first sutta (Brahmayācana Sutta) is finished.

## 2. Gāravasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "udapādi" means this thought arose in the fifth week. "Agāravo" means being without respect for others, not placing anyone in a position of respect. "Appatisso" means being without deference, not placing anyone in the position of a superior.

In the terms beginning with "sadevake," the world together with devas is called "sadevaka." Although Māra and Brahmā are included in the term "deva," Māra is a wielder of power (vasavattī) who exercises authority over all, and Brahmā is of great majesty, able to radiate light through a thousand world-systems with one finger... two fingers... and with ten fingers, he can radiate light through ten thousand world-systems. To prevent it being said that "these are more perfect in virtue than this [Ascetic Gotama]," they are mentioned separately as "samārake sabrahmake." Similarly, recluses (samaṇa) are learned, virtuous, and wise according to the Nikāyas, etc., and brahmins (brāhmaṇa) are learned and wise according to the science of sites (vatthuvijjā), etc. To prevent it being said that "they are more perfect in virtue than this [Ascetic Gotama]," it is said "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya." "Sadevamanussāya" is said by including what was already included to show completeness. Alternatively, the first three terms are spoken in terms of the world (loka), and the last two in terms of beings (pajā). "Sīlasampannataraṃ" means more perfect in virtue, more excellent. The same method applies to the rest. Here, the four dhammas beginning with virtue (sīla) are spoken of as both mundane and supramundane, but "vimuttiñāṇadassana" is spoken of as purely mundane. This is because it is reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa).
187:
"Pāturahosi" means: "This Teacher, from Avīci to the highest plane of existence (Bhavagga), sees no one superior to himself in virtue and so forth. He thinks, 'I will dwell honoring, respecting, and depending on the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (nava-lokuttara-dhamma) that I have realized.' The Blessed One considers the cause; He considers the special benefit. Thinking, 'I will go and arouse effort in Him,' Sahampati Brahma thought and appeared clearly before the Blessed One; he stood in front of Him."

In these words "Viharanti ca," if someone says, "Because of the plural word 'viharanti' (they dwell), there are many Buddhas in the present," they should be refuted with the words: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is even now the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."

Through such suttas as "I have no teacher, no one like me exists; in the world with its devas, I have no rival," the non-existence of other Buddhas [at the same time] should be shown. Therefore, because all Buddhas honor the True Dhamma, it is said "tasmā" (therefore). "Mahattamabhikaṅkhatā" means one who desires greatness. "Saraṃ buddhānasāsanaṃ" means one who remembers the teaching of the Buddhas should honor the True Dhamma. This is the second [Sekha Sutta].

## 3. Brahmadatta Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "Eko" means being alone in postures such as standing and so forth; one who dwells alone. "Vūpakaṭṭho" means physically secluded and withdrawn from the crowd. "Appamatto" means established in non-negligence (mindfulness). "Ātāpī" means endowed with the energy that burns away defilements. "Pahitatto" means having a mind directed [towards Nibbāna]. "Kulaputtā" means sons of good family by way of conduct. "Sammadeva" means not out of being oppressed by debt, fear, or difficulty in livelihood, but even if they went forth in any way, those who fulfill the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (anuloma-paṭipadā) are said to have rightly gone forth from the home life into homelessness. "Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ" means the Noble Fruit (ariya-phala) which is the consummation of the holy life of the Path. "Diṭṭheva dhamme" means in this very life. "Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā" means having known by oneself and realized through direct experience. "Upasampajja" means having attained and accomplished. While dwelling thus, he understood: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being." By this, the stage of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-bhūmi) of the Elder Brahmadatta is shown.
188:
If it is asked: 'Which birth of his is destroyed, and how did he know that destruction?'—it is said: It is not his past birth that is now destroyed, for that was already destroyed by being in the past. It is not the future birth, for there is no effort [to produce it] in that future time (or it is of the nature of non-arising). It is not the present birth, for it is currently existing. However, there is the birth that would have arisen in the realms of one, four, or five constituents, categorized by one, four, or five aggregates, because the Path had not yet been developed. That birth, because the Path has been developed, has reached the state of non-arising and is thus destroyed. Having reflected on the defilements abandoned through the development of the Path, he knows: 'When there are no defilements, even if kamma exists, there will be no rebirth in the future.'

'Vusitaṃ' means that which has been used or practiced; the meaning is that the practice has been completed. 'Brahmacariyaṃ' refers to the Noble Life of the Path. 'Kataṃ karaṇီyaṃ' means that the sixteenfold task—by way of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing through the four Paths regarding the Four Noble Truths—has been completed. 'Nāparaṃ itthattāya' means that now there is no further development of the Path to be done for the sake of such a state of existence, or for the sake of these sixteen tasks, or for the destruction of defilements. Alternatively, 'itthattāya' means that from this present continuity of aggregates of such a nature, there will be no further continuity of aggregates; he understood that these five aggregates remain fully understood, like a tree whose roots have been cut. 'Aññataro' means a certain person. 'Arahatam' means he became one among the Arahants, the disciples of the Blessed One.

'Sapadānaṃ' means undertaking the practice of house-to-house alms round, wandering in sequence without skipping any house that is reached. 'Upasaṅkami' means while approaching. The mother of that venerable one, upon seeing her son, came out of the house, took his bowl, led him inside, and made him sit on the prepared seat.

'Āhutiṃ niccaṃ paggaṇhāti' means the constant bringing and offering of food and offerings. On that day, however, there was a ritual of offering to spirits (bhūtabalikamma) in that house. The entire house was smeared with fresh cow dung, parched rice was scattered, it was surrounded by wild flowers, and banners and flags were raised. Water-filled pots were placed here and there, lamps were lit, and it was decorated with scented powders, flowers, and so on; it was covered all around with smoke and flames. That Brahmin woman also rose early, bathed with sixteen pots of scented water, and adorned herself with all kinds of ornaments. At that time, having seated the Great Arahant, without giving even a ladleful of gruel, she thought, 'I will feed the Great Brahma,' and filled a golden bowl with milk-rice, mixed it with ghee, honey, and sugar, and at the house's...
189:
...filling it with milk-rice and mixing it with ghee, honey, sugar, and so on. At the back of the house, there was a platform for Brahma, decorated by smearing with fresh cow dung and such. Taking that golden bowl and going to that place, she placed a lump of milk-rice at each of the four corners and one in the middle. Holding one lump in her hand, with ghee dripping down to her elbows, she knelt with her knees on the ground and said, 'May the Great Brahma eat; may the Great Brahma enjoy; may the Great Brahma be satisfied,' thus feeding the Brahma.

'This thought occurred' means: the scent of the Great Arahant's virtue pervaded the six deva worlds and reached the Brahma world. To the Great Brahma who smelled it, this thought occurred. 'I shall inspire [her]' means: I shall urge her and join her to the right practice. 'This person, having seated such a supreme recipient of offerings, a Great Arahant, does not give even a ladleful of gruel, but says "I will feed the Great Brahma." Like one who discards a scale to weigh with the hand, or discards a drum to beat the belly, or discards a fire to blow on a firefly, she wanders about performing spirit-offerings. I will go and break her wrong view, lift her from the path to the states of loss, and act so that she may distribute her eighty crores of wealth in the Buddha's Dispensation and ascend the path to heaven.'

'It is far from here' means: the Brahma world is very far from this ground where humans live. If a stone the size of a gabled house were dropped from that Brahma world, falling at a rate of forty-eight thousand yojanas per day, it would take four months to reach the earth. Even the lowest Brahma world is this far away. 'To whichever Brahma she makes an offering' means: the Brahma world of that Brahma you are worshipping is very far away. In this context, 'Brahmapatha' (the path to the Brahma world) refers to the four wholesome jhānas. Resultant jhānas, however, are merely the way of life (lifespan) of those Brahmas. Not knowing that Brahmapatha, why do you mutter and lament? For Brahmas live on jhāna accompanied by rapture; they do not eat cow-milk liquid cooked with grass seeds (grain). Do not tire yourself in vain.

Having said this, that Great Brahma, with hands joined in reverence and facing downwards, pointed to the Elder and said, 'Brahmin woman, this is your Brahmadeva,' and so on. In that passage, 'Nirūpadhika' means one who is free from the acquisitions (upadhi) of defilements, volitional formations, and the cords of sensual pleasure. 'Atidevapatta' means one who has reached the state of a god surpassing gods, a Brahma surpassing Brahmas. 'Ananyaposီ' means one who does not support another, because he does not support another person or a wife and children, apart from maintaining this own body. 'Āhuneyya' means one worthy of receiving offerings brought from afar. 'Vedagū' means one who has reached the end of suffering through the four Path-knowledges. 'Bhāvitatta' means one who stands having developed himself through virtues such as morality. 'Anupalitta' means one who is unstained by impurities such as craving. 'Wanders for alms' means he seeks food for his sustenance. In this Pali, 'He has no past,' 'putta' is said to be the past, and 'purattha' is said to be the future. He is one who is free from desire and lust for the aggregates of the past and the future.
190:
"Ananyaposī" means one who does not support another self-identity or a wife and children, excluding this own self-identity; thus, he is called "Ananyaposī." "Āhuneyyo" means one who is worthy of receiving offerings brought from afar. "Vedagū" means one who has reached the end of suffering through the "Vedas," which are the four paths. "Bhāvitatto" means one who remains having developed oneself (through virtue, etc.). "Anūpalitto" means one who is not smeared by the "smearings" such as craving. "Ghāsesanaṃ iriyati" means he wanders in search of food.

In the phrase "Na tassa pacchā na puratthamatthi," "pacchā" is said to be the past, and "puratthamaṃ" is said to be the future. It means that for one who is free from desire and lust regarding the aggregates of the past and future, there is no past or future. In the words beginning with "santo," he is called "santo" (peaceful) because of the calming of lust and so on. He is called "vidhūmo" (smokeless) because the smoke of anger is gone. He is called "anīgho" (painless) because of the absence of suffering. Even if he wanders holding a staff or a walking stick, he is called "nikkhittadaṇḍo" (one who has laid down the stick) because of the absence of the intention to kill. In the phrase "tasathāvaresu," worldlings (puthujjanas) are called "tasa" (the trembling), and Arahants (khīṇāsavas) are called "thāvara" (the stable). The seven types of noble learners (sekhas) cannot be called "tasa," nor are they "thāvara," but in their practice, they follow only the side of the stable. "So tyāhutiṃ" means "May that Brahmā receive your offering."

"Visenībhūto" means having become one whose army is gone, referring to the army of defilements. "Anejo" means one without craving. "Susīlo" means one with good virtue, through the virtue of an Arahant. "Suvimuttacitto" means one whose mind is well-liberated through the liberation of fruition (phala-vimutti). "Oghatiṇṇaṃ" means one who has crossed the four floods. With this much sequence of words, the Brahmā, while speaking of the Elder's virtues, urged the Brahmin woman in the house. The concluding verse was placed by the Elders who performed the Recitation (Saṅgītikārakas). "Patiṭṭhapesi dakkhiṇaṃ" means he established the offering of the four requisites. "Sukhamāyatikaṃ" means having a happy result in the future, meaning it brings happiness. The third sutta is finished.

## ၄။ ဗကဗြဟ္မသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the fourth sutta, "pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ" means a low eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). "Idaṃ niccaṃ" means saying that this Brahma realm, which exists along with the body, is "permanent" even though it is impermanent. The words "dhuva" and so on are just synonyms for that word "nicca." Among them, "dhuva" means stable. "Sassataṃ" means existing at all times. "Kevalaṃ" means complete without limit. "Acavanadhammaṃ" means not having the nature of passing away. In the words "Idaṃ hi na jāyati" and so on, [Baka Brahmā thinks] there is no one who is reborn, ages, dies, passes away, or reappears in this realm.
191:
It refers to the absence of passing away and rebirth, meaning there is no one who passes away or reappears. "There is no other besides this" means there is no other escape superior to this Brahma realm along with this Brahma state. Thus, a strong eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) arose in that Baka Brahmā. That Brahmā, holding such a view, denies all the three higher Jhana realms, the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna. When did that view arise in him? It arose when he was born in the first Jhana realm. Some teachers say it arose when he was born in the second Jhana realm.

The sequential story regarding this matter is as follows: It is said that this Baka Brahmā was one who used to be born in lower realms. In the time before a Buddha appeared, he went forth as a hermit (isi), performed the preliminary work for Kasina, and attained meditative attainments (samāpatti). Having died with his Jhana unimpaired, he was born in the Vehapphala Brahma world, the fourth Jhana realm, with a lifespan of five hundred great aeons (mahākappa). Having stayed there for the full lifespan, he then took birth in a lower realm, developed the noble third Jhana, and was born in the Subhakiṇha Brahma world with a lifespan of sixty-four aeons. Having developed the second Jhana there, he was born in the Ābhassara realm with a lifespan of eight aeons. Having developed the first Jhana there, he was born in the first Jhana realm with a lifespan of one aeon. In the early period of that life, he knew his own past karma and his place of birth. However, as time went by, he forgot both and developed the eternalist view.

"Avijjāgato" means one who is possessed of ignorance, unlearned, and has become like a blind person. "Yatra hi nāma" means "the one who." "Vakkhati" means "will say." Because it is joined with the particle "yatra," it is expressed in the future tense.

When this was said, that Brahmā was like a highway robber who, while receiving two or three blows, endures without naming his companions, but when struck with a further blow, says, "So-and-so and so-and-so are my companions." Similarly, when threatened by the Blessed One, he regained his mindfulness and, fearing that "The Blessed One, looking at my every move, wishes to crush me," he said the words beginning with "dvāsattatī" wishing to name his companions. The meaning of that verse is: "Friend Gotama, we seventy-two people performed meritorious deeds and were born here because of those meritorious deeds. We are masters (vasavattino); without falling under the control of others, we bring others under our own control. We have transcended birth and aging. We have reached the designation 'Vedagū' because we are known through the Vedas. Venerable Sir, this is our final Brahma birth. 'Asmābhijappanti janā anekā' means many people desire and cherish us seventy-two."
192:
Many people long for and admire us (the seventy-two Brahmas). They long for and admire us, saying: 'This venerable one is indeed Brahma, Mahābrahma, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-seeing, the Controller, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Best, the Apportioner, the Master, the Father of those who have been and those who are to be.'

Then the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'Appaṃ hi etaṃ.' In that context, 'etaṃ' means: this life of yours in this Brahma realm, which you think is 'long,' is actually very little, very short. 'Sataṃ sahassānaṃ nirabbudānaṃ' means: I, the Buddha, know the life span of a hundred thousand nirabbudas. 'I know that your remaining life is now only this much.' You say, 'I am an Anantadassī (one who sees infinite things to be known), one who has transcended birth and so forth.' Baka Brahma said, 'If you are truly an Anantadassī, then tell me this: what was my ancient habit of virtue and practice? Tell me this matter.' 'Vatasīlavattaṃ' refers to virtue (sīla) itself. He said, 'I wish to know the matter spoken by you, O Buddha; please tell me that matter.'

Now, the Blessed One, wishing to tell Baka Brahma, spoke the words beginning with 'Yaṃ tvaṃ apāyesi.' The meaning is: In the past, it is said that this Baka Brahma was born in a noble family. Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he thought, 'I will make an end to birth, aging, and death,' and went forth as a hermit (isi). Having attained the meditative attainments (samāpatti) and the jhānas which are the basis for psychic powers (abhiññā), he built a leaf hut on the bank of the Ganges and spent his time delighting in jhāna. At that time, from time to time, merchants with five hundred wagons would enter the Maru desert. In the Maru desert, it is impossible to travel by day; travel occurs only at night. Then, the great oxen yoked to the front of the lead wagon, as they went along, turned back and faced the path they had come from. All the wagons turned back in the same way, and only when the dawn rose did they realize they had turned back. That day was supposed to be the day they crossed the desert, but all the wood and water were exhausted. Therefore, thinking, 'Now there is no life left for us,' they tied the oxen to the wagon wheels, and the people entered the shade of the wagons and lay down.

The hermit also came out of his leaf hut early and, sitting at the door of the hut looking at the Ganges, saw the great river coming full of a great flood of water, like a rolling mass of jewels. Seeing this, he thought, 'Are there any beings in this world suffering from not obtaining such sweet water?' As he was thus reflecting, he saw that caravan in the Maru desert and, thinking 'May these beings not perish,' he resolved: 'Let a great mass of water break off from here and there...'
193:
...and go toward the caravan in the desert.' He resolved with his mind of psychic power (abhiññā-citta). Simultaneously with the arising of the thought, the water went to that journey as if it were being poured into a canal. The people, hearing the sound of water, got up and, seeing the water, were greatly delighted. They bathed, drank, and gave water to the oxen, and then proceeded safely to their desired destination. The Blessed One, wishing to show Baka Brahma's past deed, spoke the first verse. In that verse, 'apāyesi' means 'you caused to drink.' The 'a' prefix is merely a particle. 'Gammantī' means 'in the summer.' 'Samparete' means 'afflicted or reached by the heat of the summer sun.'

At another time, the hermit created a leaf hut on the bank of the Ganges and lived depending on a small forest village. At that time, bandits attacked that village, took away valuable property, and departed, seizing cows and captives. The cows, the dogs, and the people all wailed loudly. The hermit, hearing that sound, reflected, 'What is this?' and knowing that danger had arisen for the people, he thought, 'While I am watching, let these beings not perish.' He entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for psychic power, and after emerging from the jhāna, he created a fourfold army in the path of the bandits with his mind of psychic power. The bandits, seeing the army coming in battle array, thought, 'The King has surely come,' and abandoning their loot, they fled. The hermit resolved, 'Let whatever belongs to whomever be theirs alone,' and it happened exactly so. The people reached safety and happiness. The Blessed One, wishing to show this past deed of Baka Brahma as well, spoke the second verse. In that verse, 'Eṇikūlasmiṃ' means 'on the bank of the Ganges.' 'Gayhakaṃ nīyamānaṃ' should be understood as 'when being taken as a captive' or 'when the one captured by hand is being led away.'

Again, at another time, a family living on the upper Ganges made a friendship with a family living on the lower Ganges. They tied boats and rafts together, loaded them with many kinds of food, perfumes, flowers, and so on, and came down with the current of the Ganges. The people, eating, drinking, dancing, and singing, were filled with great joy as if they were traveling in a celestial mansion. A Naga named Gaṅgeyyaka saw them and became angry, thinking, 'These people do not even show me a sign of recognition. Now I will send them to the very ocean.' He created a huge physical form, split the water in two, emerged, spread his hood, and stood there making a hissing sound. The people, seeing him, cried out in terror. The hermit living in the leaf hut heard them and reflected, 'These people were coming with joy, dancing and singing, but now they are wailing with the sound of danger. For what reason?'
