When it is time for alms-round, he adjusts his inner robe, fastens his waistband, puts on his upper robe, and takes his bowl. Sometimes alone, sometimes surrounded by the Sangha of monks, he enters a village or a market town for alms. Sometimes he enters in his natural form, and sometimes accompanied by many miraculous wonders.

These are the wonders: As the Lord of the World enters for alms, gentle winds precede him and cleanse the ground. Clouds sprinkle drops of water to settle the dust on the path and then remain above as a canopy. Other winds bring flowers and scatter them on the path. High places on the ground level out, and low places rise up. When he sets down his feet, the ground becomes perfectly even, or else soft-to-the-touch lotus flowers receive his feet. As soon as he places his right foot inside the threshold, six-colored rays emit from his body, running here and there, making palaces and pinnacled gables appear as if sprinkled with liquid gold or draped with variegated cloth. Elephants, horses, birds, and other animals, remaining in their respective places, make sweet sounds. Likewise, musical instruments such as drums and lutes, and even the ornaments worn by people, produce melodious sounds.

By these signs, people know, "Today the Blessed One has entered here for alms." Dressed and robed properly, they take scents, flowers, and other offerings, leave their houses, reach the street, and respectfully worship the Blessed One with scents and flowers. They request, "Venerable Sir, give us ten monks," "Give us twenty," or "Give us a hundred monks," and taking the Buddha's bowl, they prepare seats and respectfully serve them with alms-food.
225:
After the Blessed One had finished his meal, he surveyed the mental dispositions of the people and taught the Dhamma in such a way that some were established in the Three Refuges, some in the Five Precepts, some in one of the fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, or Non-returning, and some, having gone forth, were established in the supreme fruit of Arahantship. Having thus benefited the multitude, he rose from his seat and went to the monastery. There, he sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the perfumed pavilion, waiting for the monks to finish their meal. Then, when the monks' meal was finished, the attendant monk informed the Blessed One. Thereupon, the Blessed One entered the Gandhakuṭi. This is the pre-meal duty (purebhattakicca).

Then, the Blessed One, having performed the pre-meal duties, sat in the attendance hall of the Gandhakuṭi, washed his feet, and standing on the footstool, exhorted the assembly of monks: "Monks, strive with diligence; the arising of a Buddha in the world is rare, the attainment of human birth is rare, the perfection of faith is rare, going forth is rare, and hearing the True Dhamma is rare." Then, some monks asked the Blessed One for meditation subjects. The Blessed One gave them meditation subjects suitable for their temperaments. Then, all the monks, having paid homage to the Blessed One, went to their respective places for the night and day. Some went to the forest, some to the foot of a tree, some to a mountain or similar place, some to the realm of the Four Great Kings... and some to the realm of the Vasavatti devas. Then, the Blessed One entered the Gandhakuṭi and, if he so desired, mindfully and clearly comprehending, he would lie down for a moment in the lion's posture on his right side. Then, with his body refreshed, he rose and, in the second part of the afternoon, surveyed the world of beings to be guided. In the third part, he would stay depending on a village or market town; there, the people, having given alms before the meal, would gather at the monastery after the meal, well-dressed and well-robed, bringing perfumes, flowers, and so on. Then, the Blessed One, proceeding with suitable psychic power to the assembled company, sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma hall and taught the Dhamma appropriate to the time and occasion. Then, knowing the time, he dismissed the assembly, and the people, having paid homage to the Blessed One, departed. This is the post-meal duty (pacchābhattakicca).

Having thus completed the post-meal duties, if he wished to bathe his body, he rose from the Buddha-seat, entered the bathroom, and refreshed his body with water prepared by the attendant monk. The attendant monk also brought the Buddha-seat, dusted it, and spread it in the courtyard of the Gandhakuṭi. The Blessed One, having put on his well-dyed lower robe, fastened his waistband, and properly adjusted his upper robe, came there and...
226:
He sat alone for a moment in the seclusion of fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti). Then, monks came from various places to attend upon the Blessed One. There, some asked questions, some asked for meditation subjects, and some requested to hear the Dhamma. The Blessed One, fulfilling their desires, spent the first watch of the night. This is the duty of the first watch (purimayāmakicca).

At the conclusion of the first watch, when the monks had paid homage to the Blessed One and departed, the deities of the entire ten thousand world systems, obtaining the opportunity, approached the Blessed One and asked questions as they had prepared them, even those as short as four syllables. The Blessed One, answering the questions of those various deities, spent the middle watch of the night. This is the duty of the middle watch (majjhimayāmakicca).

The last watch of the night, however, he divided into three parts. To relieve the fatigue of the body caused by sitting since before the meal, he spent one part in walking meditation. In the second part, he entered the Gandhakuṭi and, mindfully and clearly comprehending, lay down in the lion's posture on his right side. In the third part, he rose and sat down, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye (buddhacakkhu) to see those individuals who had performed meritorious deeds such as giving and virtue in the presence of former Buddhas. This is the duty of the last watch (pacchimayāmakicca).

At that time, while thus surveying, he saw the Brahmin Kasibhāradvāja, who was endowed with the supporting conditions for Arahantship. He thought: "When I go there, a conversation will take place. At the end of the conversation, having heard the Dhamma teaching, this Brahmin, along with his wife and children, will be established in the Three Refuges. Having distributed eighty crores of wealth in my dispensation, he will later renounce the world, go forth, and attain Arahantship." Knowing this, he went there, initiated a conversation, and taught the Dhamma. To show this matter, the words beginning with "Atha kho Bhagavā" were spoken.

In that Pali text, "pubbaṇhasamayaṃ" is the second case (accusative) used in the sense of the seventh case (locative), meaning "in the morning." "Nivāsetvā" means having dressed. This is said in the sense of changing into the monastery robe. "Pattacīvaramādāya" means taking the bowl with the hands and the robe with the body, receiving and carrying them. It is heard that, as the Blessed One desired to enter for alms, the stone bowl, having the color of an emerald (indranīla), came into the middle of his two hands like a bee coming into the middle of two blooming lotuses. Having received the bowl that came thus with his hands, and carrying the robe that was wrapped around him evenly with his body, is what is meant.
227:
'Te nupasaṅkami' means that the Blessed One approached alone by the very path that one must take to reach the plowing festival. Why did the monks not follow the Blessed One? Whenever the Blessed One wished to go somewhere alone, he would close the door and stay inside the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) until the time for the alms-round. By that sign, the monks knew, "Today the Blessed One wishes to wander for alms alone; he has surely seen someone who is fit to be tamed." Those monks would then take their own bowls and robes, circumambulate the Fragrant Chamber, pay their respects, and go on their alms-round. On that occasion, too, the Blessed One acted in this manner, which is why the monks did not follow him.

'Parivesanā vattati' means that the task of serving the five hundred plowmen, who sat holding golden vessels and so forth, was not yet finished. 'Ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi' means he stood in a high place where the Brahmin could see him, where it was easy to hear his words, and within sight. While standing there, he emitted a bodily radiance from all directions, yellow like liquid silver and gold, surpassing the brilliance of the moon and the sun. Due to the pervading influence of that radiance, the walls of the Brahmin's workshop, the trees, and the clods of earth turned up by the plow appeared as if they were made of gold. Then the people, whether eating or plowing, abandoned all their tasks. They saw the Fully Enlightened One standing in a suitable place, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) and accompanied by the eighty minor characteristics (Asīti-anubyañjana), beautified by a fathom-wide aura, with a pair of arms like a moving lotus pond, like the sky filled with a host of stars shining with nets of rays, and like a golden mountain peak entwined with lightning, blazing with glory. They washed their hands and feet, raised their joined palms in salutation, and stood surrounding the Blessed One. Seeing the Blessed One standing for alms while surrounded by the crowd, the Brahmin Kasibhāradvāja said to the Blessed One, "O ascetic, I plow and I sow."

Why did the Brahmin say this? Was it because he lacked faith in the Tathāgata, who is inspiring in every direction and has attained supreme self-control and tranquility? Or was it out of stinginess regarding a single spoonful of alms-food, even though he had prepared milk-rice for two thousand five hundred people? It was not for either of those reasons. Rather, seeing his people abandon their work because they were not satisfied with gazing at the Blessed One, he felt displeased, thinking, "He has come to ruin my work."

Furthermore, seeing the perfection of the Blessed One's marks, he thought, "If this person were to engage in work, he would be like a crest-gem on the heads of the people in the whole of Jambudīpa. Why should his welfare not be fulfilled? Why does he, out of laziness, not work and instead wander for alms at festivals such as this plowing ceremony?" Thus he was displeased. Therefore, he said, "O ascetic, I plow and I sow; only after plowing and sowing do I eat."
228:
Therefore, he spoke thus. Seeing the perfection of the Blessed One's marks, he thought: "If this person were to manage affairs and work, he would be like a crest-gem on the heads of the people in the whole of Jambudīpa. Why should his prosperity not be complete? In this way, due to laziness, he does not manage affairs but wanders for alms at plowing festivals and the like." Thus, the Brahmin was displeased. Therefore, he said: "O ascetic, I plow and I sow; having plowed and sown, I eat."

This was his intention: "My works are not ruined; I am still striving. I am not endowed with marks like you. You, too, should plow and sow and eat. For one endowed with such marks as you, what prosperity would not be fulfilled?" Alternatively, he had heard: "A prince was born in the Sakyan royal family; he renounced the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) and went forth." Knowing now that "This is he," and wishing to reproach him, he said: "Having renounced the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch, you are now exhausted." There is yet another view: this Brahmin was one of sharp wisdom. He did not speak because he lacked faith in the Blessed One. Rather, seeing the perfection of the Blessed One's physical form and honoring the perfection of his merit, he spoke thus to initiate a conversation. Then the Blessed One, according to the disposition of the one to be tamed, showed his own status as the supreme plowman and sower in the world with its devas, saying: "O Brahmin, I too..." and so on.

Then the Brahmin thought: "This ascetic says, 'I too plow and sow.' Yet I do not see his coarse plowing implements such as the yoke and plow. How is this? Does he speak a falsehood?" Examining the Blessed One from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair using the science of body marks (Aṅgavijjā), and knowing that he was endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks of a Great Man because of his performed merits, he thought: "It is impossible for such a person to speak a falsehood." With great respect arising, he abandoned the address 'ascetic' (Samana) and addressed the Blessed One by his clan name, saying: "We do not see the Venerable Gotama's..." and so on. Because it is the power of the Buddhas to speak in accordance with the Dhamma previously established, the Blessed One, demonstrating the Buddha-power, said: "Faith is the seed," and so on.

What is this "accordance with the Dhamma previously established"? Did the Brahmin not ask the Blessed One about the connection with plowing implements like the plow? Yet the Blessed One spoke of the seed, which was not asked about, as being of a similar nature: "Faith is the seed." If this is so, the speech would also be disconnected and inconsistent in its sequence (Anusandhi). For the Buddhas...
229:
In the speech of the Buddhas, there is no such thing as disconnected discourse, nor do they teach in a manner that is inconsistent with the Dhamma previously taken up. In this teaching, the connection of sequence (anusandhi) should be understood as follows: The Brahmin asked the Blessed One about farming by way of the components of farming such as the yoke and the plow. Out of compassion for that Brahmin, the Blessed One, not omitting even the unasked matters, wished to make known the nature of farming together with its root, its support, its components, and its fruit. Thus, showing it starting from the very foundation, He said: "Faith is the seed," and so forth.

In that statement, the seed is the foundation of farming. This is because farming is performed only when there is seed, and not when there is no seed; and it is performed according to the measure of the seed. Skilled farmers plow the field in accordance with the amount of seed, thinking, "Let our crops not diminish," and they do not plow in excess, thinking, "Let our effort not be in vain." Since the seed alone is the foundation, the Blessed One, showing the components of farming starting from the foundation, and wishing to show the Dhamma first taken up in His own farming which is consistent with the seed first taken up in that Brahmin's farming, said: "Faith is the seed." In this way, the consistency of the Dhamma first taken up should also be understood.

If it is asked, "Why were the unasked matters not spoken after first stating only what was asked?" it is because such a teaching is beneficial and is capable of connecting with the benefit of the Dhamma. Indeed, this Brahmin was wise, but having been born in a family of wrong view, he was devoid of faith. A wise person who is devoid of faith cannot practice in a matter that is not his own domain through the faith of others, and thus cannot attain distinction. Furthermore, his weak faith, being overwhelmed by the defilement of impurity, even if it exists alongside powerful wisdom, cannot accomplish the goal, just like an ox yoked to the same shaft as an elephant. Thus, faith is beneficial to him. Wishing to establish that Brahmin in faith, this meaning which should have been spoken later was spoken first due to skillfulness in teaching. Moreover, rain is beneficial to the seed; stating the matter of rain immediately after that [seed] is capable of connecting it with the benefit. Thus, because of the ability to connect the Dhamma, this meaning which should have been spoken later, as well as other meanings such as the plow-pole and the bond, should be understood as having been spoken first.

In that teaching, faith has the characteristic of clarity (sampasāda) or the characteristic of conviction (okappana). "Seed" (bīja) refers to five kinds of seeds: root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, bud-seed, and seed-seed as the fifth. All of these are designated as "seed" in the sense of germinating and growing.
230:
In that teaching of "Faith is the seed" and so forth, by way of analogy, the seed which is the cause in the Brahmin's farming performs two functions: it stands firmly below by the root and it causes the sprout to rise above. Similarly, faith, which is the cause in the Blessed One's farming, stands firmly below by the root of virtue (sīla) and causes the sprout of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā) to rise above. Furthermore, just as that grain seed, taking the essence of earth and the essence of water through the root, grows through the stalk to receive the ripening of the grain, so this faith, taking the essence of tranquility and insight meditation through the root of virtue, grows through the stalk of the Noble Path (ariya-magga) to obtain the ripening of the grain of the Noble Fruit (ariya-phala).

Just as that grain seed, being established in good soil, reaches growth, increase, and abundance through the development of roots, sprouts, leaves, stalks, and stems, and producing milk, accomplishes the rice-ear filled with countless grains; so this faith, being established in the mental continuum, reaches growth, increase, and abundance through the six purifications (visuddhi), and producing the milk of the purification of knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi), accomplishes the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) filled with many analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and direct knowledges (abhiññā). Therefore, He said: "Faith is the seed."

But why is only faith called the "seed" when more than fifty other wholesome states arise together with it? It is because it performs the function of a seed. Just as among those states, consciousness (viññāṇa) alone performs the function of cognizing, so faith performs the function of a seed. And it is the foundation of all wholesome states. As it is said: "One who has faith approaches; approaching, he attends... and through wisdom, he fully penetrates and sees that Dhamma."

It is called "tapa" (ardor/austerity) because it causes unwholesome states and the body to burn. This is a designation for sense restraint (indriya-saṃvara), energy (vīriya), ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and difficult practices (dukkara-kārikā); however, in this context, sense restraint is intended. "Vuṭṭhi" (rain) is of many kinds, such as rainfall and wind-rain, but here rainfall is intended. Just as the seed and the crops caused by the seed, being well-supported by the Brahmin's rainfall, grow and reach completion without withering; so the faith and the states such as virtue rooted in faith, being well-supported by the Blessed One's sense restraint, grow and reach completion without withering. Therefore, He said: "Ardor is the rain."

In the phrase "paññā me" (my wisdom), the word "me" should also be applied to the preceding terms as "my faith is the seed, my ardor is the rain." What is shown by this? It should be understood thus: "Brahmin, in the field sown by you, if there is rain, it is well. If there is no rain, water must be brought from rivers, lakes, or dams. Similarly, when I have yoked the oxen of energy, having bound them together with the bond of the mind to the plow-pole of shame (hiri) and the yoke and plow of wisdom, and having prodded them with the goad of mindfulness, there is no such thing as a lack of rain when the seed of faith is sown in the field of my own mental continuum. Indeed, for me, this state of sense restraint is always like the rain of ardor."

Although wisdom (paññā) is of many kinds, such as that of the sense sphere, in this context, the Path-wisdom (magga-paññā) together with tranquility and insight is intended. "Yuganangalaṃ" means the yoke and the plow. Brahmin, just as you yoke the yoke and the plow, the twofold wisdom of the Blessed One is the yoke and the plow. In that statement, just as the yoke is the support for the plow-pole and is bound to the plow-pole at the front, and being the support for the bonds, it restrains the oxen by knowing their movement so they go straight without swerving to one side; so wisdom is the support for states such as shame. Therefore, it is said: "All wholesome states have wisdom as their chief," and "Among wholesome states, wisdom is said to be the best."
231:
Once (the seed of faith) is sown, there is no such thing as a lack of rain; indeed, for me, this practice of sense-restraint (indriya-saṃvara-tapa) is always like rain.

Although wisdom (paññā) is of many kinds, such as those belonging to the sense sphere and so on, in this context, it refers to Path-wisdom (magga-paññā) together with insight (vipassanā). 'Yuganangala' refers to the yoke and the plow. Just as a Brahmin has a yoke and a plow, the Blessed One also has both insight and wisdom. In that context, just as the yoke is the support for the shaft (īsā), is tied to the shaft in front, is the support for the ropes (yotta), and maintains the oxen moving together, so too wisdom is the supporting condition (upanissaya) for states such as shame (hirī).

Therefore, it was said: "All wholesome states have wisdom as their chief," and "The wise say wisdom is best among wholesome states, like the moon among stars." Wisdom stands in front because it precedes wholesome states. As it is said: "Virtue, glory, and the Dhamma of the virtuous follow one who possesses wisdom." Because it arises without being separated from shame, it is like being tied to the shaft. Because it is the supporting condition for the rope of concentration (samādhi) known as 'mind' (mano), it is the support for the ropes. By preventing over-exertion and laxity, it maintains the oxen of energy (vīriya) moving together. Just as a plow fitted with a plowshare breaks the hard earth and cuts through the roots when plowing, so too wisdom coupled with mindfulness breaks the compactness (ghana) of continuity (santati), group (samūha), function (kicca), and object (ārammaṇa) during insight meditation, and destroys all the roots of defilements. That wisdom is indeed supramundane (lokuttara), though it could also be mundane (lokiya). Therefore, He said: "Wisdom is my yoke and plow."

Hirī is so called because one is ashamed of evil states. By mentioning hirī, the dread of wrongdoing (ottappa) which is inseparable from it is also included. The shaft (īsā) is the wooden pole that holds the yoke and plow together. Just as a Brahmin's shaft holds the yoke and plow, so too the Blessed One's shame (hirī) carries the yoke and plow known as mundane and supramundane wisdom. This is because without shame, there is no wisdom. Just as the yoke and plow tied to the shaft perform their task steadily and without loosening, so too wisdom tied to shame performs its task steadily, without loosening, and without being mixed with shamelessness (ahirika). Therefore, He said: "Shame is my shaft." 'Mano' is so called because it knows; it is a name for the mind (citta). But here, with 'mind' as the head, concentration (samādhi) associated with it is intended. 'Yotta' means the binding rope. That rope is of three kinds along with the shaft...
232:
...binding the yoke, binding the oxen to the yoke, and binding the oxen together with the charioteer. In this context, just as a Brahmin uses the rope to unite the shaft, yoke, and oxen into one to accomplish his plowing, so too the Blessed One's concentration (samādhi) binds all those states of shame, wisdom, and energy to a single object with the nature of non-distraction to accomplish its task (such as insight). Therefore, He said: "Mind is the rope."

Sati (mindfulness) is so called because it remembers what was done long ago, etc. Phāla (plowshare) is so called because it breaks. Pācana (goad) is so called because one drives (the oxen) with it. In this sutta, it is called "pācana" (driving-stick). This is a name for the goad (patoda). Phālapācana means the plowshare and the goad. Just as a Brahmin has a plowshare and a goad, the Blessed One has mindfulness associated with insight and the Path. In that context, just as the plowshare protects the plow and goes before it, so too mindfulness, while searching for the course of wholesome and unwholesome states or establishing them in the object, protects the plow of wisdom. For this reason, it is called "protection" (ārakkha), as in "He dwells with a mind protected by mindfulness." By virtue of non-forgetfulness, it stands before that wisdom. Indeed, wisdom understands only the states that are made present by mindfulness, not those that are forgotten. And just as the goad, by showing the danger of being pricked, does not let the oxen sink down and prevents them from going off-track, so too mindfulness, by showing the danger of the lower realms (apāya) to the oxen of energy, does not let them sink into sloth. By preventing them from wandering into the wrong pastures of the five cords of sensual pleasure and engaging them in the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), it prevents them from going off-track. Therefore, He said: "Mindfulness is my plowshare and goad."

'Kāyagutto' means guarded by the three types of bodily right conduct. 'Vacīgutto' means guarded by the four types of verbal right conduct. By this, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) is stated. In the phrase 'āhāre udare yato' (restrained in food and stomach), since all four requisites are included by way of food, it means being restrained in the four requisites and being free from defilements. By this, the virtue of purity of livelihood (ājီva-pārisuddhi-sīla) is stated. 'Udare yato' means being restrained in the stomach, eating in moderation, and knowing the measure in food. By this statement, with moderation in eating (bhojane mattaññutā) as the head, the virtue regarding the use of requisites (paccaya-paṭisevana-sīla) is stated. What does this show? Brahmin, just as you sow seeds and make a fence of thorns, trees, or a surrounding wall to protect the crops, so that herds of cattle, buffaloes, and deer cannot enter and destroy the crops, so too I, having sown the seed of faith, to protect the various crops of wholesome states, have made a threefold enclosure consisting of restraint in body, speech, and food...
233:
I perform (the three circles). Because of this, the herds of cattle, buffaloes, and deer, which are the unwholesome states such as lust, do not gain entry and cannot destroy the various crops of merit.

In the phrase 'Saccaṃ karomi niddānaṃ', 'Sacca' (Truth) refers to truthful speech (vaci-viññatti) that does not deviate in two ways: stating what is true as true and what is not true as not true. 'Niddāna' means cutting, reaping, or uprooting. In this context, it should be understood as 'Saccena karomi niddānaṃ' (I perform the weeding with truth). What is meant is this: 'Brahmin, just as you perform weeding in an external field by cutting, reaping, or uprooting weeds that destroy crops with your hands or a sickle, even so, I perform weeding in the internal field by cutting, reaping, or uprooting the weeds of falsehood (vissaṃvādana) that destroy the crops of merit with truth.' Alternatively, 'Sacca' should be understood here as the knowledge of things as they truly are (yathābhūta-ñāṇa). It is shown that with that knowledge, one cuts down the weeds such as the perception of self (atta-saññā). Or else, 'Niddāna' refers to the one who cuts, reaps, or uproots (a laborer). Just as you employ a slave or a laborer for weeding, saying 'Uproot the weeds,' making them the cutter, reaper, or uprooter, it is shown that I make Truth (that laborer). Or else, 'Sacca' refers to the truth of views (diṭṭhi-sacca). It means I make that truth of views something to be cut, reaped, and uprooted. Between these two interpretations, the meaning using the accusative case (upayoga) is more appropriate.

In the phrase 'Soraccaṃ me pamocanaṃ', although the virtue (sīla) of restraint in body and speech is often called 'soracca' (gentleness/restraint), it is not intended here. This is because virtue has already been mentioned by the phrase 'kāyagutto' (guarded in body) and so on. Rather, the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) is intended. It is called 'soracca' because it delights in the sublime Nibbāna. 'Pamocana' means the release from the yoke of effort (yoga). This is what is meant: 'Brahmin, your release (unyoking the oxen) is not yet a true release because it must be yoked again in the evening, or the next day, or in the coming year. My release is not like that. For me, there is no such thing as being yoked again in the interval. From the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, having yoked the draft oxen of energy to the plough of wisdom, I performed the great cultivation for four incalculable periods (asaṅkhyeyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa), and I did not release them until I attained Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi). And when, after all that time had passed, the Fruit of Arahantship accompanied by all noble qualities arose for me as I sat upon the Unconquered Throne (aparājita-pallaṅka) at the foot of the Bodhi tree, then I was released through the subsiding of all strenuous effort; now, there will be no need to yoke them again.' Intending this meaning, He said, 'Soraccaṃ me pamocanaṃ.'
234:
In the phrase 'Energy is my beast of burden' (vīriyaṃ me dhuradhorayhaṃ), 'energy' (vīriya) refers to the exertion of energy in both body and mind. 'Dhuradhorayha' means being capable of bearing the load placed upon the yoke; it means carrying the burden. Just as the plow pulled by the brahmin's beasts of burden breaks the hard crust of the earth and tears through the tangles of roots, even so, the plow of wisdom (paññā) pulled by the Blessed One's energy breaks the aforementioned 'hardness' [of self-view, etc.] and tears through the tangles of defilements (kilesa). Therefore, He said, 'Energy is my beast of burden.'

Alternatively, it is called 'dhura' because it carries the initial burden, and 'dhorayha' because it carries the fundamental/original burden; being both dhura and dhorayha, it is 'dhuradhorayha.' Thus, just as the team of four oxen for each plow of the brahmin carries the burden and destroys whatever grass roots have grown, thereby accomplishing the perfection of the crop, even so, the beast of burden consisting of the Blessed One's fourfold Right Efforts (sammappadhāna) carries the burden and destroys whatever unwholesome states (akusala) have arisen, thereby accomplishing the perfection of wholesome states (kusala). Therefore, He said, 'Energy is my beast of burden.'

In the term 'yogakkhemādhivāhanaṃ,' Nibbāna is called 'yogakkhema' because it is secure from the four bondages (yoga). It is called 'adhivāhana' because it carries [the practitioner] on account of that Nibbāna, or because it carries one directly toward Nibbāna. Carrying one toward Nibbāna, which is the security from bondage, is 'yogakkhemādhivāhana.' The meaning is this: just as your beast of burden travels directly toward one of the directions such as the East, so too my beast of burden travels directly toward Nibbāna.

In being thus carried, it goes forward without turning back. It is not like your beast of burden pulling the plow, which turns back upon reaching the edge of the field; rather, [my beast of burden] has been going forward without turning back since the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. Alternatively, it is because the defilements abandoned by this or that Path (magga) do not need to be abandoned again. It is not like the grass cut by your plow, which needs to be cut again at another time; rather, it goes forward without turning back, abandoning the defilements associated with wrong view by the first Path, the gross defilements by the second, the subtle defilements by the third, and all defilements by the fourth Path. Alternatively, 'gaccati anivattaṃ' means it goes in a manner that is devoid of turning back. 'Taṃ' refers to that beast of burden. Thus should the meaning be understood here.

Furthermore, while it goes in this way, your beast of burden does not go to a place where, having arrived, the farmer becomes sorrowless, free from dust, and does not grieve. But this [my] beast of burden goes to a place where, having arrived, one does not grieve. When one goes driving this beast of burden of energy with the goad of mindfulness (sati), a farmer like me becomes sorrowless, free from dust, and no longer grieves. It should be understood that it goes to the Unconditioned (asaṅkhata) state called Nibbāna, which is the uprooting of the shafts of all sorrow.
235:
Now, the Blessed One, wishing to conclude, spoke the verse "Evamesā kasī". The brief meaning of that verse is: O Brahmin, for whoever has this seed of faith (saddhā), nurtured by the rain of penance (tapo) as described, this is the farming. Having made the yoke and plow of wisdom (paññā), the pole of shame (hiri), and the tie of mind (mano) into one; striking the plowshare of mindfulness (sati) with the plow of wisdom; holding the goad of mindfulness; guarding the actions of body and speech for protection; using truth (sacca) as the weeding to cut away the weeds of unwholesome states; and bearing the burden of right effort (sammappadhāna-vīriya) which is the great ox that leads to the fruit of Arhatship (arahatta-phala), free from exertion—one proceeds towards Nibbāna, the end of the four yokes, without turning back. By this farming, one reaches the fourfold fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala), which is the conclusion of the work. That fruit has the deathless Nibbāna as its result; thus, this farming bears the fruit of the deathless. Nibbāna is called the deathless (amata); the meaning is that it has Nibbāna as its benefit.

This farming does not bear the fruit of the deathless for me alone; indeed, any Khattiya, Brāhmaṇa, Vessa, Sudda, householder, or renunciant who performs this farming, all of them are liberated from all suffering by such farming.

In this way, the Blessed One concluded the teaching with Arhatship as the pinnacle and Nibbāna as the end. Then the Brahmin, having heard the teaching of profound meaning, realized: "Even if I eat the fruit of my farming, I become hungry again on that very day. But the farming of this Venerable Gotama has the fruit of the deathless; if one eats that fruit, one is liberated from all suffering." Being inspired, he showed his devotion and said, "May the Venerable Gotama eat," and so on. All those words and the subsequent ones have the meaning already stated. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Udayasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "Odanena pūresi" means he filled [the bowl] with rice along with curry prepared for himself and offered it. It is said that the Blessed One, while surveying the world at dawn, saw that Udaya Brahmin. Early in the morning, after attending to his physical needs, he entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), closed the door, and stayed there. Seeing the Brahmin's food being brought near, he took his bowl on his shoulder alone, left the Fragrant Chamber, took out the bowl at the city gate, entered the city, and walking in order, stood at the doorway of the Brahmin's house. The Brahmin, seeing the Blessed One, offered the food he had prepared. This was said in reference to that offering. "Dutiyampi" means on the second day also. "Tatiyampi" means on the third day also. For those three days...
236:
While the Blessed One was going continuously to the doorway of Udaya Brahmin's house, no one else was able to stand up and take the bowl in the presence of the Blessed One; the great multitude just stood looking on.

"He spoke these words" means that although the Brahmin filled the bowl and gave for three days, he did not give out of faith. He gave out of fear of reproach, thinking, "He eats without giving even a morsel of alms-food to the renunciant who has come and stood at the doorway." While giving, after having given for two days, he turned back without saying a single word. The Blessed One also departed without saying anything. But on the third day, being unable to endure it, he spoke these words: "Pakaṭṭhako" and so on. The Blessed One also went until the third day specifically to make him utter those words. In that context, "Pakaṭṭhako" means one who is greedy for flavors.

"They sow the seed again and again" (Punappunaṃ ceva vapanti bījaṃ) is the verse the Teacher started after hearing the Brahmin's words, saying, "Brahmin, you shrink back after giving alms-food for three days; in the world, there are sixteen things that are done again and again," to show those things. In that teaching, "They sow again and again" means they do not shrink back after sowing once, thinking "This is enough," but they sow again in subsequent sowing seasons. "It rains again and again" means it does not stop after raining for one day, but it rains again on subsequent days and in subsequent years; only when it rains like this do the districts become prosperous. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

In the word "Yācakā" (beggars), the Teacher, through his skill in teaching, included himself among the recipients of alms. "Khīranikā" are the milk-makers, the cow-milkers. They do not pull the teat only once; the meaning is that they milk the cow by pulling again and again. "Is weary and trembles" means this being is weary and trembles due to that posture. "Gabbhaṃ" (womb) refers to the bellies of animals such as domestic dogs and jackals. "Sivathikaṃ" means the cemetery; the meaning is that they carry dead beings to that cemetery again and again. "Having attained the Path for non-rebirth" means having attained Nibbāna, which is called the Path (Magga) for the sake of not being born again.

"When this was said" means when the sixteen things done again and again were thus taught by the Blessed One while standing in the middle of the street. "He spoke these words" means at the end of the teaching, being inspired...
237:
Together with his wife, children, friends, and relatives, he paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One and spoke these words: "Excellent, O Venerable One!" and so forth. (This is) the second sutta.

## 3. Commentary on the Devahita Sutta

In the third sutta, "vātehi" means by wind ailments in the stomach. It is said that while the Blessed One was practicing austerities for six years, consuming only a handful of green gram soup and such, his internal wind was disturbed due to poor food and uncomfortable lodging. Later, even after attaining Enlightenment and consuming refined food, that ailment would manifest itself from time to time. It was in reference to that wind ailment that the words "vātehi" and so forth were spoken. "Upaṭṭhāka hoti" means he became an attendant during the early period of Enlightenment when there was no permanent attendant. At that time, among the eighty great elders, there was almost no one who had not served as an attendant to the Teacher. Nāgasamāla, Upavāṇa, Sunakkhatta, the novice Cunda, Sāgata, and Meghiya are the attendants mentioned in the Pāḷi texts. During this time, the Elder Upavāṇa would rise early in the morning, sweep the precinct, offer tooth-sticks, prepare water for bathing, take the bowl and robes, and follow behind—performing all the duties of an attendant for the Blessed One.

"Upasaṅkami" refers to the fact that during the first twenty years after Enlightenment, the Buddha lived only in the forest where there was no smoke (fire). The Blessed One had not yet permitted the heating of water for the Saṅgha of monks. That brahmin Devahita had built fireplaces, placed large pots on them, and made hot water, which he sold along with bathing powders and such to make a living. Those who wished to bathe would go there, pay a fee, bathe, apply perfumes, wear flowers, and then depart. Therefore, the Elder Upavāṇa approached that brahmin Devahita.

"Kiṃ patthayāno" means what does he desire? "Kiṃ esan" means what is he seeking? The Elder began to speak these words, "pūjito pūjaneyyānaṃ", to praise the virtues of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala). It is a duty that a monk who goes for a sick person's medicine should speak of the sick person's virtues. Hearing of such virtues, people think they should respectfully offer medicine. When suitable medicine is obtained, the sick person recovers quickly. When speaking of the sick person's virtues, it is not appropriate to speak based on jhāna, vimokkha, samāpatti, magga, or phala. It is only appropriate to speak of the practices that are the foundation for the paths and fruits, such as: "He is virtuous, conscientious, scrupulous, learned, a bearer of the scriptures, and a protector of the lineage." "Pūjaneyyānaṃ" means the eighty great elders are called pūjaneyya because they are worthy of worship by the world of devas and humans. Those eighty great elders themselves are worthy of respectful worship. To those eighty great elders who are worthy of worship by devas and humans...
238:
...they are called pūjaneyya because they are worthy of worship by the world. They are called sakkareyya because they are worthy of honor and respect. They are called apaceyya because they are worthy of reverence. The Elder Upavāṇa spoke thus, wishing to manifest the virtue of the Blessed One as being worshipped, honored, and revered by those great elders. "Hātave" means to carry away.

"Phāṇitassa ca puṭaṃ" refers to a large, overflowing lump of molasses. It is said that the brahmin Devahita asked, "What is the ailment of the ascetic Gotama?" and hearing "stomach wind," he said, "In that case, we know the medicine for this; dissolve this molasses in a little water and give it to him to drink after his bath. Thus, the hot water will cause perspiration externally, and this medicine will provide relief internally. In this way, the ascetic Gotama will be at ease." Saying this, he placed it in the Elder's bowl and offered it.

"Upasaṅkami" means that when the ailment subsided, the news spread: "Devahita the brahmin gave medicine to the Tathāgata, and by that, the disease was cured. Oh, what a supreme gift from the brahmin!" Hearing this, the brahmin, who desired fame, thought, "Even with just this much, my reputation has spread far," and feeling joyful, wishing to make his deed known, he approached the Ten-Powered One with confidence born of that act.

"Dajjā" means should one give? "Kathaṃ hi yajamānassa" means for what reason does it "ijjhati"—succeed or become highly fruitful for one who makes an offering? "Yovēdī" means he who knows, he who makes it clear. There is also a variant reading "yovētī", which also means one who knows. "Passati" means he sees with the divine eye. "Jātikkhayaṃ" refers to the fruit of Arahantship. "Abhiññāvosito" means one who has known with higher knowledge and reached the completion of the task. "Evaṃ hi yajamānassa" means for one who makes an offering in this manner of worshipping such Arahants. The third sutta is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Mahāsāla Sutta

In the fourth sutta, "lūkho lūkhapāvuraṇo" means one who is old and worn out, wrapped in tattered clothes. "Upasaṅkami"—why did he approach? It is said that in that brahmin's house, there had been eight hundred thousand in wealth. He arranged marriages for his four sons and distributed four hundred thousand among them. Later, when his wife died, the sons consulted each other: "If our father takes another wife, our lineage will be ruined by the children born of that woman. Therefore, let us take good care of our father." Those four sons cared for him with good food and clothing and massaged his hands and feet. One day, while massaging the hands of their father as he rose from bed, they spoke of the faults of household life and pleaded, "We will care for you like this for the rest of your life; please give us the remaining wealth." Thus, the brahmin distributed another hundred thousand to each son, leaving only his cloak for himself, and handed over all his possessions to his four sons.
239:
(The Brahmin) gave (the wealth to his four sons). Later, when the Brahmin's wife passed away, the sons consulted each other: "If our father takes another wife, our family lineage will be ruined because of the children born from her womb. Let us take good care of our father."

The four brothers supported him with fine food and clothing, and provided services such as massaging his hands and feet. One day, while massaging the hands and feet of the Brahmin father who had just woken up from a daytime nap, they each spoke about the disadvantages of household life and pleaded: "We will support you in this manner for the rest of your life; please give us the remaining wealth as well." The Brahmin then distributed one hundred thousand to each son once more, keeping only his own clothing, and handed over all his belongings and wealth in four portions. The eldest son cared for him for a few days.

Then one day, as the Brahmin was returning from bathing, his daughter-in-law stood at the gateway and said: "O Brahmin, did you give an extra hundred or thousand to the eldest son? Did you not give two hundred thousand to each of all the sons? Do you not know the way to the houses of the other sons?" The Brahmin became angry, saying, "Perish, you low-caste woman!" and went to another son's house. After a few days, he was driven out from that house in the same manner and had to go to another son's house. In this way, unable to find a place to stay in any house, he went forth as a Paṇḍaraṅga ascetic, wearing white, and wandered for alms. As time passed, he became old and decrepit. His body withered due to poor food and miserable sleeping conditions. Returning from his alms round, he lay down on a bench and fell asleep. Upon waking and sitting up, he reflected on himself and, seeing no support from his sons, thought: "It is said that the ascetic Gotama is not one who frowns, has an open countenance, speaks pleasantly, and is skilled in hospitality. It might be possible to approach the ascetic Gotama and receive a warm welcome." He adjusted his inner and outer robes, took his alms bowl, and approached the Blessed One.

"Dārehi sampuccha gharā nikkhāmenti" means: "After taking all my wealth and knowing that I have nothing left, they consulted with their wives and drove me out of the house."

"Nandissanti" means: "Having become joyful, I was once happy and delighted." "Bhavamicchisaṃ" means: "I longed for prosperity." In the phrase "Sāva vārenti sūkaraṃ," for example, dogs forming a pack...
240:
...barking and barking, they surround the pig and make it cry out loudly again and again; in this way, together with their wives, they say many things to me and drive me away while I am lamenting—this is the meaning.

"Asantā" means those who are not virtuous (wicked). "Jammā" means those who are vile. "Bhāsare" means they speak. "Puttarūpena" means in the guise of a son. "Vayogataṃ" refers to me, who has passed through the three stages of life and stands in the final stage. "Jahanti" means they abandon.

"Nibbhogo" means being of no use due to old age. "Khādanā apanīyati" means—indeed, as long as a horse is young and possessed of speed, they give that horse food of various flavors. When it is old and useless, they remove it from that feeding. In its final stage of life, it does not receive such care and wanders in the forest eating dry grass along with the cows. Just like that horse, when I am old and have been robbed of all my wealth, I am useless; even though I am the father of these foolish sons, I, an old man, must beg at others' houses.

"Yañca" is a particle. The meaning is: "My sons who are disobedient, disrespectful, and do not follow my wishes—compared to them, a walking stick is indeed better and more excellent." Now, to show the excellence of that walking stick, the words beginning with "Caṇḍampi goṇaṃ" are spoken.

"Pure hoti" means being in front; the meaning is that it is pleasant to walk with that stick placed in front. "Gādhamedhati" means finding a firm footing in deep water when descending into the water.

"Pariyāpuṇitvā" means having learned or having mastered by heart. "Sannisinnesu" refers to the day of the assembly of such Brahmins, when the sons, adorned with all ornaments, entered that assembly and were sitting in noble seats in the midst of the Brahmins. "Abhāsi" means, thinking "This is the right time for me," he entered the midst of the assembly, raised his hand, and said, "Sirs, I wish to recite verses to you; will you listen to what I say?" When they replied, "Speak, Brahmin, we will listen," he recited them while standing. At that time, there was a human custom: "He who consumes the property of his parents but does not support them shall be killed." Therefore, those Brahmin sons fell at their father's feet and pleaded, "Father, give us our lives." Because a father's heart is soft toward his sons, the Brahmin said, "Sirs, do not destroy my foolish sons; they will support me."
241:
Then the people said to the sons of that Brahmin, "Sirs, if from this day forward you do not properly look after and care for your father, we shall kill you." Fearing this, the sons took their father to their home and cared for him. To show how they cared for him, the words beginning with "Atha kho naṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālaṃ" were spoken. In that Pali text, "netvā" means seating him on a stool and carrying him themselves. "Nhāpetvā" means anointing the body with oil, rubbing it with scented powder and the like, and bathing him. They also summoned their wives and said, "From this day forward, care for our father well; if you are negligent, we will drive you out of the house," and they fed him with choice food.

Because the Brahmin received good food and a comfortable bed, within a few days his strength was restored and his faculties became youthful. Looking at his own condition, he thought, "I have obtained this prosperity because of the Ascetic Gotama," and taking a gift, he went to the Blessed One. To show his going there, the words beginning with "Atha kho so" were spoken. In that Pali text, "etadavoca" refers to his placing a pair of garments at the feet of the Buddha and addressing him in this way. After established in the refuges, he also said to the Blessed One, "Venerable Gotama, my sons have given me four regular rations of food (dhura-bhatta); of these, I shall give two to you, and I shall consume two myself." The Blessed One said, "Brahmin, it is well; however, do not assign them separately; we will go to wherever we please." The Brahmin consented, saying, "Very well, Venerable Gotama," and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he returned home and told his sons, "Dear sons, the Ascetic Gotama is my friend; I have offered him two rations of food; when he arrives, do not be negligent in caring for him." The sons consented, saying, "Very well, father." The next morning, the Blessed One, taking his bowl and robes, went to the door of the eldest son's house. When the eldest son saw the Teacher, he took the bowl from his hand, invited him into the house, seated him on a noble couch, and offered him choice food. On subsequent days, the Teacher went to the houses of the other sons in order, and all the sons showed him the same respect and hospitality.

Then one day, a festival arose in the house of the eldest son. The eldest son asked, "Father, to whom shall we give this festive food?" The father replied, "We know no one else; is not the Ascetic Gotama my friend?" He then said, "In that case, you should invite the Ascetic Gotama along with five hundred monks for tomorrow." The Brahmin did accordingly...
242:
The Brahmin did as instructed. The Blessed One accepted the invitation and, on the following day, surrounded by the community of monks, went to the door of the eldest son's house. The eldest son invited the Teacher into the house, which had been smeared with cow dung and decorated with all kinds of ornaments. He seated the community of monks headed by the Buddha on the prepared seats and offered thick milk-rice with little water and various kinds of snacks.

While the meal was being consumed, the four sons of the Brahmin sat near the Teacher and said, "Venerable Gotama, we care for our father without negligence; look at his physical condition (how healthy and strong he has become)." The Teacher said, "You have done a good deed; caring for one's parents is indeed the practice of the wise of old," and he narrated the Mahānāga Jātaka. Then, revealing the Four Noble Truths, he preached the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, the Brahmin, together with his four sons and four daughters-in-law, directed his knowledge according to the teaching and was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). From that time on, the Teacher did not go to their house all the time. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Mānatthaddha Sutta

In the fifth sutta, "Mānatthaddha" refers to one whose mind is stiff with pride, like a bellows filled with air. "Ācariya" (teacher) refers to the fact that during the time of learning a craft, a teacher might not give the craft to one who does not pay respect; at other times, such a person might not pay respect to the teacher and might act as if he does not even know the teacher is there. It is said that this Brahmin Mānatthaddha thought, "Since this ascetic does not even perform a simple greeting when a Brahmin of perfect birth like me arrives, he must not know anything."

"Abbhutavittajātā" means being possessed of a joy that is wonderful and has never occurred before. "Kesu cassa" means in whom should it be. "Kyassa" means who should be (the ones worthy of respect) for that person. "Apacitā assū" means who would be suitable to show respect to. With this verse "arahante," because of his skill in teaching, the Buddha included himself among those worthy of worship and showed who should be honored. The fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Paccanīka Sutta

In the sixth sutta, he is called "Paccanīkasāta" because he finds pleasure and happiness only in acting in opposition, such as saying "everything is black" when it is said "everything is white."
243:
"Whoever abandons overbearingness" (Yo ca vineyya sārambhaṃ) means that a person listens after abandoning sārambha, which has the characteristic of excessive or presumptuous action. The sixth sutta (Ends).

## 7. Navakammikasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "Navakammika Bhāradvāja": It is said that this brahmin had trees cut in the forest, and right there, he constructed palaces, gabled houses, and so on, then brought them to the city to sell. Thus, because he made his living depending on the work of new construction (navakamma), he is called "Navakammika"; and because his clan name was Bhāradvāja, he is called "Navakammika Bhāradvāja." "Seeing him, this occurred to him" (disvānassa etadahosi) means that upon seeing the Blessed One sitting and emitting the six-colored rays, this thought occurred to that brahmin. "In the forest" (vanasmiṃ) means in this grove. "My forest is uprooted" (ucchinnamūlaṃ me vanaṃ) means "My forest of defilements is uprooted." "Free from the forest" (nibbanatho) means one who is without the forest of defilements. "Delights alone" (eko rame) means "I delight alone." "Abandoning discontent" (aratiṃ vippahāya) means abandoning dissatisfaction both in secluded dwellings and in meditation. The seventh sutta (Ends).

## 8. Kaṭṭhahārasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "disciples" (antevāsikā) refers to the dhammantevāsika disciples who perform services and learn the arts. "Sitting" (nisinnaṃ) refers to [the Buddha] sitting and emitting the six-colored rays. "In the profound" (gambhīrarūpe) means in the forest that has a profound nature. "With many terrors" (bahubherave) means in the forest that is very frightening due to the sentient and non-sentient dangers therein. "Having entered" (vigāhiya) means having gone into. The words beginning with "with an unmoving [body]" (aniñjamānena) are terms describing the body; it means "with such a body." "How beautiful indeed" (sucārurūpaṃ vata) is the brahmin saying, "It is very excellent indeed; he is practicing meditation."

"The Sage dwelling in the forest" (vanavassito muni) refers to the Buddha-sage who dwells depending on the forest. "This" (idaṃ) means "This reason for your dwelling in the forest appears to me as something wonderful." "With a joyful mind" (pītimano) means having a delighted mind. "Dwells in the forest" (vane vase) means he dwelt in the forest. "I think" (maññāmahaṃ) means "I consider." "Companionship with the Lord of the World" (lokādhipatisahabyataṃ) refers to being together with Mahābrahmā, the ruler of the world. "Desiring" (ākaṅkhamāno) means wishing for. The words "the unsurpassed heaven" (tidivaṃ anuttaraṃ) refer specifically to the Brahma world. "Why does the venerable one resort to the secluded forest?" (kasmā bhavaṃ vijanamaraññamassito) is a question: "I first thought you desired the Brahma world; if that is not so, then tell me, why does the venerable one resort to the secluded forest?" "For the attainment of Brahma" (brahmapattiyā) means...
244:
...for the sake of reaching the sublime state (brahmapattiyā). He also asks in another way, "Why do you practice this austerity here?"

"Doubt" (kaṅkhā) refers to craving (taṇhā). "Delight" (abhinandanā) refers to craving itself by way of excessive delight. "In many elements" (anekadhātūsu) means in objects of various natures. "Many" (puthū) refers to various kinds of craving or the remaining defilements. "Always clutched" (sadāsitā) means always depending and staying close. "Originating from the root of ignorance" (aññāṇamūlappabhavā) means arising with ignorance (avijjā) as the root. "Muttered" (pajappitā) is called so because craving causes one to mutter, "This is mine, this is mine." All cravings have been completely removed and ended by the Buddha through the Path of Arahantship (sabbā mayā byantikatā). "With the root" (samūlikā) means [abandoned] together with the root of ignorance.

"Not approaching" (anūpayo) means not clinging. By the phrase "pure vision in all things" (sabbesu dhammesu visuddhadassano), he shows Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). "Unsurpassed Enlightenment" (sambodhimanuttaraṃ) is said in reference to the Fruit of Arahantship. "Auspicious" (sivaṃ) has the meaning of "sublime." "I meditate" (jhāyāmi) means "I contemplate with both types of meditation: ārammaṇူpanijjhāna (meditation on an object) and lakkhaṇူpanijjhāna (meditation on characteristics)." "Confident" (visārado) means free from fear. The eighth sutta (Ends).

## 9. Mātuposakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "having passed away" (pecca) means going forward from this human life (after death). The ninth sutta (Ends).

## 10. Bhikkhakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "here" (idha) means in this monkhood. "Foul state" (vissaṃ dhammaṃ) refers to unwholesome states that have a bad odor. "Having discarded" (bāhitvā) means having completely abandoned through the Path of Arahantship. "With understanding" (saṅkhāya) means with wisdom. "He is truly called a Bhikkhu" (sa ve bhikkhūti vuccati) means that person is indeed called a Bhikkhu because he has destroyed the defilements. The tenth sutta (Ends).

## 11. Saṅgāravasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eleventh sutta, "desires" (pacceti) means he wishes or longs for. He speaks the words "It is well, Bhante" (sādhu bhante) by way of entreaty. It is heard that this Saṅgārava Brahmin was a lay friend of the Venerable Ānanda Thera. Therefore, the Elder entreats and urges him, thinking, "May this young man, even though he has me as a friend, not hold wrong views and become one who fills the lower realms." Alternatively, this brahmin has a large following.
245:
Thinking, "If this brahmin gains faith, five hundred families will also follow and gain faith," he also made a request. "Atthavasaṁ" means the benefit, the advantage, or the cause/reason. "Pāpaṁ" refers to unwholesome states such as the destruction of life. "Pavāhemi" means descending into water as deep as the neck and floating [something] away, or making it go far away. The verse containing the word "Dhamma" is just as previously explained. The eleventh sutta is finished.

## 12. Commentary on the Khomadussa Sutta

In the twelfth sutta, the village named Khomadussa is so called because of the abundance of linen cloths (khoma-dussa). "Sabhāyaṁ" means in the hall or the assembly hall. "Phusāyati" means releasing raindrops, or raining. It is said that the Teacher wished to approach that assembly hall. He thought, "If I approach in this manner, it will be uncomfortable for them; I will approach by relying on a certain cause." Thus, by the power of his resolve, he caused rain to fall. "Sabhādhammaṁ" (the etiquette of the assembly): Entering from the side without disturbing those sitting comfortably [inside the hall] is called their assembly etiquette. Entering directly after making the crowd move aside is not their etiquette.

The Blessed One entered directly. Therefore, they were angry and, disparaging the Blessed One, said, "Who are these shaveling petty recluses? Who among them would know the etiquette of the assembly?" "Santo" refers to the wise and virtuous people. "Pahāya" means having abandoned those [defilements] such as lust, they teach the Dhamma for the sake of subduing lust and so on; therefore, they are called "virtuous ones" (santa). The twelfth sutta is finished.

## The Second Chapter: The Chapter on Lay Followers (Upāsaka Vagga).

## Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

## The Commentary on the Brāhmaṃa Saṃyutta is finished.
246:
## 8. Vaṅgīsa Saṃyutta

## 1. Commentary on the Nikkhanta Sutta

In the first sutta of the Vaṅgīsa Saṃyutta, "aggāḷave cetiye" means at the noble shrine near the city of Āḷavī. Before the Buddha arose, there were shrines and abodes of yakkhas and nāgas, such as Aggāḷava and Gotamaka. When the Buddha arose, people removed those shrines and built monasteries. Those monasteries were given the same names. "Nigrodhakappena" means with the Elder Kappa (the preceptor) who usually lived at the foot of a banyan tree. "Ohiyyako" means one who is left behind. "Vihārapāla" (monastery guardian): It is heard that at that time, that venerable one had no seniority (avassika) and was not yet skillful in handling the bowl and robes. Then the senior elders said, "Friend, stay here looking after these requisites such as umbrellas, sandals, and walking sticks," and having appointed him as the monastery guardian, they entered [the town] for alms. Therefore, he is called "monastery guardian." "Samalaṅkaritvā" means having adorned with ornaments suitable to one's wealth. "Cittaṁ anuddhaṃseti" means it destroys or ruins the wholesome mind. "Taṁ kutettha labbhā" means "When this lust has arisen, from where can that cause be obtained?" "Yaṁ me paro" means "By what cause would another person or the Dhamma dispel my discontent and produce delight right now? Even my teachers and preceptors have left me in the monastery and gone."

"Agārasmā" means coming out from the household life. "Anagāriyaṁ" means attaining the state of homelessness (monkhood). "Kaṇhato" means they come running, being oppressed by the dark side of unwholesomeness, the side of Māra. "Uggaputtā" means sons of noblemen, powerful princes. "Daḷhadhammino" means those with strong bows, holding the best bows of a master. "Sahassaṁ apalāyinaṁ": To show the number of those who do not flee even if shot at with arrows from all sides, he said "a thousand." "Etato bhiyyo" means even more than that thousand. "Neva maṁ byādhayissanti" means they will not be able to make me shake. "Dhamme samhi patiṦṭhitaṁ" means being established in one's own Dispensation (Sāsana) Dhamma, which is capable of dispelling discontent and producing delight. The meaning is this: Just as when a thousand archers shoot arrows from all sides, a trained man takes a stick and strikes all the arrows in mid-air, making them fall at his feet without letting them hit his body.
247:
Among those archers, not even one can shoot two arrows at once. These women, however, shoot five arrows at once through the power of visual objects and so forth. Even if there were more than a thousand such women shooting in this way, they would not be able to move me.

'Sakkhī hi me sutaṃ etaṃ' means 'I have heard this in the presence of the Buddha.' 'Nibbānagamanaṃ maggaṃ' refers to insight (vipassanā). Although that path of insight is the preliminary part of the path to Nibbāna, it is called 'maggaṃ' (path) due to a change in grammatical gender (liṅgavipallāsa). In that phrase, 'me' means the mind delights in that path of mine, which is called tender insight, leading to Nibbāna. 'Pāpimā' and 'Maccū' refer to defilements (kilesa). 'Na me maggampi dakkhasi' means 'In such a way that you will not see even the path I have traveled in the realms of existence and modes of birth, in that way I shall act.' The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Arati Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, 'nikkhamati' means he departs from the monastery. 'Aparajju vā kāle' means either on the second day or at the time of going for alms. It is said that the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita was one who deeply respected the monastery. 'Aratiñca ratiñca' refers to discontent in the Dispensation and delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Sabbaso gehasitañca vitakkaṃ' means having abandoned in every way the evil thoughts based on the 'home' of the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Vanathaṃ' refers to the great forest of defilements. 'Kuhinci' means in any object. 'Nibbanatho' means one who is without the forest of defilements. 'Arato' means one who is free from the delight of craving.

'Pathaviñca vehāsaṃ' refers to the appearance of men, women, clothes, ornaments, etc., situated on the earth, and the light of the moon, sun, etc., situated in the sky. 'Rūpagataṃ' means just the visual form. 'Jagatogadhaṃ' means immersed within the earth; the meaning is that it reaches the Naga realm inside the earth. 'Parijīyati' means it decays. 'Sabbam-aniccaṃ' means all that visual form is indeed impermanent. This is said to be the Elder's Great Insight (Mahāvipassanā). 'Evaṃ samacca' means having known well in this way. 'Caranti mutatā' means they live having understood their own nature (attabhāva).

'Upadhīsu' refers to the acquisitions of the aggregates (khandha), defilements (kilesa), and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra). 'Gadhitā' means they are greedy. 'Diṭṭhasute' refers to visual forms seen with the eye and sounds heard with the ear. In the phrases 'paṭighe ca mute ca,' the word 'paṭighe' includes smells and tastes, and the word 'mute' includes tactile objects. 'Yo ettha na limpati' means the person who is not smeared by the smears of craving and views regarding these aforementioned five cords of sensual pleasure.

'Atha saṭṭhinissitā savitakkā, puthū janatāya adhammā niviṭṭhā' means furthermore, many unrighteous thoughts based on the six objects are established in the multitude of people.
248:
Through the power of a person who has reached the group of defilements, one would not reach the group of defilements anywhere. 'No pana duṭṭhullabhāṇī' means speaking coarse words connected with sensuality should also not occur. 'Sa bhikkhū' means such a person of this nature is called a bhikkhu.

'Dabbo' means a wise man of good birth. 'Cirarattasamāhito' means one who has a concentrated mind for a long time. 'Nipako' means a mature wise person endowed with prudence. 'Apihālū' means one who has no craving. 'Santaṃ padaṃ' refers to peaceful Nibbāna. 'Ajjhagamā munī' means the sage (monk) who has reached Nibbāna. That monk, who has attained Parinibbāna through the quenching of defilements by relying on Nibbāna, only awaits the time of final passing (Parinibbāna). The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Pesala Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'atimanyati' means thinking, 'These monks are old; they do not know the Pali, nor the Commentary, nor the sweetness of words and phrases. But for us, the Pali and the Commentary appear in hundreds and thousands of ways.' Thus, it is the act of exalting oneself while overlooking and disparaging others. 'Gotamā' is addressing himself by that name because he is a disciple of the Buddha Gotama. 'Mānapatha' refers to the states that have conceit as their object and the states that arise together with conceit. 'Vippaṭisārī huvā' means he became remorseful. 'Maggajino' means one whose defilements have been conquered by the Path. 'Kittiñca sukhañca' refers to words of praise and physical and mental happiness. 'Akhilodha padhānavā' means being free from the five fallows (impurities) and being endowed with effort and energy in this Dispensation. 'Visuddho' means one should be exceptionally pure. 'Asesaṃ' refers to the nine types of conceit without remainder. 'Vijjāyantakaro' means one who makes an end of defilements through the knowledge (vijjā) of the Path of Arahatship. 'Samitāvī' means a person whose lust and so forth have been calmed. The third sutta is finished.

## 4. Āနန္ဒသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ (Ānanda Sutta Vaṇṇanā)

In the fourth sutta, 'rāgo': Venerable Ānanda was of great merit and was esteemed by all. Kings, royal ministers, and others would invite him and have him stay inside their houses. Women adorned with all kinds of ornaments would approach the Elder, pay homage, and fan him with palm-leaf fans. They would sit nearby, ask questions, and listen to the Dhamma. At that time, lust for the visual forms of the women disturbed the mind of Venerable Vaṅgīsa, who was newly ordained and unable to restrain his senses. Since Venerable Vaṅgīsa was a man of good birth with an honest nature who had ordained out of faith, he thought, 'If this lust of mine increases, it will destroy my welfare in both this life and the next.' While remaining in that very place, he revealed his condition to Venerable Ānanda and addressed him with the words starting with 'kāmarāgena.' In that verse, 'nibbāpanaṃ' means the cause for the quenching of lust. 'Pariyesatī' means seeking the 'beautiful sign' (subhanimitta), which is the cause for the arising of lust, through the power of the perversion of the perception of beauty (subhasaññā-vipallāsa).
249:
Thinking, 'If this lust of mine grows, it will destroy my welfare in both the present life and the future,' he revealed his state to the Venerable Ānanda while sitting nearby and spoke the words beginning with 'kāmarāgena'.

In those verses, 'nibbāpanaṃ' means the cause for the extinguishing of lust. 'Vipariyesā' means occurring through perversion (vipallāsa). 'Subhaṃ rāgūpasañhitaṃ' means a desirable object that is a basis for lust. 'Parato passa' means 'see it as impermanent (anicca)'. 'Mā ca attato' means 'do not see it as self (atta)'. 'Kāyagatā tyatthu' means 'let mindfulness directed to the body be with you'. 'Animittañca bhāvehi' means 'develop signless insight (animitta-vipassanā)', so called because the signs of permanence and so on have been discarded. 'Mānābhisamayā' occurs because of the realization through seeing (dassanābhisamaya) and the realization through abandoning (pahānābhisamaya) of conceit. 'Upasanto' means one who is at peace because of the calming of lust and so on. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Subhāsita Sutta

In the fifth sutta, 'aṅgehi' means by causes or by parts. The four factors such as abstaining from false speech are the causes of well-spoken speech, and the four such as truthful speech are the parts. When the word 'aṅga' is used in the sense of cause, it takes the ablative case (nissakka) as 'catūhi'; when used in the sense of part, it takes the instrumental case (karaṇa). 'Samannāgatā' means well-followed, occurring, or endowed with. 'Vācā' means the spoken word; that speech appears as 'vācā girā byappatho' and 'nelā kaṇṇasukhā'. Although the term 'vācā' also appears as the intimation (viññatti) in 'the action done by speech', as the abstinence (virati) in 'abstaining from the four types of vocal misconduct is called right speech', and as the volition (cetanā) in 'monks, harsh speech... leads to hell', that volition is not intended here. Why? Because it is not something that is spoken. 'Subhāsitā' means well-spoken. By this term, its quality of bringing benefit is shown. 'No dubbhāsitā' means not ill-spoken. By this term, the abandoning of bringing harm is shown. 'Anavajjā' means free from faults such as lust. By this, the purity of its cause and the absence of the four faults are shown. 'Ananuvajjā' means free from blame or censure. By this, its perfection in every aspect is shown. 'Viññūnaṃ' means of the wise. By this, it is shown that the praise or blame of fools is of no account.
250:
'Speaks only what is well-spoken' refers to speech that is free from any of the faults among the four factors of speech, according to the teaching based on the individual (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). 'Does not speak what is ill-spoken' is the prohibition of speaking the opposite of those factors of speech. By 'no dubbhāsitā', the abandoning of wrong speech (micchāvācā) is shown. By 'subhāsitā', the characteristic of the speech that should be spoken by one who has abandoned wrong speech is shown. To clarify the factors, in this sutta, the speech that should be spoken is mentioned first without mentioning the speech that should not be spoken. This same method applies to 'only the Dhamma' and so on. Among these four, by the first phrase, speech that is free from the fault of slander and creates harmony is meant. By the second, thoughtful speech that is free from the fault of frivolous talk and is not separate from the Dhamma is meant. By the other two, pleasant and truthful speech free from harshness and falsehood are meant.

'With these four factors' and so on, he concludes that speech by demonstrating those factors clearly. Other teachers outside the Dispensation consider even speech such as false speech to be 'well-spoken' if it is endowed with parts like the proposition (paṭiññā), and with the perfection of words like nouns, and of gender, number, case, tense, and agency (kāraka); he rejects that. For even if it is endowed with such parts, such speech is indeed ill-spoken because it brings harm to oneself and others.

However, speech endowed with these four factors, even if it belongs to a barbarian language (milakkhu-bhāsā) or is contained in the song of a potter's servant girl, is still well-spoken because it brings the benefit and happiness of the mundane and supramundane. For instance, sixty monks practicing insight, while traveling along a road, heard the sound of a Sinhalese servant girl guarding crops by the roadside singing a song in the Sinhalese language about birth, old age, and death, and they attained Arahantship. Likewise, a monk named Tissa, who had begun insight practice, was walking near a lotus pond and, having plucked lotuses in the pond, heard a servant girl singing this song:

'The red lotus that bloomed early in the morning is destroyed by the sunlight.
Even so, beings who have reached the human state are crushed by the violent force of old age.'

Having heard this, he attained Arahantship. Also, in the interval between Buddhas, a certain man came from the forest with his seven sons and heard a certain woman pounding rice with a pestle...
251: "This body is oppressed by aging; it is dependent on withered skin. This body is subject to destruction by death; it is but food for Death. This body is an abode for worms; it is filled with various corpses. This body is a vessel for impurities; this body is just like a banana trunk." Hearing this song and reflecting upon it, that person attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha along with his sons. Thus, speech endowed with these four factors, even if it belongs to a Milakkha (local/barbarian) language or the song of a potter's slave-woman, should still be understood as "well-spoken" (subhāsita). Because it is well-spoken, it is faultless; the wise who seek the benefit and rely on the meaning rather than the syllables do not find it blameworthy. "Sāruppāhi" means with words appropriate (to the Buddha). "Abhitthavi" means praised. "Na tāpaye" means one should not burn or torment oneself with remorse. "Pare" means even if others cut one down (with criticism), one should not be oppressed. Thus, with this verse, he praises the Blessed One by way of non-slanderous speech (apisunavācā). "Paṭinanditā" means speech that is cherished and beloved. "Yaṃ anādāya" means that a person speaking does not take up the evil, unloved, and harsh words of others, but speaks only sweet and beloved words complete in meaning and phrasing; by way of such speech, he praises the Blessed One for His endearing speech. "Amatā" means "Deathless" (Amata) because it is like ambrosia due to its excellence, or because it is the cause for the Deathless Nibbāna, as it is said: "Of tastes, truth is indeed the sweetest." "Esa dhammo sanantano" means this truthful speech is an ancient law, a traditional practice. This is indeed the practice of the ancients; they did not speak what is false. Therefore, it is said: "The virtuous are established in truth, in benefit, and in the Dhamma." In that Pali, because one is established in truth, one is said to be established in the benefit of oneself and others; because one is established in benefit, one is known to be established in the Dhamma. Alternatively, these (benefit and Dhamma) are merely attributes of truth. The meaning is: they are established in truth. What kind of truth? Truth that is not devoid of the benefit of others and thus does not conflict with benefit, and truth that is not devoid of the Dhamma and thus accomplishes a benefit that is in accordance with the Dhamma. Thus, with this verse, he praises the Blessed One by way of His truthful speech.
252:
"Khemaṃ" means being without danger, free from peril. For what reason is it free from peril? It is because it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna, the making an end of suffering, and brings one to Nibbāna where defilements are extinguished, and because it conduces to the making an end of the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭadukkha). Alternatively, it should be understood that the Buddha speaks the "safe word" (khemaṃ vācaṃ) for the sake of the two Nibbāna elements—attaining Nibbāna and ending suffering—by revealing the safe path; that word is indeed the most excellent of all words. Thus, with this verse, praising the Blessed One through the power of the spoken word, he concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship. The fifth (sutta) is finished.

## 6. Sāriputtasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the sixth sutta, "poriyā" refers to (speech) that is perfect in syllables and so on. "Vissaṭṭhā" means (speech) that is unobstructed and unhindered. Indeed, when the Captain of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) speaks, his speech is unhindered by the influence of bile and so on; it issues forth (clearly) like the sound from a bronze gong struck with an iron rod. "Anelagalā" means being faultless in meaning and sound, and without error in words and syllables. For when the Elder speaks, neither word nor syllable is lost. "Atthassa viññāpaniyā" means (speech) capable of making the meaning understood. "Bhikkhūnaṃ" means (teaching) to the monks.

"Briefly also" means he teaches briefly thus: "Friends, there are these four Noble Truths. Which four? The Noble Truth of Suffering... etc... Friends, these are the four Noble Truths; therefore, friends, an effort should be made (to realize) 'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering'."
