"In detail also" means he speaks in detail, analyzing those same truths in the manner beginning with "What, friends, is the Noble Truth of Suffering?" The same method applies to teachings on the aggregates (khandha) and so on. "Like the sound of a Salika bird" means that just as the sound of a Salika bird, which, having eaten a sweet ripe mango and fanned the air with its wings, utters a sweet sound, so too is the sweet sound of the Elder when he preaches the Dhamma. "Gives rise to inspiration (paṭibhāna)" means that infinite analytical inspiration arises like waves from the ocean. "Odhenti" means they listen (odahanti). The sixth (sutta) is finished.
253:
## 7. Commentary on the Pavāraṇā Sutta

In the seventh sutta, 'tadahu' means it occurred on that day; it means on that day. It is called 'Uposatha' (Observance) because they dwell in observance (upavasanti) on this day. 'Upavasanti' means they dwell being endowed with virtue or by fasting. That Uposatha day is of three kinds: the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth. To exclude the other two kinds of Uposatha, it is said 'pannarase' (on the fifteenth). 'Pavāraṇāya' refers to the Pavāraṇā at the end of the rains retreat (vassa). This Pavāraṇā is also named 'Visuddhipavāraṇā' (Pavāraṇā of Purity).

'Nisinno hoti' (He is seated) means that in the evening, after preaching the Dhamma suitable for the time to the assembled audience, the Blessed One poured water over his body in the bathroom, dressed in his lower robe, placed the noble great robe over one shoulder, and sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared leaning against the central pillar, outshining the glory of the moon rising in the eastern direction with his own glory. 'Tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ' (Silent, silent) means that wherever he looked, there was only silence. In that assembly, not even a single monk had any restlessness of hands or feet; all the monks sat with a silent and peaceful posture. 'Anuviloketvā' means having looked around with eyes possessing the five clear sensitivities.

The word 'handa' is a particle in the sense of relinquishing (offering). In the phrase 'Na ca me kiñci garahatha,' the words 'na ca kiñci' contain the letter 'na' in the sense of questioning. It means: 'Do you have any reproach for me? If you have any reproach, speak; I wish to give you the opportunity to speak.' By the words 'kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā' (whether bodily or verbal), he invites (makes Pavāraṇā) only regarding the bodily door and the verbal door, not the mind door. Why? Because the mind door is not manifest. Indeed, a fault is manifest in the bodily and verbal doors, but not in the mind door. In fact, even for one sleeping on the same couch, one only knows the course of the mind after asking, 'What are you thinking?' Thus, he does not invite regarding the mind door because it is not manifest, not because it is impure. Even when he was a Bodhisatta, in the times of Bhūridatta, Chaddanta, Saṅkhapāla, Dhammapāla, and so on, his mind door was pure; now, in this state, there is certainly nothing to say.

'Etadavoca' (He said this) means that standing in the position of the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati) and bearing the burden of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, he spoke this. 'Na kho mayaṃ, bhante' (Not indeed we, Venerable Sir) means 'Venerable Sir, we do not reproach the Blessed One in any way.' The Elder said 'kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā' referring to the four things that do not need guarding (arakkhiya). The Blessed One has four things that do not need guarding. As he said:
254:
'Monks, these four are the things not needing guarding for the Tathāgata. Which four? The Tathāgata, monks, is of perfectly pure bodily conduct; there is no bodily misconduct for the Tathāgata that the Tathāgata would need to guard, thinking, "May another not know this of me." The Tathāgata, monks, is of perfectly pure verbal conduct; there is no verbal misconduct for the Tathāgata that the Tathāgata would need to guard, thinking, "May another not know this of me." The Tathāgata, monks, is of perfectly pure mental conduct; there is no mental misconduct for the Tathāgata that the Tathāgata would need to guard, thinking, "May another not know this of me." The Tathāgata, monks, is of perfectly pure livelihood; there is no wrong livelihood for the Tathāgata that the Tathāgata would need to guard, thinking, "May another not know this of me."' (Aṅguttara Nikāya, 7.58).

Now, wishing to speak of the Blessed One's qualities as they really are, he said 'Bhagavā hi, bhante,' and so on. Therein, 'anuppannassa' (of the unarisen) refers to the Dhamma that has not been previously arisen in the continuum of any other recluse or brahmin since the time of Kassapa Sammāsambuddha. 'Asañjātassa' is just a synonym for 'anuppanna.' 'Anakkhātassa' means not preached by others. 'Pacchā samannāgatā' means those who have followed and arrived well after the Blessed One who arose first. Thus, since all the Blessed One's qualities such as virtue (sīla) come only by depending on the Path of Arahatship (Arahattamagga), the Elder spoke of the qualities by depending on the Path of Arahatship. By that, all qualities such as Omniscience are indeed spoken. The Elder said 'Ahañca kho, bhante' (And I, Venerable Sir), wishing to invite (make Pavāraṇā) regarding his own and the Saṅgha's bodily and verbal actions to the Blessed One, who is the Supreme Person in the world with its devas.

'Pitara pavattitaṃ' (Set in motion by the father) means that when a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) passes away or ordains, the Wheel Treasure disappears after seven days. Thereafter, for the eldest son who dwells fulfilling the ten or twelve duties of a Wheel-turning Monarch, another Wheel Treasure appears. He sets it in motion. Because it is made of jewels and is similar in meaning, it is said to be 'set in motion by the father' by performing the same duties. Or, because that son says, 'Sire, remain at ease, I will instruct,' he is said to set in motion the wheel of authority following the father. 'Sammadeva anuppavattesi' means he set it in motion in the right way, by the right method, and with the correct cause. The Blessed One preaches the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; the Elder preaches the same in follow-up; therefore, he said this. 'Ubhatobhāgavimuttā' means by two parts...
255:
Those who are 'liberated' (vimuttā) are the 'both-ways liberated' (ubhatobhāgavimutta), being liberated from the form-body through the formless attainments and from the name-body through the Path of Arahantship. Those 'liberated by wisdom' (paññāvimutta) are the Arahants who have exhausted the taints through wisdom, even though they have not reached those attainments.

'For the sake of purity' (visuddhiyā) means for the sake of the Pavāraṇā of purity. Those who remain after cutting through the defilements known as 'fetters' (saṃyojana) and 'bonds' (bandhana) are called 'cutters of fetters and bonds' (saṃyojanabandhanacchida). One is called a 'victor in battle' (vijitasaṅgāma) because of having conquered the battle of greed, hatred, and delusion, and also because of having conquered the army of Māra. The Blessed One is called a 'caravan leader' (satthavāha) because he leads the caravan of beings to be tamed onto the carriage of the Eightfold Path and brings them across the wilderness of Saṃsāra; (I pay homage to) that caravan leader. 'Chaff' (palāpa) refers to an immoral person who is hollow inside, lacking the essence of virtue and so on. 'Kinsman of the Sun' (ādiccabandhu) means the Teacher, the Ten-Powered One; the meaning is 'I pay homage to him.' The seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Parosahassasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, 'more than a thousand' (parosahassa) is a numerical count exceeding one thousand. Nirvana is called 'fearless' (akutobhaya) because there is no fear from any direction in Nirvana, or because there is no fear from any direction for one who has reached Nirvana. 'The seventh of the Sages' (isisattama) means the seventh Sage counting from Vipassī Buddha.

'Vangīsa, how is it with you?'—the Blessed One said this based on the occasion that had arisen. It is said that a conversation arose in the midst of the Saṅgha: 'The Elder Vangīsa has abandoned the training; he does not apply himself to the recitation of texts, to questioning the commentaries, or to wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), but wanders about composing verses and creating prose passages.' Then the Blessed One thought: 'These monks do not know Vangīsa’s accomplishment in spontaneous analytical insight (paṭibhāna); they think he speaks only after much reflection. I will make them know his accomplishment in spontaneous insight.' Having thought thus, he said, 'Vangīsa, how is it with you?' and so on.

'The path of emergence' (ummaggapatha) refers to the emergence of many hundreds of defilements, yet it is called a 'path' (patha) because it is the cause of the round of suffering. 'Having broken the spikes' (pabhijja khilāni) means you wander after having broken the five spikes such as the spike of greed. 'See him' (taṃ passatha) means see the Buddha who wanders having thus overcome and broken the defilements. He is the 'releaser from bonds' (bandhapamuñcakara). 'Unattached' (asita) means not clinging (through craving and views). 'Dividing into parts' (bhāgaso pavibhajanta) means dividing the Dhamma into sections such as the foundations of mindfulness. There is also a variant reading 'pavibhajja,' meaning 'see him after he has divided the Dhamma into major and minor parts.' He shows the various distinctions of the four floods through the power of the foundations of mindfulness and so on. He teaches that noble Nirvana. That Blessed One remains, making the Four Noble Truths manifest.
256:
'Of the flood' (oghassa) refers to the four floods. 'Manifold' (anekavihitaṃ) refers to the Dhamma which has various distinctions through the power of the foundations of mindfulness and so on. In that Nirvana taught by the Blessed One, 'seers of the Dhamma' (dhammaddasā) are those who see the Four Noble Truths. 'Steadfast and unshakeable' (ṭhitā asanhīrā) means they remain established, unable to be moved or shifted by the whirlwinds of views.

'Piercing through' (ativijjha) means knowing by piercing through. 'Of all standings' (sabbaṭṭhitīnaṃ) refers to all the bases of views or the bases of consciousness. 'Saw the transcendence' (atikkamamaddasā) means he saw Nirvana, which is of a transcendent nature. 'The supreme' (aggaṃ) refers to the supreme Dhamma. There is also a reading 'agge,' meaning 'at first.' 'To the five' (dasaddhānaṃ) means he taught the supreme Dhamma to the five monks of the group of five (half of ten); or it means he taught the Dhamma to the group of five monks first. Therefore, one who knows that this Dhamma is well-expounded should not be negligent; thus, 'one should train' (anusikkhe) means one should practice the three trainings. The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Koṇḍaññasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'Aññāsi Koṇḍañña' is the Elder who received this name because he was the first to understand the Four Noble Truths. 'After a very long time' (sucirasseva)—how long? After twelve years. Where did he live for this long a time? On the shore of the Mandākinī Lake at the dwelling place of the Chaddanta elephant king, where Paccekabuddhas reside. Why did he live there? Because he valued secluded living (viharagarutā). That Venerable Koṇḍañña was a wise Great Disciple. Just like the Blessed One, his virtues were spread among the gods and humans within the ten thousand world systems. After gods and humans approached the Blessed One and worshipped him with scents and garlands, they would approach and worship the Elder, saying, 'He is the disciple who first penetrated the supreme Dhamma.' It is customary to provide a suitable Dhamma talk or a friendly greeting to those who arrive. Since the Elder valued secluded living, such interaction with gods and humans appeared to him as an impediment (papañca). Thus, valuing secluded living, he went and lived there.

There is also another reason. At the time of the alms round, all disciples go according to their seniority. However, at the time of a Dhamma teaching, when the Teacher is seated on the adorned Buddha-seat in the center, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, sits on the right side, and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna sits on the left side. Behind these two Chief Disciples, they prepare a seat for the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña. The remaining monks sit surrounding him. The two Chief Disciples, because of his first penetration of the supreme Dhamma and because of his seniority, were very respectful toward the Elder. They regarded the Elder Koṇḍañña like a Great Brahmā, like a great bonfire, or like a highly venomous snake, and they felt apprehensive, fearful, and bashful about sitting in front of him. The Elder Koṇḍañña thought: 'These Chief Disciples fulfilled the perfections for an incalculable period and a hundred thousand aeons for the sake of these foremost seats. Now, out of respect for me, they are apprehensive and bashful about sitting in the foremost seats. I will act so that these Chief Disciples can live in comfort.' Having thought thus, at a suitable time, he approached the Blessed One and requested, 'Venerable Sir, I wish to live in the countryside,' and the Blessed One granted him permission. Venerable Koṇḍañña...
257:
The two Chief Disciples regarded Elder Koṇḍañña as like the Great Brahmā, a great mass of fire, or a venomous snake; thus, they were fearful and hesitant to sit near him. Then the Elder thought: 'These Chief Disciples are those who fulfilled the perfections for one hundred thousand aeons and an incalculable period to attain their positions. Now, they are fearful and hesitant to sit near me. I will make arrangements so they may live comfortably.' At a suitable time, the Elder approached the Blessed One and said, 'Venerable Sir, I wish to live in the countryside,' and the Teacher granted him permission.

The Elder put his lodging in order, took his bowl and robes, and went to the shore of Lake Mandākinī in the Chaddanta forest. Eight thousand noble elephants, who were accustomed to serving Paccekabuddhas in the past, saw the Elder and said, 'Our field of merit (puññakkhetta) has arrived.' They cleared the walking path with their nails, removed obstructing branches, cleaned his dwelling place, and performed various duties. Then all the elephants assembled and consulted together: 'If we all hesitate, thinking "this elephant will serve him" or "that elephant will serve him," the Elder will leave with his bowl just as it was washed, like one who has arrived at a village with many relatives. Therefore, let us serve him in turns; when one's turn comes, one must not be negligent.' Thus, they established a rotation. The elephant on duty would prepare water for washing the face and tooth-sticks for the Elder early in the morning and perform other duties.

Lake Mandākinī is fifty leagues wide. In the middle of the lake, for about twenty-five leagues, there are no weeds or moss, only water as clear as crystal. Beyond that, in water waist-deep, a forest of white lotuses half a league wide surrounds the fifty-league lake. Next to that is a forest of red lotuses of the same width, followed by forests of red lilies (kumuda), white lilies, blue lotuses (uppala), red lotuses, and fragrant red rice, all surrounding it in order. Beyond those are sweet climbing fruits such as cucumbers, gourds, and pumpkins, and a sugarcane forest half a league wide. Those sugarcane stalks are as thick as betel palms. Beyond that is a banana grove, where humans would become full and exhausted after eating just two fruits. Beyond that are forests of jackfruit with fruits the size of large water jars, rose-apple forests, mango forests, and wood-apple forests. In short, it cannot be said that there is no edible fruit in that lake. When the flowers bloom, the wind carries the pollen and places it upon the lotus leaves. When raindrops fall onto those lotus leaves, they are cooked by the heat of the sun and become like well-cooked thickened milk. This is indeed lotus honey (pokkharamadhu).
258:
They would bring that lotus honey and offer it to the Elder. The lotus stalks are the size of plow heads; they would bring those and offer them as well. A large lotus leaf is the size of a great drum's face; in one joint of that leaf, there is milk-like sap the size of a footprint, which they would bring and offer. They also offered lotus honey mixed with sugar. They would place sugarcane on flat rocks and tread on it with their feet. The juice would flow out, fill small rock hollows, and when cooked by the heat of the sun, it would become like blocks of molasses; they would bring those and offer them. As for the ripe jackfruit, bananas, and mangoes, there is no need to even mention them.

A young deity (devaputta) named Nāgadatta lived on Mount Kelāsa. From time to time, the Elder would go to the door of his celestial mansion. That deity would fill the Elder's bowl with milk rice (pāyāsa) made without water, mixed with fresh ghee, lotus pollen, and sugar. It is said that during the time of Kassapa Buddha, he had offered milk rice (salāka-bhatta) with fragrant ghee for twenty thousand years. Due to that merit, such food arose for him. Thus, the Elder lived there for twelve years. While reviewing his life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra), he realized it was exhausted and thought, 'Where shall I attain Parinibbāna?' He considered: 'The noble elephants have performed a difficult task by serving me for twelve years. Having asked permission from the Teacher, I shall attain Parinibbāna in the presence of these very elephants.' He then traveled through the air to the presence of the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said, 'After a long time, he approached the Blessed One.'

Regarding 'nāmañca' (and the name), why did he announce his name? Some knew the Elder, while others did not. Then the Elder thought: 'Those who do not know me might have corrupt thoughts, thinking, "Who is this old man with a white head, a bent body, and crooked like a roof-rafter, who is conversing familiarly with the Teacher?" They would thus fill the states of misery (apāya). But those who know me will have clear and confident hearts, thinking, "He is a great disciple, as famous and well-known in the ten thousand world-systems as the Teacher." They will thus be headed for heaven.' Wishing to close the path to the states of misery and open the path to heaven for beings, he announced his name.

'Buddhanubuddha' means that first the Teacher realized the Four Truths, and afterwards the Elder realized them; therefore, he is called 'Buddhanubuddha' (one who enlightened after the Buddha). 'Tibbanikkama' means one with great energy/exertion. 'Vivekānaṃ' refers to the three kinds of seclusion (viveka). 'Tevijjo cetopariyāyakovido' mentions four of the six supernormal knowledges (abhiññā). Although the other two are not mentioned, the Elder was indeed possessed of the six supernormal knowledges. At the conclusion of this verse, the assembly sat in silence.
259:
Knowing that the assembly was seated, the Elder exchanged greetings with the Teacher and requested permission for his Parinibbāna, saying: "Venerable Sir, my life-formations are exhausted; I shall now attain Parinibbāna." The Teacher asked: "Koṇḍañña, where will you attain Parinibbāna?" He replied: "Venerable Sir, the noble elephants who have attended upon me have performed a difficult task; I shall attain Parinibbāna in their presence." The Teacher granted permission.

The Elder circumambulated the Possessor of Ten Powers and said: "Venerable Sir, my first sight of you was the beginning; this sight is the last." While the great multitude wept, he paid homage to the Teacher and departed. Standing at the gateway, he exhorted the people: "Do not sorrow, do not lament. Whether it be Buddhas or their disciples, there are no conditioned things that arise and do not perish." Then, while the multitude watched, he rose into the air and descended at the banks of Lake Mandākinī. After bathing, he put on his lower robe, placed his upper robe over his shoulder, tidied his dwelling place, and spent the three watches of the night in the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. At the break of dawn, he attained Parinibbāna. Simultaneously with the Elder’s Parinibbāna, all the trees in the Himavantā forest bowed down, laden with flowers and fruits.

The noble elephant whose turn it was to serve, unaware of the Elder’s Parinibbāna, prepared the water for washing and tooth-sticks early in the morning. Having performed his duties and brought edible fruits, he stood at the end of the walkway. Not seeing the Elder emerge by sunrise, he thought: "Why is this? Previously, the Venerable One would walk on the path and wash his face early. Today, he has not even come out of the leaf-hut." He shook the door of the hut and looked in. Seeing the Elder sitting, he extended his trunk and touched him. Searching for breath and finding none, he realized: "The Elder has attained Parinibbāna." He placed his trunk in his mouth and let out a great cry of lamentation. The entire Himavantā forest was filled with a single echoing roar.

Eight thousand elephants gathered, placed the Elder on the frontal globe of the lead elephant, and carrying blossoming branches, they surrounded him and processed throughout the Himavantā before returning to their place. Sakka addressed Vissakamma: "Friend Vissakamma, our elder brother, the Elder Koṇḍañña, has attained Parinibbāna. Let us perform the funeral rites. Create a gabled pavilion made of all kinds of jewels, nine leagues in size." Vissakamma did as commanded, placed the Elder’s body in the pavilion, and handed it over to the noble elephants. Those elephants lifted the pavilion and repeatedly processed around the Himavantā forest, which is three thousand leagues in extent, as an act of worship.
260:
They swung the pavilion. The sky-dwelling deities took it from the hands of those noble elephants and celebrated with a festival. From there, the gabled pavilion reached as far as the Brahma world in this manner: through the rain-cloud deities, cool-cloud deities, hot-cloud deities, the Four Great Kings, and the Tāvatiṃsa deities. Then the Brahmas gave it back to the deities, and in due order, they returned the gabled pavilion to the hands of the noble elephants. Each deity brought a piece of sandalwood four finger-breadths in size, and the pyre (citaka) became nine leagues high. They placed the gabled pavilion upon the pyre. Five hundred monks arrived through the air and performed recitations throughout the night. The Venerable Anuruddha preached the Dhamma, and many deities attained the realization of the Dhamma.

At dawn the next day, after the pyre was extinguished, they filled a water-strainer with relics that had the color of jasmine buds. When the Blessed One had departed and reached the gateway of the Veḷuvana Monastery, they brought them and placed them in the Teacher’s hands. The Teacher took the water-strainer containing the relics and extended his hand toward the earth. The great earth split open, and a stupa resembling a silver bubble emerged. The Teacher, with his own hand, enshrined the relics in the stupa. It is said that even today, that stupa still stands. The Ninth Sutta is finished.

## 10. Moggalānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "samannesati" means searching or reflecting. "Nagassa" refers to Mount Isigili. "Muniṃ" refers to the Great Sage, the Buddha. "Dukkhassa pāraguṃ" refers to one who has reached the far shore of the suffering of the round of rebirths. "Samannesaṃ" means searching. "Evaṃ sabbanga-sampannaṃ" refers to one endowed with all the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha. "Anekākāra-sampannaṃ" refers to being endowed with many inspiring qualities. The tenth sutta is finished.

## 11. Gaggarāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eleventh sutta, the term "tyāssudaṃ" should be resolved as "te assudaṃ". "Te" refers to those deities and humans, while "assudaṃ" is merely an indeclinable particle without specific meaning. "Vaṇṇena" means by the beauty of his body, and "yasasā" means by his retinue; he was exceedingly magnificent. "Vigatamalova bhāṇumā" means like the sun free from impurities. The eleventh sutta is finished.

## 12. Vaṅgīsasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the twelfth sutta, the word "āyasmā" is an affectionate form of address. "Vaṅgīsa" is the name of that Elder. It is said that formerly, in the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he saw a disciple endowed with inspired wit (paṭibhāna), gave alms, and made an aspiration. Having fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons, in the time of our Buddha, he wished to engage in debate in Jambudīpa, and carrying a rose-apple branch, he was a debater along with a wanderer...
261:
Having given gifts and made aspirations, and having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for a hundred thousand aeons, during the time of our Blessed One, he wandered throughout the whole of Jambudīpa desiring debate, carrying a rose-apple branch. Due to the consequences of victory and defeat in a debate with a certain wanderer (paribbājaka), he lived together with that wanderer and was conceived in the womb of a female wanderer (paribbājikā). When he reached the age for learning, he learned a thousand doctrines—five hundred from his mother and five hundred from his father—and wandered about. He also knew a certain mantra; by reciting this mantra and tapping the skulls of the deceased with his finger, he could know, 'He is reborn in such and such a place.' This was his art. Wandering through villages and market towns in due course, he arrived at Sāvatthī with five hundred young disciples and stayed at a rest house by the city gate.

At that time, the city dwellers, having given alms before the meal and after the meal, dressed properly in their upper robes and carrying perfumes, flowers, etc., in their hands, went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. The young man saw them and asked, 'Where are you going?' They replied, 'We are going to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the Dasabala (the Buddha).' Vangīsa, along with his retinue, went with them, exchanged greetings, and stood in a suitable place. Then the Blessed One said to him, 'Vangīsa, is it true that you know a good art?' 'Venerable Gotama, I know many arts. Which art are you referring to?' 'I am referring to the art of Chavadūsaka (skull-tapping),' He said. 'Yes, Venerable Gotama, I know it,' he replied. Then the Blessed One, by his own psychic power, showed the skull of one reborn in hell and asked, 'Vangīsa, where is this one reborn?' He recited the mantra, tapped it with his finger, and said, 'In hell.' 'Well done, Vangīsa, you have spoken correctly,' the Blessed One said, and showed the skull of one reborn in the deva world. He answered that in the same way. Then He showed the skull of one who had destroyed the taints (an Arahant). Although he recited the mantra repeatedly and tapped it with his finger, he could not see the place of rebirth.

Then the Blessed One said, 'Vangīsa, are you weary?' 'Yes, Venerable Gotama, I am weary,' he replied. 'Investigate again and again,' He said. Even though he did so, he could not see, and asked, 'Venerable Gotama, do you know?' 'Vangīsa, it is true; I know. This person has gone relying on me, and I know his destination (gati),' He said. 'Venerable Gotama, do you know it by a mantra?' he asked. 'Vangīsa, it is true; I know it by a single mantra,' He said. 'Venerable Gotama, please give this mantra to me,' he requested. 'Vangīsa, my mantra is not without a foundation (not to be given for free),' He said. 'Venerable Gotama, please give it to me,' he requested again.
262:
'It is not possible to give it to one who has not gone forth in my presence,' He said. Then Vangīsa addressed his disciples, 'Friends, the ascetic Gotama knows a superior art. I will go forth in his presence and learn that art. After that, there will be no one in the whole of Jambudīpa who knows more than us. You all wander about without becoming discouraged until I return.' Having sent them away, he said, 'Please ordain me.' The Teacher assigned him to the Elder Nigrodhakappa. The Elder took him to his dwelling and ordained him. After being ordained, he came to the Teacher, paid homage, and requested, 'Please give me the art.' 'Vangīsa, just as you perform preliminary preparations such as eating saltless food and sleeping on the ground when learning an art, this art also has a preliminary preparation. Perform that first.' 'Very well, Bhante,' he agreed. Then the Teacher taught him the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of the thirty-two parts of the body. Vangīsa, reflecting on that meditation subject in forward and reverse order, developed insight and gradually attained Arahantship.

'Vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī' means experiencing the bliss of liberation after attaining Arahantship. 'Kāveyyamattā' means being skilled in the composition of poetry. 'Khandhāyatanဓာတုယော' refers to teaching the Dhamma by explaining the aggregates, sense bases, and elements. 'Ye niyāmagataddasā' refers to those who have reached the fixed path of rightness (sammatta-niyāma) by standing in fruition, and those who see the fixed path of rightness by standing in the path. 'Svāgataṃ' means a good arrival. By the words 'Iddhippattomhi,' the knowledge of psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa) is taken. By the words 'Cetopariyāyakovido,' the knowledge of discerning the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa) is taken. Although the divine ear (dibba-sota) is not specifically mentioned, it is included. Thus, this great disciple should be understood as one who attained the six supernormal knowledges (abhiññā). The twelfth (sutta).

## Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Vangīsa Saṃyutta is finished.
263:
## 9. Vana Saṃyutta
## 1. Vivekasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Vana Saṃyutta, the phrase 'Kosalesu viharati' (dwelling among the Kosalans) means that after taking a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in the presence of the Teacher, the monk went to and dwelt in the Kosala country because almsfood was easily obtainable there. 'Saṃvejetukāmā' (desiring to stir him up) means desiring him to attain the three kinds of seclusion (viveka). 'Vivekakāmo' (desiring seclusion) means longing for the three kinds of seclusion. 'Niccharati bahiddhā' (goes out externally) refers to wandering among various external objects such as visual forms, other than the alms-resort village.

'Jano janasmiṃ' (a person among people) means: You, a person who is a monk, should remove the desire and lust for other people. 'Pajahāsī' means to abandon. 'Bhavāsī' means to become. 'Sataṃ taṃ sārayāmase' (we remind you, the virtuous one) means: We also remind you, who are mindful and wise; or it means: We remind you of the Dhamma that leads to the removal of defilements found in virtuous people.

'Pātālarajo' (the dust of the abyss) refers to the dust of defilements called 'Pātāla' (the abyss) because it has no standing ground. 'Mā taṃ kāmarajo' (let not the dust of sensuality [carry] you) means: May this dust of sensual lust not carry you away; may it not lead you to the states of deprivation (apāya). 'Paṃsukunthito' means being smeared with dust. 'Vidhunaṃ' means shaking off. 'Sitaṃ rajaṃ' refers to the dust clinging to the body. 'Saṃvegamāpādī' (he attained a sense of urgency) means that reflecting, 'Even the deities remind me thus,' he attained seclusion (samatha and vipassanā); or it means that by exerting supreme energy, he entered the Path (magga), which is the highest seclusion. The commentary on the first sutta is finished.

## 2. Upaṭṭhānasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'supati' (he sleeps) refers to this monk who is said to be an Arahant. After going to a distant alms-resort village and returning, he put away his bowl and robes in the monastery cell, went down to a nearby lake to cool his body, swept the day-quarters, spread a small low couch there, and lay down without falling asleep. Since even an Arahant experiences bodily fatigue (kāyadaratha), 'supati' is said in reference to his lying down to dispel that bodily fatigue.

'Ajjhabhāsī' (addressed) means that a forest deity, thinking, 'This monk took a meditation subject in the presence of the Teacher but sleeps during the day; such day-sleeping destroys the benefits to be cultivated for both the present life and the future,' and intending, 'I will urge him,' spoke to him.

'Āturassa' (of the afflicted) refers to the three kinds of affliction: the affliction of old age, the affliction of disease, and the affliction of defilements; here, it is said in reference to the affliction of defilements. 'Sallaviddhassa' (of one pierced by an arrow) means being pierced in the heart by the arrow of craving (taṇhā) tipped with the poison of ignorance (avijjā), just as one is pierced by a poisoned arrow. 'Ruppato' means being oppressed. Now, the deity speaks the words beginning with 'Aniccā' (impermanent), pointing out the danger in sensual pleasures. In those verses, 'anissito' means one who does not depend on the supports of craving and views (taṇhā-diṭṭhi). It means that for such an Arahant who has completed the monkhood, day-sleeping is appropriate.
264:
...just as one is pierced by a poisoned arrow, it means being pierced in the heart by the arrow of craving tipped with the poison of ignorance and thus being oppressed. 'Ruppato' means being struck or oppressed.

Now, desiring to show the danger in sensual pleasures to that deity, the Buddha (or the Elder) spoke the words beginning with 'Aniccā'. In those verses, 'asitaṃ' refers to one who is unattached to the supports of craving and views. Why should it trouble the monk? For such an Arahant, day-sleeping does not cause distress. Alternatively, these are the words of the Elder himself. Therefore, the meaning here is: Why should day-sleeping trouble an Arahant monk like me, who is free and unattached among those who are bound? It will not trouble me. In the remaining verses, the method is the same. From the deity's perspective, the meaning is: 'Day-sleeping does not trouble such an Arahant monk, but why would it not trouble one who is not like that? It certainly will trouble them.' From the Elder's perspective, the meaning is: 'Why should day-sleeping trouble one like me, an Arahant monk? It certainly does not.'

This is the explanation of the obscure terms. 'Vinayā' means through discipline (attaining detachment). 'Samatikkamā' means by transcending ignorance, which is the root of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). 'Taṃ ñāṇaṃ' refers to that knowledge of the Four Noble Truths. 'Paramodānaṃ' means supreme purity. 'Pabbajitaṃ' refers to a monk endowed with such knowledge. 'Vijjāya' means through the knowledge of the fourth path (arahantship). 'Āraddhavīriyaṃ' means having exerted and fulfilled energy. The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Kassapagottasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'chetaṃ' refers to a hunter. 'Ovadati' (admonishes) means: That hunter, having eaten early in the morning, entered the forest thinking, 'I will kill deer.' Seeing a red deer (rohitamiga), he chased it, intending to strike it with a spear. While chasing, he passed near the Elder who was sitting in his day-quarters as described in the first sutta. Then the Elder said to him: 'Lay follower, that which is called killing living beings leads to the states of deprivation and leads to a short life. One can support a wife and children through other work such as farming or trade; do not do such a cruel deed.' The hunter, out of respect, thinking, 'The Great Rag-robe Wearing Elder is speaking,' stood still and began to listen. Then, the Elder, intending to inspire in him a greater desire to hear the Dhamma, made his thumb burst into flames. The hunter saw it with his eyes and heard with his ears, but his mind...
265:
“The deer will go to such a place; it will descend to such a landing place. I will go there, kill it, eat as much meat as I want, and carry the rest on a shoulder pole to please my children.” In this way, he runs only following the tracks of the deer. Regarding the Elder who preached the Dhamma to this hunter with such a distracted mind, it is said, “he advises.”

“Ajjhabhāsī” refers to the deity who spoke, thinking, “This Elder, like a carpenter hewing what is not wood, or like one sowing seeds where there is no field, is destroying his own effort; I shall restrain this Elder.”

“Appapaññaṃ” means one without wisdom. “Acetasaṃ” means one devoid of a mind capable of knowing the cause. “Mando vā” means a fool, like one who is dull-witted. “Suṇāti” means he listens to your Dhamma talk merely by hearing. “Na vijānāti” means he does not know the meaning of that Dhamma. “Āloketi” means he looks at your thumb, which is glowing through your mundane psychic power. “Na passati” means he does not see the cause: “There is no oil, no wick, no lamp-bowl; indeed, this radiance shines only through the power of the Elder.” “Dasa pajjote” refers to the ten lamps on the ten fingers. “Rūpāni” refers to the visual objects that are the cause. “Cakkhu” is the eye of wisdom. “Saṃvegamāpādī” means he thought, “What benefit is there for me with this wicked person?” and exerting effort, he reached the path of Arahantship, the supreme seclusion. The third sutta is finished.

## 4. Sambahula Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the fourth sutta, “Sambahulā” refers to many monks who are experts in the Suttas, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya. “Viharanti” means they stay near the Teacher, having taken a meditation subject. “Pakkamiṃsu” means that seeing those monks approaching an obscure village in that region, the people, with devoted hearts, prepared rugs and other seats in the refectory, offered gruel and food, and sat nearby. The Mahāthera told one Dhamma-preacher monk, “Preach the Dhamma.” That monk gave a wonderful Dhamma talk. The people, being devoted, offered exquisite food at mealtime. The Mahāthera gave a pleasant appreciation (anumodanā) for the meal. The people, even more devoted, made a promise, saying, “Venerable sirs, please spend the three months of the Rains Retreat right here,” and having built monastery compounds in a place easy to come and go, they supported them with the four requisites. On the day of entering the Rains, the Mahāthera advised the monks: “Friends, you have taken a meditation subject from the presence of the esteemed Teacher; the appearance of a Buddha is rare. Listen to the Dhamma eight days a month, abandon socializing, and live diligently.” From that day on, they strove and exerted themselves. Sometimes, throughout the three watches of the night...
266:
Sometimes they listen to the Dhamma, sometimes they answer questions, and sometimes they practice meditation. On the day of listening to the Dhamma, dawn breaks while they are still preaching. On the day of answering questions, dawn breaks while a skilled monk asks and a wise one answers, engaging in the process of questioning and answering. On the day of meditation, at sunset, they strike the wooden gong, descend to the walkway, and dawn breaks while they are still meditating. Having spent the rainy season in this manner and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they departed. This was said in reference to those monks.

'Paridevamānā' means lamenting and crying, saying things such as, 'Where can I now obtain such sweet Dhamma listening and discussion of questions?'

'Khāyati' means to be apparent or to appear before one.

'Ko me' means 'Where have these monks gone?'

'Vajjibhūmiyā' means they have gone towards the Vajjī country.

'Magā viya' (like deer) means, for example, when deer wander at the foot of various mountains or in forest thickets, they do not cling to a place thinking, 'This belongs to my mother or father, it is an ancestral place.' Instead, they wander wherever food is easy to find and where there is no danger. In the same way, monks who have no fixed home or house do not cling to a place thinking, 'Friends, this is the place of our teachers and preceptors, it is an ancestral place.' Instead, they dwell wherever the climate, food, persons, lodgings, and listening to the Dhamma are suitable (sappāya) and easily available. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Ānandasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, 'Ānando' refers to the Elder Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma. 'Ativelaṃ' means for an excessively long time. 'Gihisaññattibahulo' means spending much time, both day and night, instructing and admonishing laypeople to remember the teachings well.

After the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa said to the Elder Ānanda, 'Friend Ānanda, we shall enter the rainy season retreat in Rājagaha and recite the Dhamma (perform the Saṅgāyana). Go into the forest and strive for the sake of the three higher paths.' That Elder Ānanda, taking the bowl and robes of the Blessed One, went to the Kosala country, stayed in a forest dwelling, and entered a village for alms the next day. When the people saw the Elder, they lamented, saying much: 'Venerable Ānanda, previously you used to come with the Teacher. Today you come alone. Where have you left the Teacher? Whose bowl and robes do you carry now? To whom do you give the water for washing the face and the tooth-stick? Whose monastery grounds do you sweep, and for whom do you perform the major and minor duties?'

The Elder consoled the people, saying, 'Lay followers, do not grieve, do not lament; conditioned things are indeed impermanent,' and so on. After finishing his meal, he returned to his dwelling. In the evening, the people went to that monastery and lamented just as they had in the village. The Elder admonished them in the same manner as before. It is in reference to this admonishing that the words 'ativelaṃ' and so on were spoken.

'Abhāsi' means that although this Elder Ānanda had entered the forest to admonish the assembly of monks and practice the Dhamma of a recluse, he was now only admonishing laypeople. Thinking that the Buddha's Dispensation remains like a heap of unstrung flowers and the recitation of the Dhamma has not yet been performed, the forest deity spoke, wishing to urge him.

'Pavisitvā' means entering into the heart. Entering into the heart means that one who makes an effort, thinking 'I shall reach Nibbāna,' by way of task or by way of object, is said to establish Nibbāna in the heart by way of task. The deity spoke in reference to both of these.

'Jhāyino' means by the two kinds of jhāna...
267:
“Do not weep; conditioned things are impermanent,” and so forth. Having spoken these words to make those people understand, he went back to his usual dwelling place after finishing his meal. Even in the evening, people went there and wept in the same way. The Elder also gave instructions in the same manner. With reference to that instruction, it was said: “Ajjhabhāsi” (spoke to). This means he spoke after thinking: “This Elder, having heard the words of the Saṅgha of monks and entered the forest thinking ‘I will practice the Dhamma of a recluse,’ now lives merely explaining things to laypeople to make them understand. The Buddha’s Dispensation remains like a large heap of unstrung flowers. He does not perform the rehearsal of the Dhamma. I shall urge and prompt this Elder.”

“Pasakkiya” means having entered. “Hadayasmiṃ opiya” means having placed in the heart, both in terms of task and object of mind. One who strives thinking “I shall reach Nibbāna” is said to place Nibbāna in the heart by way of task. One who sits having attained the meditative attainment that takes Nibbāna as its object is said to place it in the heart by way of object. The deity spoke with reference to both of these. “Jhāyā” means “be one who meditates with the two types of jhāna.” “Biḷibiḷikā” refers to this kind of chatter with laypeople. The fifth Sutta is finished.

## 6. Anuruddhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth Sutta, “Purāṇadutiyikā” refers to the one who was the chief queen in the immediately preceding life. “Sobhasi” means “you were beautiful before, and you are beautiful now.” “Duggatā” (miserable) does not mean miserable in terms of the destination (gati). This is because those deities are established in a happy destination (sugati) and are enjoying prosperity. However, they are miserable in terms of the misery of practice (paṭipatti-duggati), which is the ruin of conduct and virtue. Because they may even be reborn in hell after passing away from that deva realm, they are called “duggatā” (miserable ones). “Patiṭṭhitā” (established) means that one who is established in the existing body (sakkāya) is established through eight causes: one who is lustful is established by the power of lust (rāga); one who is hateful, by the power of hatred (dosa); one who is deluded, by the power of delusion (moha); one who is bound, by the power of conceit (māna); one who is wrongly attached, by the power of views (diṭṭhi); one who has reached strength, by the power of underlying tendencies (anusaya); one who is unable to decide, by the power of doubt (vicikicchā); and one who is restless, by the power of agitation (uddhacca). Those deities are also established in the existing body in this way. “Naradevānaṃ” means “of gods and men.”

“Natthi dāni” (not now) means—that deity Jālinī reportedly had a strong affection for the Elder Anuruddha; therefore, she did not dare to come into his presence. She would come at appropriate times to sweep the courtyard and prepare water for washing the face, tooth-sticks, drinking water, and water for use. The Elder used them without investigating. One day, as the Elder was wandering in search of rags (paṃsukūla) because his robes were worn out, the deity placed a divine cloth on a rubbish heap and left. The Elder saw that cloth, picked it up, and while looking at it...
268:
Seeing the cloth and knowing “This is a cloth,” he took it, thinking, “This much cloth is enough.” With that cloth, the Elder’s robe was completed. At that time, three persons—the two chief disciples and the Elder Anuruddha—sewed the robe. The Teacher (the Buddha) threaded the needle and gave it. To the Elder who was wandering for alms after the robe was finished, the deity inspired [people to give] almsfood. That deity would come to the Elder sometimes alone and sometimes with a companion.

On that occasion, however, three deities came and approached the Elder while he was at his daytime resting place, saying, “Venerable Sir, we are deities called Manāpakāyikā (those with pleasing bodies). We can create any appearance we desire with our minds.” The Elder thought, “These deities speak thus; I shall test them. Let them all become blue in color.” Knowing the Elder’s mind, they all became blue in color. Similarly, they created colors of gold, red, and white. Then those deities thought, “The Elder is enjoying our appearance,” and began to perform a musical dance. One sang, one danced, and one snapped her fingers. The Elder lowered his sense faculties (he remained composed and did not look). Then, knowing “The Elder does not enjoy our appearance,” the deities, failing to get affection or intimacy, became weary and prepared to leave. Knowing that those deities were about to leave, the Elder, declaring his Arahantship so that they would not come again and again, spoke this verse. In that verse, “Vikkhīṇo” means “exhausted” or “ended.” “Jātisaṃsāro” means the round of rebirths known as birth in various existences. The sixth Sutta is finished.

## 7. Nāgadattasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh Sutta, “Atikālena” (too early) means entering [the village] very early for alms-gruel after sleeping all night, sweeping a little at dawn, and washing the face. “Atidivā” (too late in the day) means taking the gruel, going to the rest house, drinking it, and then lying down to sleep in one place, thinking, “I will get excellent almsfood at the people’s mealtime.” Then, rising near midday, taking water with a water-strainer, rubbing the eyes, wandering for alms, eating as much as desired, and returning after midday has passed. “Divā ca āgantvā” (having come during the day) means that although one who enters very early should return before other monks, you have returned very late in the day. “Bhayāmi Nāgadattaṃ” means “I fear that Nāgadatta.” “Suppagabbhaṃ” means “very bold” or “impudent.” “Kulesu” means “among the families,” such as the families of supporters like the khattiyas. The seventh Sutta is finished.
269:
## 8. Kulagharaṇī Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the eighth sutta, the Kulagharaṇī Sutta, the term 'ajjhogāḷhappatta' means reaching the state of being deeply immersed through familiarity. It is said that this monk, having taken a meditation subject from the Teacher, entered that forest grove. On the second day, he entered the village for alms with a graceful manner in his movements, such as his approach. A certain family, being inspired by his deportment, bowed with the five-point prostration and offered alms-food. Having heard the talk of appreciation (anumodanā) for the meal, they became even more inspired and invited him, saying, "Venerable Sir, please always accept alms-food only at our house."

The Elder accepted, and while consuming their food and nourishment, he put forth effort and strove until he attained Arahantship. Then he thought, "This family has been very helpful to me; what would I do by going elsewhere?" Thus, enjoying the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), he continued to reside right there.

The term 'ajjhabhāsī' refers to the forest deity who, not knowing the Elder's state as one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), thought: "This Elder goes to no other village, nor to any other house; he does not sit at the foot of trees or in rest houses, etc. He always enters this house and sits there. These two have reached a state of great intimacy and affection. Sometime this monk might ruin this family; I shall urge him." Thinking thus, the deity spoke.

'Saṇṭhāne' refers to a place near the city gate where people unload their goods and rest. 'Saṅgamma' means having assembled together in harmony. 'Mantentī' means they are talking. 'Mañca tañca' means they talk about me and they talk about you. 'Kimantaraṃ' is a question: "For what reason?" In the world, there are many such conflicting sounds. For that reason, or because of that, the monk of austere practice should not be dejected. It is shown that a being is not defiled by the words spoken by others, but is defiled only by the evil deeds committed by oneself.

'Vātāmigo yathā' means just as a forest animal called a 'wind-deer' is startled by the sound of leaves moved by the wind, so too is the person who is startled by mere lowly words spoken by others. For such a one with a flighty mind, the undertaken practice (vow) cannot be fulfilled. The Elder, however, being an Arahant, should be known as one who has fulfilled his practice. The eighth sutta ends.

## 9. Vajjiputta Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the ninth sutta, the Vajjiputta Sutta, 'Vajjiputtaka' refers to a prince in the Vajjī country who renounced the royal parasol and went forth as a monk. 'Sabbaratticāra' refers to the all-night festival that was held throughout the entire city after the Kattika constellation festival was proclaimed...
270:
It is a festival celebrated all night long, adorned with banners, flags, and so on. This festival is bustling and continuous all the way up to the Realm of the Four Great Kings. 'Tūriyatāḷitavāditanigghosasaddam' refers to the sound of drums and other musical instruments, the sound of striking gongs and the like, the sound of playing lutes and the like, and the sound of playing xylophones and the like, which resounds in the eight directions.

'Abhāsi' means that in the city of Vesālī, it is said that seven thousand seven hundred and seven kings, along with an equal number of viceroys, generals, and others, descended to the main street in full finery to enjoy the festival. The Elder, while walking on a great walkway sixty cubits long, saw the moon positioned in the middle of the sky, and leaning against a plank at the end of the walkway, he spoke thus.

'Apaviddhaṃva vanasmiṃ dārukaṃ' means 'I have become like a useless piece of wood discarded in the forest because I am devoid of the finery of head-cloths and ornaments.'

'Pāpiyo' means 'Is there anyone else more base than us?'

'Pihayanti' means that because the Elder is a forest-dweller, a wearer of rag-robes, an alms-collector, one who follows the uninterrupted alms-round, one of few desires, and one who is content, many people admire and revere the venerable one. This is the meaning.

'Saggagāminaṃ' refers to those who are going to the heavenly realm as well as those who have already arrived. The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10. Sajjhāyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, 'yaṃ sudaṃ' is merely a particle. 'Sajjhāyabahulo' refers to one who spends a great deal of time reciting the scriptures (pariyatti) as a means of liberation from the round of suffering. That monk would sweep the teacher's daytime resting place and stand waiting for the teacher. Then, seeing the teacher coming, he would go out to meet him, take his bowl and robes, and while the teacher sat on the prepared seat, he would fan him with a palm-leaf fan, ask for and offer drinking water, wash his feet, apply oil, and after paying homage, he would stand and receive the Pali lesson, reciting it until sunset. That monk would prepare water in the bathhouse and make a fire in the charcoal brazier. He would wipe the feet of the teacher who returned from bathing, massage his back, pay homage, receive the Pali lesson, and recite it during the first watch of the night. In the middle watch, he would rest his body, and in the last watch, he would receive the Pali lesson and recite it until dawn. After reciting, he would contemplate the sound that had ceased in terms of its destruction (impermanence). From there, he developed insight (vipassanā) into the five aggregates—namely, derived matter, primary matter, and mental phenomena—and attained Arahatship.

'Appossukko' means no longer having concern or making effort in the tasks of receiving Pali lessons and reciting.

'Saṅkasāyati' means reflecting: 'The Arahatship for the sake of which I performed the recitation has now been attained by me; what further benefit is there now in recitation?'
271:
(That monk) has reached the summit (the fruition of Arahatship). Thinking, "What use is recitation to me now?", he spends his time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). "Ajjhabhāsi" means that (the deity), wondering, "Has this elder become unwell, or has his teacher become unwell? For what reason does he not recite with a sweet voice as before?", came and stood nearby and spoke.

"Dhammapadāni" here refers to all the words of the Buddha (Buddhavacana). "Nādhīyasi" means not reciting. There is also a variant reading "nādiyasi", which means not learning (not taking up). "Pasaṃsanti" means the Dhamma-preacher receives praise; people praise such a person as an expert in Abhidhamma, an expert in Suttanta, or a bearer of the Vinaya. "Virāgena" means by the Noble Path. "Aññāya" means having known (having penetrated). "Nikkhepanaṃ" means that the virtuous say it is the relinquishing of what has been seen, heard, etc., and it does not mean the relinquishing of the Buddha's words. By this, it is not meant that in the phrase "the elder does not relinquish the Buddha's words," one must be reciting constantly; rather, after reciting, one should know, "I am capable of being a bearer of this much of the meaning or the Dhamma," and then practice for the sake of making an end to the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭadukkha). The tenth sutta (commentary) is finished.

## 11. Akusalavitakka Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the eleventh sutta, "akusale vitakke" refers to the three great unwholesome thoughts, such as sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka). "Ayoniso manasikārā" means by improper attention (anupāya-manasikāra). "So" refers to you (the monk). "Ayoniso paṭinissajja" means to avoid that improper attention. With this verse beginning with "Satthāraṃ", the Buddha teaches the inspiring meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). "Pītisukhamasaṃsayaṃ" means that one will certainly attain powerful rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha). The eleventh sutta (commentary) is finished.

## 12. Majjhanhika Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the twelfth sutta, what needs to be said has already been stated in the Nandana Vagga of the Devatā Saṃyutta. The twelfth sutta (commentary) is finished.

## 13. Pākatindriya Sutta Vaṇṇanā
The thirteenth sutta has been explained in detail in the Jantu Devaputta Sutta of the Devaputta Saṃyutta. The thirteenth sutta (commentary) is finished.
272:
## 14. Gandhatthena Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourteenth sutta, "abhāsi" means that upon seeing the monk holding a lotus stalk and smelling a paduma lotus, (the deity) thought: "This monk has taken a meditation subject from the Teacher and entered the forest to practice the Dhamma of a recluse, yet he remains fixated on the object of scent. He smells it today, and he will smell it again tomorrow and the day after. If this continues, his craving for scents (gandhataṇhā) will increase and destroy his welfare in both this life and the next. Let him not perish while I am watching; I shall urge him to feel spiritual urgency (saṃvega)." Thus, she approached and spoke.

"Ekangametaṃ theyyānaṃ" means that among the five groups of stealable objects such as visual forms, etc., this object of scent is one part (one category). "Nā harāmi" means "I am not taking it away." "Ārā" means that he says, "I am smelling it while standing at a distance, having held and bent the stalk from afar." "Vaṇṇena" means by reason (or cause).

"Yvāyaṃ" is "yo ayaṃ". This was said in reference to a person from the countryside who, while the monk was speaking with the deity, descended into the water and began digging for lotus roots, etc. "Ākiṇṇakammanto" means one whose actions and work are impure. There is also a variant reading "akhīṇakammanto", meaning one whose work is coarse. "Na vuccati" is a question: Why is he not called a "scent-thief" or a "flower-thief"?

"Ākiṇṇaluddo" means one who has many evils or whose evils are grave. Therefore, that person is not called (a scent-thief). "Dhāticeḷaṃva makkhito" means just as a nurse's worn, dirty cloth is stained with excrement, urine, dust, soot, mud, etc., so too is that person stained with the impurities of greed, hatred, etc. "Arahāmi vattave" means "it is proper for me to speak." Indeed, the deity's warning and instruction are like the well-spoken guidance of the Buddha. Such guidance is not obtained by those who are base, of low inclination, or practitioners of wrong conduct. However, only those worthy persons (bhabba-puggala) who are capable of attaining the paths and fruits in this very life receive it. Therefore, this was said.

"Sucigavesino" means for one who seeks pure virtue, concentration, and wisdom. "Abbhāmattā vā" means as small as a fragment of a cloud. "Jānāsi" means "you know that this monk is pure." "Vajjāsi" means "you should speak." "Neva taṃ upajīvāma" means the deity thought: "If this monk thinks, 'I have a deity who desires my welfare, and that deity will warn me,'"
273:
"...she will warn me," he might repeatedly practice negligence (pamāda). "Therefore, I will not accept his word," she thought and thus said this. "Twameva" means you yourself. "Jāneyyā" means you should know. It means, "By whatever action you may go to a happy destination (sugati), you yourself should know that action." The fourteenth sutta is finished.

## Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī,
the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,
## The Commentary on the Vana Saṃyutta is concluded.
274:
## 10. Yakkha Saṃyutta
## 1. Indaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the Indaka Sutta, which is the first sutta of the Yakkha Saṃyutta, "Indakassa" refers to the name of the yakkha residing on Mount Indakūṭa. Indeed, the mountain peak received its name from the yakkha, and the yakkha received his name from the mountain peak. "Rūpaṃ na jīvanti vadanti" means: if the Buddhas do not speak of form as the soul (jīva), and if they do not speak of form as a being or a person. In the phrase "kathaṃ nwayaṃ," the words should be analyzed as "kathaṃ nu ayaṃ." By what cause does this being obtain this body? "Kutassa aṭṭhīyakapiṇဍameti" means: from where do the skeleton and the mass of flesh (liver) come to that being? Here, by the word "aṭṭhi" (bone), the three hundred bones are taken; by the word "yakapiṇḍa" (mass of liver/flesh), the nine hundred pieces of flesh are taken. The question asks: if form is not the soul, then from where do these bones and these pieces of flesh come to that being? "Kathaṃ nwayaṃ sajjati gabbharasmiṃ" means: for what reason does this being stick and remain in the mother's womb?

It is said that this yakkha was a proponent of the person (puggalavādī). Holding the view that "a being is born in the mother's womb all at once," he thought: the mother of the being dwelling in the womb eats fish, meat, and so on; all that food is digested in a single night and dissolves like foam. If form were not a being, it would dissolve just like this food. He asked this question based on that view. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show that "one is not born in the mother's womb all at once, but rather grows gradually," spoke the words beginning with "paṭhamaṃ kalalaṃ hoti."

In that text, "paṭhamaṃ" means that at first, along with the rebirth-consciousness, there is no name such as Tissa or Phussa; rather, there is the kalala (embryo in the first stage), which is the size of a drop of oil resting on the tip of a thread made of three strands of wool. Regarding that kalala, it is said:

"Just like a drop of sesame oil,
Or like clear, undisturbed ghee,
Such is the appearance of the form
That is called the kalala."

"Kalala hoti abbuḍaṃ" means that after seven days have passed from that kalala, the stage called abbuḍa occurs, which is the color of meat-washing water, and the name kalala disappears. It is also said:

"For seven days it is the kalala;
When it matures and accumulates,
That state transforms and revolves,
And what is called the abbuḍa is born."
275:
"Abbuḍā jāyate pesi" means that after seven days have passed from that abbuḍa, the stage called 'pesi' (a mass of flesh) occurs, which resembles a melting cucumber. The appearance of that pesi should be understood through the analogy of ripe chili syrup. Village girls take well-ripened chilies, wrap them in a piece of cloth, squeeze them, and then place the clear liquid in a pot shard to set in the sun. When that liquid dries, it peels away from all sides. Such is the nature of the pesi, and the name abbuḍa disappears. It is also said:

"For seven days it is the abbuḍa;
When it matures and accumulates,
That state transforms and revolves,
And what is called the pesi is born."

"Pesi nibbattatī ghano" means that after seven days have passed from that pesi, a solid mass of flesh called 'ghana' occurs, shaped like a hen's egg, and the name pesi disappears. It is also said:

"For seven days it is the pesi;
When it matures and accumulates,
That state transforms and revolves,
And what is called the ghana is born.
Just as a hen's egg is round all over,
So is the shape of the ghana,
Produced by the condition of karma."

"Ghanā pasākhā jāyantī" means that in the fifth week, five protuberances (knobs) appear for the two hands, the two feet, and the head. Referring to this, it was said: "Monks, in the fifth week, five protuberances appear due to karma."

Passing over the sixth, seventh, and subsequent weeks, and summarizing the teaching to show the period of maturity in the forty-second week, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "kesā." In that forty-second week, the hair of the head, body hair, and nails appear.

"Tena so tattha yāpeti" means that the umbilical cord arising from the navel of the being in the mother's womb is connected to the mother's abdominal wall. That umbilical cord is hollow like a lotus stalk, and through that hollow, the nutrient-essence (āhāra-rasa) flows in, giving rise to form produced by nutriment. In this way, the child survives for ten months. "Mātukucchigato naro" means a person who has gone into the interior of the mother's womb. Thus...
276:
The Blessed One showed: "Yakkha, in this way this being grows gradually in the mother's womb; it does not arise all at once." The commentary on the first sutta ends.

## 2. Commentary on the Sakkanāma Sutta
In the second sutta, *Sakkanāmako* refers to a yakkha of this name; it is said that he was a yakkha who was a partisan of Māra. *Vippamuttassa* means for one who is liberated from the three planes of existence. *Yadanyaṃ* should be analyzed as *yaṃ aññaṃ*. *Vaṇṇena* means by way of cause. *Saṃvāsa* means living together; it has the meaning of the state of friendship. *Sappañño* refers to the Buddha, who possesses excellent wisdom. The commentary on the second sutta ends.

## 3. Commentary on the Sūciloma Sutta
In the third sutta, *Gayāyaṃ* means in the village of Gaya, depending on a village situated near the Gaya river. *Ṭaṅkitamañca* refers to a couch made by piercing the middle of the legs of a long couch and inserting the frame-rails. For that couch, there is no designation of "this is the top, this is the bottom"; even if it is spread after turning it over, it remains the same; they usually place such a couch in a shrine. A house made by spreading a stone slab over four stones is also called a *ṭaṅkitamañca*. *Sūciloma* refers to one who has hair like the needles used for sewing thick robes. It is said that he had gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, and having come from a distant place, he lay down without respect and without spreading a cover on a well-prepared Saṅgha-owned couch with a body smeared with sweat and dirt. That disrespectful act of that monk, who possessed pure virtue, was like a black spot on a clean cloth. Being unable to attain any distinction in that existence, when he passed away, he was reborn as a yakkha at a refuse heap at the gate of Gaya village. As soon as he was reborn, his entire body became as if pierced by thick robe-sewing needles, like a cow's eye lattice. 

Then one day, when the Blessed One was surveying the world at dawn, he saw that yakkha appearing in his first reflection and thought: "This yakkha has experienced great suffering for the interval between two Buddhas. Could there be a cause for his welfare by depending on me?"
277:
Reflecting thus, he saw the strong support (*upanissaya*) for the first path. Then, desiring to show him favor, he dressed in a well-dyed double-layered undergarment, put on the great robe of the Sugata, and leaving the Gandhakuti which was like a divine mansion, he went to the refuse heap which had a foul smell of the carcasses of elephants, cattle, horses, humans, dogs, and so on, and sat there as if in the Great Gandhakuti. With reference to this, it was said: "In the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma."

*Khara* means one with a rough body like the back of a crocodile or like an unevenly tiled roof. It is said that in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, he was a lay follower endowed with virtue. One day, at the monastery, he lay down on a Saṅgha-owned mat spread on the ground with ornate coverings, without spreading his own upper robe. Some also say that without sharing the Saṅgha-owned oil, he smeared his body with it with his own hands. Being unable to be reborn in heaven due to that kamma, he was reborn as a yakkha at the refuse heap at the gate of that same village. As soon as he was reborn, his entire body became rough in the manner described. Those two became friends. Thus, the roughness of the yakkha Khara should be understood. *Avidūre atikkamanti* means they were passing nearby while searching for food or going to a meeting place. Between those two, Sūciloma did not see the Teacher; Kharaloma saw him first and said to the yakkha Sūciloma: "Friend, this is a recluse; a recluse has entered your abode and is sitting there." Sūciloma replied: "This is not a recluse, he is a mere shaveling (*samaṇaka*)." It is said that he used to call anyone who fled in fear upon seeing him a "samaṇaka," and anyone who did not fear him a "samaṇa." Therefore, thinking "This one will flee in fear upon seeing me," he spoke thus. 

*Kāyaṃ upanāmesi* means he created a terrifying form, opened a huge mouth, made the hairs on his entire body stand up, and leaned his body toward [the Buddha]. *Apanāmesi* means [the Buddha] slightly moved away his body, which was beautiful like a golden block weighing a hundred units. *Pāpako* means a low, disagreeable touch. That touch is something to be avoided like excrement, like fire, or like a cobra; it means "it should not be touched by this golden-colored body of mine." When this was said, Sūciloma became angry, thinking "My touch is said to be evil," and asked the question beginning with "I will ask you a question, recluse." In the phrase *cittaṃ vā te khipissāmi* (or I will scatter your mind): when non-humans wish to scatter the minds of humans, they create and show a terrifying form with a distorted face, a blue belly, extremely red hands and feet, a large head, and dripping eyes, as described before, or with other frightening appearances.
278:
Certain yakkhas, desiring to distract the minds (of beings), manifest a terrifying physical form (attabhāva) to them—having a white face, a blue belly, very red hands and feet, a large head, and blazing eyes—or they make a terrifying sound. Or, while they are speaking, they thrust their hands into their mouths and squeeze their hearts; for that reason, those beings become insane and distracted in mind. Referring to one who has reached such insanity and distraction, it is said: "Pāragangāya" means seizing that monk by his two legs and dragging him, saying, "I will throw you to the other side of the Ganges so that you cannot return." The words beginning with "Sadevake" have the meaning already stated. "Pucccha yadākaṅkhasi" means "Ask whatever you desire, all of it; I will answer you without remainder"—thus the All-knowing Buddha offers an invitation (pavāraṇā).

"Kuto nidānā" means: What is the cause? What is the condition? "Kumārakā dhaṅkamivossajanti" means: Just as boys catch a crow and release it, so too, from what do these low thoughts (vitakka) arise and release the mind?

"Ito nidānā" means: This physical form (attabhāva) is the cause of those (lust, etc.), hence "ito nidānā". "Ito jā" means: They are born from this physical form. "Ito samuṭṭhāya manovitakkā" means: For example, boys tie a crow's leg with a long string, wind the end of the string around their finger, and release it; even if that crow flies far, it falls back again at the feet of those boys. In the same way, arising from this physical form, low thoughts release the mind.

"Snehajā" means: Born from the moisture of craving (taṇhā). "Attasambhūtā" means: Produced within oneself. "Nigrodhasseva khandhajā" means: Like the aerial roots or shoots born from the trunk of a banyan tree. "Puthū" means: Many various low thoughts and the defilements (kilesa) associated with those thoughts. "Visattā" means: They are attached or clinging. "Kāmesu" means: In the objects of sensuality (vatthukāma). "Māluvā va vitatā vane" means: Just as in the forest, the māluvā creeper depends on a tree to grow, and from the root to the top, and from the top to the root, it repeatedly entwines, overwhelms, and stands spreading all around; in the same way, many defilements of sensuality (kilesakāma) cling to the objects of sensuality, or many beings cling to the objects of sensuality through those defilements of sensuality. "Ye naṃ pajānanti" means: Those who know the physical form (attabhāva) mentioned in this word "attasambhūtā".
279:
"Yatonidānaṃ" means: They know the cause of this physical form (attabhāva) as well as the (to be known) Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) of that physical form. "Te naṃ vinodenti" means: They completely dispel the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca), which is the cause of the Truth of Suffering known as the physical form, by means of the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). "Te duttaraṃ" means: When they completely dispel the Truth of the Origin, they cross over this flood of defilements (kilesogha) which is difficult to cross. "Atiṇṇapubbaṃ" means: (The flood) which has never been crossed before, even in a dream, in the beginningless round of rebirths (saṃsāra). "Apunabbhavāya" means: For the sake of the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) known as the non-arising of a new existence. Thus, by showing the Four Noble Truths with this verse, He concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahatship. At the end of the teaching, the yakkha Sūciloma, standing in that very place, directed his knowledge according to the teaching and was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). As it is said that Stream-enterers do not remain in a defiled physical form, as soon as he attained the Fruit, all the white pustules and needle-like hairs on Sūciloma's body fell off. He put on divine garments, wrapped himself in a noble divine shawl, wore a divine turban, adorned himself with divine ornaments, scents, and garlands, and having a golden complexion, he obtained the retinue of a terrestrial deity (bhummadeva). (Commentary on Sūciloma Sutta) The third is finished.

## 4. Maṇibhadda Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "sukhamedhati" means he obtains happiness. "Suve seyyo" means he is noble day by day, he is always noble. "Verā na parimuccati" means one is not freed from enmity merely by having mindfulness, thinking "I am mindful." "Yassa" refers to that Arahant. "Ahiṃsāya" refers to (delighting in) the jhāna of compassion (karuṇā) and the access concentration (upacāra) which is the preliminary stage of the meditation on compassion. "Mettāṃsa" means that person develops the jhāna of loving-kindness (mettā) and the access concentration which is the preliminary stage of the meditation on loving-kindness. Alternatively, "aṃsa" means a portion or part. Because he has a portion of the mind of loving-kindness, he is called "mettāṃsa". The intended meaning is: "O Yakkha, the mind of that Arahant always delights in non-violence (ahiṃsā) toward beings; for him who has a portion of the mind of loving-kindness toward all beings, there is no such thing as enmity with any person." The fourth is finished.

## 5. Sānu Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "yakkena gahito hoti" means: It is said that the novice Sānu was the only son of that female lay follower (upāsikā). Then, that lay follower had her son ordained as a novice while he was still young. From the time of his ordination, Sānu was virtuous and accomplished in his duties.
280:
He performed the duties toward his teachers, preceptors, and visiting monks. On the eighth day of the month, he would rise early, place water on the water-stand, sweep the preaching hall, light the lamps, and announce the time for hearing the Dhamma in a sweet voice. Knowing the novice's capability, the monks would urge him, "Novices, recite the sarabhañña (intoned chanting)." Without making any excuses such as "I have a pain in my chest caused by wind" or "I am suffering from a cough," he would ascend the preaching seat and recite the sarabhañña as if bringing down the celestial Ganges. Upon descending, he would say, "I share the merit of this sarabhañña recitation with my parents."

His human parents did not know of this sharing of merit. However, in her next life, the novice's mother had become a yakkhiṇī. She came along with the deities, and after listening to the Dhamma, she said, "Dear ones, I rejoice in the merit shared by the novice."

Monks endowed with virtue are beloved by the world including the deities. Therefore, the deities felt a sense of shame and respect toward that novice, regarding him like a Great Brahmā or a great mass of fire. Out of respect for the novice, they also looked upon that yakkhiṇī with great esteem. At gatherings of yakkhas for hearing the Dhamma and so on, they would offer her the best seat, the first water, and the first portion of food, saying, "Sānu's mother, Sānu's mother." Even powerful yakkhas, upon seeing her, would step aside from the path and rise from their seats.

Later, as the novice grew up and his faculties matured, he was oppressed by dissatisfaction (anabhirati) with the holy life. Unable to dispel this dissatisfaction, with his nails and hair grown long and wearing soiled robes, he took his bowl and robes without informing anyone and went alone to his mother's house. Seeing her son, the laywoman paid homage to him and asked, "Dear son, previously you used to come here with your teachers and preceptors or with young novices. Why have you come alone today?" He informed her of his weariness with the holy life. Although the faithful laywoman admonished him by showing the various disadvantages of the household life, she was unable to convince him. Thinking, "Perhaps he will come to his senses on his own," she said, "Wait a moment, dear son, until I prepare gruel and a meal for you. After you have drunk the gruel and finished your meal, I will bring out and give you pleasant clothes."

She prepared a seat for him, and the novice sat down. In a moment, the laywoman prepared the gruel and snacks and gave them to him. Then, saying, "I shall prepare the meal," she sat nearby and began washing the rice. At that time, the yakkhiṇī reflected, "Where is the novice? Has he received any alms-food or not?"

Knowing that he was sitting there with the intention to disrobe, she thought, "Let me not be put to shame among the deities. I shall go and create an obstacle to my son's intention to disrobe." She came and possessed the novice's body, twisted his neck, and threw him to the ground. The novice, with his eyes rolling and saliva flowing, writhed and struggled on the ground. Thus, it is said, "He was seized by a yakkha."

Seeing her son's affliction, the laywoman quickly went to him, embraced him, and laid him on her lap. All the villagers came and performed rituals such as making offerings to spirits. The laywoman, weeping, spoke these verses. Regarding "pāṭihāriyapakkhañca," it means people say, "We shall observe the preliminary and concluding days of the eighth-day Uposatha," and thus they undertake the Uposatha factors on the seventh and ninth days...
281:
Reflecting on whether he had received alms-food or not, and knowing that he was sitting there with the desire to disrobe, she thought, "Let me not be put to shame among the deities. I shall go and create an obstacle to his disrobing." She came, possessed his body, twisted his neck, and threw him to the ground. With eyes rolling and saliva flowing, he writhed on the ground. Therefore, it is said, "He was seized by a yakkha."

"Abhāsi" means the laywoman, seeing her son's affliction, went quickly, embraced him, and laid him on her lap. All the villagers came and performed rituals such as making offerings. The laywoman, weeping, spoke these verses.

"Pāṭihāriyapakkhañca" means people say, "We shall observe the preliminary and concluding days of the eighth-day Uposatha," and thus they undertake the Uposatha factors on the seventh and ninth days as well. Those who observe the preliminary and concluding days of the fourteenth and fifteenth-day Uposatha undertake them on the thirteenth day and the first day of the waning/waxing moon.
