Saying, "We shall observe the conclusion of the Rains Retreat," they become regular observers of the Uposatha for the half-month between the two Pavāraṇā days. It is in reference to such Uposatha observance that "pāṭihāriyapakkhañca" is said. "Aṭṭhaṅgasusamāgataṃ" means well-endowed with the eight factors; the meaning is "associated with." "Brahmacariyaṃ" means the noble practice. "Na te hi yakkhā kīḷanti" means the yakkhas do not seize and harass such persons.

With the verse beginning "Puna cātuddasiṃ," the yakkhiṇī possessing the novice's body spoke. "Āvi vā yadi vā raho" means whether in the presence of someone or in private. "Pamutyatthi" means there is liberation. "Uppaccāpi" means even by flying up. It means, "Even if you fly away like a bird, there is no escape for you." Having said this, she released the novice. The novice opened his eyes and saw his mother with her hair disheveled, sobbing and weeping. The novice did not know that he had been seized by a non-human being. Looking around, he thought, "Previously I was sitting on a bench. My mother was sitting nearby washing rice. Now I am on the ground, and my mother is sobbing and weeping, and all the villagers have gathered. What has happened?" While still lying there, he spoke the verse beginning with "Mataṃ vā amma."
282:
"Kāme cajitvānā" means abandoning both types of sensuality: sensual objects (vatthukāma) and sensual defilements (kilesakāma). "Punarāgacchate" means returning by way of disrobing. "Puna jīvaṃ mato hi so" means that although he lives again after disrobing, he is like a dead person; therefore, it is said that they weep for that disrobed person as if he were dead.

Now, wishing to show this novice the disadvantages of the household life, she speaks the verse beginning with "Kukkuḷā." In that verse, "Kukkuḷā" means that the household life is like hot embers because of its burning nature. "Kassa ujjhāpayāmase" means, "Dear son, run here; may it be well with you," and it implies, "To whom shall we complain or report this perversion caused by a yakkha, since you desire to disrobe?" "Puna ḍayhitumicchasi" and so on means: like goods taken out of a burning house, having left the home and ordained in the Buddha's Dispensation, do you now wish to be burned again in the household life, which is like a great conflagration? Having noted what his mother said, that novice regained his sense of shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa) and said, "I have no desire for the state of a layman." Then his mother, being delighted, said, "Excellent, dear son," and after feeding him with choice food, she asked, "Dear son, how many years (vassa) have you?" He replied, "Laywoman, I have completed twenty years." She said, "In that case, dear son, undergo the higher ordination," and she gave him robes and cloths. Having had the three robes made, he received the higher ordination. While studying the Word of the Buddha, he became a bearer of the Tipitaka. Fulfilling the virtues such as morality (sīla), he soon attained Arahantship and became a great Dhamma preacher. He lived for one hundred and twenty years, moved the entire Jambudīpa, and then attained Parinibbāna. The fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Piyaṅkarasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "Jetavane" refers to a dwelling called Kosambaka-kuṭi at the edge of the Jetavana monastery; he was staying there. "Dhammapadāni" here refers to the text of the twenty-six chapters that were separately included in the Council. At that time, the Elder Anuruddha, sitting inside the monastery, was reciting the Appamāda-vagga in a sweet voice using the sarabhañña intonation. "Evaṃ tosesi" means that the mother of Piyaṅkara, a yakkhinī, carrying her son Piyaṅkara on her hip, was searching for food starting from the back of the Jetavana monastery. Gradually heading towards the city, while searching for loathsome food such as excrement, urine, saliva, and snot, she reached the Elder's dwelling and heard the sweet voice. For her, that sound pierced the skin and so on...
283:
...piercing the skin and so on, hitting the marrow, it entered and remained in her heart. Then, not even a slight thought of searching for food arose in that yakkhinī; she stood still, lending an ear and listening only to the Dhamma. However, the young yakkha, being small, had no mind for listening to the Dhamma. Being oppressed by hunger, he repeatedly urged his mother, saying, "Mother, why do you stand like a stump wherever you go? Why do you not search for food or meals for me?" That yakkhinī, thinking, "This child is creating an obstacle to my listening to the Dhamma," consoled him, saying, "Do not make a sound, Piyaṅkara." In that context, "Mā saddaṃ kari" means do not make a noise.

With the verse beginning "Pāṇesu ca," she shows the five precepts (pañcasīla) she had undertaken of her own accord. In that verse, "Saṃyamāmase" means we shall restrain ourselves, we shall be restrained. By the words "Pāṇesu ca saṃyamāmase," abstinence from taking life (pāṇātipāta) is taken. By the second foot, abstinence from false speech (musāvāda) is taken. By the third foot, the remaining three abstinences are taken. "Api mucceama pisācayoniyā" means, "Dear ones, having abandoned these five enmities that arise in the world of yakkhas, and by practicing properly, might we be released from this womb of hungry ghosts and yakkhas which is plagued by hunger and famine?" The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Punabbhasusutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "Tena kho pana samayena" refers to what time? It was at the time of sunset. At that time, the Blessed One, having preached the Dhamma to the great crowd in the afternoon and dismissed them, bathed in the bathhouse and sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the precinct of the Gandhakuṭi, looking towards the eastern world-system. Then, monks who were forest-dwellers and alms-food gatherers, who usually travel alone or in pairs, came out from their respective dwellings, approached and paid homage to the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala), and sat down surrounding him as if encircling him with a red curtain. Then, knowing their inclination, the Teacher preached a Dhamma discourse related to Nibbāna.

Regarding the words "Evaṃ tosesi," it is heard that the mother of Punabbhasu, a yakkhinī, carrying her young daughter on her hip and holding her son by the hand, was searching for excrement, urine, phlegm, and snot near the enclosure wall at the back of the Jetavana monastery. Gradually, she arrived at the gateway of the Jetavana monastery. When the Blessed One said, "Ānanda, bring the bowl; bring the robe; give the gift to those who eat the leftovers," his voice spread only about twelve cubits around. But when he was preaching the Dhamma...
284:
While the Blessed One was preaching, even if the assembly extended to the edge of the universe, His voice would reach the entire assembly. Lest the sweet voice be wasted without cause, it did not extend even a finger's breadth beyond the assembly. At that time, this ogress, standing outside the assembly, could not hear the voice; however, as she stood at the gateway, the Gandhakuṭī (Fragrant Chamber) situated directly in front of the great road became clearly visible to her.

Seeing the assembly sitting as still as a lamp flame in a windless place out of respect for the Buddha, without any movement of hands or feet, she thought, "Surely there must be some food being distributed here; I might obtain some ghee, oil, honey, molasses, or something else dripping from a bowl or a hand, or perhaps fallen on the ground," and she entered the monastery. The guardian deity standing at the gateway to prevent entry saw the ogress's strong potential (upanissaya) and did not stop her. When she became one with the assembly, the sweet voice penetrated her skin and reached her bone marrow. As she stood still to listen to the Dhamma, her young sons urged her as they had done before. Thinking, "They are creating an obstacle to my listening to the Dhamma," she comforted them, saying, "Sons, be quiet; Uttara, be quiet."

In that verse, 'yāva' means 'as long as I am listening to the Dhamma.' 'Sabbaganthappamocanaṃ' means 'release from all bonds,' so called because all bonds of defilements (gantha) are released through Nibbāna. 'Ativelā' means exceeding the limit or exceeding the measure. 'Piyāyanā' means seeking or longing. 'Tato piyataraṃ' means 'this seeking and longing for the Dhamma is dearer to me than those children.' There is also a variant reading 'piyatarā.' 'Pāṇinaṃ' is as if it means 'releasing beings from suffering.' If one asks, "Whom does He release?", it is said by bringing forth the word 'beings' (pāṇine). 'Yaṃ dhammaṃ abhisambuddhaṃ' refers to the Dhamma that the Blessed One fully realized. 'Tuṇhībhūtāyamuttarā' means "Not only am I silent, but my sister Uttara is also silent." 'Saddhammassa anaññāyā' means "Mother, because we did not know this True Dhamma before, we now wander and live in suffering, experiencing this misery of hunger and thirst."

'Cakkhumā' refers to the Blessed One who is endowed with the five eyes. While preaching the Dhamma, the Blessed One, observing the assembly and seeing the potential (upanissaya) for the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) in both the ogress and the young yakkha, changed the discourse to explain the Four Noble Truths. Upon hearing that Dhamma, the ogress, standing in that very place, together with her son...
285:
...attained the Fruit of Stream-entry along with her son. Although the ogress's daughter also had the potential (upanissaya), she was unable to accept the teaching because she was too young.

Now, that ogress, rejoicing in her son's realization, said, "How good it is to be wise," and so on. "Today I have well emerged" means "Today I have emerged from the round of suffering (vaṭṭa)," or "I have become well-known in the Dispensation." "Seen" means "seen (the Truths) by both me and you." "May Uttara also hear my words" means "May my daughter Uttara also hear of our realization of the Four Noble Truths." Simultaneously with the realization of the Truths, she, like the yakkha Sūciloma, discarded her entire state of having dry and wet scabs and sores, and obtained divine splendor along with her son. As for her daughter Uttara, just as in the world when parents obtain wealth and power, it also belongs to the children, so she obtained splendor through her mother's power. From then on, she, together with her young sons, obtained a dwelling tree near the Gandhakuṭī and lived there for a long time, seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dhamma every evening and morning. The seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Sudatta Sutta

In the eighth sutta, "on some business" refers to trading business. Anāthapiṇḍika and the Treasurer of Rājagaha were brothers-in-law. When goods produced in Rājagaha became expensive, the Rājagaha Treasurer would take those goods with five hundred carts to Sāvatthī, and stopping about a league away, he would send word of his arrival. Anāthapiṇḍika would go out to welcome him, pay him great honor, place him in a single carriage, and enter Sāvatthī. If the goods sold quickly, the Treasurer would sell them. If not, he would leave them at his sister's house and depart. Anāthapiṇḍika also did the same. At that time, Anāthapiṇḍika had also gone to Rājagaha on that very business. This was said in reference to that journey.

On that day, however, the Rājagaha Treasurer did not hear the message sent by Anāthapiṇḍika, who was standing a league away, to inform him of his arrival, as he had gone to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma discourse, he invited the community of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha for the next day and had pits dug for stoves and wood split in his house. Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, "He will welcome me now; he will welcome me now," was waiting at the house door for the welcome...
286:
Even though he entered the house, he did not receive much of a welcome. "Great Merchant, are the children well? Are you not tired from the journey?" This was the extent of the greeting. Seeing the great preparations of the Rajagaha merchant, he asked, "Merchant, is there to be a marriage ceremony?" following the account in the Senāsanakkhandhaka. Upon hearing the word "Buddha" from the merchant's mouth, he attained the fivefold joy. That joy arose from his head and went down to the balls of his feet; it arose from the balls of his feet and went up to his head. It arose from both sides and descended into the middle of his body; it arose from the middle and went to both sides. Being continuously touched by this joy, he asked three times, "Merchant, did you say 'Buddha'?" "Merchant, I said 'Buddha,'" [the other replied]. Then he said, "Even the sound of the word 'Buddha' is rare in the world." It is with reference to this hearing that it is said, "The householder Anāthapiṇḍika heard that a Buddha had appeared in the world."

The thought occurred to him, "Today is not the right time." He asked the merchant, "Great Merchant, where is the Blessed One staying?" Then the Rajagaha merchant informed him, "Buddhas are difficult to approach, like fierce poisonous snakes. The Blessed One is staying in the cemetery. People like you are not able to go there at this time of night." Then this thought occurred to Anāthapiṇḍika. "He slept with mindfulness directed towards the Buddha" means that on that day, his mind did not even turn toward his carts of goods or his attendants, and he did not even eat his evening meal. Having ascended to the seven-storied mansion, he lay down on a well-prepared and decorated noble bed, reciting "Buddha, Buddha," and fell asleep. Therefore, it is said, "He slept with mindfulness directed towards the Buddha."

"In the night, thinking it was dawn, he rose three times" means that when the first watch had passed, he rose and recollected the Buddha repeatedly. Then, powerful devotion arose in him, and the light of joy appeared. All darkness vanished, and it became as if a thousand lamps were lit, or as if the moon and sun had risen. Thinking, "I have reached the light; the sun has risen," he got up and looked at the moon in the sky, realizing, "Only one watch has passed; two more remain," and went back to sleep. In this manner, he rose three times, at the end of the middle watch and at the end of the last watch. At the end of the last watch, in the very early dawn, he rose, went out into the open, and proceeded to the main gate. The gate of the seven-storied mansion opened by itself. From the mansion...
287:
(Anāthapiṇḍika) arrived in front of the main gate, and the gate of the seven-storied mansion opened by itself. He descended from the mansion and entered the main street.

"They opened" means that the deities thought, "This great merchant has set out to attend upon the Buddha. Upon his first sight, he will be established in the fruit of Stream-entry and become the foremost supporter of the Triple Gem. He will build an incomparable monastery for the Saṅgha and will be one who keeps the doors always open for the Noble Saṅgha coming from the four directions. Therefore, it is not proper to keep his door closed." Thus, they opened it.

"Vanished" refers to the fact that Rajagaha was extremely populous, with ninety million people living inside the city and ninety million outside, totaling one hundred and eighty million people. When people died at an improper time and could not be carried out of the city, they were often thrown over the watchtowers to the city gates.

As soon as the great merchant stepped outside the city, he stepped on a fresh corpse with his foot and struck another with the top of his foot. Flies flew up and swarmed around. A foul, putrid smell struck his nostrils. At that moment, his devotion toward the Buddha diminished. Because of that, his light vanished and darkness appeared. "He made a sound heard" means that [the spirit], intending to arouse the merchant's effort, proclaimed in a sweet voice like the tinkling of golden bells.

In the phrase "a hundred thousand maidens," the preceding terms should also be connected with the word "a hundred thousand." It means a hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, and a hundred thousand chariots, just as there are a hundred thousand maidens. Thus, it shows a hundred thousand of each kind. "Of a single step" (padavītihāra) refers to the distance of about a fist's width between the two feet during normal walking.

"Not worth a sixteenth part" means that if one divides the distance of that single step into sixteen parts, and then divides one of those parts again into sixteen, and repeats this sixteen times, the resulting minute fraction is called a "soḷasī-kalā." Those four hundred thousand (elephants, horses, chariots, and maidens) are not worth even that sixteenth part.

This is what is meant: The intention (cetanā) that arises in even that tiny fraction of space called a "soḷasī-kalā" for one going to the monastery is far more excellent and noble than obtaining a hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, a hundred thousand chariots, and a hundred thousand maidens from all over Jambudīpa wearing ruby earrings.

However, by whose power should this journey to the monastery be understood? It should be understood by the power of one who, having gone to the monastery, will be established in the fruit of Stream-entry without hindrance. Or, "I will worship with perfumes and garlands..."
288:
(I shall worship the) shrine, listen to the Dhamma, perform the offering of lamps, invite the Saṅgha and give alms, and establish myself in the precepts or the refuges—it is indeed appropriate that such a thought (volition) is considered noble for one who goes with such intention.

"The darkness vanished" means that the merchant thought, "I considered myself alone, but I have companions following me; why should I fear?" and thus became brave. Then, a powerful faith in the Buddha arose in him. Therefore, the darkness vanished. In the remaining sections, the method is the same. Furthermore, as he proceeded forward, he saw various kinds of corpses—skeletons, flesh, and blood—on the terrifying cemetery path. He heard the sounds of village dogs, wild dogs, and so forth. He went on, suppressing all those dangers by repeatedly increasing his faith in the Buddha.

"Come, Sudatta" means that while the merchant was going, he thought, "In this world, many heretics like Pūraṇa Kassapa and others say, 'We are Buddhas, we are Buddhas.' How can I know the Teacher's true state as a Buddha?" Then this thought occurred to him: "The name that arose due to my virtues is known to the public, but no one besides me knows the name given by my family. If he is truly a Buddha, he will address me by my family name." The Teacher, knowing his mind, spoke thus.

"Parinibbuta" means extinguished through the extinction of defilements. "Āsatti" refers to cravings. "Santi" refers to the peace of the extinction of defilements (Nibbāna). "Pappuyya" means having reached. Having spoken these words, the Teacher taught him the gradual discourse (Anupubbikathā) and, at the conclusion, revealed the Four Noble Truths. Having heard the Dhamma teaching, the merchant was established in the fruit of stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). He invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha and began to give a great donation starting from the next day. King Bimbisāra and others sent messages to the merchant, saying, "You are a guest; if there is anything insufficient, have it brought from us." He declined them all, saying, "It is enough; you have many duties," and gave a great donation for seven days with the wealth brought by five hundred carts. At the conclusion of the donation, he requested the Blessed One to spend the rains retreat in Sāvatthī, and from Rājagaha...
289:
...and on the journey between Sāvatthī and Rājagaha, he spent one hundred thousand [kahāpaṇas] at every league (yojana) to build forty-five monasteries. Upon reaching Sāvatthī, he built the Jetavana Mahāvihāra and offered it to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, pouring the water of dedication. The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Paṭhamasukkāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the ninth, the First Sukkā Sutta, "rathikāya rathikaṃ" means moving from one main street to another, or approaching a main street. The same method applies to crossroads. Here, "rathikā" means a main road, and "siṅghāṭaka" means a four-way crossroads. "Kiṃ me katā" means "What are these people doing?" "Madhupītāva seyare" means they are sleeping like those who have drunk the beverage called gandhamadhu. It is said so because one who has drunk the gandhamadhu beverage cannot even lift his head and sleeps in a state of unconsciousness.

That Dhamma is also called "appaṭivānīya." He taught it as a Dhamma that should not be rejected and of which one does not tire. Even very sweet food in the external world, if eaten repeatedly, is rejected and removed, with one saying, "Take it away, what is the use of this food?" But this Dhamma is not like that. Even if wise men listen to this Dhamma for a hundred years or a thousand years, they do not reach satiation. Therefore, it is called "appaṭivānīya." "Asecanakamojavaṃ" means being naturally full of essence (flavor) without needing to pour in other things. In the external world, even unmixed milk-rice and such are sweet and flavorful only when mixed and poured with ghee, honey, and sugar; but this Dhamma is not like that. This Dhamma is sweet and flavorful by its own nature; it is not seasoned by anything else. Therefore, it is called "asecanakamojavaṃ." "Pivanti maññe sappaññā" means that wise persons drink it, as it were. It is like travelers exhausted by the heat of the sun drinking water that has come out from among the clouds. The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10-11. Dutiyasukkāsuttādi-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "puṇyaṃ vata pasavi bahuṃ" means "he has indeed generated much merit." The tenth sutta is finished.

The eleventh sutta has a clear meaning. The eleventh sutta is finished.

## 12. Āḷavakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the twelfth, the Āḷavaka Sutta, "Āḷaviyaṃ" refers to both the country of Āḷavī and the city of Āḷavī. The mansion of that yakkha Āḷavaka is situated not far from the city, about a gāvuta away. It should be understood that while the Blessed One was staying in that yakkha's mansion, he was residing in the country of Āḷavī depending on that city. Here, the sequential account is as follows: The king who ruled the kingdom of Āḷavī, while enjoying royal splendor, used to go hunting once every seven days to prevent the danger of thieves, to ward off enemies from border regions, and to mark the boundaries. One day, they made a pact: "If a deer escapes from the side of a certain person, that person must be responsible." Then, a female deer (eṇī) escaped from the king's side. The king, who possessed great speed, took his sword and followed the deer on foot for a distance of three leagues (yojanas). Although the deer could run for three leagues, its speed was exhausted after that.
290:
It is said, "He dwells in the country of Āḷavī, relying on the city of Āḷavī." Regarding the phrase "in the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka," the following is the sequential account (the background story): King Āḷavaka, having abandoned various theatrical entertainments and royal enjoyments, used to go hunting every seven days to prevent the danger of thieves, to deter enemy kings, and for the sake of physical exercise. One day, together with his army, he made a pact: "Whoever lets a deer escape from his side, he alone shall bear the burden of that deer." Then, a deer escaped from the king's side itself. The king, endowed with great speed, took his bow and, though on foot, pursued that deer for three yojanas. Deer of the Eṇī species are capable of running with a speed of three yojanas. Then, the deer, its speed exhausted, stood still as if entering water. The king killed it, cut it into two pieces, and although he had no need for the meat, he carried it on a shoulder pole to avoid the reproach that he "could not catch the deer." Not far from the city, seeing a large banyan tree (nigrodha) with thick foliage, he approached the foot of that tree to relieve his exhaustion.

In that banyan tree, the yakkha Āḷavaka had received an abode from the Great Kings (Mahārāja), and he lived there eating any living beings that entered the shaded area of that tree at the time of noon. Seeing the king, the yakkha approached to eat him. The king made a pact with him, saying, "Release me, and I will send you one human and one pot of rice every single day." The yakkha said, "You, being intoxicated with royal enjoyments, will forget and not remember. Moreover, I am not allowed to eat anyone who has not approached my abode or who has not been granted to me. If so, I would lose you as well," and he did not release him. The king granted himself by saying, "On whatever day I fail to send them, on that day you may seize and eat me." Only then was he released by the yakkha, and he headed back toward the city.

The army, which had been waiting in a camp on the road, saw the king and went out to meet him, saying, "Great King, why are you so exhausted because of a danger that is merely the fear of death?" The king, without informing anyone of the incident, returned to the city, and after having his breakfast, he summoned the city guard (nagaraguttika) and informed him of the matter. The city guard asked, "Sire, did you set a time limit?" The king replied, "Friend, I did not." The guard said, "Sire, you have done poorly. For non-humans (amanussa) receive only as much as is specifically defined, but if it is undefined, the entire countryside will be afflicted. However, let it be, Sire. Despite this, you may enjoy royal happiness without concern; I will do what needs to be done in this matter." That city guard, rising early and standing at the prison gate, addressed those who were to be executed, saying, "Whoever desires to live, that person..."
291:
"...let him come forth."

He took the one who came out first to his house, had him bathed, fed him, and sent him, saying, "Give this pot of rice to the yakkha." As soon as that person reached the foot of the tree, the yakkha manifested a terrifying form and ate him like a root or a tuber. It is said that by the power of the yakkha, the entire body of humans, starting from the hair, becomes like a lump of butter. The royal servants who went to deliver the yakkha's food saw this, became terrified, and told their friends. From then on, knowing that "the King catches thieves and gives them to the yakkha," people abstained from theft. Subsequently, due to the absence of new thieves and the exhaustion of old ones, the prisons became empty.

Then the city guardian informed the King. The King, thinking, "Perhaps someone will take it out of greed," had his wealth placed on the city streets. No one touched that wealth even with their feet. Not finding any thieves, the King told the ministers. The ministers suggested, "Let us send one elderly person from each household in order; such a person is naturally on the path of death anyway." The King forbade it, saying, "The people will be agitated, saying that I am sending their fathers and grandfathers. Do not let this plan please you." "In that case, Great King, let us send an infant who is just beginning to lie on its back; such a child has no affection, thinking 'this is my mother' or 'this is my father'," they suggested. The King consented. The ministers did as planned. Mothers of infants and pregnant women in the city took their children and fled to other districts, returning only after the children had grown up there. In this way, twelve years passed.

Then one day, after searching the entire city and not finding a single infant, the ministers informed the King, "Great King, there is no infant in the city except for your own son, Prince Āḷavaka, in the inner palace." The King said, "Just as my son is dear to me, so is he dear to all people; however, there is no one dearer than oneself. Go, give that prince and protect my life." At that time, the mother of Prince Āḷavaka had bathed the prince, adorned him, wrapped him in a fine cloth, and was sitting with him in her lap. By the King's command, the royal servants went there and took the prince, along with his nurse, from the weeping and wailing Queen Mother and the sixteen thousand queens. They said, "Tomorrow, he will be the yakkha's food." On that day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One...
292:
The Blessed One, having arisen from his seat at dawn, entered the Attainment of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) of the Jetavana Monastery. Looking out upon the world with the Buddha-eye, he saw the potential (upanissaya) for Prince Āḷavaka to attain the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmī-phala), for the Yakkha Āḷavaka to attain the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), and for eighty-four thousand beings to obtain the Dhamma-eye at the conclusion of the discourse. After the night had passed and he had performed his morning duties, and having finished his meal-time duties, on the day of the new moon Uposatha, as the sun was setting, he took his bowl and robes and, being alone without a companion, travelled thirty yojanas on foot from Sāvatthī and entered the abode of that Yakkha. Therefore, it is said, "In the abode of the Yakkha Āḷavaka."

As to whether the Blessed One stayed at the foot of the banyan tree where the abode of the Yakkha Āḷavaka was located, or in the abode itself—he stayed in the abode itself. Just as the Yakkhas see their own abode, so too did the Blessed One see it. The Blessed One went there and stood at the entrance of the abode. At that time, the Yakkha Āḷavaka had gone to an assembly of Yakkhas in the Himalayas. Then, a Yakkha named Gadrabha, who was the gatekeeper for Āḷavaka, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable Sir, why has the Blessed One come at an improper time?" The Blessed One replied, "Yes, Gadrabha, I have come. If it is no trouble to you, I would like to stay for one night in the abode of Āḷavaka." Gadrabha replied, "Venerable Sir, it is no trouble to me. However, that Yakkha is fierce and harsh; he does not even perform acts of respect such as saluting his own parents. May the Blessed One not find pleasure in staying here." The Blessed One said, "Gadrabha, I know his nature. No harm whatsoever will come to me. If it is no trouble to you, I would like to stay for one night."

For a second time, the Yakkha Gadrabha said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, Āḷavaka is like a pan heated red-hot by fire. He knows not parents, nor ascetics and brahmins, nor the Dhamma. He causes those who come here to go mad, he splits their hearts, and seizing them by the feet, he tosses them to the other side of the ocean or to the other side of the world system." For a second time, the Blessed One said, "I know, Gadrabha. If it is no trouble to you, I would like to stay for one night." Gadrabha replied, "Venerable Sir, it is no trouble to me. However, that Yakkha might even deprive me of life for allowing this without informing him. Venerable Sir, let me first inform him."
293:
The Blessed One said, "Gadrabha, go and inform him as you please." The Yakkha Gadrabha replied, "In that case, Venerable Sir, you yourself shall know," and having paid homage to the Blessed One, he departed towards the Himalayas. The door of the abode opened for the Blessed One of its own accord. The Blessed One entered the abode and sat upon the celestial jeweled throne where Āḷavaka used to enjoy his splendor on auspicious days and such, and he emitted a golden radiance. Seeing that radiance, the Yakkha women came, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down surrounding him. The Blessed One gave them a discourse on various topics (pakiṇṇaka-dhammakathā) in this manner: "In the past, you attained this prosperity because you gave gifts, undertook the precepts, and honored those worthy of honor. Now, do likewise; do not live overcome by envy and stinginess toward one another." Hearing the sweet voice of the Blessed One, those Yakkha women gave thousands of sadhu-calls and remained sitting, surrounding the Blessed One. Gadrabha, having reached the Himalayas, informed Āḷavaka: "Behold, friend, you should know that the Blessed One is seated in your mansion." Āḷavaka gave a sign to Gadrabha, saying, "Be quiet; I will go and do what needs to be done." It is said that he acted this way because he felt ashamed in his manly pride, thinking, "Let no one in the midst of the assembly hear this."

At that time, the devas Sātāgira and Hemavata, having paid homage to the Blessed One at the Jetavana monastery, were travelling through the air with their retinues in various vehicles, saying, "We shall go to the assembly of Yakkhas." In the sky, there is no path everywhere for Yakkhas; they must avoid the mansions situated in the sky and travel only where there is a path. Āḷavaka’s mansion, however, was situated on the ground and was well-secured, surrounded by a wall, and complete with well-constructed gates, watchtowers, and portals, covered above with a bronze net, resembling a casket, and was three yojanas in height. There was a path above that mansion. When they reached that place, they were unable to proceed further. This is because no one is able to pass over the place where Buddhas are seated, up to the highest point of existence (bhavagga). They reflected, "What is this?" and seeing the Blessed One, they descended like a stone thrown from the sky, paid homage, listened to the Dhamma, and having circumambulated him, said, "Venerable Sir, we shall proceed to the assembly of Yakkhas." Praising the Three Jewels, they went to the assembly of Yakkhas. When Āḷavaka saw them, he moved aside and gave them a place, saying, "Sit here." They said to Āḷavaka, "It is a gain for you, Āḷavaka, that the Blessed One is staying in your abode. Go, friend, and attend upon the Blessed One." Thus, the Blessed One stayed in the abode itself, not at the foot of the banyan tree where Āḷavaka’s abode was. Therefore, it is said, "At one time, the Blessed One was staying in the abode of the Yakkha Āḷavaka." Then, why did Āḷavaka say, "Ascetic, get out"? He said it because he wished to harass him. Thus should the connection of the Pali words be understood.
294:
The abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka was in a banyan tree; it was not at the foot of that banyan tree (that the Buddha stayed). Therefore, it is said: "At one time, the Blessed One was staying in Āḷavī, in the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka."

Then the yakkha Āḷavaka ... (p) ... said this: "Get out, ascetic!" Why did he say this? He said it because he desired to harass and annoy. In this matter, the connection of the story from the beginning should be understood as follows: Just as talk about virtue is unpleasant to those who are immoral, talk about faith is unpleasant to one who is faithless. Therefore, upon hearing the praise of the Blessed One from those yakkhas, his heart began to crackle with anger within him, like a lump of salt thrown into a fire, and he said, "Who is this so-called Blessed One who has entered my abode?"

Those yakkhas said, "Friend Āḷavaka, do you not know the Blessed One, our Teacher? That Blessed One, while staying in the Tusita heaven, performed the five great investigations," and so on, recounting the story up to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and mentioning the thirty-two omens starting from the conception. They urged him, saying, "Friend Āḷavaka, have you not seen such wonders?" Although he had seen them, due to the power of his anger, he said, "I have not seen them."

"Friend Āḷavaka, whether you wish to see or not, what benefit is there in someone like you seeing or not seeing? What can you do to our Teacher, the Blessed One? Compared to that Blessed One, you appear like a newborn calf beside a great bull with a prominent hump; like a newborn elephant calf beside a great tusker in threefold rut; like an old jackal beside a lion king adorned with a brilliant, flowing mane on its shoulders; like a broken-winged young crow beside the king of Garuḍas whose body extends for a hundred and fifty yojanas. Go and do what you must do!"

When this was said, the wicked Āḷavaka stood up, and placing his left foot on the Manosilā stone slab, he said, "Now see whether your Teacher is more powerful, or I am!" and with his right foot, he stepped on the peak of Mount Kelāsa, which is sixty yojanas in size. That mountain peak shattered into layers and flakes like a red-hot iron mass struck by an iron sledgehammer. Standing there, he shouted, "I am Āḷavaka!" and the sound spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

It is said that four great sounds have been heard throughout the whole of Jambudīpa: the sound of the yakkha general Puṇṇaka shouting "I have won!" while clapping his hands after defeating King Dhanañjaya Koravya at dice; the sound of Sakka, the king of devas, who, when the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa was declining, created the deva Vissakamma in the form of a great black dog and caused him to shout, "I shall devour the evil monks..."
295:
...and evil nuns, and laymen, and laywomen, and all those who profess false doctrines." In the Kusa Jātaka, while seven kings were surrounding the city because of Princess Pabhāvatī, the Great Being (King Kusa) placed Pabhāvatī with him on the back of an elephant, and as he left the city, he shouted, "I am the great King Kusa, who has a voice like a lion's roar!" And the sound of Āḷavaka standing on the peak of Mount Kelāsa shouting "I am Āḷavaka!" was also such a sound. At that time, it was as if he were standing at the door of every house in the whole of Jambudīpa and shouting. Even the great Mount Himavā, three thousand yojanas in extent, trembled due to the power of the yakkha.

That yakkha Āḷavaka thought, "I will make the ascetic flee with this windstorm alone," and he created a windstorm. Those winds arose from the east and other directions, splitting mountain peaks of half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and three yojanas in size, uprooting forests and trees, and rushing toward the city of Āḷavī, crushing old elephant stables and the like, and scattering roof tiles into the sky. The Blessed One made a resolution: "Let no harm come to anyone." When those winds reached the Dasabala, they were unable to move even the hem of his robe.

Then, thinking, "I will kill the ascetic by overwhelming him with water," he created a great rainstorm. By his power, clouds arose in hundreds and thousands of layers and rained down. Due to the force of the rain, the earth became full of holes. Although a great flood came over the forest trees, it was unable to wet even a dewdrop's worth of the Dasabala's robe.

Then he created a shower of stones. Great mountain peaks, smoking and flaming, came through the sky, but when they reached the Dasabala, they turned into celestial flower garlands.

Then he created a shower of weapons. Swords, spears, and arrows, both single-edged and double-edged, smoking and flaming, came through the sky, but when they reached the Dasabala, they became celestial flowers.

Then he created a shower of live coals. Coals with the color of flame-of-the-forest flowers came through the sky and, becoming celestial flowers, scattered at the feet of the Dasabala.

Then he created a shower of hot ashes. Extremely hot ashes came through the sky and, becoming sandalwood powder, fell at the feet of the Dasabala.

Then he created a shower of sand. Very fine sand, smoking and flaming, came through the sky and, becoming celestial flowers, fell at the feet of the Dasabala.

Then he created a shower of mud. That shower of mud, smoking and flaming, came through the sky and, becoming celestial scented mud, fell at the feet of the Dasabala.
296:
Then, thinking, "I will frighten the ascetic and make him flee," he created a thick darkness. That darkness, resembling the fourfold darkness, vanished upon reaching the Ten-Powered One, like darkness destroyed by sunlight. Thus, the yakkha Āḷavaka, unable to make the Blessed One flee with these nine rains—of wind, rain, stones, weapons, live coals, hot ashes, sand, mud, and darkness—approached the Blessed One himself with a fourfold army, carrying various weapons and crowded with many types of spirit beings. Those spirit beings, making various terrifying gestures and shouting "Seize him! Kill him!", seemed to descend upon the Blessed One. However, just as flies are unable to approach a red-hot iron ball, they were unable to approach the Blessed One. Even so, unlike Māra who retreated as soon as he arrived at the Bodhi-mandala, they did not retreat but caused a disturbance until midnight. Unable to shake the Blessed One even by showing various terrifying sights until midnight, Āḷavaka thought: "What if I release the Dussāvudha (cloth weapon), which is invincible to anyone?"

It is said that there are four supreme weapons in the world: Sakka's Vajirāvudha, Vessavaṇa's Gadāvudha, Yama's Nayanāvudha, and Āḷavaka's Dussāvudha. If Sakka, being angry, were to strike the summit of Mount Sineru with the Vajirāvudha, it would pierce through Mount Sineru, which is one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas high, and pass through to the bottom. The Gadāvudha released by Vessavaṇa when he is angry strikes off the heads of many thousands of yakkhas and returns to his hand. When Yama is angry, by merely looking with his Nayanāvudha, many thousands of Kumbhaṇḍas perish, crackling like sesame seeds on a hot pan. If the angry Āḷavaka were to release the Dussāvudha into the sky, it would not rain for twelve years. If he were to release it on the ground, all trees, grass, and so on would wither and not grow again for twelve years. If he were to release it into the ocean, all the water would dry up like a drop of water on a hot pan. If he were to strike a mountain as large as Sineru, it would be shattered into pieces and scattered. He then unfolded and took hold of that Dussāvudha, the upper garment of great power. Most of the deities from the ten-thousand world systems quickly assembled.
297:
"Today the Blessed One will tame Āḷavaka; we shall hear the Dhamma during that taming," thinking thus, the deities who wished to see the battle also assembled. Thus, the entire sky became filled with deities.

Then Āḷavaka, hovering in the sky near the Blessed One, released the cloth weapon. That cloth weapon, making a terrifying sound in the sky like a thunderbolt, smoking and flaming, reached the Blessed One and, in order to crush the yakkha's pride, turned into a foot-wiping cloth and fell at his feet. Seeing this, Āḷavaka became like a bull with broken horns or a snake with its fangs extracted—powerless, humbled, with his banner of pride fallen—and thought: "Even my Dussāvudha could not overcome this ascetic. What could be the reason?" [He realized,] "This is the reason: the ascetic is endowed with the dwelling of loving-kindness (metta-vihāra). Now, I will provoke him and separate him from his loving-kindness." It was in this connection that it was said: "Then the yakkha Āḷavaka [went] to where the Blessed One was... (and so on) ... 'Get out, ascetic!'"

The meaning therein is: "Why have you entered my abode without my permission and sat in the midst of my harem like the master of the house? For an ascetic, using what is not given and associating with women is improper. Therefore, if you are established in the Dhamma of an ascetic, get out, ascetic!" Some teachers, however, say: "He said this after saying these and other harsh words."

Then the Blessed One, knowing, "A stubborn person cannot be tamed by stubbornness; if one acts stubbornly, he will become even more stubborn, just as if one were to burst the gall bladder on the nose of a fierce dog, it would become even more fierce; but he can be tamed with gentleness," accepted his word with the pleasant address, "Very well, friend," and went out. Referring to this going out, it is said: "The Blessed One, saying 'Very well, friend,' went out."

Then Āḷavaka thought: "This ascetic is indeed easy to speak to; he went out with just a single word. I have been fighting all night for no reason against an ascetic who is so easy to make leave." Having become gentle-hearted, he thought again: "Even now, it is not yet easy to know; did he leave because he is easy to speak to, or because he is angry? Now, I will test him." Then he said, "Enter, ascetic!" Then the Blessed One, speaking pleasant words again to demonstrate that he was easy to speak to and gentle-hearted, said, "Very well, friend"...
298:
The Blessed One entered [the dwelling]. The yakkha Āḷavaka, wishing to repeatedly test that very quality of being easy to speak to (suvaca), said for a second and third time, "Monk, go out; enter." The Blessed One did as requested. If he had not done so, the heart of the yakkha, who was naturally fierce, would have become even fiercer and would not have been a fit vessel for a Dhamma discourse. Therefore, just as a mother soothes her crying young son by giving or doing whatever he desires, so the Blessed One, in order to make the yakkha—who was crying with the 'crying' of defilements—understand, did whatever he said.

Just as a nurse, giving something to a child who does not want to suckle, coaxes him to drink milk, so the Blessed One, in order to make the yakkha drink the milk of the Supramundane Dhamma (Lokuttara-dhamma), coaxed him by doing as he requested. Just as a man, wishing to fill a gourd with the 'four sweets' (catumadhura), cleans its interior, so the Blessed One, wishing to fill the yakkha's heart with the supramundane 'four sweets', went out and entered up to three times to clean the stain of anger within him.

Then the yakkha Āḷavaka thought: "This monk is indeed easy to speak to; when told 'Go out,' he goes out; when told 'Enter,' he enters. What if I exhaust this monk in this way for the whole night, then seize him by his feet and throw him to the other side of the Ganges?" Having given rise to such an evil thought, he said for the fourth time, "Monk, go out." Knowing that thought, the Blessed One said, "I will not go out, friend." Having said this, [the Buddha knew] the yakkha would seek something further to do and would think of asking a question. Knowing that this would be the opening for a Dhamma discourse, he said, "I will not go out." In that statement, 'na' is for negation; 'kho' is for emphasis; 'ahaṃ' refers to oneself; 'taṃ' is the reason. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "Friend, because you think thus, I shall not go out at all; do whatever you must do."

Then, because in the past, while traveling through the air, Āḷavaka would think, "Is this a golden mansion, or one of the silver or ruby mansions? Let us see," and would harass powerful ascetics and wanderers who came to his mansion by asking questions they could not answer, causing them to go mad and so on; thinking he would harass the Blessed One in the same way, he spoke the words beginning with "Pañhaṃ taṃ" (A question for you).
299:
From where did these questions come to this yakkha Āḷavaka? It is said that his parents, having attended upon the Blessed One Kassapa, learned eight questions along with their answers. They made Āḷavaka learn them when he was young, but with the passage of time, he forgot the answers. Because he had forgotten the answers, thinking "Let not these questions be lost," he had them written on a golden plate with vermilion and kept them in his mansion. Thus, these asked questions are indeed within the range of a Buddha (Buddhavisaya). The Blessed One, knowing this, and because no one is able to cause an obstacle to the gains, an obstacle to the life, or an obstruction to the Omniscient Knowledge and the fathom-wide radiance (byāmappabhā) of the Buddhas, wishing to show the power of a Buddha which is uncommon in the world, said: "Friend, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas..." and so on.

Thus, the Blessed One, having thwarted the yakkha's desire to harass him and encouraging him to ask questions, said: "Furthermore, friend, ask whatever you desire." The meaning is: "If you desire, ask; I have no burden in answering questions. Or rather, ask what you desire; I will answer everything for you." Thus he made an invitation of omniscience (sabbaññupavāraṇā), which is not shared by Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, or great disciples. When the Blessed One had thus made the invitation of omniscience, the yakkha Āḷavaka addressed the Blessed One with a verse.

In that verse, "Kiṃ sūdha vittaṃ" means "What wealth is best in this world?" Vitta means wealth. It is called vitta because it produces the delight known as pīti. Suciṇṇa means a practice well-performed. Sukha means physical and mental pleasantness. Āvahati means it brings, gives, or conveys. The word have is a particle in the sense of certainty. Sādutara means exceedingly sweet. There is also a reading sādhutara. Rasānaṃ means among those things known as tastes. Kathaṃ means in what manner. Kathaṃjīvino jīvitaṃ means the living of one who lives in what way. For the sake of the verse's meter, it is said with a nasal as kathaṃjīviṃ jīvitaṃ. There is also a reading kathaṃjīviṃ jīvataṃ, the meaning of which is: "Among those who live, what kind of living is best?" Thus, with this verse, he asked these four questions: "What is a man's best wealth in this world? What practice, when well-performed, brings happiness? What is the sweetest among tastes? What way of living do they say is the best living?"

Then the Blessed One, wishing to answer in the same manner as the Ten-Powered Kassapa had answered, spoke this verse: "Faith is the best wealth here..." In that verse, just as wealth such as gold and silver brings the happiness of use, prevents the suffering of exhaustion, ends the state of being poor, is the cause for obtaining pearls and jewels, and carries on the lineage of the world; so too, mundane and supramundane faith (saddhā) brings mundane and supramundane resultant happiness. For those who practice with faith as the forerunner, it prevents the suffering of rebirth, aging, and so on. It ends the state of being poor in virtues. It is the cause for obtaining jewels such as the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). A clansman endowed with faith is also endowed with virtue, and endowed with attendants and wealth. To whatever region that clansman approaches, in those various regions...
300:
(Mundane wealth such as gold and silver) brings the happiness of enjoyment, wards off suffering such as hunger and thirst, alleviates poverty, is the cause for obtaining treasures such as pearls, and maintains the continuity of the world. Similarly, faith (saddhā), whether mundane or supramundane, brings mundane or supramundane resultant happiness accordingly. For those who practice with faith as the lead, it wards off the suffering of birth, aging, and so on; it alleviates the poverty of lack of virtue; and it is the cause for obtaining treasures such as the factors of enlightenment like mindfulness (satisambojjhaṅga).

According to the words: "One who has faith and is endowed with virtue, possessed of fame and wealth, is honored wherever he goes" (Dhp. 303), it is called "wealth" (vitta) because it maintains the continuity of the world. Because their wealth of faith follows them to future lives, is not shared with others, is the cause of all attainments, and is also the root cause for obtaining mundane wealth such as gold and silver. Only one with faith, having performed meritorious deeds like giving (dāna), acquires wealth; whereas the wealth of one without faith leads only to harm. Therefore, it is called supreme. The phrase "for a man" is a teaching given by way of the highest category of beings. Therefore, it should be understood that not only for a man, but also for women and others, the wealth of faith is indeed supreme.

"Dhamma" refers to the ten wholesome courses of action, or the practices of giving, virtue, and mental development (dāna, sīla, bhāvanā). "Suciṇṇo" means well-performed or well-practiced. "Sukhamāvahati" means it brings human happiness like that of the merchant's son Soṇa or Raṭṭhapāla, divine happiness like that of Sakka and others, and ultimately the happiness of Nibbāna like that of Prince Mahāpaduma and others.

The word "Sacca" (truth) is seen in various meanings. These are: in the sense of truthfulness of speech (vācā-sacca) in such passages as "Speak the truth, do not get angry" (Dhp. 224); in the sense of the truth of abstinence (virati-sacca) in "Ascetics and Brahmins established in truth" (Ja. 2.21.433); in the sense of the truth of views (diṭṭhi-sacca) in "Why do they say various truths..." (Sn. 891); in the sense of Brahmanical truths (brāhmaṇa-sacca) in "Monks, there are these four Brahmanical truths" (AN 4.185); in the sense of ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca) in "Truth is one, there is no second" (Sn. 890); and in the sense of the Noble Truths (ariya-sacca) in "How many of the four truths are wholesome?" (Vibh. 216). Here, however, including the ultimate truth of Nibbāna and the truth of abstinence within...
301:
...truthful speech is intended. By the power of that truthful speech, they make water and so on follow their will, and they cross over to the other shore of birth, aging, and death. As it is said:

"By truthful speech one runs upon the water,
By truth the wise even destroy poison,
By truth the rain-god thunders and pours down rain,
Established in truth, they aspire for Nibbāna.

Whatever tastes there are on this earth,
Truth is indeed the sweetest of those tastes;
Ascetics and Brahmins established in truth,
Cross over to the other shore of birth and death."

"Sādutaraṃ" means especially sweet or excellent. "Rasānaṃ" refers to things to be tasted according to the method of "root-taste, trunk-taste," etc. (Dhs. 628-630); the "fruit-taste" (phala-rasa) in "Monks, I allow all fruit juices" (Mahāvagga 300); the tastes in "The venerable Gotama is without taste; Brahmin, there are these tastes of forms and tastes of sounds" (Pārājika 3, AN 8.11); the tastes in "There is no offense in taste-taste" (Pācittiya 605-611); the taste in "This Dhamma-Vinaya has one taste, the taste of liberation" (Cūḷavagga 385, AN 8.19); and the tastes in "The Blessed One is a partaker of the taste of the goal and the taste of the Dhamma" (Mahāniddesa 149). Apart from the taste of physical objects (rūpācāra-rasa), the remaining syllables and so on are called "Dhamma-rasa." Among those tastes, truth is indeed the sweetest. Or, it is the best, most praised, or supreme. Root-tastes and so on nourish the body and bring happiness accompanied by defilements. In the taste of truth, the taste of abstinence-truth and speech-truth nourish the mind through serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā), and bring happiness free from defilements. The taste of liberation (vimutti-rasa) is sweet because it is repeatedly infused with the happiness of Nibbāna, which is the ultimate truth. The taste of the goal (attha-rasa) and the taste of the Dhamma (dhamma-rasa) are also sweet because they occur depending on the cause and effect which are the means to attain that happiness of Nibbāna.

Regarding "Paññājīviṃ jีvitaṃ" (living a life of wisdom): among the blind, the one-eyed, and the two-eyed persons, the two-eyed person (di-cakkhu) who knows both mundane and supramundane benefits—if a layperson—lives by fulfilling the lay practice such as diligence in work and trade, taking refuge, giving, sharing, undertaking precepts, and observing the Uposatha through wisdom. If a monk, he lives by fulfilling the monastic practice through wisdom, starting from virtue characterized by lack of remorse up to the higher purification of mind (citta-visuddhi) and so on.
302: The life of one who lives by wisdom, or that living by wisdom, is said to be the most excellent; this is how the meaning should be understood. Having heard these four questions answered by the Blessed One, the delighted Yakkha Āḷavaka, wishing to ask the remaining four questions, spoke the verse beginning with, "How does one cross the flood?" Then, the Blessed One, wishing to answer him in the same manner as before, spoke the verse beginning with, "By faith one crosses the flood." In that verse, whoever crosses the fourfold flood also crosses the ocean of saṃsāra, overcomes the suffering of the round of rebirths, and is purified from the stains of defilements. This being so, a person without faith, not believing in the possibility of crossing the flood, cannot enter into it; being heedless by letting the mind loose in the five cords of sensual pleasure and being attached only to those pleasures, they cannot cross the ocean of saṃsāra. A lazy person, being mixed with unwholesome states, lives in suffering. An unwise person, not knowing the path to purity, cannot be purified. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show the qualities such as faith which are the opposites of faithlessness and so on, taught this verse. By this verse thus spoken, since the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is the proximate cause for the factors of the path of Stream-entry, the Blessed One, with the phrase "By faith one crosses the flood," revealed the path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga), which is the means of crossing the flood of views (diṭṭhogha), and the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). Since the Stream-enterer is endowed with heedfulness (appamāda), characterized by constant effort in the development of wholesome states, and having attained the second path, the path of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-magga), they cross the ocean of saṃsāra, which is the ground of the flood of existence (bhavogha) not yet crossed by the path of Stream-entry, leaving aside only the path that leads to returning to this human world once more. Therefore, with the phrase "By heedfulness one crosses the ocean," He revealed the path of Once-returning and the Once-returner. The Once-returner, having attained the third path, the path of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-magga), through energy (vīriya), overcomes the sensual realm which is the ground of the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha) not yet overcome by the path of Once-returning, as well as the suffering of sensual lust called the flood of sensual desire. Therefore, with the phrase "By energy one overcomes suffering," He revealed the path of Non-returning and the Non-returner. The Non-returner, having attained the wisdom of the fourth path, the path of Arahantship (Arahatta-magga), which is absolutely pure, through wisdom purified by the absence of sensual perceptions, abandons the supreme stain called ignorance (avijjā) not yet abandoned by the path of Non-returning. Therefore, with the phrase "By wisdom one is purified," He revealed the path of Arahantship and the fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala), which is the means of crossing the flood of ignorance (avijjogha). At the conclusion of this verse, which was taught with Arahantship as its climax, the Yakkha Āḷavaka was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).
303: Now, taking up the word 'wisdom' (paññā) mentioned in the phrase 'By wisdom one is purified,' and wishing to ask a question mixed with mundane and supramundane aspects through his own intellectual wit, he spoke this six-line verse: "How does one gain wisdom?" In that verse, the word 'kathaṃsu' (how) is an inquiry into the logical reasoning in all respects. Indeed, this Yakkha Āḷavaka, having known the meaning of wisdom and so on, asks about its logic: "How, by what logic, and for what reason does one gain wisdom?" This same method applies to wealth and so forth. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show the Yakkha the attainment of wisdom through four causes, spoke the words beginning with 'saddahāno' (one who has faith). The meaning of that Pali is: by whatever Dhamma—in the preceding stage through the divisions of bodily good conduct and so on, and in the subsequent stage through the divisions of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma)—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples who are free from defilements have reached Nibbāna; one who has faith in that Dhamma of the Arahants for the sake of attaining Nibbāna gains mundane and supramundane wisdom. And that wisdom is not gained by mere faith alone. Because one who has developed faith approaches [a teacher]; one who approaches attends [to them]; one who attends lends an ear; and one who lends an ear hears the Dhamma. Therefore, from the moment of approaching until the hearing of the Dhamma, one gains the desire to learn (sussūsa). What is meant is this: even if one has faith in that Dhamma, by approaching teachers and preceptors at the proper time and attending to them by performing major and minor duties, when the teachers' minds are pleased by such attendance, they desire to speak something. Then, by lending an ear with the acquired desire to learn, the one who hears gains wisdom. Even with such a desire to learn, only one who is heedful, not being devoid of mindfulness, and who is discerning, knowing what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, gains it; not anyone else. Therefore, He said, "one who is heedful and discerning." Thus, because of faith, one practices the path that leads to the gain of wisdom; through the desire to learn, one respectfully hears the means of acquiring wisdom; through heedfulness, one does not forget what has been learned. Through being discerning, one takes the meaning without deficiency, excess, or distortion, and expands upon it. Or, through the desire to learn, one who lends an ear hears the Dhamma which is the cause for the acquisition of wisdom; through heedfulness, one retains the Dhamma that has been heard; through being discerning, one investigates the meaning of the Dhammas that have been retained; thereafter, one gradually realizes the ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca). Therefore, when asked by the Yakkha, "How does one gain wisdom?", the Blessed One, showing these four causes, spoke this verse.
304: Now, wishing to answer the next three questions, He spoke this verse beginning with 'Patirūpakārī'. In that verse, one is called 'Patirūpakārī' (one who acts appropriately) because they employ the means to acquire worldly or supramundane wealth without neglecting the proper place, time, and so on. 'Dhuravā' refers to one who bears the burden without laying it down (one with unflagging effort) by the power of mental energy. 'Uṭṭhātā' refers to one who is endowed with initiative and has unrelaxed exertion by the power of bodily energy, in the manner of 'one who does not think of cold or heat more than a blade of grass' and so forth. 'Vindate dhanaṃ' (acquires wealth) means obtaining it just as the young pupil of the Little Treasurer soon acquired 400,000 in worldly wealth with only a single dead mouse, or as Elder Mahallaka Mahātissa acquired supramundane wealth. That Elder Mahallaka Mahātissa made a vow, saying, 'I will dwell only in three postures.' When the time of drowsiness came, he soaked a straw wreath in water, placed it on his head, and entered water deep up to his neck. Warding off drowsiness and striving for ten years, he attained Arahantship. 'Saccena' (by truth) means one attains fame through verbal truth, being 'one who speaks the truth, one who speaks what is real,' and also through ultimate truth, being 'a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a Noble Disciple.' 'Dadaṃ' (one who gives) means that by giving whatever is desired or longed for, one binds, fulfills, or makes friends. Or it means one binds that friendship by giving what is difficult to give. It should also be understood that by the mention of giving, all four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) are included; it means one makes friends through those bases of sympathy. Having thus answered the four questions by the method mixed with worldly and supramundane aspects common to both householders and monastics, He now wished to answer the fifth question, 'How does one not sorrow in the hereafter?' from the perspective of a householder, and so He spoke the verse beginning with 'Yassete'. The meaning of that verse is: For a householder who enjoys sense pleasures, seeking a home or seeking the five cords of sensual pleasure, who is 'Saddha' (faithful) because of being endowed with faith that gives rise to all wholesome states as mentioned in the phrase 'Saddahāno arahataṃ'; there is 'Sacca' (truth) of the kind mentioned in the phrase 'Saccena kittiṃ pappoti'; 'Dama' (restraint) which is mentioned by the names of desire to learn and wisdom in the phrase 'Sussūsaṃ labhate paññaṃ'; 'Dhiti' (fortitude) which is mentioned by the names of diligence (dhura) and initiative (uṭṭhāna) in the phrase 'Dhuravā uṭṭhātā'; and 'Cāga' (generosity) of the kind mentioned in the phrase 'Dadaṃ mittāni ganthati'. If these four qualities exist, 'Sa ve pecca na socati' means that when going from this world to the next world, he certainly does not sorrow.
305: The Blessed One, having thus answered the fifth question, spoke the words beginning with 'Ingha aññepi' (Come now, ask others too) to urge the Yakkha. In that text, 'Ingha' is a particle in the sense of urging. 'Aññepi' means 'ask other numerous recluses and brahmins,' or 'ask other numerous recluses and brahmins like Pūraṇa Kassapa and others who claim to be omniscient.' If there is in this world any cause for attaining fame greater than Truth (Sacca) as mentioned here in 'By truth one attains fame'; or any cause for acquiring worldly and supramundane wisdom greater than Restraint (Dama) mentioned here by the designation of wisdom as 'One who desires to learn acquires wisdom'; or any cause for binding friends greater than Generosity (Cāga) as mentioned here in 'By giving one binds friends'; or any cause for acquiring worldly and supramundane wealth greater than Patience (Khanti)—which is described here as energy (viriya) that has reached the state of great exertion because of its nature of enduring great burdens, mentioned by the names of diligence (dhura) and initiative (uṭṭhāna) in 'Dhuravā uṭṭhātā'—or if there is any cause for not sorrowing after passing from this world to the next greater than these four qualities mentioned as 'Truth, Restraint, Fortitude, and Generosity,' (then ask them). This is the explanation of the meaning together with the brief connection (yojanā). In detail, however, each word should be understood by analyzing it through the methods of extracting the meaning, extracting the word, and word-description. When this was said, the Āḷavaka Yakkha, because the doubt for which he might ask others had been abandoned, thought, 'How could I ask now?' and wishing to make those who did not yet know the reason for his not asking understand, he said, 'I now understand the benefit for the future life' and so on. In those words, 'Ajja' (today) means 'starting from today.' 'Pajānāmi' (I understand) means 'I understand in the manner already described.' By the words 'Yo attho' (what benefit), he shows the benefit in the present life mentioned by the method of 'One who desires to learn acquires wisdom' and so forth. By the word 'Samparāyiko' (relating to the future), he shows the benefit for the future life, which is the cause for the absence of sorrow after passing away, as mentioned in 'To whom these four qualities belong.' The word 'Attha' is a synonym for cause (kāraṇa). This word 'Attha' occurs in the sense of the meaning of the text (pāṭhattha) in such places as 'Sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ'. It occurs in the sense of 'object of desire' (vicakkhaṇa) in such places as 'Householder, I have need (attho) of gold and silver'. It occurs in the sense of 'growth' (vuḍḍhi) in such places as 'There is benefit (attho) for the virtuous'. It occurs in the sense of 'wealth' (dhana) in such places as 'Many people associate for the sake of wealth (attha-hetu)'. It occurs in the sense of 'welfare/benefit' (attha) in such places as 'He practices for the benefit (atthaṃ) of both'.
306:
(The word 'attha') occurs in the sense of benefit, and in such passages as 'Atthe jāte ca paṇḍitaṃ' (Jātaka 1.1.92), it occurs in the sense of cause. In this scripture, however, it occurs in the sense of cause. Therefore, I have now personally understood in detail, through the method taught by the Blessed One today, that benefit which is the cause for the attainment of wisdom and so forth in the present life, and the cause for the absence of sorrow in the future life. Having understood thus, why should I now ask many recluses and brahmins? Thus the meaning should be understood in brief.

Thus, the yakkha Āḷavaka, having said, "I understand the benefit pertaining to the future life," and wishing to show that this knowledge has the Blessed One as its root, said, "The Buddha has indeed appeared for my benefit." In that statement, 'atthāya' means for benefit and for growth. "In whatever place a gift given bears great fruit" means that through the generosity mentioned in the phrase 'yassete caturo dhammā', I have known the Buddha, the supreme recipient of offerings, in whom a gift given bears great fruit. Some teachers, however, say that this was said in reference to the Saṅgha.

Thus, having shown his attainment of benefit through this verse, and now wishing to show the practice accompanied by that benefit, he said, "I shall wander," and so forth. In that statement, "from village to village" means from one celestial village to another celestial village. "From city to city" means from one celestial city to another celestial city. "Paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One and the excellence of the Dhamma" means praising the Buddha's perfect enlightenment and the Dhamma's excellent proclamation through such methods as "The Blessed One is indeed the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Dhamma of the Blessed One is indeed well-proclaimed," and by the word 'ca' (and), praising the Saṅgha's good conduct through such methods as "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has indeed practiced well," and thus paying homage and becoming a proclaimer of the Dhamma, he meant "I shall wander."

Thus, at the conclusion of this verse, the clear dawning of the night, the arising of the sounds of "Sādhu," and the bringing of Prince Āḷavaka to the yakkha's mansion occurred all at the same moment. When the king's men heard the sound of "Sādhu," they reflected, "Such a sound of 'Sādhu' does not arise for anyone except the Buddha; has the Blessed One perhaps arrived?" Seeing the radiance of the Blessed One's body, they did not stand outside as before but entered inside without hesitation and saw the Blessed One seated in the yakkha's mansion and the yakkha standing with palms joined in reverence. Seeing the yakkha, they said, "O great yakkha, we have brought this prince to you as a sacrificial offering; now eat him, consume him, or do with him as you please." That Āḷavaka yakkha, being a Sotāpanna, was filled with shame.
307:
Especially when spoken to in this way in the presence of the Blessed One, that yakkha (being a Sotāpanna and thus very ashamed) lifted the prince with both hands and offered him to the Blessed One. "Venerable Sir, this prince has been sent to me; I offer this prince to the Blessed One. May the Buddha, who is compassionate for the welfare of beings, accept this child for his benefit and happiness," he requested and recited this verse:

"This prince, who possesses marks resulting from countless merits,
Who is endowed with all limbs and complete in physical characteristics,
With a joyful and clear mind, I give him to You.
O Visionary One, accept him for the benefit of the world."

The Blessed One accepted the prince. While accepting, He recited a verse lacking one foot (pādūna-gāthā) to bring blessings to both the yakkha and the prince. Then the yakkha, wishing to establish the prince in the Refuges, completed the fourth foot by reciting it three times. It was as follows:

"May this prince be long-lived,
And may you, O yakkha, be happy.
Being free from disease, may you both remain for the benefit of the world.
This prince goes to the Buddha for refuge.
This prince goes to the Dhamma for refuge.
This prince goes to the Saṅgha for refuge."

Then the Blessed One gave the prince to the king's men, saying, "Nurture this prince until he grows up, and then give him back to me." Thus, because the prince went from the hands of the king's men to the hands of the yakkha, from the hands of the yakkha to the hands of the Buddha, and from the hands of the Buddha back to the hands of the king's men, he became famously known by the name "Hatthaka Āḷavaka" (Āḷavaka of the Hands). Seeing the king's men returning with the prince, farmers, forest-workers, and others asked in fear, "Did the yakkha not want the prince because he was too young?" The king's men told them everything, saying, "Do not be afraid. The Blessed One has made things safe." Then, with shouts of "Sādhu, Sādhu," the entire city of Āḷavī turned toward the yakkha's dwelling in a great commotion. The yakkha also, when the time for the Blessed One's alms-round arrived, took the bowl and robes and followed Him halfway before returning.

Then the Blessed One, having wandered for alms in the city and finished His meal, sat upon the Buddha-throne prepared at the foot of a certain secluded tree near the city gate. Thereafter, the King and the citizens, gathering together with a great multitude of people, approached the Blessed One...
308:
(The King and the people) approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down surrounding him. They asked, "Venerable Sir, how did you tame such a fierce yakkha?" To them, the Blessed One related the Āḷavaka Sutta itself, starting from the battle, saying, "In this way, I caused the nine kinds of rain to fall; in this way, he created terrifying sights; in this way, he asked questions; and in this way, I answered him." At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya).

Afterward, the King and the citizens built an abode for the yakkha Āḷavaka near the residence of the Great King Vessavaṇa and maintained regular offerings of flowers, scents, and so forth. When the prince reached the age of discretion, they sent him away, saying, "You have gained your life because of the Blessed One; go and attend upon the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks." While attending upon the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, Hatthaka Āḷavaka soon established himself in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). Having mastered the entire word of the Buddha, he was surrounded by five hundred lay followers. The Blessed One designated him as the foremost, saying, "Monks, among my lay disciples who win over an assembly by the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), the foremost is Hatthaka Āḷavaka." This is the twelfth sutta.

## Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Yakkha Saṃyutta is finished.
309:
## 11. Sakka Saṃyutta

## 1. First Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the Suvīra Sutta

In the first sutta of the Sakka Saṃyutta, regarding the word "abhiyaṃsu": When did they march against (in battle)? They marched against when the Asuras were powerful. In this regard, the following is the sequential account:

It is said that Sakka was once a young man named Magha in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha. Taking thirty-three men as companions, he performed meritorious deeds and fulfilled the seven vows (vattapada). Having passed away there, he was reborn in the world of the gods (Tāvatiṃsa). Seeing that this new son of the gods, along with his retinue, surpassed the existing gods in ten respects due to the power of his great merit, the old inhabitants (the former gods) prepared a fragrant drink called Gandha. Sakka gave a sign to his followers, saying, "Friends, do not drink this fragrant liquor; only make a gesture as if drinking." They did as he said.

The old gods drank as much as they desired of the liquor brought in golden bowls, became intoxicated, and fell asleep here and there on the golden ground. Sakka said, "Seize these people who are drunk and asleep," and having them grasped by their feet, he had them thrown down into the ocean at the foot of Mount Sineru. By the power of Sakka's merit, all those who followed his will also fell there at the foot of Mount Sineru. When they regained consciousness in the midst of Mount Sineru, they said, "Friends, we shall not drink liquor (surā); we shall not drink liquor." From then on, the name Asura (non-drinker) came into being.

Then, due to the influence of their past karma and the physical environment (kamma-paccaya-utu), the Asura realm, ten thousand yojanas in extent, appeared at the lower base of Mount Sineru. Sakka established guards to prevent them from returning. Referring to those guards, the teachers said:

Between the two cities difficult to conquer by battle,
Five kinds of guards are stationed:
Nāgas, Garuḍas, Kumbhaṇḍas,
Yakkhas, and the four powerful Great Kings.
310:
Because they cannot be taken by war, the two cities—the city of the devas and the city of the asuras—are known as Ayujjhapura (the city unconquerable by war). When the asuras are powerful, the devas flee and enter the city of the devas; once the gates are closed, even a hundred thousand asuras cannot do anything. When the devas are powerful, the asuras flee and close the gates of the asura city; then even a hundred thousand Sakkas cannot do anything. Thus, these two cities are called Ayujjhapura. Between these two cities, Sakka has placed guards at five places, starting with the water.

Among those five places, by the word 'udaka' (water), the nāgas are meant. These nāgas are powerful in water. Therefore, they are placed as guards on the first terrace (alinda) of Mount Sineru. By the word 'karoṭi', the supaṇṇas (garuḍas) are meant. It is said they have a drink and food called 'karoṭi', hence they received that name. They are placed as guards on the second terrace. By the word 'payassahārī', the kumbhaṇḍas are meant. They are dānavarakkhasas (ogres). They are placed as guards on the third terrace. By the word 'madanayuta', the yakkhas are meant. They are said to be unruly and fond of fighting. They are placed as guards on the fourth terrace. By the word 'caturo ca mahantā', the Four Great Kings are meant. They are placed as guards on the fifth terrace. Therefore, if the asuras, with angry and agitated minds, ascend to the city of the devas for war, the nāgas on the first terrace of Mount Sineru block them. In this manner, the remaining forces, such as the supaṇṇas, block them on the remaining terraces.

Those asuras are equal to the Tāvatiṃsa devas in terms of lifespan, appearance, retinue, and power. Therefore, not realizing they were asuras in the interim, it is only when the trumpet flower trees (cittapāṭalī) bloom that they say: "This city is not the city of the devas; in that city, the pāricchattaka (coral tree) blooms, but here the cittapāṭalī blooms. The old Sakka has deceived us by making us drink liquor (surā) and has taken our city of the devas. Let us go and fight with that old Sakka." Mounting elephants, horses, and chariots, holding shields of gold, silver, and gems, and being prepared for war, they strike the asura drums and emerge, splitting the waters of the great ocean in two. When the devas appear, those asuras begin to climb Mount Sineru like termites and flies climbing a termite mound. Then, first, a battle occurs between them and the nāgas.
