In that battle, no one's outer or inner skin is cut, nor does blood flow. It is merely like a battle between children playing with wooden sticks, where they [frighten] each other...
311:
...it is merely a matter of frightening one another. Hundreds of millions, even thousands of millions of nāgas, after fighting with those asuras, drive them back into the asura city and return.

When the asuras are powerful, the nāgas retreat and fight together with the supaṇṇas on the second terrace. This same method applies to the supaṇṇas and others. When the asuras crush all five places, the five forces, even when combined, retreat. Then the Four Great Kings go and report the matter to Sakka. Sakka, hearing their words, either goes out himself mounting the Vejayanta chariot, which is one hundred and fifty yojanas long, or sends one of his sons. At this time, wishing to send his son, he says: "Dear Suvīra," and so on.

"Evaṃ bhaddantavāti kho" means "May it be well with you." "Pamādaṃ āpādesi" means he became negligent. Surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, he descends to the great golden street, sixty yojanas wide, and wanders in the Nandana Grove and other places, playing at the festival of the stars.

"Anuṭṭhahanti" means not making personal effort. "Avāyāmanti" means not making an exertion. "Alasvassā" should be broken down as "alaso assa" (if one were lazy). "Na ca kiccāni kāraye" means one should not perform any task at all. "Sabbakāmasamiddhassa" means one would be endowed with all desires. "Taṃ me sakka varaṃ disā" means "O Sakka, best among devas, tell me of that excellent place where one is fulfilled without performing any work." "Nibbānassa hi so maggo" is said (ironically) meaning that living without performing any livelihood task is the path to Nibbāna (the Ariyan Path). This is the first sutta.

## 2. Susīmasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "Susīmaṃ" refers to one particular son of that name among his thousand sons. This is the second sutta.

## 3. Dhajaggasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "samupabyūḷho" means gathered together in a mass. "Dhajaggaṃ ullokeyyatha" means Sakka's Vejayanta chariot, which is one hundred and fifty yojanas long, is fifty yojanas wide.
312:
The rear part of the Vejayanta chariot is fifty yojanas, the middle carriage body is fifty yojanas, and from the junction of the chariot to the front is fifty yojanas. Teachers also say that by doubling that measure of one hundred and fifty yojanas, the length is three hundred yojanas. In that chariot, a jeweled throne of one yojana is spread; at the top, a white umbrella of three yojanas is placed; and to a single yoke, one thousand thoroughbred horses are harnessed. There is no limit to the measure of the remaining ornaments. The banner of that chariot rises two hundred and fifty yojanas high; when struck by the wind, a sound like that of a five-fold musical ensemble issues from that banner. It is said, "Look at the tip of that banner." Why? Because for the devas who see that banner, the fear does not arise, thinking, "Our king, Sakka, has come and stands like a firmly planted pillar at the edge of the host; whom should we fear?"

Pajāpati refers to that deva king who is said to be equal in appearance and lifespan to Sakka; he receives the second seat immediately following Sakka. Deva kings Varuṇa and Īsāna are likewise. Varuṇa receives the third seat, and Īsāna receives the fourth seat. "Palāyī" (the fleer) refers to one who, when defeated by the Asuras, has the nature of fleeing even upon seeing the banner of a few soldiers while standing on that chariot.

The terms beginning with "Itipi so bhagavā" have already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. "Idamavoca" means the Blessed One spoke this Dhajagga Paritta, whose majesty prevails throughout the hundred thousand million world systems that constitute its domain of authority (āṇākhetta). There is no end to the number of those who, by reflecting on this Dhajagga Sutta, have been liberated from sufferings such as the danger of yakkhas and the danger of thieves. Let alone the subsiding of other dangers and sufferings; one who reflects on this Paritta with a confident mind finds a footing even in the sky.

In this regard, there is this supporting story—it is heard that while plastering work was being done at the Dīghavāpi Cetiya, a young monk fell from the base of the pinnacle (muddha-vedikā) and was sliding down the flank of the stupa. The community of monks standing below said, "Friend, reflect on the Dhajagga Paritta!" That young monk, being threatened by the fear of death, said, "May the Dhajagga Paritta protect me!" At that very moment, two bricks came out from the flank of the stupa and stood as a flight of steps, and the monks standing above lowered a vine ladder. When that monk stood on the ladder, the bricks returned to their original places. This is the third sutta.
313:
## 4. Vepacittisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, Vepacitti is said to be the eldest among the Asuras. The words "yena" and "naṃ" are merely particles. "Kaṇṭhapañcamehi" refers to being bound with five types of bonds: on the two hands, the two feet, and the neck. Those bonds, like lotus fibers or spider webs, are visible to the eye but obstruct one's movements. However, one is bound by those bonds only through the mind and is freed only through the mind.

"Akkosati" (he reviles) means reviling with these ten grounds of abuse: "You are a thief, you are a fool, you are confused, you are a stealer, you are a camel, you are an ox, you are a donkey, you are a hell-being, you are an animal; there is no good destination for you, only a miserable destination is to be expected for you." "Paribhāsati" (he threatens) means threatening by saying things such as, "O old Sakka, you will not always be the winner; when the Asuras gain victory, I will bind you like this, make you lie down at the gate of the Asura abode, and beat you." Sakka, having achieved victory, does not take that threat to heart, but shaking his noble upper robe over his head, he repeatedly enters and leaves the Sudhammā hall of the devas. "Ajjhabhāsi" means Mātali spoke because he wished to investigate, thinking, "Does this Sakka endure these harsh words out of fear, or because he is endowed with endurance-patience (adhivāsana-khanti)?"

"Dubbalyā no" means "is it because of weakness?" "Paṭisaṃyuñje" means "shall I compete as an enemy?" or "shall I overwhelm and oppress?" "Pabhijjeyyuṃ" means they fail or are faulty. There is also a variant reading "pakujjheyuṃ." "Paraṃ" refers to the enemy. "Yo sato upasammati" means the one who, being mindful, is at peace; the meaning is "I consider that very peace of his to be the restraint of the fool." "Yadā naṃ manyati" means "because he considers it so." "Ajjhāruhati" means he overwhelms or tramples upon. "Go va bhiyyo palāyinaṃ" means, for example, while two oxen are fighting, the herd of oxen stands watching, and when one flees, the entire herd of oxen further overwhelms that fleeing ox. Likewise, the one of little wisdom further overwhelms the one who is patient.

"Sadatthaparamā" means taking one's own benefit as supreme. "Khantyā bhiyyo na vijjati" means among such supreme benefits of one's own, there is no other benefit greater than patience. "Tamāhu paramaṃ khantiṃ" means when one who is strong endures, they call that patience the supreme patience. The strength of a fool is merely the strength of ignorance. That strength, to whomsoever...
314:
"That strength is indeed no strength; that strength is called strength," it is explained. *Dhamma-guttassa* means of one protected by the Dhamma, or of one who protects the Dhamma. *Paṭivattā* means one who speaks by overpowering or oppressing; or one might even say "the strength of a fool" by overpowering; however, there is no one capable of shaking one established in the Dhamma. *Tasseva tena pāpiyo* means that for one who reacts with anger toward an angry person, it is worse for that person because of that anger. *Tikicchantānaṃ* is a plural used in place of the singular, meaning "one who heals." Ordinary foolish people think of such a person—who acts for the benefit of both himself and others as if treating them—as "this person is a blind fool." *Dhamma-akovida* refers to those unskilled in the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. *Idha* means in this Dispensation (*Sāsana*). *Kho* is merely a particle. The fourth sutta [is finished].

## ၅။ သုဘာသိတဇယသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the fifth sutta, he said this to the Lord of Asuras. This was said because of his skillfulness. It is said that Sakka had this thought: "It is burdensome to speak first by disregarding the name of another; however, it is easy to speak later by following the words of another." *Pubbadevā* refers to the ancient rulers who lived in the deva realm for a long time. "Speak the words that have come down from your lineage," is the meaning. *Adaṇḍāvacarā* refers to those who are free from oppression by punishment. It means that there is no need to take up a stick or a weapon here. The fifth sutta [is finished].

## ၆။ ကုလာဝကသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the sixth sutta, *ajjhabhāsi* means: as Sakka headed toward the silk-cotton forest (*simbali-vana*), the sound of the chariot, the sound of the thoroughbred horses, and the sound of the banners were like the sound of thunderclaps all around. Hearing that sound, the powerful Garuḍas (*supaṇṇa*) in the silk-cotton forest fled. The old birds, those weak from disease, and the young chicks whose wings had not yet grown, being unable to flee and terrified by the fear of death, cried out with a great wail all at once. Sakka heard that sound and asked Mātali, "Friends, whose sound is this?" "Great King, hearing the sound of the chariot, the Garuḍas are unable to flee and are wailing," he replied. Hearing those words, his heart was moved by compassion, and he spoke. *Īsāmukhena* means with the tip of the chariot's pole. Let these birds be avoided by this chariot pole so that the tip of the pole does not crush or destroy their nests. For that chariot, born of the power of merit...
315:
...even if the Cakkavāḷa mountains or Mount Sineru stand in its way, it goes right through them; it travels without sticking, as if traveling through the sky. If it were to go through that silk-cotton forest, just as a large cart going through a grove of castor-oil plants or a grove of reeds destroys and crushes the entire forest, so too would it happen to that silk-cotton forest. The sixth sutta [is finished].

## ၇။ နဒုဗ္ဘိယသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the seventh sutta, *upasaṅkami* means: this Sakka thought, "Even if he were my greatest enemy, I would not betray him." Vepacitti thought, "There is no one who is more of an enemy to me than Sakka; I will test him first to see whether he will betray me or not upon seeing me," and so he approached. "Stop, Vepacitti, you are caught!" Sakka said. As soon as he said this, Vepacitti the Asura was bound by the fivefold bonds, including the neck. "Make an oath not to betray me," Sakka said. By the phrase *yaṃ musābhaṇato pāpaṃ*, he refers to the evil of false speech committed by King Cetiya among the first inhabitants of this aeon. *Ariyūpavādino* refers to evil like that of the monk Kokālika. *Mittadduno ca yaṃ pāpaṃ* refers to the evil of the one with a corrupt mind toward the Bodhisatta in the Mahākapi Jātaka. *Akataññuno* refers to the evil of an ungrateful person like Devadatta. It is said that these four are the great evils in this aeon. The seventh sutta [is finished].

## ၈။ ဝေရောစနအသုရိန္ဒသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the eighth sutta, *aṭṭhaṃsu* means they stood like statues of gatekeepers. *Nipphadā* means accomplishment. Verocana the Asura means that one should strive as long as the goal is not yet accomplished. The second verse belongs to Sakka. Therein, *khantyā bhiyyo* means that among accomplished and beautiful benefits, there is no benefit superior to patience. *Atthajātā* means having business or tasks. Starting from animals such as dogs and jackals, there is no being that is without business. Even just going from here to there is a task. *Saṃyoga-paramā tveva sambhogā sabbapāṇinaṃ* means that because things like leftover rice are unfit for consumption, they become fit for consumption only when they are heated again, roasted, or combined with ghee, honey, molasses, and so on. Therefore, it is said, "The enjoyments of all beings are primarily based on combination."
316:
"Sabbapāṇinaṃ" means of all living beings. "Nipphannasobhano attho" means these matters are beautiful only when they are accomplished. Furthermore, the fourth verse is the verse of Sakka. In that verse also, the meaning should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Araññāyatanaisisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "paṇṇakuṭīsu" means they live in leaf-roofed huts equipped with night quarters, day quarters, walking paths, and so on, in a delightful forest region of the Himālaya. Sakka, the lord of devas, and Vepacitti, the lord of asuras—these two persons, being son-in-law and father-in-law, sometimes quarrel and sometimes travel together. At this time, however, they are traveling together. "Paṭaliyo" refers to [wearing] layered sandals. "Khaggaṃ olaggetvā" means slinging a sword over the shoulder. "Chattena" means holding a divine white parasol over the head. "Apabyāmato karitvā" means acting without respect. "Ciradikkhitānaṃ" means of those who have long-undertaken practices after becoming hermits. "Ito paṭikkamma" means "Go away from here, avoid this place, do not stand upwind." "Na hettha devā" shows that devas do not have a perception of repulsiveness regarding the scent of these virtuous ones' bodies, but rather have a perception of it as pleasant, delightful, and dear. The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10. Samuddakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "samuddatīre paṇṇakuṭīsu" means they live in the aforementioned leaf-roofed huts on the sandy shores, which have the appearance of silver plates, on the surface of the Great Ocean of the Cakkavāḷa. "Siyāpi no" means "Might there be [danger] for us?" "Abhayadakkhiṇaṃ yāceyyāma" means "We shall ask for the gift of safety." Generally, the war between devas and asuras tends to occur on the surface of the Great Ocean. The asuras do not always win; they are defeated many times. When those asuras flee after being defeated by the devas, they pass near the hermits' ashrams and, becoming angry, thinking, "Sakka consults with these hermits to destroy us; seize these sons of [hermits] who are asleep," they destroy the water-pot stands, walking paths, and so on in the ashram. When the hermits return from the forest bringing various fruits and see the destruction, they have to repair it again with great difficulty. Those asuras also destroy it again and again in the same manner. Therefore, hearing that "now the battle between those two celestial armies is imminent," they consulted thus. "Kāmaṅkaro" means one who can act according to his will. "Bhayassa abhayassa vā" means [one who can grant] fear or safety. It is intended to show: "King Sambara, if you wish to give safety, you are capable of giving safety; if you wish to give fear, you are capable of giving fear. Please give us the gift of safety." "Duṭṭhānaṃ" means of those who oppose evilly. "Pavuttaṃ" means like seeds sown in a field. "Tikkhattuṃ ubbijjī" means waking up screaming as if being pierced by a hundred spears just after falling asleep upon going to bed after dinner. The entire asura realm of ten thousand yojanas was agitated, wondering "Why is this?"
317:
When the hermits brought back various fruits from the forest and saw the destruction, they began the task [of repairing] again with great difficulty. Those asuras also destroyed it again and again in the same manner as before. Therefore, hearing that "now the battle between those two celestial armies is imminent," they consulted thus.

"Kāmaṅkaro" means one who can act according to his will. "Bhayassa abhayassa vā" means fear or safety. This is the intended meaning: "If you, King of Asuras, wish to give safety, you are capable of giving safety. If you wish to give fear, you are capable of giving fear. Please give us the gift of safety." "Duṭṭhānaṃ" refers to those who oppose evilly. "Pavuttaṃ" refers to seeds sown and established in a field.

"Tikkhattuṃ ubbijjī" means waking up screaming as if being struck by a hundred spears by those standing around just after falling asleep upon going to bed after dinner. At that time, the entire asura realm of ten thousand yojanas fell into agitation, wondering "What is this cause?" Then the asuras came and asked, "Great King, what is this cause?" That king of asuras said, "It is nothing." In the second watch and so on, it was the same way. Thus, while the asuras were comforting the king, saying "Do not fear, Great King," dawn broke. In this way, from that time on, a severe illness arose in that king, and his heart trembled. For that very reason, another name, "Vepacitti," became well-known for that king of asuras. The tenth sutta is finished.

## First Chapter.

## 2. Second Chapter

## 1. Vatapadasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the second chapter, "vatapadāni" means the sets of well-practiced dhammas. "Samattāni" means being complete without breakage or defect. "Samādinnāni" means being well-undertaken. "Kule jeṭṭhāpacāyī" means one who pays respect to the elders in the family, such as grandfathers, grandmothers, junior uncles, junior aunts, maternal uncles, maternal aunts, and so on. "Saṇhavāco" means one who has endearing, gentle, and sweet speech. "Muttacāgo" means one who has generous giving, free from stinginess. "Payatapāṇi" means one whose hands are always washed for the purpose of giving gifts. "Vossaggarato" means one who delights in relinquishing. "Yācayogo" means one who is worthy of being asked by others, or one who is suitable for requests. "Dānasaṃvibhāgarato" means one who delights in both giving and sharing. The first sutta is finished.
318:
## 2. Sakkanāmasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, 'manussabhūto' refers to the time when he was a human being in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha. 'Āvasathaṃ adāsi' means he built and donated a resting place for the public at the four great crossroads. 'Sahassampi atthānaṃ' means that whether it be a thousand matters, or when presented by a thousand people or with a thousand words, he could decide instantly (remaining on a single point), saying, "This is the meaning of this; this is the meaning of that." The explanation of the second sutta ends.

## 3. Mahālisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'upasaṅkami' means he approached with the thought, "They speak of Sakka, the King of Devas; is there anyone who has seen that Sakka before? I will ask the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala) about this matter." 'Tañca pajānāmi' is the use of the singular in place of the plural, meaning "I also know those dhammas that lead to the state of Sakka."

It is said that in his previous life immediately preceding the present one, Sakka was a wise and skillful youth named Magha in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha. His conduct was like that of a Bodhisatta. That youth Magha, taking thirty-three companions, performed meritorious deeds. One day, reflecting with his own wisdom, he cleared the rubbish at the place where the public gathered in the middle of the village and made that place pleasant and delightful. Again, he had a pavilion (maṇḍapa) built at that very spot. Later, as time passed, he had a rest house (sālā) built. Leaving the village, he traveled as far as a gāvuta, half a yojana, three gāvutas, and one yojana, and together with those companions, he made the uneven roads level.

All of them, being of one mind, performed many merits by building bridges where bridges were needed, and by constructing pavilions, rest houses, ponds, and planting flower gardens in suitable places. Having fulfilled the seven vows (vatapada), the youth Magha, upon the breaking up of the body, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven together with his companions. The Blessed One knows all of those matters. Therefore, He said: "I know those dhammas by the undertaking of which Sakka attained the state of Sakka." This is the brief account of Sakka's attainment of the state of Sakka. The detailed account, however, has been stated in the explanation of the Sakkapañha Sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī. The explanation of the third sutta ends.
319:
## 4. Daliddasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, 'manussadaliddo' refers to a poor human being without wealth. 'Manussakapaṇo' refers to one who has reached a pitiable state among humans. 'Manussavarāko' refers to a wretched or lowly human. 'Tatra' means in that place, or in that surpassing splendor [of other devas]. 'Ujjhāyanti' means they complain or scorn; they think of him as lowly. 'Khīyanti' means they speak of faults; they make them known. 'Vipācenti' means they speak about it in various places; they spread and elaborate upon it.

In the phrase "Friends, this person indeed," there is this sequential narrative: It is said that before the appearance of a Buddha, that person was the King of Bārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāsi. Because of his possession of glorious wealth, he made a clockwise procession around the city, which was well-decorated with various ornaments and hoisted banners and flags, while being gazed upon by the masses whose eyes were drawn to him. At that time, a Paccekabuddha came from Mount Gandhamādana and was wandering for alms in that city; he was one with peaceful faculties, a peaceful mind, and possessed the highest self-control.

The masses, abandoning their respect for the King, gazed only at the Paccekabuddha. The King thought, "Now, among these people, not even one looks at me. Why is this?" Looking around, he saw the Paccekabuddha. That Paccekabuddha was elderly, being in the last stage of life. His robes were also worn out, and threads were falling from here and there. Although the King saw the Paccekabuddha who had fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) for two incalculable periods (asaṅkhyeyya) and a hundred thousand aeons, there was neither even a moment of devotion in his mind nor even the mere stretching out of his hands in salutation.

That King, becoming angry with the thought, "I suppose this ascetic does not look at me out of envy," said, "Where is this fellow from, wearing robes as loathsome as a leper's?" and having spat, he departed. Due to the result of that evil deed, he was reborn in the great hell (Mahāniraya). When he came to the human world as a residual result, he took conception in the womb of an extremely poor woman in the city of Rājagaha. From the time of conception, that woman did not even get enough sour gruel (kañjika) to fill her stomach. While he was still in the womb, his ears and nose disappeared, and he was born from his mother's womb as one with white leprosy. Parents are indeed those who perform what is difficult to do; therefore, the mother of that child brought him sour gruel and water until he was able to go about holding an alms bowl. When he was able to wander for alms, she placed a bowl in his hand and said, "You will be known by your own karma," and departed.
320:
From then on, pieces of flesh fell from his entire body, pus and putrid fluids oozed out, and he suffered intense pain. On whichever street he lay down to sleep, he would cry out with a loud voice throughout the night. Because of his pitiful wailing and lamentation, the people in the entire street could not sleep all night. From that time on, he came to be known as 'Suppabuddha' because he awakened those who were sleeping peacefully.

Later, on another occasion, when the Blessed One arrived at Rājagaha, the townspeople invited the Teacher and, having constructed a large pavilion in the middle of the city, gave alms. Suppabuddha the leper also went and sat not far from the alms pavilion. While the townspeople were serving the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with choice food and delicacies, they also gave him gruel and rice. Having eaten the choice food, his mind became concentrated. At the conclusion of the meal, the Blessed One gave a talk of appreciation and revealed the Four Noble Truths. While sitting in his very place, Suppabuddha followed the teaching with his wisdom and was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala).

The Blessed One rose from his seat and departed for the monastery. He too, placing a head-pad, taking his bowl-shard, and leaning on a staff, was going to his dwelling place when a fierce cow took his life. Just like breaking an earthen bowl and receiving a golden bowl, in the second thought-moment (dutiyacittavāra), he was reborn in the celestial realm. Relying on his own merit, he surpassed and outshone the other devas. Desiring to show this matter, Sakka, the lord of devas, said, "Friends, this person..." and so forth.

'Saddhā' (faith) refers to the faith attained through the Path. In the phrase 'sīlañca yassa kalyāṇaṃ', 'kalyāṇa-sīla' (virtuous conduct) refers to the virtue loved by the noble ones (ariyakanta-sīla) of a noble disciple. Although there is no virtue that is not loved by a noble disciple, in this context, it refers to the Five Precepts which are not abandoned even in another life. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Rāmaṇeyyakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'ārāmacetyā' refers to shrines in parks (gardens) that are worthy of respect. 'Vanacetyā' refers to shrines in forests that are worthy of respect. In both cases, they should be understood as 'cetya' in the sense of being honored. 'Manussarāmaṇeyyassa' means the state of being delightful to humans. Now, desiring to show the delightfulness of the ground by way of its delightfulness to humans, he said 'gāme vā' and so forth. The fifth sutta is finished.
321:
## 6. Yajamānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'yajamānānaṃ' means for those who perform offerings and honors. At that time, the people living in the kingdoms of Anga and Magadha would annually take the best portions of ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth, and having made a great pile of wood about sixty cartloads in one place, they would set it on fire. When the fire blazed up, they would say, "We sacrifice to the Great Brahmā," and throw all those items into the fire. It is said they held the view that "throwing it in once yields a thousandfold benefit."

Sakka, the king of devas, thought, "All these people are taking all the best things and burning them in the fire, saying, 'We sacrifice to the Great Brahmā.' They are performing a fruitless act. Let them not perish while I am watching. I will act so that they may gain much merit by giving to the Buddha and the Saṅgha." Having caused the woodpile to blaze, while the people were watching on the full-moon day, he assumed the form of Brahmā and appeared as if emerging by splitting the lunar disk right before the eyes of the multitude. When the multitude saw him, they stood worshiping with joined palms, kneeling on the ground, saying, "The Great Brahmā has come to accept this sacrifice!" The Brahmins also said, "Do you think we speak only by conjecture? Look now, this Brahmā of yours has come in person to accept the sacrifice."

Sakka came and stood in the air above the woodpile and asked, "For whom is this honor intended?" They replied, "For you, Lord Brahmā; please accept our sacrifice." He said, "If so, come; do not abandon the great scale and weigh with your hands. This Teacher dwells in the nearby monastery; let us ask him, 'To whom does giving yield great fruit?'" Thus, taking the people from both kingdoms, he went to the Blessed One and, while questioning, addressed him in this way.

In that verse, 'puññapekhānaṃ' means for those who desire merit, those who seek merit. 'Opadhikaṃ puññaṃ' is merit that can produce the result of rebirth (upadhi-vipāka). 'Saṅghe dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ' means that an offering given to the Noble Saṅgha is of great fruit. At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings drank the nectar of the Dhamma (Amata). From then on, people gave all their best offerings to the Saṅgha of monks. The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Buddhavandanāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'uṭṭhehi' means 'arise', 'strive', 'exert'. 'Vijitasaṅgāmaṃ' (one who has won the battle) is a title for the Blessed One because he has conquered the defilements such as lust, as well as the army of Māra which extended for twelve leagues.
322:
(Sakka) calls out. *Pannabhārā* refers to one whose burden—the aggregates, defilements, and volitional formations—has been laid down. *Pannarasāya rattiṃ* means on the night of the fifteenth day, the full moon night. The seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Gahaṭṭhavandanāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, *puthuddisā* refers to the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions. *Bhummā* refers to the deities dwelling on the earth. *Cirarattasamāhite* refers to those with minds concentrated for a long time through access concentration and absorption concentration. *Vande* means "I pay homage." *Brahmacariyaparāyaṇe* refers to those practicing the noble life (*brahmacariya*), such as sleeping alone and eating one meal a day, for ten years, twenty years... sixty years, or until the end of life. *Puññakarā* refers to those who perform meritorious deeds, such as offering the four requisites, worshipping with *kusumbha* and jasmine flowers, and lighting a thousand lamps. *Sīlavanto* refers to those established in the status of lay followers (*upāsaka*) and endowed with the five or ten precepts. *Dhammena dāraṃ posenti* means supporting one's wife and children righteously through farming, cattle-rearing, and trade, without committing acts like tunneling or housebreaking. *Pamukho rathamāruhi* means Sakka, the chief of the devas, mounted the Vejayanta chariot. The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Satthāravandanāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, *bhagavantaṃ namassati* means paying homage by placing the upper robe (*dukula*) over one shoulder, kneeling down, and placing the joined palms on the head. *So yakkho* refers to that Sakka. *Anomanāmaṃ* refers to one whose name is full of qualities, as there is no inferiority in any of his virtues. *Avijjāsamatikkamā* means by overcoming ignorance (*avijjā*), the root of the cycle of rebirth, which veils the Four Noble Truths. *Sekkhā* refers to the seven types of trainees (*sekha*). *Apacayārāmā* refers to those who delight in destroying the cycle of rebirth. *Sikkhare* means they are training. The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10. Saṅghavandanāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, *ajjhabhāsī*: if it is asked, "Why does this Sakka speak thus repeatedly?" it is because the voice of Sakka, the king of devas, is sweet, his lips are beautiful, and when he speaks, it sounds like the tinkling of golden bells. He speaks because he wishes to hear that sound again and again. *Pūtidehasayā* refers to those who sleep in a foul body, either by being enveloped in the foul body of the mother or in one's own body.
323:
*Nimuggā kuṇapamhete* means those beings are submerged in the foulness of the mother's womb for ten months. *Etaṃ tesaṃ pihayāmi* means "I cherish and long for this practice of these venerable ones." *Na te saṃ koṭṭhe openti* means those venerable ones do not put their own grain into granaries. This is because they do not possess grain. *Na kumbhī* means they do not store it in pots. *Na kaḷopiyaṃ* means they do not store it in baskets. *Paraniṭṭhitamesānā* means seeking alms-food that has been prepared by others and cooked in others' houses, according to the duty of alms-gathering. *Tenā* means by such a livelihood sought in this way. *Subbatā* means those with excellent vows well-undertaken for ten years up to sixty years.

*Sumantamantino* means those who are habituated to speaking well-spoken words such as, "We shall recite the Dhamma, we shall undertake the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), we shall enjoy the Deathless (*amata*), we shall practice the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*)." *Tuṇhībhūtā samañcarā* means that even though they preach the Dhamma for the three watches of the night, roaring like thunder, they are said to be silent and to practice evenly because they do not engage in useless talk. *Puthumaccā ca* means many beings are in conflict with one another. *Attadaṇḍesu nibbutā* means those who have laid down weapons and are peaceful among beings who hold weapons to harm others. *Sādānesu anādānā* means those who are free from grasping, as they do not have even a fraction of attachment to existence (*bhava*), birth (*yoni*), etc., among beings who have attachment. The tenth sutta is finished.

## Dutiya Vagga

## 3. Tatiya Vagga

## 1. Chetvāsutta-vaṇṇanā
The first sutta of the third chapter has the same meaning as previously stated. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Dubbaṇṇိယသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the second sutta, *dubbaṇṇo* refers to one whose appearance is like a burnt stump. *Okoṭimako* refers to one who is short and pot-bellied. *Āsane* means on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat. *Kodhabhakkho* is merely a name given by Sakka. That person was a Brahma of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) who, having heard that "Sakka is endowed with the power of patience," came to test him...
324:
Having heard that he was complete, he came to investigate. Truly, the earth-dwelling deities (bhummasso) who are prohibited cannot enter a place with such well-arranged protection.

"Upaśaṅkami" means: Having heard the words of the deities, he thought, "This anger-eating deity (kodhabhakkha) cannot be moved by harsh words; indeed, he can only be made to flee by one who is humble and established in patience." Desiring to make him flee in that manner, he approached.

"Antaradhāyi" means: When he (Sakka) stood in patience, manifesting great respect and showing a humble manner, the deity was unable to remain on Sakka's throne and disappeared.

In the phrase "Na sūpahatacittomhi", the word "su" is merely a particle. It means "I am not one who has a mind that harms others." "Nāvattena suvānayo" means he is not to be led by following the turn of anger; it means "I am not one who is easily made to be under the power of anger." In the phrase "Na vo cirāhaṃ", the word "vo" is merely a particle. It means "I do not remain angry for long." The twelfth sutta is finished.

## 3. Sambaramāyāsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the thirteenth sutta, "Ābādhiko" means being afflicted with a disease that arose when the group of hermits cursed him. "Vācehi maṃ" means "If you teach me the magic (māyā) of the Asura named Sambara, I will likewise treat that disease." "Mā kho tvaṃ mārisa vācesi" means: Even without learning the Sambara magic, Sakka is already oppressing us; if he comes to know that magic, we will be destroyed. Do not destroy us for the sake of your own benefit alone—thus they spoke and forbade him.

"Sambaro va sataṃ samaṃ" means: Just as the Asura king named Sambara, being deceitful and using magic, was cooked in hell for a hundred years, so too is he cooked. It means: You are those who conform to the Dhamma; magic is not suitable for you.

How is it? Is Sakka able to cure the anger of that Asura king? Yes, he is able. How? At that time, it is said that the group of hermits was still alive. Therefore, he should have taken that Asura king to the hermits and made him ask for forgiveness. By making him ask for forgiveness in this way, there would be well-being for that Asura king. However, because that Asura king was deceitful, he did not do so and simply departed. The thirteenth sutta is finished.

## 4. Accayasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourteenth sutta, "Sampayojesuṃ" means they engaged in a quarrel. "Accasarā" means he transgressed. The meaning is that one monk spoke words of transgression to another monk. "Yathādhammaṃ na ppaṭikaroanti" means they do not forgive. "Do not follow the power of anger," he showed. In the Pali "Mā mitte jarā", the word "hi" is merely a particle. Let there be no change (corruption) in your behavior towards friends. Alternatively, it is the instrumental case in the sense of the locative. It means: Let there be no corruption in your friends; let there be no change into something other than the state of being a friend. "Agarahiyaṃ mā garahittha" means: Do not blame the person who should not be blamed. The fourteenth sutta is finished.
325:
"Yathādhammaṃ na ppaṭiggaṇhāti" means he does not forgive. "Kodho vo vasamāyātu" means: Let anger come under your control; do not follow the power of anger—thus it is shown. In the Pali "Mā ca mitte hi vo jarā", the word "hi" is merely a particle; let there be no such thing as "decay" (destruction) in your practice of friendship. Alternatively, using the instrumental case in the sense of the locative, it means: Let there be no decay in your friends; let there be no change into something other than the state of being a friend. "Agarahiyaṃ mā garahittha" means: Do not blame the Arahant who should not be blamed. This is the opening of the fourth sutta.

## 5. Akkodhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "Mā vo kodho ajjhabhavī" means: Let not anger overcome you; you yourselves should overcome and crush anger. "Mā ca kujjhittha kujjhataṃ" means: Do not get angry back at those who are angry. "Akkodha" refers to loving-kindness (mettā) and the preliminary stages of loving-kindness. "Avihiṃsā" refers to compassion (karuṇā) and the preliminary stages of compassion. "Atha pāpajanaṃ kodho, pabbatovābhimaddati" means: Just as a great mountain crushes (things below it), anger crushes the wicked person. This is the opening of the fifth sutta.
